• This course has been structured for group and individual activities.  Group discussions will center around 
readings, lectures, and your own research interest, with the aim of spawning meaningful peer bonds.
• Goals include improving listening comprehension, enhancing leadership capabilities, summarizing and 
connecting ideas, building vocabulary and expressions, addressing cultural topics, and sharing views/ideas 
with others. 
• Midterm and final tasks will be in the form of academic papers (midterm being a topic proposal and the final 
being a longer paper on the topic).  There are no formal presentations in this class.

address provided, not through EKU email. Missed assignments receive a zero; missing a midterm or final may result in

Conspiracies, Controversies, & Mysteries
• From the JFK assassination to the events of 9/11, and even to recent controversies surrounding COVID-19, conspiracy 
theories have long captivated the public imagination. Likewise, many controversies and mysteries fill our world.
• Throughout the semester, students will engage in discussions, research, and analysis of specific cases—both alleged and 
confirmed conspiracies, ongoing controversies, and mysteries of our world. By examining the topics, students will deepen 
their understanding of how ideas come about and are challenged.
• Students will select a conspiracy theory, controversy, or mystery of their own choosing to research and will analyze the 
evidence supporting or undermining its validity. Their work will include evaluating who supports the idea, assessing 
whether the proponents sound paranoid or credible, and examining the available evidence to estimate the likelihood of the 
theory’s truth.
• The coursework will culminate in a written analysis of their chosen topic—a research paper discussing the strongest 
evidence, the arguments presented, and the overall probability that the conspiracy, controversy, or mystery has validity.
Learning Outcomes:
By the end of the semester, students will be able to:
• Produce evidence-based writing that demonstrates logical reasoning and argumentative skills.
• Critically evaluate the reasoning and arguments presented in assigned and researched texts.
Texts and Resources:

Research Tips:
Maximize your research efforts by utilizing KU’s excellent library resources, including FRIC—a comprehensive database 
offering journals, articles, and books. Relying solely on general search engines like Google or YouTube may lead to an 
overload of paranoid or unreliable information. Librarians are happy to assist you in finding credible sources—just explain 
your assignment when you visit.

COURSE INTRODUCTIONS  
Course overview 
You will learn about thermodynamics, especially specialized in energy engineering, which is one of 
the most fundamental knowledge in all engineering disciplines. 
1.
Dynamics is fundamentally the most foundational discipline in engineering, elucidating the correlation 
between motion or work and the force exerted on a mass-bearing object.
2.
In thermodynamics, force translates into (i) heat and (ii) the objects upon which force is applied 
encompass all scales of matter, from microscopic points of view such as electrons/atoms/molecules to 
macroscopic points of view. Thus, thermodynamics can be understood as the study of the motion/work 
induced by heat in objects.
3.
These thermodynamic phenomena are common fundamental occurrences in our surroundings where 
thermal energy is prevalent. This implies that diverse interpretations are possible from an academic 
perspective, leading to various applications. Therefore, there exist diverse thermodynamic 
methodologies/applications across different disciplines. In reality, subjects such as "Physical 
Chemistry" in Chemistry, "Statistical Thermodynamics" in Physics, "Chemical Thermodynamics" in 
Chemical Engineering, "Material/Metal Thermodynamics" in Materials Engineering, and "Process 
Thermodynamics" or "Heat and Thermodynamics" in Mechanical Engineering are taught in various 
forms.
4.
Energy thermodynamics involves (i) a rigorous understanding of widely accepted fundamental laws of 
thermodynamics and (ii) learning about their application in the field of energy engineering. Especially in 
the latter case, it encompasses thermodynamic knowledge necessary for understanding solar energy 
technologies, batteries, low-power electronic components, and photosynthesis.
Course objectives 
Through interactive concept learning, we aim to deeply understand the concepts necessary for 
comprehension of energy thermodynamics: the goal is to be able to explain thermodynamic concepts in 
one's own words by the end of the semester. As mentioned, thermodynamics, like a chameleon, 
encompasses various aspects, meaning that diverse interpretations are possible depending on the 
academic perspective. Thus, a unidirectional teaching method such as providing definitions followed by 
memorization or presenting formulas followed by memorization may have limitations in revealing the 
essence of thermodynamics. This approach is even less suitable for the study of thermodynamics. We 
aspire to broaden our understanding of thermodynamics through collaborative learning, where each 
individual shares and discusses their understanding of thermodynamic concepts/laws, leveraging collective 
intelligence. Instead of simply imparting equations, we will teach the physical/chemical implications of each 
term within the equations. We will strive to make thermodynamic concepts more accessible by utilizing 
various everyday examples encountered in daily life.

출석 확인은 1) LMS의 자율 출석(스마트출석), 2) 출석 설문으로 진행한다.
4.3.1. LMS의 자율 출석(스마트 출석)
매 교시(4교시, 5교시)의 출석은 LMS의 자율 출석으로 진행한다. 
출석 코드는 공개 후 10분이 지나면 자동 만료되며, 만료 이후에는 입력할 수 없다. 제한 시간 내 출석을 완료하

수업에 지각하여 LMS 상에 ‘결석’ 처리 되었을 경우, Zoom 채팅을 통해 조교에게 알려 ‘지각’으로 출석을
정정받는다.
LMS의 출석 정정은 정규 강의시간 이내 조교에게 직접 알린 경우에만 이루어지며, 강의 종료 이후의 정정
요청은 받지 않는다.
4.3.2. 출석 설문(Check-in)
수업 도중 랜덤한 시점에 ‘오늘의 단어’를 공개하며, 해당 단어를 설문에 올바르게 입력하여 제출한다. 출석 설
문은 매주 강의 종료 즉시 제출해야 한다. 
매 교시의 LMS 자율 출석을 모두 완료했더라도, 출석 설문을 제출하지 않으면 5교시는 ‘지각’으로 처리된다.
기타 출결 안내사항:
지각 차시 3회가 누적될 경우 결석 1 차시로 처리되며, 결석은 성적에서 감점 요인이 된다. 
중간고사 및 기말고사 주간은 출석을 진행하지 않으며, 과제 및 프로젝트 제출 여부로 출석이 기록된다.
결석일이 5일 이상이면 과제나 기말 프로젝트 점수와 관계없이 F를 부여한다.

COURSE OBJECTIVES 
This course aims to help students think beyond the classroom and act more entrepreneurially by 
creating opportunities and taking action in uncertain environments. To achieve this goal, it provides 
a comprehensive introduction to the entrepreneurial process, guiding students from idea generation 
to the development and presentation of a business plan. However, this course is not solely intended 
for students who wish to start a new business. That view reflects a narrow, traditional definition of 
entrepreneurship. Instead, we explore a broader concept, one that emphasizes the mindset, skillset, 
and toolset necessary to create change, improve the world, and make a meaningful impact on 
people’s lives. While students interested in launching a business will certainly benefit, more 
importantly, the world benefits when individuals act entrepreneurially. 
In the 21st century, especially in the wake of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, it is essential for all 
students to become comfortable with generating and testing new ideas, navigating uncertainty, and 
taking action to learn. This aligns closely with KUBS’s 3C values: Curiosity in exploring new possibilities, 
Collaboration through teamwork and peer feedback, and Contribution by creating solutions that 
address real-world problems. The course also encourages students to consider entrepreneurial 
opportunities in 4T industries: AI, AI-related semiconductors, AI-embedded robotics, and the energy 
sector, all of which are rapidly transforming today’s business landscape. Through hands-on exercises, 
case studies, and team collaboration, students will explore creativity, opportunity recognition, 
customer identification, and business model development. By engaging with real-world challenges 
and refining their ideas, students will develop the essential skills to succeed in entrepreneurial 
endeavors.

Exams – Individual (15%+20%) 
Both midterm and final exams will be close-book exams. Exams will cover all the materials during 
the course by the time of the exam, including all the assigned readings and cases. Detailed 
information will be given before each exam. Questions include true/false, multi-choices, and short 
answer questions.  
Class Participation – Individual (10%)  
Class participation does not mean your attendance check merely; It also includes your active 
contribution to the class discussion. Your contribution can help the conversation go forward. 
Therefore, participation scores (10 points) will be based on two components: base attendance (BA, 
5 points) and active participation (AP, 5 points).  
 
Base Attendance (5%) 
 
Attendance will be checked every class since the second week, and students are allowed 
up to THREE legitimate absences without penalty. For any non-legitimate absences or 
additional absences beyond the three allowed, points will be deducted from the overall 
attendance score. The deduction increases progressively: 1 absence results in a 1-point 
deduction, 2 absences result in a 2-point deduction, and so on. If you have no non-
legitimate or excessive absences but do not participate at all, you will receive the base 
attendance score of 5 points. 
 
Student will FAIL the course automatically when BA reaches 0.  
 
Legitimate absences must apply officially on the Korea University portal.  
 
Active Participation (5%) 
 
Active participation can be achieved through two methods: (1) in-class participation, by 
engaging in discussions, answering questions, contributing personal insights or external 
knowledge, and/or asking questions that advance the conversation; and (2) online 
participation, by initiating or contributing to discussions related to class topics in a 
meaningful way. For online discussions, contributions should be made within 24hours of 
the specific lecture or discussion to be eligible for grading. While you may continue the 
discussion beyond this timeframe, comments made after it will not be graded. Additionally, 
simply agreeing with others’ ideas will not earn participation points. 
 
To earn the full participation score of 5, students must be recognized for active 
participation 10 or more times across in-class and online methods. Online and offline 
participation for the same day lecture is considered as one participation. The score 
decreases incrementally based on the frequency of participation, with 9 participations 
earning 4.5, 8 earning 4, and so forth, down to 0 points for 0 participation.  
Assignment – Individual (25%)  
 
Business Ideas (10%) 
 
You will post your business ideas on the LMS system during the 3rd (5%) and 6th (5%) 
weeks of the semester. The focus of this activity is participation, so all submitted ideas, 
regardless of quality, will guarantee you full credit for this part of the course. 
 
Idea Discussion (5%) 
 
Each student should comment on at least TWO business ideas by offering additional 
insights, constructive feedback, or alternative perspectives on the LMS.  
 
In the second round (6th week), students will evaluate the posted ideas by ranking their 
top 5 favorites. Based on the collective rankings, the top 20 ideas will automatically 
determine the 20 team leaders for the final project. Students whose ideas do not make it 
into the top 20 must choose one of the selected teams to join and collaborate with to 
complete the final project. (What is so good about being a leader? An extra 0.2 points will 
be added to your final scores!) (*the number of teams is subjected to change) 
 
The detailed formats and content requirements will be given on the LMS later. 
 
Pitch Comments (5%)  
 
Each student should comment on at least TWO pitch ideas during the pitch session. 
Comments may include questions related to the pitch itself, suggestions for improvement, 
or compliments on how the pitch has developed from the initial business idea.  
 
Peer Evaluation (5%) 
 
Each student should evaluate their team members in the final session. The peer evaluation 
score will be calculated as the average of the scores given by team members. If you do not 
complete the peer evaluation, you will receive a score of 0, even if others evaluate you. 
Also, if your average peer evaluation score is below 2.5, all your group-based project scores 
will be adjusted accordingly. 
Final Project – Group (30%) 
The final project is a comprehensive group assignment designed to develop and refine your 
business planning and presentation skills. It includes multiple components to ensure a well-rounded 
learning experience. Each group will submit both business plan and give a 6-min pitch.   
• 
Business Plan (20%) 
 
Three versions of the business plan draft will be collected over the semester. The first draft 
(2%) serves as the foundation of your work, the second draft (3%) should be an almost 
finished version, and the final draft (15%) must be a completed version. The first two drafts 
should be submitted through the LMS, and the final version must be submitted as a hard 
copy.   
 
I will provide a template based on a Korean government grant application program format, 
along with detailed instructions on structuring and writing your business plan.  
 
• 
Pitch (10%) 
 
Each group should prepare the initial version of pitch materials before the designated pitch 
clinic session. I will provide feedbacks to every group. The final pitch should incorporate all 
the comments.  
 
Each group will have 6 minutes to pitch their business idea, followed by 6 minutes of Q&A 
from peers and the instructor. 
 
Each group can have 1, 2, or up to 3 members presenting. It is NOT required for all 
members to present. 
 
The presentation will be graded by me, but your peers will need to choose whether they 
would "Invest" or "Not Invest" in the business after each presentation immediately.  


different business ideas. Each team can have up to 3-4 members (*this is subject to change

개요
이 수업에서는 인류 역사의 다양한 지적 성찰 및 실천적 가치를 종합적으
로 탐구하고, 이를 바탕으로 현재의 사회를 이해하고 미래의 변화에 대응
할 수 있는 토의·토론의 장을 마련한다. 개별 전공들 간의 장벽을 넘어 비
판적·융합적·창의적 사고 능력을 함양하고, 나아가 새롭고 다양한 관점에서 
문제의식을 생성하며 타인과의 소통 및 협력을 통해 문제를 해결할 수 있
도록 하는 것이 이 교과의 목표이다. 이를 위해 플립트 클래스(Flipped 
Class) 기반의 학습자 중심 교수학습 방법을 도입하여, 질문 중심 학습
(QBL: Question Based Learning)과 토론 및 발표를 통해 학습자가 배
움의 주체가 될 수 있도록 한다.

Technological Innovation Management: A Pre-requisite for 
Successful Entrepreneurship  
(BUSS 410) 
 
Spring 2026 
 
Course Outline 
 
 
Professor: Se-Joon Hong 
Email: sejoon@korea.ac.kr 
 
 
Course Overview: 
 
Managing technology and innovation is essential to the survival and growth of companies, but it 
is a tricky business. Even well-established companies often lose their edge, finding their very 
existence to be threatened by their inability to manage for innovation. Clearly there is no “one 
best way” to manage innovation.  
 
The course aims to meet three objectives as the following: first, this course stimulates your 
curiosity and broadens your perspective by posing you puzzling critical dilemmas that deny 
some of your long-held assumptions and guiding you to think critically about them. You will 
understand that there is a critical gap between designing and developing innovative technologies 
and making them commercially successful (i.e., widely adopted); second, the course exposes you 
to various concepts and frameworks that will help you understand different aspects of 
technological innovation from a business strategy perspective; third, you will be able to apply the 
concepts and theoretical frameworks learned from the course to analyze the innovation of a 
company of your choice and propose sound and implementable recommendations to the 
company. 
 
Course Readings: 
 
⚫ Lecturer’s lecture notes 
⚫ Supplementary readings will be pointed 
 
Group Project/Assignment:  
 
As for the group project, each group can freely choose a company considered to be very 
innovative (in terms of technology, business model, target market, and so on) and conduct 
research about the company. Each group is responsible for delivering the company’s innovative 
business activities clearly to the classmates. The presentation may include the company’s 
background, competitors, business models as well as the future prospect.  
 
 
Exam:  
 
Final Exam 
 
Grading: 
 
Final Exam: 40%

Peer Evaluation: 
 
As the substantial part of the class work is to be done in groups, a peer evaluation will be 
conducted for each group work. The main purpose of this evaluation is to know whether all team 
members contributed equally to the group work.

Course objective:
• SPGE400: From Galileo to Einstein (Undergraduate/Credits: 3)
We investigate the history of science since its birth by Galileo through the discovery of the
special theory of relativity by Albert Einstein.
We focus on the fact that revolutionary
transitions in human history always stem from scientific observations of natural phenomena,
followed by the leading escape from scientific absurdity by physicists like Galileo, Newton,
and Einstein.
– Goal 1: enhance the ability of quantitative reasoning
– Goal 2: enhance the ability of qualitative reasoning
– Goal 3: investigate the history of science starting from Galileo to Einstein.
• SPGE401: Escape from Scientific Absurdity (Undergraduate/Credits: 3)
We mainly focus on escaping from the ignorance of the physics background of various math-
ematical formulas. Calculus and differential equations originate not from pure mathematics
branches but from physicists’ pioneering efforts to solve problems such as classical mechanics
and electrodynamics. We first deal with Euclidean Geometry with vector algebra, which is
also developed by physicists. We experience the analytic properties of power-series expansions
to approximate useful functions appearing in physics problems. The analytic nature of physi-
cal functions leads us to explore the nature of the Newtonian equation of motion. Finally, we
investigate the equivalence of the Euler-Lagrange equation to Newtonian mechanics and the
development of the calculus of variations, resulting in the discovery of Hamilton’s least-action
principle.
– Goal 1: enhance the ability of quantitative reasoning
– Goal 2: enhance the ability of qualitative reasoning
– Goal 3: investigate first principles of the physical universe
• SPGE412: Intellectual Beauty Hiding in Physics (Undergraduate/Credits: 3)
We appreciate and enjoy the intellectual beauty hiding in physics by investigating the his-
torical and philosophical aspects of the fundamental theoretical structure that has led to the
scientific revolution.
– Goal 1: enhance the ability of quantitative reasoning
– Goal 2: enhance the ability of qualitative reasoning
– Goal 3: appreciate and enjoy the intellectual beauty hiding in physics
1
• UNIV534: KPOPE Physics Series X (Undergraduate/Credits: 3)
We study fundamental concepts of classical mechanics of particles and waves, thermal and
statistical mechanics.
– Goal 1: understand elementary concepts of classical mechanics of a particle and a system
of particles
– Goal 2: understand elementary concepts of wave
– Goal 3: understand elementary concepts of thermal and statistical physics
• UNIV535: KPOPE Physics Series Y (Undergraduate/Credits: 3)
We study fundamental concepts of electromagnetism, interference of light waves, relativity,
and quantum mechanics.
– Goal 1: understand elementary concepts of electromagnetism
– Goal 2: understand elementary concepts of the light wave
– Goal 3: understand elementary concepts of relativity and quantum mechanics
• PHY505: Quantum Mechanics I (Graduate/Credits: 3)
We study the fundamental theoretical framework of quantum mechanics. The first part covers
the review of classical mechanics, including relativity and classical electrodynamics. After
constructing the Lorentz covariant form of Maxwell’s equations, we construct Schr¨odinger
equation. The second part covers the time evolution of state kets. We focus on the state kets
for a free particle state and a harmonic oscillator to evaluate the propagators. Feynman’s
path integral approach is also employed to reproduce them. The third part is devoted to the
unitary transformations of translation and rotation.
• PHY506: Quantum Mechanics II (Graduate/Credits: 3)
We study fundamental concepts for quantum mechanical descriptions of hydrogen atom, per-
turbation theory, and scattering theory

ENGL281 US Literature and Popular Culture 
Spring 2026 
 
Instructor: Kyungjin Jo 
E-mail: kyungjin.jo.seoul@gmail.com 
Class Hours: Tue/Thu 12:00-1:15 
Class Location: 법학관 구관 206 호 
 
Course Description 
 
Within elitist and Eurocentric cultural hierarchies, US musical theatre has long been dismissed as 
overly popular, commercially oriented, and aesthetically lightweight. It has often been treated as 
mere entertainment rather than as a serious subject of academic study. Yet a closer examination 
reveals that American musicals engage with social, historical, and political topics, such as 
nation-building, US imperialism, urban problems, immigration, the AIDS epidemic, and 
resistance to white supremacy, while also employing innovative approaches to musical style, 
choreography, and scenic design. 
 
This course examines eight to nine U.S. musicals considered milestones in musical theatre 
history. We will explore these works from multiple perspectives, including how the musicals 
engage with the topics mentioned above, represent diverse identities related to gender, sexuality, 
race, ethnicity, and class, participate in the (re) construction and (re) imagination of national 
identity and history. We will also study how these musicals have been adapted across different 
media and revived in different historical moments. Through this approach, we will examine how 
musical theatre has contributed significantly to the evolution of US drama and theatre, as well as 
to the formation of American culture. 
 
Class activities include lectures, discussions, student presentations, and in-class writing. Students 
will have regular reading, listening, and viewing assignments. 
 
Course Objectives 
 
By the end of the course, students will be able to:  
 
• demonstrate their knowledge and analytical skills to interpret the selected musicals’ 
narratives, characters, musical genres and styles, and themes and conventions.  
• understand the cultural and historical contexts and significance of the musicals.   
• gain insight into how musicals both reflect and shape various identities and their voices in 
American culture—including gender, sexuality, race, ethnicity, and class—and how these 
representations of identity have evolved over time.

➢ Attendance 
 
You are expected to attend class regularly and punctually. Attendance will be taken at each 
meeting. Unexcused absences will result in a deduction of 1 point from your attendance score 
starting from the third unexcused absence. In other words, the first two unexcused absences will 
not affect your attendance score, but from the third unexcused absence onward, 1 point will be 
deducted for each additional unexcused absence. 
 
Students with more than 15 absences (including excused absences) will fail the course. Two late 
arrivals will count as one absence. Arriving more than 20 minutes late or leaving more than 20 
minutes early will also count as one absence. If you cannot attend a class for any reason, you 
must notify me in advance via email. In general, supporting documentation is required for any 
excused absences due to illness, emergency, or contingency.  
 
➢ Participation 
This course is designed as a discussion-oriented class rather than a series of lectures, so active 
participation is essential. Your engagement will be strongly encouraged and monitored. Students 
are expected to: 
• 
Demonstrate preparation by engaging with the assigned readings, listening, and viewing 
materials 
• 
Offer thoughtful interpretations or critical questions 
• 
Respond constructively to classmates’ ideas 
• 
Help sustain an atmosphere of respectful intellectual exchange 
Participation will be evaluated according to both the frequency and quality of verbal and written 
contributions throughout the semester: 
• 
12 or more: 20 points 
• 
8–11 contributions: 17 points 
• 
4–7 contributions: 14 points 
• 
3–6 contributions: 11 points 
• 
0–2 contributions: 8 points 
Multiple comments within a single session will count as one participation contribution. This 
policy is designed to encourage balanced engagement across the semester rather than repeated 
speaking in a single class.  Simply speaking without engaging the material meaningfully will not 
result in a high participation grade. 
➢ Staged Reading and Analysis Presentation  
For this assignment, you will work in groups to select one scene (including a number) from the 
assigned musical of the week and present a staged reading. The goal is to explore how 
interpretation deepens when text is voiced, shared, and experienced collectively. The emphasis 
of this assignment is not on acting or singing ability or theatrical effects. Rather, it focuses on 
interpretive choices, clarity of analysis, and collaborative teamwork. 
Part 1: Brief Context (5 minutes) 
Provide only the essential information necessary for the class to understand your selected scene. 
Avoid extensive plot summary. Your task is not to explain the entire musical, but to clarify why 
this particular scene and/or number merit closer attention. 
Part 2: Staged Reading (10 minutes) 
Present a staged reading of your selected scene. 
• 
Scripts must be printed and brought as hard copies. 
• 
Memorization is not required. 
• 
Minimal blocking or gesture is welcome but not required. 
• 
Acting skill is not evaluated. 
• 
Hats and masks are not permitted during the reading. 
For sung-through musicals, singing is encouraged but optional. You may: 
• 
Read lyrics rhythmically, 
• 
Play a short musical excerpt  
• 
Sing selectively if you feel comfortable.  
• 
In addition, groups that choose to perform an entire musical number receive up to 3 
bonus points for exceptional engagement and collaborative effort.  
Part 3: Q&A and Class Discussion  (10-15 minutes) 
Following the presentation, the presenting group will facilitate a brief Q&A session with the 
class. The group should prepare at least one discussion question for the audience. 
➢ Midterm and Final 
 
There will be two written exams—a midterm and a final. These exams will include questions 
requiring explanations of key terms and identification questions where you will need to identify 
the name of the musical, composer, book writer, lyricist, or character and discuss the significance 
of the specific excerpts (e.g., their dramatic function, thematic relevance, and character insight). 
There may also be one or two short essay questions.

■ 강의 개요
  이 강의는 일상생활과 학교생활에서 만나는 과제를 처리하고 학업과 직접적으로 관련된 문제를 해결할 
수 있는 수준의 한국어 실력을 갖추는 것을 목표로 한다. 또한 학습자는 이 강의에서 제시된 사회적 주제
로 비교적 유창하게 의사소통을 할 수 있을 것이다. 이에 더하여 이 강의에서는 한국어 지식의 확장을 위
해 일상적 주제와 사회적 주제의 주요 어휘, 중급의 핵심적인 문법을 집중적으로 학습한다. 또한 읽고 쓰
기, 듣고 말하기의 기능 통합 활동으로 유창하게 한국어를 이해하고 표현할 수 있도록 한다.

(3) 비교적 친숙한 사회적 주제에 대한 대화를 듣고 이해할 수 있다.

Overview 
This course is an introductory macroeconomics, the second part of 
Principles of Economics. This course introduces you to key concepts 
of macroeconomics and develops a simple macroeconomic model 
which we use to analyze short run economic fluctuations. Further, this 
course introduces you to important topics in macroeconomics, such as 
growth, unemployment, and inflation.  
By the end of the course, students should have a general understanding 
of macroeconomic phenomena and theory and be able to understand 
the methods used by macroeconomists. Furthermore, you should be 
able to link the knowledge learned in the class to the real world and to 
understand newspaper and magazine articles on current 
macroeconomic issues.

Office Hours: By appointment 
E-mail: leekats@korea.ac.kr 
 
Course Description: 
 
The course utilizes information and communication technologies to foster global 
communication in English. Students use English as an International Language (EIL) to engage 
in discussions and promote a better understanding of varieties of English and different cultures.  
 
NOTE:  
1. The class will be held with Waseda University (WU) in Japan and Tamkang University 
(TKU) in Taiwan. 
2. The class will be graded on an absolute grading scale regardless of enrollment size. 
3. There are no prerequisites.  
 
Course Objectives: 
 
1. Use EIL for meaningful communication. 
2. Engage in cross-cultural communication in English.  
3. Discuss socially critical issues in English.  
 
Course Expectations and Additional Information: 
 
• Academic Integrity 
 
Academic integrity is the foundation for successful learning. If you choose to engage in 
dishonest acts including, but not limited to, copying homework, plagiarizing all or part of a 
written assignment, relying heavily on AI, or fabricating sources, etc., you will be sanctioned 
according to the severity of the offense.   
 
• LMS (https://lms.korea.ac.kr/) and Communications 
 
Students are required to access LMS for course-related announcements and post presentation 
materials. All course communications will be sent to your email address registered on 
LMS. You are therefore strongly encouraged to monitor that email account. 
Announcements and all course materials will be available on LMS. You should be 
comfortable accessing LMS regularly. 
 
• Required Materials 
 
Students must bring a designated notebook for ENGL 173, a folder to keep handouts and 
readings, and a pen or pencil to every class. There is no required textbook. 
 
 
ENGL 173 
 
 
2 
 
● Netiquette 
 
All audio, video, screen captures, or other materials from this class are for your use only 
to help you learn and review class materials. Any public posting or sharing of these 
materials is NOT allowed and will be treated as a violation of the Honor Code.  
 
• Counseling Services  
 
If you need counseling services, please contact the Korea University Student Counseling 
Center. Refer to the website http://kuscc.korea.ac.kr/kuscc/index.do or telephone number 
02-3290-1540. 
 
• Learning Services 
 
If you need help with your coursework, please contact the Center for Teaching and 
Learning. Refer to the website https://ctl.korea.ac.kr/ or telephone number 02-3290-1577. 
 
   
Grading Criteria: 
 
• Attendance  
 
Students are expected to attend all classes, as attendance is paramount in this course. Points 
will be deducted from the final grade for being tardy and being absent. 
 
Tardy:  
-1 point <5 mins.; -5 points <15 mins.; -10 points > 15 mins. 
Absence:  
-5 points (KU-only session) 
-10 points (Joint session) 
 
Students will be excused only in outstanding cases where written documentation is provided. 
Note that requested absences (유고결석) are not excused for KU-WU-TKU sessions. Students 
absent from 2 or more classes (including the first class) cannot earn an A or A+.  
 
• Class participation & preparation (30%) 
 
Active participation in all classroom activities is essential for success in this course.  
Participation entails a consistent willingness to play a strong role in both whole-class and small-
group discussions by offering opinions, comments, and questions; careful reading, in advance, 
of assigned material; the completion of homework assignments in a thorough and timely 
fashion; and bringing the appropriate materials to class. Your performance will be evaluated 
on a weekly basis according to a relative scale.   
 
Students help create an environment conducive to learning where everyone feels comfortable 
in participating. Everyone is expected to be considerate and respectful of others and their 
opinions. Lively discussions and disagreements are expected and healthy but should always be 
civil. Be attentive to your language and word choice.   
 
• Presentations (30% + 5%) 
 
ENGL 173 
 
 
 
3 
 
Students will directly engage in the selection and presentation of discussion topics for the 
course. Topics should be socially critical and debatable to ensure a lively and meaningful 
discussion. Possible topics can include but are not restricted to the following: politics, 
economy, society, international affairs, culture, arts, sports, and science.  
 
Students will then form small groups and prepare a major presentations and reading materials 
for the class discussions. Major presentations (30%) must utilize PowerPoint. Reading 
materials can include but are not restricted to the following publications: newspapers, 
magazines, Internet resources, books, etc. At least 2 sources must be prepared for each topic 
and uploaded on BB with the presentation file by noon (12:00 p.m.) on the Tuesday before the 
presentation. A smaller presentation (5%) will also be assigned with details forthcoming. 
 
NOTE:  
 
1. The PPT file and 2 readings for the presentation must be uploaded onto Google 
Classroom by the Tuesday before the presentation by noon (12:00 p.m.). If you post 
your materials after the deadline, 10% will be deducted from your presentation score. 
2. If you would like feedback on your PPT file or reading selections, you must email me 
by 23:59 on the Saturday before your scheduled presentation. 
3. ALL students MUST read and bring the assigned readings to class. If you fail to do so, 
10% will be deducted from your final grade.  
 
• BBS (Bulletin Board System) Comments (25%) 
 
Students will extend the topic of the class discussion by writing comments and asking questions 
on Google Classroom. The comments must focus on the topic of the session’s contents for that 
week and include personal opinions and questions. The length of the comments should be at 
least 200 words. Ten percent will be deducted for each day that the posting is late. Points will 
also be deducted for postings that do not meet the guidelines and misspellings. Comments must 
be uploaded onto the BBS by the following Saturday 23:59 after the class.  
 
• BBS Reply (10%) 
 
First, students must reply to a student’s posting in a meaningful way for each class topic. These 
replies must be posted by the following Monday 23:59. After receiving the reply from another 
student, students must respond to the reply by the following Wednesday 23:59.

개요
이 수업에서는 인류 역사의 다양한 지적 성찰 및 실천적 가치를 종합적으
로 탐구하고, 이를 바탕으로 현재의 사회를 이해하고 미래의 변화에 대응
할 수 있는 토의·토론의 장을 마련한다. 개별 전공들 간의 장벽을 넘어 비
판적·융합적·창의적 사고 능력을 함양하고, 나아가 새롭고 다양한 관점에서 
문제의식을 생성하며 타인과의 소통 및 협력을 통해 문제를 해결할 수 있
도록 하는 것이 이 교과의 목표이다. 이를 위해 플립트 클래스(Flipped 
Class) 기반의 학습자 중심 교수학습 방법을 도입하여, 질문 중심 학습
(QBL: Question Based Learning)과 토론 및 발표를 통해 학습자가 배
움의 주체가 될 수 있도록 한다.

Overview
One of the most important bilateral relationships today is 
between the United States and the People’s Republic of China. 
The two nations are the most influential figures in global 
politics. Thus, it is crucially important for us to understand the 
relationship between the two countries. This seminar explores 
the relationship between the United States and China from 
1949 to the present. We will cover some of the main events 
that shaped and influenced the current relationship between the 
United States and China. The events that will be covered in 
this course include The Cold War, Ping-pong diplomacy, The 
Tiananmen Square incident, The trade war, and COVID-19. 
Based on the past and current relationship between the two 
countries, we will ultimately discuss the future relationship 
between the two countries and their impact on the globe. In 
this course, students will explore the past and present 
relationship between the United States and China. We will 
critically analyze the past, present, and future relationship of 
the two states based on data.

지식을 다져나가고자 합니다. 말하기, 듣기, 쓰기, 읽기의 외국어 습득의 4가지 영역의 능력을 
향상시키는 것을 목표로 문법을 체계적으로 습득하고, 단어를 늘려서 일상생활에 활용할 수 
있게 구성하였습니다. 시간이 허락된다면 강의 중간중간에 문화적인 요소를 포함하여 일본 
문화나 일본인의 생활에 흥미와 관심을 더하고자 합니다. 
다음 3가지에 초점을 두고 강의를 진행한다.
첫째, 히라가나(ひらがな)+가타가나(カタカナ)와 일상생활에서 사용되는 기본적인 한자로 쓰
여진 정형화된 어구나, 문장을 읽고 이해할 수 있다.
둘째, 명사문+い형용사+な형용사, 「です」용법을 활용할 수 있다. 
셋째, 일상생활에서 자주 접하는 장면에서 느리고 짧은 회화로부터 필요한 정보를 얻어
낼 수 있다.
 추천과목은 없습니다. 일본어에 대한 관심이 있는 학생이라면 누구든지 수강할 수 있습니다.
 일본어 능력이 초급 이상인 학생들은 타분반 수업을 수강해 주실 것을 부탁드립니다.

Evaluation 
Method 
Description
Students will be evaluated through a balanced mix of class participation, a 
team project on global expansion strategy, and written exam that emphasizes 
applying international business frameworks to real-world situations. Assessment 
focuses on understanding, application, and critical judgment rather than rote 
memorization, with clear rubrics shared in advance to ensure transparency and 
fairness.
Attendance Policy
No grade may be assigned for absences of 1/3 or more of the class days, 
except in cases of unavoidable absences deemed necessary by the instructor.
Overview
The course focuses on the dynamic nature of international business, 
highlighting opportunities and challenges in global markets. It examines 
the business implications of market internationalization and analyzes how 
economic, political, legal, cultural, and ethical factors impact multinational 
corporations (MNCs), governments, and financial markets. Additionally, this 
course 
aims 
to 
differentiate 
between 
general 
international 
business 
operations and domestic business management, facilitating a deeper 
understanding 
of 
their 
divergent 
principles 
and 
practices. 
Through 
discussions and case studies, students develop skills in analyzing strategic 
choices 
for 
internationalization 
and 
assessing 
their 
effectiveness.

Who Should Take 
This Course
This course is designed for undergraduates who wish to understand how 
firms compete and make strategic decisions in global markets. It is 
especially suitable for Business School students and non-business majors 
interested in international careers, multinational corporations, or graduate 
study in international business.
Prerequisites 
(Recommended)
There are no strict formal prerequisites, but students will benefit from 
prior 
exposure 
to

Principles

Management, Economics, or Marketing, as well as comfort reading English 
textbook chapters and business articles. A willingness to engage with data, 
real-world cases, and group work is strongly recommended.
Class Rules
Students are expected to attend class regularly and on time, sit in a 
consistent seat with a visible name tag, and come prepared by completing 
the 
assigned 
readings 
before 
each 
session. 
Active 
and 
respectful 
participation in discussions and group work is required, and absences, 
lateness, or lack of preparation will negatively affect the participation 
grade. All students must follow university policies on academic honesty; 
unauthorized collaboration, plagiarism, recording, or sharing of course 
materials is strictly prohibited.
Changes and 
improvements
In this offering, the course places stronger emphasis on data-based group 
projects, real-world case analysis, and structured in-class discussions to 
deepen 
application 
of 
international 
business 
frameworks. 
Evaluation 
rubrics, peer assessment for group work, and feedback opportunities have 
been refined to enhance fairness, transparency, and the overall learning 
experience for students.
Objectives  
General
This course aims to equip undergraduate students with a comprehensive 
understanding of how firms operate and compete in the global business 
environment by integrating core international business theories with 
real-world applications.
Detailed Objective 1
Students will be able to explain the drivers and consequences of 
globalization for countries, firms, and individuals, and describe how major 
international institutions 
and agreements 
shape the global business 
environment.
Detailed Objective 2
Students will be able to analyze how economic, political, legal, and cultural 
differences influence international business activities and apply key 
frameworks to evaluate market entry modes, multinational strategies, and 
global operations.
Detailed Objective 3
Students will be able to apply basic concepts of international finance, 
global value chains, marketing, and cross-cultural management to develop 
evidence-based strategic recommendations for firms operating across 
borders.

Syllabus: General Physics 1 (PHYS151) 
  
Spring Semester, 2026 
Credit: 3  
 
Lecturer: Se-Jong Kahng (sjkahng@korea.ac.kr) 
 
Description: 
This course introduces fundamental principles of classical mechanics, fluid dynamics, and 
thermodynamics. Emphasizing conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills, it covers 
topics ranging from Newton’s laws of motion to the laws of thermodynamics. 
 
Objectives: 
Develop a solid foundation in the fundamental principles of classical mechanics. Acquire 
problem-solving skills applicable to motion, forces, energy, wave, and thermodynamics. 
Understand the various types of Newton’s laws that govern the motion particle systems, 
collisions, rotational motion, oscillations, and waves. Explore thermodynamic concepts, 
including temperature, heat, entropy, and conservation laws. 
 
Textbook: 
Halliday, Resnick, and Walker, Principles of Physics, 10th or later Edition (John Wiley 
& Sons, Inc) 
 
Schedule 
 
Week 1   Ch 1 : Measurement 
Ch 2 : Motion Along a Straight Line 
Week 2   Ch 3 : Vectors 
Ch 4 : Motion in Two and Three Dimensions 
Week 3   Ch 5 : Force and Motion - I                           
Ch 6 : Force and Motion - II 
Week 4   Ch 7 : Kinetic Energy and Work                                   
Week 5   Ch 8 : Potential Energy and Conservation of Energy 
 
   
Week 6   Ch 9 : Center of Mass and Linear Momentum 
Week 7   Ch 14 : Fluids 
Week 8   Ch 10 : Rotation 
Week 9   Ch 11 : Rolling, Torque, and Angular Momentum 
Week 10  Ch 12 : Equilibrium and Elasticity 
Ch 13 : Gravitation  
Week 11  Ch 15 : Oscillations 
Ch 16 : Waves - I                         
Week 12  Ch 17 : Waves - II 
Week 13  Ch 18 : Temperature, Heat, and the First Law of Thermodynamics 
Week 14  Ch 19 : The Kinetic Theory of Gases  
Week 15  Ch 20 : Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics 
 
Grade: 300 (3 exams) + alpha

* 본 과목은 flip learning의 양방향 토론식 수업이며, 수업시간에 적극적으로 참여해야 하는 것이 
  가장 중요하며, 평가에도 가장 크게 반영되는 요소입니다.
** 첫 수업시간부터 정상 수업을 진행하며, 출석체크에 반영합니다. 
   정정기간에 수강신청하여 들어올 경우, 출석 점수에 큰 지장이 생길 수 있음. 
 
본 과목의 가장 큰 특징은 ‘창업을 통한 사회 혁신’에 대한 이론과 실무를 협업 수업을 
통해 직접 배우고 경험해 볼 기회가 제공된다는 것입니다. 
먼저 우리가 속해있는 사회의 정치, 경제, 문화, 기술 부분 등에서 어떤 변화가 일어나고 
있는지, 어떤 사회적 문제가 야기되고 그 영향은 무엇인지를 파악하기 위해 매 수업마다 
한 주간에 있었던 주요 경제 신문의 기사 내용을 토론하는 시간을 갖습니다. 매 수업시간
마다 학생들은 한국경제신문/매일경제신문을 구독하여 읽고 수업시간에 내용[PESTI]을 정
리하여 가지고 오는 것이 필수 과제입니다
중간고사 이전의 전반기(Part 1)에는 창업에 대한 주요 요소들을 이론 수업을 통해 학습하
고, 중간고사 이후의 후반기(Part 2)에는 ‘MIT스타트업바이블‘ 교재를 통해서 창업의 단계
별 준비를 어떻게 진행해야 하는지를 점검할 것입니다. 
특히, 후반기에는 학생들은 조별 과제를 통해 임팩트 벤처 기업의 사업 내용 분석을 토대
로 신규 사업 계획을 수립하고 이를 기말고사때 회사의 관계자들에게 발표할 것입니다. 본 
기말 발표는 기말 고사를 대신할 예정이며, 현장에서 기업 관계자가 평가한 내용을 성적에 
반영할 것입니다. 
이러한 일련의 프로세스를 통해 본 과목을 수강하는 학생들은 실제 임팩트 벤처 기업을 
창업하고 사업 계획을 수립하는 것과 같은 경험을 하게 될 것입니다.
창업(Entrepreneurship)과 사회적 혁신(Social Innovation), 두 가지 모두에 대해 구체적인 
이해도를 높이는 것이 본 과목의 학습 목표입니다. 
창업, 경제, 경영, 사회적 혁신 등에 대한 기본 지식이 있을 경우 도움을 받을 수 있습니
다. 단, 배우고자 하는 적극적인 자세만 있다면 충분히 수업을 즐길 수 있습니다. 
수업시간에는 아래의 제한 사항이 있습니다. 
  (1) 수업시간에는 모든 스마트 기기와 노트북 사용 금지
  (2) 빈말을 줄이기

이 수업에서는 인류 역사의 다양한 지적 성찰 및 실천적 가치를 종합적으
로 탐구하고, 이를 바탕으로 현재의 사회를 이해하고 미래의 변화에 대응
할 수 있는 토의·토론의 장을 마련한다. 개별 전공들 간의 장벽을 넘어 비
판적·융합적·창의적 사고 능력을 함양하고, 나아가 새롭고 다양한 관점에서

도록 하는 것이 이 교과의 목표이다. 이를 위해 플립트 클래스(Flipped 
Class) 기반의 학습자 중심 교수학습 방법을 도입하여, 질문 중심 학습
(QBL: Question Based Learning)과 토론 및 발표를 통해 학습자가 배
움의 주체가 될 수 있도록 한다.

BUSS313-02 INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS (국제경영론-영강) 
TUESDAY, THURSDAY 9:00AM-11:45PM 
2026 SPRING SEMESTER 
COURSE SYLLABUS 
 
Professor: Yoojung Ahn  
Contact: yjahn@korea.ac.kr 
Office: LP615 
Office hours: Tuesdays 2PM-3PM or by appointment 
 
COURSE DESCRIPTION 
The purpose of this course is to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of international 
business. It will provide students with a basic understanding of the global business environment. 
This course covers the macro-level environmental factors that affect international businesses 
today. We will discuss such topics as globalization, country environments (political, legal, and 
economic), culture, global trade and foreign direct investment, regional economic integration, 
international strategy, and international management. Students should leave this course with an 
increased appreciation of the challenges and opportunities of doing business internationally. 
COURSE OBJECTIVES 
By completing this course, students will:   
§ Develop an understanding and knowledge of basic principles and concepts of international 
management.  
§ Examine the various cultural, political, and legal issues that impact international business 
activity 
§ Examine the international institutions and practices that impact international business 
§ Understand the different challenges business face when they operate in an international 
environment 
§ Develop intellectual skills so that students are able to integrate previously learned aspect of 
business and organization in the global context 
 
2 
 
TEACHING METHODS 
The lectures will focus on equipping students with knowledge about international management. 
During the lectures, students will be expected to actively participate by responding to and 
answering questions and by sharing their understanding and critique of the course readings to 
facilitate explanation, evaluation, analysis and comparison, application, and communication. 
During the lectures, students will discuss with peers during exercises, debates, etc. to facilitate 
description, explanation, evaluation, analysis and comparison of fundamental theories, and apply 
them into current international business context.  
 
For the group projects, students are expected to demonstrate their critical thinking by analyzing 
and evaluating global business environments and providing appropriate solution to firms. Students 
will give presentation on their analysis of their selected country and company. Students are 
expected to effectively communicate their skills on evaluation, analysis, and application with 
audience. 
 
The online quiz and final reaction paper assignments will help students to assess their learning of 
the main topics, cases, and other materials covered in class. 
REQUIRED READINGS 
Course Powerpoint Slides 
There is no required textbook for this class. Instead you will have slides as the main course material. 
The slides for each class will be uploaded ahead of time. Please download it before coming to class.  
 
Casepack: 
There will be 2 cases used throughout the semester. Please download them via the following link: 
https://hbsp.harvard.edu/import/1378042 (USD $9.90). Student registration is required.  
 
Others:  
We will spend 10-15 minutes every week discussing weekly international business news around 
the world. Please read and bring any interesting pieces of news to share with the class! 
EVALUATION

Group project and presentation (40%)  
Group project report will be evaluated in content, writing, and presentation. The content portion 
will be based on how well the students have analysed and evaluated topics by incorporating their 
thoughts. The writing portion will be based on spelling, grammar, syntax, and organization and 
flow etc.  Presentation will be graded on the basis of content and presentation skills. The project 
should be done in a group of 4-5 members (depending on the total class size).   
The project will focus on the new market entry activities of a firm (i.e. an entry within the last four 
years).  New market entry refers either to a firm entering a new country, or a firm offering a new 
product or service in a non-domestic market in which it already is active.  Market entry can consist 
of a variety of activities such as exporting, licensing, franchising, or foreign direct investment. As 
part of your research and presentation, your group is expected to explain the market entry and 
evaluate whether it was a success or a failure. More details on the content will be shared in class.

share their analysis in a 20-minute presentation, which consists of a 15-minute PowerPoint 
presentation and a 5-minute Q&A session after the presentation. Your presentation will be 
evaluated by the professor as well as your peers. 
  
        Report (10%): Each group will submit a project report to the professor after incorporating the 
feedback from the presentation one week after the presentation date. The report should be between 
10-15 pages (double-spaced, one inch margins, 12 point Times New Roman font), excluding 
figures, tables, and references. The report will be evaluated based on its argument and its written 
quality. Late assignment is subject to 5% penalty per calendar day after the due day.

11:59PM. Late submissions will not be graded.

Course Description:  
This course introduces undergraduate students to the core principles and practices of 
social research in sociology and related social science disciplines. Students will learn how 
sociologists generate reliable knowledge about social phenomena through systematic, ethical, 
and theory-informed research. The course covers key stages of the research process and the 
methodological concepts needed at each stage, such as conceptualization, operationalization, 
measurement, and sampling. Students will also be introduced to major research strategies, 
including experiments, surveys, qualitative field research, unobtrusive methods, and evaluation 
research, along with the fundamentals of data analysis and research reporting. 
 
Student Learning Outcomes:  
By the end of this course, students will be able to: 
 
Define and explain key concepts and terminology associated with quantitative and 
qualitative social research methods. 
 
Describe the role of research methods in sociological inquiry and in the production of 
evidence relevant to social policy and public debate. 
 
Compare and evaluate the strengths and limitations of major research designs and 
data collection strategies used in social research. 
 
Critically assess existing empirical studies by examining their research questions, 
design choices, measurement strategies, and ethical considerations. 
 
Apply fundamental research-methods concepts to formulate research questions and 
assess appropriate methodological approaches to studying social phenomena. 
2 
 
 
Course Materials: 
Students are expected to read all required textbook chapters prior to every class (see the 
Tentative Course Schedule table on pages 4 and 5). We use the textbook below, and the main 
textbook will be reserved and available at the designated book section in the KU’s main library.  
 
 
Main Textbook: Babbie, Earl R. 2020. The Practice of Social Research (15th edition). 
Cengage learning. 
 
In addition to the textbook, I will use my own lecture slides for each module. They will 
largely overlap with the book but there will be material in the slides that is not in the book and 
vice versa. I will do my best to post the slides on KU-LMS before class although this is not a 
guarantee. If I cannot post them before class, I will do so after class. When I do post them in 
advance, I might make edits or additions in class. Be prepared to make notes on your slides to 
reflect these changes. 
 
Course Requirements / Grading: 
Your final grade will be based on the sum of two (2) in-class exams (midterm and final; 
worth 70%, 35% each) and one (1) individual research proposal assignment submission (worth 
30%). Please know that grades are NOT subject to negotiation. Except for the case of grading 
error, your grades will not change under any circumstances. 
 
 
Exams: Two (2) in-class and closed-book exams are scheduled during the semester. 
Exams will cover all material from the textbook and lecture slides. Note that my 
lecture slides are not a substitute for the textbook; you must read the book. Both 
sources are subject to exams. One or two essay questions as well as multiple choice, 
true/false, and fill-in-the-blank questions based on textbook reading will be given to 
students. Students will be given a language option for their essay responses; their 
essay responses can be written in either Korean or English. 
 
 
Individual Research Proposal Assignment: One (1) individual research proposal 
assignment is required for assessment. This assignment requires students to develop 
an individual research proposal that demonstrates their ability to identify and define 
an important social problem that has not been sufficiently addressed in existing 
research, and to determine the most effective methodological approach for 
investigating that problem. The primary objective of this assignment is to evaluate 
students’ capacity to formulate original and meaningful sociological research 
questions and to assess how different research methodologies can be used to generate 
appropriate answers to those questions. The submission deadline is 11:59p.m. on 
June 16. As with the language option for the exam essays, students may also write 
3 
 
their proposals in either Korean or English. Further instructions about this assignment 
will be provided in class. 
 
 
Extra Credit: There will be some opportunities to earn extra credit through 
attendance and class participation. First, students who have TWO or fewer absences 
after March 12 will receive extra credit worth 1% of the total. In addition, students 
who have TWO or fewer absences for online interactive quizzes (Kahoot!) will 
receive extra credit worth 1% of the total as well.  
 
 
Grading: No rounding will be applied. 
A+: 95% and above  
 
A: 90% - 94% 
B+: 85% - 89% 
 
 
B: 80% - 84% 
C+: 75% - 79% 
 
 
C: 70% - 74%

D: 60% - 64%

Course Policies: 
 
Students are expected to attend every class; students with FIVE OR MORE 
ABSENCES AFTER MODULE 2 (MARCH 12) will receive an F. Students are 
also encouraged to be on time and not to leave early to avoid disturbing other peer 
students. If you are more than 10 minutes late after class starts or if you leave early 
before the lecture is over, your attendance may not be recorded. If students are unable 
to participate in the lecture due to family emergency or medical issues, proper 
documentation that proves emergent incidents stated above (e.g., doctor’s note, etc.) 
needs to be submitted to avoid a record of absence. 
 
No late submission of research proposal and no make-up exams will be allowed 
except in case of an emergency that can be proven by proper documentation (e.g., 
death of immediate family, admission to a hospital, etc.). 
 
Plagiarism is strictly prohibited; even a single plagiarized sentence is unacceptable. 
All submitted work must be your own original effort. If you utilize AI assistance 
(such as ChatGPT) for the written assignment, you are required to include a 
disclosure statement specifying which sections were assisted and how the tool was 
used. Presenting AI-generated text as your own original writing is considered 
plagiarism. All submissions will be screened using multiple plagiarism and AI 
detection tools. Undisclosed use of AI or any other form of plagiarism will result in 
automatic failure of the course and potential disciplinary action by the Department 
Chair or the College Dean. 
 
Recording lectures and taking pictures/videos in class are strictly prohibited. 
 
This syllabus is subject to change. If changes are necessary or desired during the 
course, I will immediately inform students of the change in class as well as via email.

개발하고, 데이터를 수집한 후 분석하여 논문을 쓰게 됩니다. 이러한 과정을 통해 사람들을 이해하는 데 
중요한 성격 및 개인차에 대해 이해하고, 이를 측정하는 데 필요한 제반 지식을 습득합니다.

로 4인 1조로 이루어질 예정입니다. 많은 과정이 조별 활동을 통해 이루어지므로, 조별 활동에 성의 있
는 참여가 어려운 학생은 수강하지 않은 것을 권고합니다. 각 조는 학생들이 자발적으로 구성하고 교수
가 일방적으로 정하지 않을 예정입니다. 미리 함께 일하고 싶은 조원과 함께 수강 신청하는 것도 좋습
니다.

본 수업에서는 한국어로 된 성격 측정 도구를 제작하고, 그에 관련된 논문을 작성할 예정이기 때문에 
한국어가 서툰 학생들은 많은 어려움이 있을 수 있습니다.

강의# 개요!
 
“정치학 배워서 뭐하나요?” 학생들과 면담할 때, 흔히 받는 질문이지만, 언제나 답변
이 궁색했다. 정치인? 외교관? 교수? 고시나 로스쿨을 진학할 때, 도움이 되나? 정치
학이 도움이 될 만한 이런저런 직업군을 떠 올려 보지만, 직업을 얻기 위한 수단으로
서 정치학은 뭔가 부족한 느낌이었다. 정치학을 배우면, 우리의 현실을 더 잘 이해하
고, 우리 사회를 더 좋게 만들 수 있다고 답하고 싶었지만, 막상 구체적인 예를 떠올
려 보려니 딱히 생각나는 것이 없었다. 그래서 학생들이 직접 그 답을 찾을 수 있는 
기회를 만들고자 했다. 2022년 한국정치세미나라는 제목으로 강의를 처음 개설했고, 
2023년과 2024년에는 “시민정치리빙랩: 교실밖의 정치학”이라는 이름으로 강의를 진
행하고, 그 결과물들을 출판해 왔다.  
 
 
 
 
 
부제가 의미하는 바와 같이 본 수업은 교실 안의 정치학을 통해 우리가 배운 이론과 
지식들이 교실 밖의 문제를 해결하는 데 얼마나 도움이 되는 가를 학생들 스스로 탐
구하는 것을 목적으로 한다. 본 수업을 통해 학생들은 지역사회 내의 문제를 발굴하
고, 지역주민, 시민단체, 지역의회, 지방행정기관 등 다양한 행위자들과 면담을 통해 
해결방안을 모색하는 활동을 하게 된다.  
 
이번 학기에는 특히 이민과 관련된 주제에 초점을 맞추고자 한다. 2026년 현재, 국내 
체류 외국인은 265만 명을 넘어 전체 인구의 5%를 상회하고 있으며, 다문화가정 출
생아가 전체 출생아의 6.5%를 차지하는 시대가 되었다. 세계 최저 수준의 출산율과 
급격한 고령화 속에서 정부는 인구 국가비상사태를 선언했고, 이민은 노동력 부족과 
인구감소에 대응하기 위한 핵심 정책 의제로 부상했다. 저출산 대책의 실효성에 대한 
회의가 커지면서, 이민 확대를 통한 인구 문제 해결이 정치권과 학계에서 진지하게

일원으로 정착하기 위해 분투하고 있지만, 대다수의 내국인들에게 이들의 삶은 여전
히 낯설고 먼 이야기로 남아 있다.  
 
본 수업은 이러한 현실을 성찰하는 계기를 마련하고자 한다. 이민을 단순히 숫자나 
정책의 관점에서만 바라보는 것이 아니라, 지역사회 현장에서 이민자들을 직접 만나
고, 그들의 목소리를 듣고, 그들이 직면한 문제를 함께 고민해 보고자 한다. 궁극적으
로 이 수업을 통해 학생들이 다문화 사회로 급속히 전환되고 있는 한국 사회에서 '우
리'는 누구이며, 서로 다른 배경을 가진 사람들과 어떻게 함께 살아갈 것인가에 대해 
스스로 답을 찾아가는 기회가 되기를 바란다. 
 
수강# 대상#
 
본 수업에는 별도의 선수과목은 없다. 그러나 다음 사항을 고려하여 수강 여부를 결
정하기 바란다.  
 
첫째, 세미나 수업인 만큼 동료 학생들과 토론, 토의 및 팀별 활동에 대해 적극적으로 
참여해야 한다.  
둘째, 문제의 발굴, 해결책의 모색과 적용에 있어 현장성을 강조하며, 이는 강의실 밖
에서 벌어지는 활동에 대한 적극적인 참여를 통해서 달성될 수 있다.  
셋째, 본 수업의 모든 활동은 그룹활동으로 진행된다. 그룹보다는 개인과제를 선호하
는 학생들에게는 부담이 될 수 있다.  
넷째, 마지막으로 학생들의 최종보고서는 이후 엮어서 책으로 출판하고자 한다. 따라
서 수업이 마무리된 이후에도 원고 작업 등 추가적인 작업에 대한 요구가 있을 수 있
다. 추가 작업에 대한 적극적인 참여를 권장한다.

▷ 과목개요 
 
 
This class offers lectures, presentations, and interactive mentoring sessions on Korean history and culture for 
foreign students without a Korean educational  background.  Specifically  for the Spring 2026 semester, the 
Visiting  Professor  places  a special  emphasis  on "communication"  and "mentorship."  Beyond  simple 
knowledge  transmission,  the course  is designed  to foster  a close  intellectual  relationship  between  the 
instructor and students.
(Spring 2026)
 
 
 
 
During the first half of the semester, emphasis will be given to Korean culture and how it relates to Korean 
identity  and “Korean- ness.” In the second  half, the course  will cover major periods  in Korean  history  in 
chronological order. Instead of focusing on Korea as a ‘single nation with a distinct history,’ the course will 
take a civilizational approach with attention paid to the position of Korea in the context of regional and world 
history. Through active discussion and mentoring, students will learn to view Korean history and culture as 
products  of interaction  with the rest of the world.  Major  events,  such as wars,  will be analyzed  in their 
geopolitical context, and lectures will attempt to eschew stereotypes through critical dialogue.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
▷ 학습목표 
이 강의는 한국에서의 교육 경험이 없는 학생들을 대상으로 하며, 2026학년도 1학기에는 특별히 초
빙교수(Visiting Professor)와의 '소통'과 '멘토링'을 강화하여 운영된다. 단순한 지식의 전달자로서의 
교수가 아닌, 학생들이 한국 사회와 문화를 이해하는 과정을 돕는 멘토로서의 역할을 수행하며, 강
의실 안팎에서의 활발한 상호작용을 통해 수업을 진행한다.
이 강의는 단순히 '일국사'로서의 한국학을 다루기보다는 문명학적인 관점을 택하여, 한국사를 동아
시아 지역사와 세계사의 맥락 속에서 다룰 것이다. 한국사 역시 세계사의 일부분이며 세계와 단절된 
것이 아니라 세계 속에서 발전하여 온 것이기 때문이다. 학생들은 교수와의 지속적인 문답과 멘토링
을 통해 이러한 거시적 관점을 자신의 것으로 소화하게 된다.
초반 강의에서는 정체성과 문화성 상징이라는 테마를 중심으로 문화적 정체성 형성에 대한 이론을 
강의하고, 한국학을 배우는 데 필요한 역사·정치 이론과 문화이론 전반을 소개한다. 이 강의에서는 ‘
문화’를 베네딕트 앤더슨의 ‘상상의 공동체’, 그리고 새뮤얼 헌팅턴이 사용하는 ‘문명’ 개념과 연계하
여 강의한다. 즉 상상의 공동체로서의 한국과 ‘문명’으로서의 한국을 구성하는 갖가지 상징(symbols
)들은 곧 한국문화를 구성하는 개별단위이기 때문이다. 따라서 각 강의마다 ‘테마’를 부여하여 각 시
대를 대표하는 개념을 설정하고 심도 있는 토론을 진행한다. 아울러 현재 세계 대중문화의 흐름을 
주도하고 있는 K-pop에 대한 강의를 통하여 한국 대중문화의 흐름을 파악하고 한국 현대사회와의 
관련성을 조명한다.
전반기 한국의 '기원'에 관한 강의에서는 역사기록은 물론 정치학, 고고학, 유전학, 민속학 등 인접 
학문의 이론과 학설을 적극 활용한다. 한반도와 인근 지역의 인간 집단 이동, 고고학적 유물들의 의
미, 고대인들의 유전학적 분석 등을 설명하고 또한 고대 한국인들에게 공동체적 정체성이 어떻게 형
성되었는지에 대하여 설명한다. 전쟁과 같은 중요사건(예: 고구려-수/당 전쟁, 몽골 침공, 임진왜란, 
병자호란, 일제 강점) 역시 '세계사 속의 한국'이라는 관점에서 설명이 될 것이며, 한국사가 아닌 세
계사적인 의미를 지니는 사건으로 자리매김될 것이다.
전쟁이나 정치적 격변 같은 사건들 못지않게 중요한 것은 그 사건들이 한국 역사 속에서 사회의 구
성에 미친 영향이다. 예를 들어 상인 집단이 건국한 고려와 성리학을 추종하는 신진사대부에 의하여 
건국된 조선 같은 경우, 그 상이(相異)함은 국가의 운영이나 사회 구성원들의 생활(경제적 활동, 남
녀관계 등)에 큰 영향을 미치며, 이를 자세히 들여다본다. 이러한 과정에서 상존하고 있는 (한국 관
련) 스테레오타입과 고정관념을 지양하고, 교수와의 멘토링을 통해 새로운 한국의 역사상(Historical 
Image)과 문화상(Cultural Image)을 정립하는 데 주력할 것이다.
 
Through this course, students are expected to achieve a comprehensive understanding of Korean history and 
culture.  The goal extends  beyond  the simple  transmission  of information;  we aim to provide  an array of 
diverse perspectives that encourage students to develop their own unique insights into Korea. In addition to 
interactive  in-class lectures, students will have the opportunity  to choose topics for weekly presentations, 
fostering active engagement. Furthermore, two scheduled excursions will complement the lectures, bridging 
theoretical  knowledge  with  actual,  out- of-class  experiences  to stimulate  greater  interest  and  deeper 
connection with the subject matter.

본 강의는 한국에서의 교육 경험이 낯선 학생들에게 단순히 역사적 사실을 전달하는 것을 넘어, 한국
과 한국인을 아우르는 깊이 있는 '이야기(Narrative)'를 들려주는 것을 목표로 합니다.
학기 전반부에는 한국 문화의 고유한 매력을 문명사적 관점에서 폭넓게 조망합니다. 특히 세계적으
로 주목받는 대중문화를 깊이 있게 들여다봄으로써, 전통과 현대가 어우러진 한국 사회를 더욱 생동
감 있게 이해할 수 있도록 이끌 것입니다. 후반부에는 고대부터 현대에 이르는 역사의 흐름을 따라
가되, 단순한 연대기적 나열은 지양합니다. 대신 각 시대의 사회적 변화를 이끈 결정적 사건들에 주
목하여, 역사의 소용돌이 속에서 한국인의 정체성이 어떻게 형성되고 변화해왔는지 여러분과 함께 
고민해보고자 합니다.
또한, 이번 학기는 교실 밖에서의 생생한 경험과 소통을 특히 중요하게 생각합니다. 학기 중 예정된 
견학(Excursion)은 글로 배운 역사를 현장에서 직접 느끼며 체화하는 소중한 계기가 될 것입니다. 더
불어 초빙교수와의 자유로운 멘토링과 토론 과정을 통해, 여러분이 타인의 관점을 답습하기보다 스
스로의 시선으로 한국을 해석하고 깊이 공감하는 의미 있는 시간을 만들어가기를 기대합니다.

 Ju Hyun Pyun, jhpyun@korea.ac.kr  (Office: HM 503)

※ This is an 8-week intensive course which will start on 28th April, 2026
Overview 
The course aims to equip future managers with the tools of economics that can help them 
think strategically and make better decisions. The entire course is divided into two parts. 
Part 1 – Basics 
In the first part, the course covers building blocks of managerial economics: supply & 
demand, theory of the firm, costs and cost curves, profit maximization, firm’s pricing and 
market structure (perfect competition, monopoly, and oligopoly). It also introduces tools 
to analyze the welfare associated with market outcomes. 
Part 2 – Economics of Strategy 
In the second part, the course discusses a firm’s strategic interactions with rivals in the face 
of various market structures and market imperfections. The course starts with basic game 
theory in order to give an insight to the strategic interactions between rival companies in 
oligopolistic settings. The conditions under which cooperation can take place are also 
discussed. Then, it moves on to topics related to information economics where information 
asymmetry plays a key role. Topics include the insurance market where adverse selection 
is a big problem, and managerial compensation where moral hazard is a major issue. The 
course concludes with a discussion of firm’s external environment in the current macro-
economy. 
Textbook (not required) 
Brickley, James A. et al. Managerial Economics and Organizational Architecture (5th 
edition, McGraw-Hill, 2009) 
Other References 
Baye, Michael and J. Prince, Managerial Economics & Business Strategy (8th edition, 
McGraw-Hill Economics, 2013)  
Froeb et al., Manageral Economics A Problem Solving Approach (3rd edition) 
 
2
Prerequisite 
Introductory knowledge of microeconomics is strongly recommended, either through 
principles of economics course or private reading any textbooks of intermediate level of 
micro-economics. Another important prerequisite of this course is the basic knowledge of 
calculus such as the concepts of derivatives, partial derivatives, and total differentiation. 
I recommend the following text for your self-study: Simon, Carl P. et al. Mathematics for 
Economists (Norton, 1994)

Midterm and Final examination: There will be an in-class exam midway through the

In-class assignment & Homework (10%): There will be in-class assignments for the

Introduction
Introduction to International Development is designed to provide a foundation for more advanced studies of in-
ternational development and cooperation. Learning goals will be pursued through intensive reading assignments
and hands-on investigation and research on four topics. First, students will interrogate the histories and theories
of international development and cooperation. Second, students will develop a familiarity with the concepts and
evolution of development and its variants, including sustainable development, economic development, human de-
velopment and capabilities, and post-development. Third, they will investigate the emergence and functioning of
international organizations involved in coordinating global cooperation. Finally, students will explore a selection
of compelling contemporary issues in international development and cooperation.
2
Objectives
By the end of this course, students will be knowledgeable on:
1. A broad range of theoretical perspectives on development, including both those that are widely accepted and
those that are contentious.
2. An understanding of the global framework for cooperation.
3. Selected foundational readings that inform contemporary theories of development.
4. The strengths and limits of a range of development data sources.
3

assigned in one night simply because there are only two chapters or a few articles to read. The readings can
be dense and take time to get through.
• You will take a short quiz about this syllabus before the first class meeting in the third week of classes. This
quiz is designed to ensure that you are familiar with the syllabus, that you understand the class requirements,
and that I can anticipate your interests. You will have unlimited time to take the quiz and are free to look at
the syllabus as you take the quiz, but you will only be able to take it once.
• For ten of the 13 weeks for which there are assigned readings, you are responsible for completing an online
quiz about that week’s readings. You are free to choose which of the ten weeks you take the quiz. You will
have 15 minutes to complete the quiz, which will typically consist of three to five questions. You will only
be allowed one attempt to take the quiz. The quiz must be taken before 9am on the first class meeting each
week. This is to ensure that you have the background needed to understand the class and that you can ask
about material you do not understand fully.

represented on the quiz. Readings marked with a † are simply the most important of the readings.

case by utilizing a range of data sets and interfaces. Each member of the group will screen record a walk-
through with a voice over explaining what they are trying to do with the data interface. Each member will
translate their walk-through into a flow chart that identifies their process. Finally, the group will compare
their findings and write up a short summary of the effectiveness of each data set or interface.

plagiarism).

Artificial Intelligence
The use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools like ChatGPT is not allowed. Your writing and your arguments should
be your own. (Note that I am not opposed to the use of AI for brainstorming, though I do not think it will help
much.) Like plagiarism, if it is determined that you have used AI tools, you will receive a zero for the given
assignment the first time. If you use AI a second time, you will fail the course.

this course will be an overview of global architecture so that students can understand the specific position 
of Western architecture within a diverse tradition of world culture. This course aims at helping students 
achieve not only supporting knowledge for their design but also a better understanding of architecture as 
one cultural phenomenon. 
 
2. Aims and objectives 
At the end of the semester, students will be able to … 
1) understand the stream of western architectural development from the origin to the 18th century; 
2) understand the cultural and historical diversity of western architecture within the frame of global 
architecture; 
3) have a critical understanding of architectural history, as well as basic knowledge of architecture. 
 
3. Performance Criteria [Revised in 2024] 
01. Architecture, Fine Art, and Technology: Understanding the relationship of architecture to the 
theories and knowledge of the arts and sciences. 
02. History and Culture of Global Architecture: Understanding the diversity of world 
architectural history and culture. 
04. Architecture and Society: Understanding the factors and interrelationship among humans, 
culture, economy and policy that influence architecture and urban environments.

Spring 2026
LECTURE
This Version: April 27, 2026
Instructor: Seunghoon Na (sna2518@korea.ac.kr)

Location: Room 101, Sangnam Hall
Instructor Office Hours: Thursdays, 3 PM–4:20 PM, Room 521, Sangnam Hall
Teaching Assistant: David Nam (kh nam@korea.ac.kr)
TA Office Hours: Wednesdays, 2 PM - 3 PM. Locations will be updated accordingly
Course Description
This course provides a rigorous introduction to the foundations of international finance and macroeco-
nomics (IFM). IFM studies the macroeconomic interactions of economic agents across national borders.
In today’s highly interconnected global economy, trade and financial globalization have tightly linked
domestic economies, allowing economic shocks originating in one country to transmit rapidly across
borders. Since the 1980s, the international capital market integration has enabled large cross-border
financial flows, raising important questions about the movement of capital, external imbalances, and
the interaction between domestic and global markets. As a result, domestic monetary and fiscal poli-
cies are increasingly shaped by international considerations, and national economic outcomes are closely
connected through exchange rates, capital flows, and external balances.
In this course, we study the theoretical determinants of the current account in both small and large
open economies, the determination of real exchange rates, the dynamic adjustment of economies to
shocks, and the roles of monetary and fiscal policies in an open-economy environment. This course
is designed for upper-level undergraduate students and adopts a rigorous, microfounded approach.
Throughout the course, we emphasize optimization and intertemporal decision-making by economic
agents—including households, firms, and governments—to develop a coherent analytical framework for
understanding global macroeconomic dynamics.
Prerequisites
• ECON 173, ECON 174, ECON 201, ECON 202, and ECON 301
Course Materials
Lecture notes will be provided throughout the course and will serve as the primary course material. The
lecture notes closely follow the following textbook, which is used as the main reference:

Modern Approach.
In addition, the following textbooks may be used as background or supplementary references for selected
topics:
• Krugman, Obstfeld, and Melitz (2023, hereafter KOM), International Economics: Theory and
Policy.
• Uribe and Schmitt-Groh´e (2017, hereafter USG), Open Economy Macroeconomics.
Nonetheless, the lecture notes constitute the core material for the course, and none of the textbooks are
required for purchase.

(10 pts)
Midterm and Final.
There will be a midterm exam on April 23, which will account for 30 points of
the final grade. A final exam will be held on June 18 and will account for 40 points of the final grade. The
final exam will be cumulative. Both the midterm and final exams will be closed-book and closed-note.
Problem Sets.
There will be four problem sets, each worth 5 points toward the final grade. Students
may work on the problem sets in teams, but each student must submit their own individual copy.
Class Participation.
Students are required to record their attendance electronically via the LMS for
each session. Full participation points (10 points) will be awarded for active class engagement. According
to university regulations, any student who is absent for more than one-third of the total sessions (i.e.,

1. Introduction 
Wouldn’t you like to design something for yourself—rather than for a user or anyone else? 
This course offers an opportunity to rediscover yourself by candidly exposing your own 
desires. The course focuses on experimenting with design methodologies, processes, and new 
digital content to carry out digital design projects (DDPs) from a 21st-century perspective. 
The digital design fields of interest in this course include editorial design (books, magazines), 
brand experience (logos, packaging), digital content (game characters, webtoons, manga, 
illustrations), etc. Still, they can be narrowed down depending on the student's level and 
interest. In the first half of the class, we will work on methodology and small design projects 
focused on ideation and the creation of DDPs. The second half of the class will build on this 
with a final team project based on a specific topic. This course is divided into two parts.

design. Based on the modern design paradigm, students will learn the concepts, methodologies, 
and experience of authentic editorial design and will design a small body of work (a 2-4-page 
design and a 10-15-page brochure design). In this part, students will learn the basics of 
storytelling and narrative for editorial design and various content designs.

This course offers a comprehensive exploration into the realms of British and American poetry, 
spanning various eras and stylistic expressions. Our analytical approach will categorize the poems 
based on thematic similarities. Among these themes are death, religion, nature, marriage, love, 
family, and more—timeless topics that resonate across different literary forms. Engaging with multiple 
poems that revolve around a common theme allows students to delve into how distinct poetic 
devices (such as structure, metaphors, imagery, word choice, and the nuances of rhythm and meter) 
are intricately woven together to highlight specific themes in a distinct manner. This deep dive not 
only sheds light on the unique attributes of poetry but also aims to cultivate students into discerning 
and adept interpreters of poetic literature. 
 
Required Text 
 
Poetry texts and lecture notes will be uploaded to Blackboard on a weekly basis.

regardless of the reason, will result in an automatic grade of F. Should you be absent 
due to illness or official university events, please provide a doctor’s note or an official 
letter from your department to validate your absence. More than two unexcused 
absences will adversely affect your overall grade. Additionally, arriving late on three 
occasions will be counted as one full absence, and arriving more than 20 minutes late 
will be considered an absence as well. 
➢ 
Active participation in class discussions is highly encouraged. Ensure you have read 
the assigned materials prior to class and come prepared to discuss both the structure 
and the themes of the poem. Feel encouraged to raise any questions about the poem 
that you find challenging to understand. 
➢ 
The use of smartphones during class is strictly prohibited. Please refrain from 
distractions, including messaging apps like KakaoTalk and social media platforms, to 
maintain focus during lectures.

introduction to the poet’s biography and significance, followed by a thorough 
examination of a selected poem’s structure and thematic elements, such as its themes, 
subject matter, tone, language use, imagery, literary devices, and its rhythm and meter

For lab activities, please bring a laptop (PC or Mac; not tablet devices and not Android OS 
devices). 
 
2. Course Description and Aims 
Seismology is one of the main geophysical methods for studying the Earth. This course 
introduces fundamental concepts and basic theory of seismic waves, and then applies them to 
earthquakes, Earth structure, and plate tectonics. Practical exercises are provided through in-
class labs and take-home assignments. The goal is to build both physical intuition and basic skills 
for reading and using seismological data. 
3. Prerequisites 
There is no formal prerequisite. 
However, you should be comfortable with basic calculus and introductory physics (e.g., 
derivatives and simple differential equations). 
4. Learning Outcomes 
ü Explain key ideas in seismology: stress and strain, the wave equation, and basic wave types. 
ü Describe and interpret body waves and surface waves, including Snell’s law and dispersion. 
ü Use seismograms to identify arrivals, estimate travel times, and connect observations to 
source and structure. 
ü Apply basic inverse ideas to earthquake location and simple tomography problems. 
ü Explain earthquake source concepts such as magnitude, focal mechanisms, and moment 
tensors. 
ü Discuss how seismology constrains Earth’s interior (crust, mantle, outer core, inner core) 
and plate-tectonic settings. 
5. Course Materials 
Primary textbook: 
ü Stein, S., and Wysession, M. (Wiley), An Introduction to Seismology, Earthquakes, and 
Earth Structure. 
Lecture materials: 
ü Lecture slides will be the main class materials. 
ü Additional readings or notes may be posted on Blackboard. 
 
6. Assignments and Assessment 
Exams are open-book tests.

achievement. 
ü To receive A+, all required reports should be completed on time. 
ü To receive B or higher, all requirements should be submitted before the end of the 
semester (late submission may be accepted within the semester). 
ü Missing one or more exams results in a failing grade (F). 
 
7. Laboratory (Lab) Policy 
Labs are individual activities in the sense that each student submits their own report. 
Lab reports are typically due 3 weeks after the lab activity (except for the last lab). 
Report evaluation rubric (typical guide): 
ü Exceptional: 10 
ü Completed all items well: 9 
ü Completed all items with some missing detail: 7 
ü Poorly completed: 5 
ü On-time submission: 2 
Specific instructions for each lab will be provided in class and on L 
 
8. Policy on LLM Tools (e.g., ChatGPT) 
You may use LLM assistance for lab reports. 
However, you must still provide your own understanding and a clear discussion. 
If you use an LLM, you must disclose it in your report and describe how you used it. 
 
9. Academic Integrity 
Academic integrity is required in all course work. 
If any violation is discovered, the student will receive a failing grade (F) strictly.
