◆ Course Plan Details ◆ 
▷ Course Outline 
Overview 
This class aims to read business related articles by means of which 
to learn technical terms and concepts, discussing questions raised 
by them. The course materials range from business to industry, 
technology, economy and market. Students will read articles from 
The Economist, which is to say that our focus is on not only 
domestic but also international topics. Reading business topics in 
English can help us improve English language skills, especially by 
learning expressions that we don't often encounter in everyday 
Korea University Syllabus 
Spring Semester 2026 
conversational situations. It can also lead us to look at the society 
we live in from various perspectives. In doing so, we are encouraged 
to think about questions such as “What are the issues that different 
business sectors raise? What are they pursuing and why? How do 
the businesses they are pursuing, or the challenges they are taking 
on, actually impact the society we live in?” In considering these 
questions, we can begin to see the society and its dynamic 
structures more closely. 
Who Should Take 
This Course 
1. Anyone interested in practicing all aspects of English: read, write 
and speak. 
2. Anyone interested in being exposed to and learning about a 
diverse range of business issues in both Korea and abroad. 
Prerequisites 
(Recommended) 
Anyone interested in taking the class is welcome. 
Class Rules 
1. This is a discussion-based class, so your attendance and active 
participation is required. Please don't feel pressured, as the 
discussions will take place in small groups and are intended for you 
to share your thoughts with each other, but neither the discussions 
themselves nor their content will count toward your grade or be 
tested. What I will be evaluating is your participation. 
2. All classes and assignment are in English, except for the final 
exam, where students have a choice of English or Korean. 
Changes and 
improvements 
In this class we will study one English article each week. The class 
will consist of an overview of the article, reading the article together, 
and then group discussion. 
 
▷ Objectives  
Objectives  
General 
This course is designed to discuss and understand major issues in 
both Korea and abroad by reading articles and columns on various 
topics from the sectors of industry, economy, market, science and

technology. Students will develop comprehension and expression 
skills through presentations and discussions in depth. As described 
in the course description, this course aims not only to increase your 
awareness of business topics and improve your English skills, but 
also to open your eyes to the society in which we live, thereby 
making you a more flexible and capable of dealing with the present 
and the future. Your active participation and discussion are essential 
for you to achieve more than just understanding the assigned 
readings in this class.

Improve overall English language skills through reading and 
discussing English articles.

Goals (과목 목표) 
The goal of this course is to understand the mechanical behavior of typical statically 
determinate structural systems such as truss, beam, frame, composite structures and to 
have the ability to analyze those structures to obtain the necessary information and results 
for the design and management of civil infrastructures. 
 
Outlines (과목 개요) 
This course is designed to introduce students to the principles and methods of modeling 
and analyzing statically determined structures. The first part of the course introduces you 
to common structural types and design loads. It follows the basic concepts of modeling 
and analyzing force systems of statically determined structures such as beams, trusses, 
frames, and cables. The concept of the statically determined internal force and influence 
line of the flexural member is studied. Various methods of calculating the deflection of a 
statically determined structure are discussed later in this lecture.

& Environmental Awareness 2026-1
  Korea University

What is this class?:
• This is a new elective course opened in the fall of 2025; however, the materials/activities have been developed and 
taught for over twenty years by the professor. Together, we will be examining trends in human evolution (from 
tribal to city-state incarnations, both past and present) that have contributed to ecological issues due to their world-
views; we will also investigate the detrimental impacts of pollution, deforestation, species extinction loss, and 
other factors often disproportionately impacting marginalized populations; finally, we will be highlighting social 
movements (both grass roots and non-profs) that have emerged to defend ecosystems and human communities 
from environmental decline. These global challenges will be analyzed through both domestic (Korean) and 
international frameworks. See also “Learning outcomes” (below). There are no formal presentations in this class.
Texts:
The Last Hours of Ancient Sunlight (A/S)	
	
	
Hartmann; one text per class
The Way of Research (EvH) (school year 2025) 	
	
Blackwood; one per student
Please do not purchase the above books yet; they will both likely be uploaded as pdf versions to the LMS; there 
may also be a hard copy of the research textbook.  We will cover 2/3 of the Hartmann text, perhaps more if time 
permits.
Course Structure:
• This course has been structured for group and individual activities.  Group discussions will center around content 
from readings, lectures, and your own research interest, with the aim of spawning meaningful peer bonds.
Participation: 
• Active participation in class, in English, is required. All discussions, exercises, and assignments must be conducted 
in English. Participation includes attendance; arrive on time and prepared. Late arrivals and absences disrupt the 
class and will result in penalties. You are allowed up to three excused absences; ten or more absences (including 
excused) will result in a failing grade, as per Ministry of Education policy.
• Excused absences and tardies do not excuse missed work; you are responsible for catching up. Excused absences 
must be documented with official paperwork, not phone photos, and communicated promptly. Email all 
correspondence to the address provided, not through EKU email. Missed assignments receive a zero; missing a 
midterm or final may result in failing the course. It is your responsibility to ask about missed work and adhere to 
deadlines.
FYI (for your information):
• Please be aware that deadlines are final. If late work is accepted (due to an excused absence, for example), it will 
be penalized by daily increments.  Deadline extension must be granted by the professor prior to the due date.  
Failure to complete the midterm or final exam, and/or failure to complete assignments or tasks could result in 
failure of the course. To ensure academic integrity and facilitate plagiarism checking, students are required to 
upload their final paper to the university website by the deadline, as well as to submit peer review sheets with their 
final paper.
• Scholarly behavior is expected: arrive on time, prepared with necessary materials, and refrain from using cell 
phones or chatting during class. Points will be deducted for lack of preparation or disruptive behavior.
• All submitted work must include your name, student number, and the class name (EvH). Incomplete information or 
late homework will result in lost points. Homework must be submitted in class when collected; do not send 
assignments by email unless specifically instructed.
• Assignments of two or more pages must be stapled in the upper left corner (one staple per assignment), but do not 
staple multiple assignments together.
• Emails must be written professionally, not like text messages. Include your name, student number, and the course 
name, and use proper spelling, grammar, and salutations. Questions about the syllabus or grading should be asked 
early in the semester, not at the end of the semester.
• Failure to follow these guidelines will result in point deductions.
AI Usage:
• Students can use generative AI tools like ChatGPT to enhance their learning outcomes (for example, asking 
ChatGPT to check work for mistakes) and have positive educational experiences (for example, asking to explain 
terms or concepts from class that the student cannot understand themselves; however, if students use generative AI 
without basic guidelines (for example, creating answers to an assignment), it may negatively impact the quality 
of teaching and learning.
• Common negative impacts include: (1) violations of academic integrity, such as plagiarism and cheating; (2) 
decline in critical thinking, creative thinking, and problem-solving skills due to exercising the “other brain” and 
not your own; (3) acquisition of inaccurate or biased information; and (4) reinforcement of entrenched stereotypes.
• In short, “There is no royal road to learning” (Euclid).  If you use generative AI to do your work for you, you have 
not learned the skills you took the course to learn and so have wasted your money.
Course Outline, Learning Outcomes, and Goals:
• Outline: This course is designed to stimulate students' thinking of the world around them, as well as to provide the 
chance to employ communication skills through reading, writing, listening, and speaking.  All activities are 
provided as a means to further stimulate students' thinking and to facilitate communication. Special effort has been 
taken to establish process rather than product goals.  Also, see attached week-by-week syllabus for further details.
• Organization (before and after midterm): The first portion of this course focuses on comprehending ideas 
presented by the key author that has helped influence the discussion of key environmental and social issues of the 
latter 20th century and early 21st century (influencing such people as celebrity Leonardo DiCaprio and politician 
Bernie Sanders); the second half of the semester involves practical “hands-on” discovery for you, the student, as 
you choose your very own issue to research, to discover what the author may have missed and even how the world 
has or hasn’t changed since the author wrote his book.
• Learning Outcomes: Write an evidence-based research paper demonstrating logical reasoning and argumentative 
skills, as well as to evaluate logical reasoning and argument in assigned and researched texts.  All assignments are 
designed to guide students towards these learning outcomes by the end of the semester.
• Goals: The goals for this course include, but are not limited to, critical thinking, a willingness to explore ideas 
contrary to one's own beliefs, as well as knowing when information or data are relevant to an issue and how to find 
that information. These steps are to foster improving listening comprehension, enhancing leadership capabilities, 
summarizing and connecting ideas, building vocabulary and expressions, addressing cultural topics, and sharing 
views/ideas with others. In addition to these general concepts, the instructor also wishes to address student 
concerns for self discovery.

Grade Codes

95-100: A+, 90-94: A, 85-89: B+, 80-84: B, 75-79: C+, 70-74: C, 65-69: D+, 60-64: D, 59 and below: F

Attendance Policy
Tardies, absences:
You are permitted up to three excused absences. For each unexcused absence beyond the third, your final course grade will be 
reduced by 1 percentage point through Participation (E.g., if you earn 87%, but have eight absences (three excused and five 
unexcused absences), then your final grade will be 82%.). Being late three times constitutes one absence.

The above system of penalties follows the spirit of university policy passed down from the Ministry of Education of 1/3 absences 
(>10 absences) being an automatic “F”.
What is excused or unexcused?
Excused: Illness (with documentation), family emergencies, university-sponsored events, military test, etc.
Unexcused: Absences beyond the allowed number, or those without valid documentation.
Counseling Services
The KU Student Counseling Center offers help to students having trouble at university or with their feelings. They are very good 
at listening. They have one to one counseling, group counseling, and even some tests people can take about their lives, feelings, 
personality, relationships, and more. During the semester, they are open from Monday-Friday from 9 a.m. - 5:30 p.m (closed for 
lunch). They are located in the Central Plaza Room 114. Tel: 3290-1540~1. Website: http://kuscc.korea.ac.kr (in Korean).

이하로 증원이 불가 합니다. 
<중요공지 사항>
■Background
제품디자인의 과정은 제품기획(Product Planning), 제품디자인(Product Designing), 그리고
제품개발(Product Development)의 3개의 단계로 나눌 수 있다.  Product Planning과정은 
   신제품이나 기성제품의 혁신적인 Concept을 생성하는 Verbalization단계라고 할 수 있고, 
Product Designing과정은 제품의 가치창출을 위해 Function과 Appearance의 조화를 고려
하여 시각화하는  Visualization단계이다. 마지막으로 Product Development과정은  실제로
   제품을 제작하여 실용화하는 Vitalization단계를 통하여 제조하여 소비자에게 판매하도록 하는 
것이다. 본 수업은 디자인 입문과정으로 기능이 단순하고 소형의 기성제품 중 1개 or 2개를     
일괄적으로 선별하여 Product Designing & Styling 과정을 중심으로 제품의 외관과 Brand 
Identity를 디자인하여 표현한다.
■Product Design Studio
주요 과제로는 디자인 3대 요소인 기능성, 심미성, 경제성 중에서 심미성과 관련 제품의 외관  
(Appearance)를 중심으로 하는 Designing & Styling 과정을 진행하여 기성 제품의 형태, 색채, 
질감의 조형적 요소를 연구한다. 디자인 대상은 3S : Simple, Small, & Stylish라는 기본적인 디자인    
설정기준을 중심으로 제품의 기능보다는 형태적 요소가 중요한 소형의 기성제품( Bluetooth 
Speaker, Pensile Sharpener, Toaster, 등 )중1개 or 2개를  일괄적 선정을 하여 1인 단독과제로 
진행한다. 기존의 시장에 나와 있는 제품을 참고로 하고 형태를 전개하는 과정의3가지 방향: 
1. From follows function. (Modern Form), 2. Form follows emotion. (Emotional Form), 
3. Form follows meaning.  (Meaningful Form)을 중심으로Ideation을 하여 형태를 창출한다.
전개과정은  Sketch,  Rendering, Drafting 등의 2D Vicom(Visual Communication)과 3D Sketch
Model 및 최종 실물 모형의 3D Viscom, 그리고 마지막으로 3D Modeling 및 Digital Rendering 등
Digital Viscom을 통해 그 결과물을제시하여 Presentation 한다. 
■Studio Process
• 제품디자인 스튜디오 수업의 기초 입문 단계로 실제 제품을 디자인하여 조형적 이고 기능적 
문제 해결을 통해 디자인하여 최종 실물 모형의 결과물을 제시하는 과정.
• 특정 제품을 대상으로  기본적인 Concept의 생성에서 입체 조형적 창출을 위한 단계를 거쳐 
인간 공학과 재료 및 생산 공정까지 디자인 프로세스의 A to Z를 경험. 
• 3 단계 프로세스 : 1. 기능적 형태 (Modern)  
2. 감성적 형태(Emotion) 
3. 의미론적 형태(Semantics)
• 2D, 3D, Digital Visual Communication 기법을 이용하여 기본적 Ideation을 시작하여 
Concept을 발전하여Sketch, Rendering, Finish Model 등 으로 최종 디자인을 제시 함.

Course Objectives
You will be able to
Lay the foundation of statistical/probabilistic concepts based on
mathematical tools. It requires abstract thinking.
Apply the statistical concepts to solve real-world problems.
Topics: axioms of probability, random variables, the most important
discrete and continuous probability distributions, expectation,
moment generating functions, conditional probability and conditional
expectations, multivariate distributions, some limit theorems.

二、課程內容結構
 
第一部分：漢字的演變歷史
作為一門以漢字為核心媒介的課程，首先將系統性介紹漢字的造字原理與歷史演變脈絡。
課程內容包括「六書」理論的基礎理解、中國歷代「書同文」與文字規範化政策之整理，以
及對篆、隸、行、楷、草等主要書體的認識，並欣賞相關代表性書法家與作品。
第二部分：漢字字源、字義分析與文化溯源
本單元將生活中常見之漢字依主題劃分為「衣食篇、戰爭篇、動物篇、信仰篇、器物篇」
五大類，從漢字文化學角度分析其構字原理、字源演變與語義關聯，並結合相關詩歌、書畫
等文本與圖像資料，探討漢字所承載之文化意涵。
第三部分：漢字文化圈共同母題（Motif）的探討
漢字文化圈在長期交流過程中，逐漸形成若干共享的文化母題，例如共同體意識、蘭亭修
禊、瀟湘八景、赤壁書寫與泛舟想像等。本單元將以漢字與漢文文本為基礎，分析這些母題
本課程以中國留學生為主要授課對象，以「漢字文化學」為理論基礎，系統性理解、考察
與探討以漢字為媒介所形成之「漢字文化圈」相關歷史與文化內涵。
所謂「漢字」，係指用以記錄漢語的傳統書寫文字體系；「漢字文化圈」（韓語：한자문
화권），亦稱漢文化圈、東亞文化圈，係指歷史上曾以漢字作為主要或重要書面語工具，並
在政治制度、思想體系與文化生活層面深受其影響之文化區域。
從歷史地理的角度觀之，漢字文化圈以中國為核心，涵蓋東亞與東南亞部分地區，主要包
括中國大陸、香港、澳門、臺灣、朝鮮半島、日本、琉球群島及越南等地。此一文化圈的形
成，與前近代東亞以農耕社會為基礎、冊封體制為外交框架，以及漢字作為官方與外交書寫
語言的歷史背景密切相關。
在長期的文化交流過程中，周邊諸國在制度、思想與文化層面大量吸收並轉化自中國歷代
王朝所傳入的服飾、建築、音樂、宗教與節慶習俗，並在本土化的過程中發展出各具特色的
文化樣態，形成「共享基礎、差異並存」的漢字文化圈格局。
本課程之研究範圍，著重於以「漢字」作為文化媒介所形成的共同文化傳統，課程重心以
中國為主，並兼及韓國、日本等地。教學內容涵蓋透過漢字傳承與發展而來之飲食文化、詩
歌文化、戰爭文化、信仰文化、書畫文化與服飾文化等面向。
此外，本課程所使用文字以漢字正體字（繁體字）為主，不包含現行中國大陸部分簡化字
形，請修課同學留意並多加參照。
2026學年度第 1 學期課程內容將分為以下三個主要單元進行授課。
在不同地域與時代中的流傳、變異與再詮釋。
  
三、學習目標
 
本課程旨在使學生充分理解以漢字為媒介所形成之共同歷史文化傳統，特別掌握漢字文化
的多元性與跨地域特質。課程完成後，學生將能實際掌握約一百個生活漢字的字源與字義，
理解其構字原理與形體演變，並能結合詩歌、書畫等文化文本，分析漢字文化圈的核心母題
與文化意涵。

Ⅰ. Objectives &
     Overview
•
Understand the basic principles and theories of AI (artificial intelligence), which 
is influencing the field of physical education and sports as well as health-
related areas, and is leading future societies. Through practical data analysis 
exercises, cultivate the practical ability to apply AI in various sports fields.
•
In the field of AI, through Machine Learning (ML), including supervised and 
unsupervised learning, you will use grouping, classification, and prediction 
models. By applying these to sports information, you will enhance scientific 
capabilities in physical education and your capacity in data science.
Ⅱ. Summary
1. Explore the concept and evolution of AI, and understand its functions, ethics, 
and impact on future society.
2. Learn about the methods and effectiveness of AI application in the field of 
physical education and various sports disciplines.
3. Explore the relationship between data science and AI, and understand the 
differences between machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL).
4. Introduce programming languages and tools capable of performing ML and 
learn how to use them. 
5. Practice and learn the processes and methods of data collection, coding, and 
data preprocessing.
6. Learn about basic statistics for ML and exploratory data analysis (EDA) methods 
through practice.
7. Learn the stages (data collection, preprocessing, feature extraction, training, 
evaluation) and methods of performing ML.
8. Acquire practical analysis skills by analyzing various types of sports-related data 
using ML models of supervised learning and unsupervised learning (Decision 
tree, Random forest, K-means, Linear regression, Logistic regression, Neural 
network, etc.).

Course Objective: Carry out fundamental laboratory experiments involving classical mechanics, rotational

Major Competency based Course Objective:
 This course aims to enhance integrative thinking by connecting the theoretical classical mechanics
learned in General Physics and Exercise I with real-world applications. Through measurement and anal-
ysis in experiments, students will deepen their understanding of physical phenomena from multiple per-
spectives.
 This course aims to enhance students’ understanding of physical phenomena encountered in everyday
life, including noise cancellation, through such experiments as superposition of wave. Building on this
knowledge, the course will help students cultivate the ability to generate innovative ideas.
 This course aims to develop problem-solving skills by identifying and defining challenges that extend
beyond the manuals, analyzing these issues, and deriving solutions to successfully carry out experiments.

Course Objectives: 
 
Academic English is not a conversation class. It is a formal class to prepare you for university and life 
beyond.  
 
This course is designed to improve your speaking, listening, reading, and writing skills for academic 
applications. Speaking and writing will be the primary focus of class activities. Listening and reading skills 
will be taught during the sixteen weeks, although they will be focused on more during assignments and self-
study activities. The primary focus will be on writing, discussion and presentation. By the end of the 
sixteen weeks, I hope that you will have:  
 
● first and foremost, improved your English ability  
● the ability to discuss and present topics appropriately and professionally in English 
● learned the importance of communication and teamwork  
● become more adept in verbal, non-verbal and written communication  
● built your academic vocabulary  
● become a critical thinker and an effective independent learner  
● gained confidence in your English ability and not rely solely on AI. 
 
 
Office Hours & Communication: 
 
My aim is to help you improve as much as possible. Therefore, I welcome your queries about anything, 
small or big. Communication is fundamental in so many aspects of life, so it is better to ask than to remain 
in the dark. I am also available by appointment or via Zoom or after class time. There will be times when I 
am unable to answer your questions right away due to my schedule and other students’ inquiries; 
please understand this and make an appointment if you want to meet me via online. I will make time 
for you if you let me know in advance. 
 
My Gmail account, hawkplynn@gmail.com and KULMS will be utilized for basic communication, 
announcements and course work uploads, so it is essential that you always check KULMS and your 
email.

2. ENGLISH 
 
You must use English in class: Do not use Korean or another language. 
You must try as best as you can to communicate all of your thoughts in English.  If you 
cannot find the correct words in English, try to find some other way to express yourself 
(description, body language, face expressions, drawing pictures, etc.).  Be creative.  
 
It is a requirement of this course that you use English in this class. 
 
 
 
3. PREPAREDNESS 
 
Be prepared for class. At a minimum, bring your notebook for note taking and file folder to 
every class. You are expected to read ahead any information, course material, pages, 
etc. your professor assigns to you. Being prepared includes by evidence of study outside 
of class; accessing and reviewing KULMS’s Announcements/Course Materials; being aware 
of due dates. 
 
One thing to get you through university is being organized and prepared for each class; 
hence the GF and file folder requirement. 
 
 
4. PARTICIPATION  
 
 Participate actively in the class.  Don’t be afraid to speak in class, and don’t worry 
about making mistakes.  
 
      It is important to remember mistakes do not matter to me at all, so please do your     
      best. 
 
 Incorrect speaking is better than no speaking. Perfect English is not necessary,  
but class participation is necessary.  It is a part of your grade.  
 
 Use your level of interest and motivation to create, expand and express your ideas, 
thoughts, feelings and questions. Even if you are not confident, you will have the chance 
to do well. Overtime, your confidence in speaking up in class will improve. 
 
 Use class time wisely and be prepared for each class.  
 
 Complete assignments thoroughly in a timely manner. 
 
Do not sleep in class. This will affect negatively on your participation grade. 
 
Involve yourself in every class activity; be positive and ready to learn and participate 
including asking questions. 
 
5. ASSIGNMENTS 
 
 Complete all assignments in a timely matter. Late assignments or projects will result in 
points deducted: 1 point for each day late including the weekends and holidays.  
 
 Copying assignments, homework or cheating on tests will automatically get you an “F/0". 
See also page 6. 
 
 Do not rehash and/or submit work (old or new) from another course/class. 
 
 
 If you are absent, make sure to contact me or ask your classmates about what you 
missed.   
 
 
 
 Submitted work must include a cover page, be paginated and include subtitles when 
necessary. Do not include the course material or lecture notes with your 
assignments. 
 
 As #4, use class time wisely and be prepared for each class and complete assignments 
thoroughly in a timely manner.

6. ABSENCES   
 
Come to class every day and on time and stay in class.  
 
 
If you are going to be absent from class for any reason, I will mark you as absent for that 
class, but I allow you 4 absences in the semester without any academic penalty.  
 
 If you will be absent for a special reason, and you wish to be excused from attending class, 
you must tell me before the class.  In addition, you can apply for an excused absence 
through the Korea University portal. It will still count as an absence, so use your free 
absences wisely.  
 
 
Just because you are absent for any reason does not absolve you of your responsibility. You 
are still responsible for content missed. 
 
 
Proper documentation must be provided for all special school-related absences: illness, 
death in the family or military. NOTE: a prescription is not valid documentation. 
 
Sleeping in class. This will affect negatively on your class attendance as well as your 
participation grade.  
 
Students missing 9 classes total will automatically receive a grade of “F”. 
 
See page 6 for more information. 
 
7. GRADES   
 
Although important to you and your GPA, learning a foreign language is not only about 
grades.  It is a skill that can be life changing for your future.  Developing good English 
language skills can open opportunities for employment and future study abroad, it can help 
you connect to the world beyond the borders of your country; and it can enhance your 
understanding of other cultures.  Please view this course as an opportunity to build your 
future, and not simply as an influence on your GPA.   
 
Furthermore, in Korea, English is often used as a measure of a person’s value in society, but 
NOT in this class.  It is a useful tool just as mathematics, critical thinking or creativity.   
The grades I assign to you are not an evaluation of you personally nor reflective of my likes 
or dislikes.  It is simply an evaluation of your performance in class tasks and activities.  
 
See page 7-8 for detailed assessments. 
 
8. TIME 
 
Be in class on time.  Students who are late are disturbing for the class and for me. Enter the 
class quietly. If you are more than 15 minutes late, I will mark you absent for that class.   
 
If you are late 3 times, I will mark you absent for one class. This will NOT count as one of 
the allowed absences in #6.

Classrooms are sometimes arranged in rows. It is advisable to avoid sitting in the back since

Therefore, sit in the front or close to the front of the class. Choose a seat for a few 
weeks, so I can remember who you are including your name.  
 
Depending on the assignment, new seating arrangements maybe created.

Please use the break time BETWEEN CLASSES for getting drinks, making phone calls and 
going to the washroom.  If it is an emergency, you don’t have to ask me for permission to go

13. MANNERS MAKETH THE PERSON 
 
Show respect and courtesy to EVERYONE in the class.  Acknowledge people with a 
simple hi or hello, or good morning/afternoon or a nod. (Basic Communication)  
 
Please be respectful of your classmates and help me to provide a positive and encouraging 
learning environment.   
 
Use of offensive language will not be tolerated (English, Korean, etc.).  
 
Your enjoyment of this class and the development of your academic English skills depend on 
the attitude you bring to this class every day.  Please be positive, be polite and be kind. 
 
 
 
Speaking English isn’t only about fluency. It’s about being in class, doing the work, understanding, 
and following instructions and making an effort. 
 
 
 
 
KU’S AI POLICY 
 
 
The use of generative AI in class without basic guidelines. It may negatively impact the quality of teaching and 
learning. Common negative impacts include: 
 
(1) Violations of academic integrity, such as plagiarism and cheating. 
(2) Decline in critical thinking, creative thinking, and problem-solving skills due  
     to over-reliance on generative AI. 
(3) Acquisition of inaccurate or biased information. 
(4) Reinforcement of entrenched stereotypes.

Evaluation Method 
 
Typically, a maximum of about 40-45% of you will receive a grade of “A” or “A+”. Evaluation in this class is 
based strictly on performance, and not on English language proficiency. All parts of the evaluation system 
must be completed in an exceptional manner (above and beyond) if you want to get an “A+”.   
 
I employ rubrics where students are evaluated on organization (see below), content (see below) and 
language (see below). More criteria will be given when the projects are assigned. Many students ask for a 
word count for written assignments. My philosophy is that students should be focusing on answering the 
question and providing enough support for their answer. So concentrate on fully exploring your answer.  
This is done through research (what have others said on the topic); planning (brainstorming and outline and 
deciding on your answer), and editing (checking your work for mistakes in organization, content and 
language).

Course overview
Linear algebra is a branch of mathematics to investigate homogeneous polynomials 
of degree one, vector space and operations on it. Linear algebra plays important 
role not only in mathematics, but also in science, engineering and economics. This 
course is an introduction to the fundamentals of linear algebra.
(This class is intended for only the students in math department. So, students in 
the other departments cannot resister this class.)

If you will successfully complete the course, you would understand very well of the 
following topics:
1) a system of linear equations
2) matrix operations
3) vector space
4) determinants

구에 정진

◆ Course Plan Details ◆ 
▷ Course Outline 
Overview 
The design of the course will consist of three blocks:  
1) Introduction to the EU: basic concepts, institutions, and indicators 
of the EU and Euro Area.   
2) Understanding the EU Policies: single market, EMU, labour and 
migration, climate and industrial policy. 
3) Current issues in the European economy: Brexit, China, COVID-19, 
the Russo-Ukrainian war, energy crisis, and shifts in the global order.  
Who Should Take 
This Course 
This is an introductory undergraduate course in European Economy, 
suitable for students from economics, political science, international

background in EU studies.  
Prerequisites 
(Recommended) 
No formal prerequisites required. Familiarity with basic economic 
concepts (such as supply and demand, inflation, and GDP) is helpful 
but not required.  
Class Rules 
Students are expected to respect deadlines, and follow university rules 
on academic integrity. 
Changes and 
improvements 
The course will integrate up-to-date EU developments, regularly 
incorporating recent policy documents, data, and news so that 
theoretical discussions are linked to ongoing debates in the European 
economy.  
 
▷ Objectives  
Objectives  
General 
This course is to enable students to explain the structure and 
evolution of the European economy, interpret major EU economic 
policies using basic theoretical tools, and critically assess 
contemporary European economic issues from an informed, 
evidence-based perspective.  
Detailed 
Objective 1 
[Understand EU institutions and integration stages]  
Students will be able to describe the main EU and Euro Area 
institutions, distinguish the stages of economic integration, and 
discuss why and how European integration has proceeded over time. 
Detailed 
Objective 2 
[Apply economic theories to EU policies]  
Students will be able to apply introductory macroeconomic, trade, and 
integration theories to interpret key EU policy domains such as EMU, 
the single market, competition policy, labour mobility, and 
climate/industrial strategies.  
Detailed 
Objective 3 
[Analyze current European economic issues]  
Students will be able to use the conceptual tools from the course to 
analyze selected current issues—such as Brexit, irregular migration, 
relations with China and the US, the COVID-19 shock, and the 
Russo-Ukrainian war and energy crisis—and articulate coherent 
arguments about policy options and their likely economic implications.

Course Objectives: 
 
This course explores a range of thought-provoking topics, including how discussions function, why people 
persuade, and what makes arguments effective across areas such as technology, science, art, education, 
and society. Students will engage with these themes through critical analysis, discussion, and reflection, 
strengthening their communication and critical-thinking skills while expanding their understanding of global 
issues. Through interactive activities and assignments, students will deepen their understanding of key 
ideas and learn how to apply these concepts to their own lives and academic goals. 
By the end of the sixteen-week course, students will have: 
 
 
developed stronger critical-thinking skills 
 
understood the purpose and structure of round-table discussions and demonstrate the ability to 
participate professionally 
 
recognized the importance of communication and collaborative teamwork 
 
improved verbal and non-verbal communication skills 
 
expanded academic vocabulary related to discussions and dialogue

DISS319: Special Topics in International Finance  
Division of International Studies (DIS), Korea University 
Spring 2026 
 
Instructor: Hyungseok Joo 
Time and Location: Tuesday& Thursday, 13:30 to 14:45 (218 International Studies Hall)  
Contact: hsjoo214@korea.ac.kr 
Office Hours: 15:00 to 17:00 on Tuesday (525 International Studies Hall) or appointment  
 
Overview and Objectives 
DISS319 is an advanced undergraduate course in international economics for students 
who have previously studied introductory macroeconomics and/or international finance. 
The course has two main aims: First, build a solid theoretical foundation in 
international macroeconomics and finance, with an emphasis on intertemporal (dynamic) 
decision-making and micro-founded models. Second, connect theory to practice by 
examining current policy issues and using the models introduced in the first part of the 
course to interpret real-world events and debates.  
The course begins with current account, real exchange rate, and exchange rate 
policy with dynamic optimization as the core analytical framework for modern 
international macroeconomics and finance. Building on this framework, we cover three 
broad topic areas. First, we will cover international financial crises: currency crises, 
banking crises, and sovereign debt crises. Second, we will investigate geoeconomics 
and international monetary system. Lastly, we will spend time on international 
capital flow including foreign direct investment.  
By the end of the course, students should be able to use formal economic models to 
analyze international macro-financial problems, evaluate policy trade-offs, and interpret 
contemporary developments in the global economy. 
Prerequisites 
A solid understanding of basic macroeconomics and international finance is required. 
Prerequisites for this course are Introduction to Economics (DISS115) and some 
intermediate level macroeconomics and international finance. It will be helpful to 
have prior knowledge from Korea Economy in a Globalized World (DISS210), 
International Finance: Theory and Practice (DISS311) and International Financial 
Markets and Institutions (DISS357). 
The structure of knowledge in economics is strongly hierarchic in that each successive 
lecture tends to build on prior material in a systematic fashion. As such it is very easy to 
fall behind if you don’t pay attention to lectures and do not study the missed material 
before the subsequent lecture.  
Grading 
Course grades will be based on a midterm test (40%), a final exam (40%), a presentation 
(10%), homework (5%), attendance (5%). The problem sets are designed to help you 
understand the course material. Moreover, reading articles are required and will be asked 
during classes.  
Basic Material 
The main material for the class is a set of lecture notes/slides that I will post on website. 
The following book is closely related to many topics that we will cover, and are highly 
recommended: 
• “International Macroeconomics “ by Stephanie Schmitt-Grohe, Martin 
Uribe, and Michael Woodford (SGUW)  
• “This Time is Different” by Carmen M. Reinhart and Kenneth S. Rogoff

Course Description 
 
This course aims to facilitate students’ understanding of South Korean society as a dynamic 
and global site. We start from viewpoints about knowledge production, incorporating 
concepts of decolonization; common historical experiences that have shaped Korea, 
including the Korean War, rapid period of development, Asian Financial Crisis, and 
globalization; and explore key themes that shape South Korean society such as class, 
gender, labour, family, and generation. Students will be asked to explore key texts and 
develop the ability to approach issues in Korean Studies critically. 
 
Assessment criteria include two open-book exams, short writing assignments and class 
participation throughout the semester. Students are required to do up to two readings each 
week and are recommended to watch a media piece.

their home universities is required as a prerequisite. It can include a Korean 
language class. If you’re not sure, please email (yisohoon@korea.ac.kr).

5. Attendance (10%): Students should attend all classes on time and ensure their

Class Rules 
 
1. Attendance 
 
As per university rules, if you are absent for more than 1/3 of total class time (that is, eight 
classes excluding exam weeks), you will automatically receive an F. If you need to be absent 
for legitimate reasons such as medical illness, you need to submit a medical certificate for it 
not to count as absent. If you come to class late after the attendance is taken, it is your 
responsibility to confirm with the professor that your attendance is marked. 
 
If you have attendance-related concerns and questions, please contact the TA at 
mjchu@korea.ac.kr 
 
2. Readings and class preparations 
 
You are expected to come to class after completing the readings each week. You are 
expected to spend 3-6 hours each week in preparation for class. The examinations will test 
your comprehension of all class materials, and students who demonstrate insightful and 
critical understandings of readings will be graded favourably. Media pieces are meant to be 
supplementary, and you are welcome to watch them to further your knowledge. 
 
3. Academic Accommodations for students with difficulties 
 
Korea University’s Center for Students with Disabilities offers support for students and I will 
make accommodations for such students as per university policies. If you have learning 
disabilities, psychological/mental conditions, or unforeseen and exceptional personal 
difficulties, please talk to me about how I can support your learning experience. 
 
4. Use of digital devices 
 
I do not allow typing in the lecture room. You are encouraged to take notes by hand or just 
listen as the lecture slides are uploaded on Blackboard. There are some exceptions, which 
include students taking notes with digital pens on their tablets and students with learning 
conditions requiring digital devices (in which case, students need to consult with me at the 
beginning of the course). Class activities may involve online participation, which you can do 
on your mobile phones or tablets. 
 
 5. Academic Integrity Use of Generative AI Tools 
 
This course allows for transparent, limited use of AI tools that do not compromise students’ 
ethics or academic capacity.  
 
You may notice that the assignment is graded on a complete/incomplete basis and there is 
no reason for you to ask a Gen AI tool to “write” the question/response paragraph for you so 
that your writing appears “polished” and “better”. It is perfectly ok for your question/response 
paragraphs, exit tickets, and other discussion writings to be rough, work/thought-in-
progress, and incomplete. In fact, the assignment in this course trains you to ask mindful 
and insightful questions, an essential skill for the efficient use of AI tools today and, 
predictably, in the future. Research on the educational impact of Gen AI tools is ongoing, 
but much of it has found harmful effects when students habitually outsource their thinking to 
an AI tool. Please be mindful that the ability to think requires repeated training, and your 
reliance on an AI tool to do the thinking for you means you forgo the opportunity to train 
during your valuable university years. Remember, true learning is active.  
 
Tools for detecting generative AI use are not perfect, and I will not use them to grade 
assignments or exit tickets. I generally value honor and trust as foundational to learning. 
However, I (and many other professors) have years of experience teaching and grading 
students and a “database” from such experiences. If you use an AI tool, I will likely know. 
 
Copying, plagiarizing, falsifying medical certificates, or other forms of academic misconduct 
will not be tolerated. Any student who abets or otherwise assists in such misconduct will 
also be subject to academic penalties.  
 
Students are expected to cite sources in all written work. If you have used an AI tool, please 
disclose how you have used it.

Disabilities may be required. Note that these documents are not automatically forwarded from the Center, so 
you must notify me directly.  Late penalties will apply to all assignments unless specific 
accommodations/extensions have been discussed and arranged with me in advance of the deadline (barring 
medical emergencies). If your condition involves difficulties getting started on tasks (e.g., some cases of 
ADHD), please see me early for support so that we can strategize together on task completion. For more 
information on support at KU for students with disabilities, please see: 
https://gsc.korea.ac.kr/usr/service/support_center.do 
 
Assessments 
      
Midterm: Problem/Solution Essay: 42%  (15% Draft 1; 25%, Referenced Essay;  2%, Typed) You will 
describe a problem and propose a solution in an in-class APA 7th edition essay about a topic related to 
Informatics. Closed book, paper-and-pencil.  
 
Elevator Pitch (10%) You will practice speechwriting and delivery by pitching your solution in a 90-second 
pitch.  
 
Workshop- Presentation + Discussion (30%) You will deliver a how-to presentation and handle Q and A. 
Then, you’ll lead your table of classmates in an engaging discussion on your topic.  
 
APA 7th Edition Quizzes (10%) You will complete a series of very short in-class closed-book quizzes on 
citing sources and the use of APA 7th edition.  
 
Assorted Weekly Tasks and Participation (8%) 
You will demonstrate learning and share your amazing insights through discussion board posts, uploads, 
classroom activities, and other small tasks, as well as through on-time attendance. You will complete work 
by the deadlines, bring your materials to every class, speak in English during class time, and volunteer 
answers without being called on. Participation and the completion of optional tasks (e.g., worksheets, 
learning journal) may make a difference to your final grade. For example, if your final grade is very close to 
the line between an A and an A+, stellar attendance, class participation, and the completion of optional 
worksheets might be able to lift the grade slightly.  
 
For small homework tasks (unless specified otherwise): 3 points = on time, complete, instructions followed, effort 
demonstrated, 2 points = late same day or incomplete, but there’s still effort, 1 point = handed in the next class, 0 
points = not completed within the time frame.  
      
Attendance: Up to four (4) absences are allowed without them affecting your final score (excused or 
unexcused absences.) No note is required for these; however, an email to me is always appreciated if 
you know you will be absent.  
3 
 
 
 
Attendance Grade Deductions: Starting from five (5) absences, 1.5% will be deducted from your total 
final grade for each absence. At eight (8) absences, the grade for the class will be an F (fail).  
 
3 minutes to 19 minutes late = late:  3 lates = 1 absence 
20 minutes+ late = 1 absence 
 
Graded Tasks: Please note that if a graded task occurs in class on the day you are absent, you will not 
be able to make up the points for that task. Please notify me in advance if you have a class in a building 
far away before this one and will be late regularly.  
 
Just as professionals are expected to show up for work, students are expected to come to class 
consistently and on time. While ultimately engagement is crucial, there is also a strong positive 
correlation between class attendance and learning achievement (Lam et al., 2025). At the same time, 
however, learners who are physically present in a classroom but mentally elsewhere are not 
maximizing their learning time. It is hoped that if you are in the classroom, it is because you are there 
to learn.  
 
     Submitting Official Absence Documentation 
At KU, students are generally excused from classes only for the following official reasons: military 
service, family bereavement, hospitalization and/or medical emergency,  or required academic events 
related to their major, including education majors’ practica. If you prefer to have recognition for an 
excused absence, you must submit official documentation through the required process in KUPID’s 
출석인정신청 system and also email me. I will then go into the KUPID system to confirm the absence. 
However, in most cases, the grade deductions starting from five (5) absences or more will still apply, 
except in the case of students receiving special dispensation for early-start military service or an 
education practicum.  
 
Mandatory Attendance Days: If you are late or absent on the days of quizzes, Essay Draft 1, Referenced 
Essay, Elevator Pitch, or your own Student-led Discussion, you will be permitted to make up the tasks if 
there was an immediate medical emergency.  You will not be allowed to make up these assignments 
unless you both 1) contact me immediately and 2) provide official documentation signed by a doctor 
(의사소견서 or 의사진단서, not 진료확인서) that there was a genuine medical emergency requiring 
urgent hospital treatment.

Purpose of Academic English 
 
1 - To prepare students for taking English mediated courses (EMC) in their major. 
2 - To prepare students to be part of the global community of academia. 
3 - To prepare students for studying abroad in an international-language  
       environment. 
4 - To prepare students to thrive (survive) in a foreign language environment 
5 - To prepare students to be independent learners and thinkers. 
 
 
 
 
 
Academic English focuses on developing students’ academic skills in 
critical thinking, argumentation, academic writing, academic 
discussion and presentation (all in English).  
 
These crucial skills are transferable to any course, any major,  
any language or taught in any country.

Typically, a maximum of about 40-50% of you will receive a grade of “A” or “A+”. Evaluation in 
this class is based strictly on performance, and not on English language proficiency. All parts of 
the evaluation system must be completed in an exceptional manner if you want to get an “A+”.   
 
 
Need Help? 
Getting adjusted to university life can sometimes be tough, dramatic even traumatic, especially 
during a pandemic.  Help is available, however.  The KU Student Counseling Center offers 
help to students having trouble at university or with their feelings. They are very good at 
listening. They have one to one counseling, group counseling, and even some tests people can 
take about their lives, feelings, personality, relationships, and more. During the semester, they 
are open from Monday-Friday from 9 a.m. – 5:30 p.m. (closed for lunch). They are located in 
the 과학도서관 307 호. Tel: 3290-4581~4582. Website: http://kuscc.korea.ac.kr (in Korean). 
 
 
 
 
3 
 
Class Expectations (Please READ CAREFULLY!) 
 
This class is not like your other classes.  It is NOT a lecture class, so you must be 
active instead of passive in this class.  The following are some guidelines for 
conduct that I expect in this class.  Following these expectations will assist in 
enhancing your academic skills as well as improving chances of a good grade.  
 
 
1. 
 
Ask me questions:  This course is about communication, and it is extremely 
important for us to understand each other.  Feel free to ask me at any time to 
repeat or explain something if you do not understand. I am also available in my 
office, Rm 711, by appointment or during my office hours. Please remember that  
it is your responsibility to tell me if there is something you do not 
understand or need help with. 
 
 
2. 
 
You must use English in class: You must try as best as you can to 
communicate all of your thoughts in English.  If you cannot find the correct words 
in English, try to find some other way to express yourself (body language, face 
expressions, drawing pictures, etc.).  Be creative! It is a requirement of this 
course that you use English in this class. 
 
 
3. 
 
Participate actively in the class!  Do not be afraid to speak in class, and do not 
worry about making mistakes.  Incorrect speaking is better than no speaking.  
Perfect English is not necessary, but class participation is necessary.  It is a 
part of your grade! 
 
 
4. 
 
Assignments and projects!  Any assignment or project not ready by the 
assigned deadline will receive a grade of “0”.  If you are absent, make sure to ask 
your classmates or contact me about what you missed.  Copying homework 
(plagiarism) will automatically get you an "0". Any assignments fully created 
with generative A.I. (like ChatGPT) will receive a grade of “0”. 
 
 
5. 
 
Grades!  Although important to you and your GPA, improving your skills in a 
foreign language is not only about grades.  It is a skill that can be life changing for 
your future.  Developing good English language skills can open opportunities for 
employment and future study abroad, it can help you connect to the world beyond 
the borders of your country, and it can enhance your understanding of other 
cultures.  Please view this course as an opportunity to build your future, and 
not simply as an influence on your GPA.  Furthermore, in Korea, English is 
often used as a measure of a person’s value in society, but NOT in this class!   
The grades I assign to you are not an evaluation of you personally nor 
reflective of my likes or dislikes.  It is simply an evaluation of your performance in 
class tasks and activities. 
 
 
6. 
 
Absences!  If you are going to be absent from class for any reason, I will mark 
you as absent for that class, but I allow you 3 absences in the semester 
without any academic penalty.  You can notify me about an absence through the 
Korea University portal, but it will still count as an absence, so use your free 
absences wisely.   
 
- Students missing more than 6 classes will receive a grade of “F”. 
 
 
 
4 
 
 
7. 
 
Be in class on time!  Students who are late are disturbing for the class and for 
me. If you are more than 10 minutes late, I will mark you absent for that class.  If 
you are late 3 times, I will mark you absent for one class.   
- This will NOT count as one of the allowed absences in #6. 
 
 
8. 
 
No distracted sessions!  The use of mobile telephones for communication 
purposes is not allowed in this class.  It is disruptive and rude to other participants.  
Use of cell phones for communicative purposes (including Kakao Talk) will

Course Description
This course, Behavioral Finance, explores the intersection between finance and psychology. It
examines how cognitive biases, emotions, and social factors affect financial decision making.
Topics include heuristic-driven biases, prospect theory, market anomalies, and the implications
of behavioral finance findings for public policy and personal investing. The primary aim of the
course is to get you thinking about or working on projects related to behavioral finance, using
theory and archival/experimental data.

▷ 강의개요
개 요
건축이 발생하는 순간
  
건축은 눈앞에 보이는 구조물이기 이전에, **인간의 관계, 언어, 정
치, 윤리, 기억이 교차하는 실존적 사건**이다. 벽과 지붕을 세우는 
기술이 중요하지만, 그것만으로 건축을 전부 설명하긴 어렵다. 건축
은 인간이 공간 속에서 어떻게 살아가고 관계 맺으며, 의미를 구성
해왔는지를 보여주는 실천적 기록이다.
  
이 강의는 건축을 이러한 관점에서 접근한다. 즉, 건축을 ‘짓는 행위’
로 보기보다, ‘사회적 의미를 공간과 물질로 번역하는 과정’으로 전제
한다. 따라서 건축은 도시를 형성하는 물리적 단위이자, 사회적 질서
를 구조화하는 언어적 기획이며, 시대정신을 담는 실존적 실천이다.
이런 관점에서, 건축가는 단순한 설계 기술자가 아닌, 세계를 해석하
고 재구성하는 기획자여야 한다. 무엇을, 왜, 어떻게 지을 것인가는 
정치적·윤리적 판단의 결과이며, 그 판단이 건축의 시작이 된다. 이 
강의는 건축을 처음 접하는 학생들과 함께, 이러한 출발점들을 사유
하고 의심하는 학문적 여정을 시작한다.
  
강의 구성 및 방법
건축학개론은 다음 세 개의 사유적 층위를 따라 구성된다.
  
첫째, 건축을 언어적 실천이자 사회적 구성물로 이해할 수 있는 이
론적 탐색을 수행한다. 이는 건축을 시각적 형태로 환원하는 대신, 
그 안에 내재한 사회적 코드와 윤리적 함의를 읽어내는 훈련을 통해 
이루어진다.
  
둘째, 설계의 개념적 구조와 건축에 작동하는 기하학을 해석하는 방
법론적 감각을 기른다. 건축의 판단 기준은 미감과 영감이 아니라, 
사회적 의미와 개념의 구상에 있으며, 이러한 의미와 개념이 어떻게 
기하학을 통해 구성되는지를 학습한다.

교육 방식 및 기대 결과
  
이 강의는 건축을 처음 접하는 학생들이 시각적 이해와 개념적 구상
을 통합할 수 있도록 설계되었다. 강의와 과제는 영상과 다양한 매
체, 현장 답사, 문화적 기호 해석 등을 포함한 비판적 독해 방식을 
적극 활용한다. 
  
건축학개론은 건물을 설계하는 기술자를 양성하는 것이 아니라, 세
계를 해석하고 재구성하는 사고자이자 기획자로서의 건축가를 준비
하는 과정이다. 이렇게 각자의 언어와 시각을 갖추게 된 학생들은, 
건축이라는 사유이자 실천의 세계에 첫발을 내딛게 될 것이다.

강의 개요 및 목적 
우리는 일상적으로 미디어를 통해 세상을 인식하고 사회적 관계를 형성하며 다양

어서 다양한 미디어에 지속적으로 둘러싸여 일상을 살아가는 미디어 환경은 우리

하는 기술적 도구가 아니라 우리의 사고와 행동을 매개하는 핵심적인 환경으로 
작동하고 있습니다.  
미디어를 이해한다는 것은 개별 기술이나 콘텐츠의 특성을 파악하는데 그치는 것
이 아니라 다양한 미디어가 어떤 방식으로 현실을 구성하고 의미를 생산하는지를 
비판적으로 살펴보는 과정입니다. 또한 우리가 속한 사회를 해석하고 그 속에서 
자신의 시각을 만들어가는 핵심 역량을 기르는 과정이라고 할 수 있습니다.  
이 수업에서는 미디어의 발달 과정과 주요 이론, 그리고 현대 사회에서 미디어가 
수행하는 역할을 폭넓게 다룹니다. 특히 일상적인 미디어 경험과 현상을 사회적, 
문화적 맥락 속에서 이해하는 사고의 틀을 제공하는 것을 목표로 합니다.  
 
수업 교재 
강의 자료가 매주 KU LMS에 업로드 됩니다. 또한 주요한 공지 사항이 이메일을 
통해 공지될 수 있으니 자주 사용하는 이메일 주소를 등록해 주시길 바랍니다.  
 
 
성적 평가 비율 및 평가 방법 
출석 (20%): 불가피한 개인 사정으로 결석할 수 있는 상황을 고려하여 한 학기 
동안 최대 3회까지 결석이 허용됩니다. 3회의 결석에는 병가, 생리 공결, 개인 사
유 등 결석 사유와 관계없이 모두 포함됩니다. 4회차 결석부터는 1회당 출석 점수
에서 2점씩 감점됩니다. 하지만 학교 규정에 따라 전체 수업 시간의 30% 이상 
(총 9회 이상) 결석 시 사유와 관계 없이 F학점이 자동적으로 부여되며 예외는 
인정되지 않습니다.  
참여 (20%): 매 수업마다 소그룹 활동에서 논의한 내용, 수업 중 제기된 질문, 수
업 내용에 대한 코멘트 등을 바탕으로 한 내용을 수업 당일 저녁 6시까지 짧게 
작성해 제출합니다 (130~150 단어). 참여가 확인될 경우 수업 당 최대 2점의 참
여 점수가 부여됩니다. 공휴일, 중간고사 기간, 기말고사 기간을 제외한 총 25회
의 수업 (3/9일 시작 기준)에 대해 시행됩니다. 출석에 대해 최대 3회 결석은 허
용 되나, 참여 점수 채점 기준이 엄격하게 적용되므로 이점을 충분히 숙지하시기 
바랍니다. 사고, 장례, 예비군 훈련 등 특별한 사유가 있는 경우에는 증빙서류 제
출 시 해당 수업의 참여 점수가 인정될 수 있습니다. 
시험 (중간고사 20% + 기말고사 20%): 중간고사와 기말고사는 수업 및 제공된 
수업 자료에서 다룬 내용을 중심으로 출제됩니다. 시험 유형은 객관식 및 단답형 
주관식으로 구성됩니다. 
기말 과제 (발표 10% + 보고서 10%): 기말 과제는 현재의 미디어 이슈 또는 사
례를 선정해 수업에서 다룬 이론과 연계해 분석하는 과제입니다. 학생은 수업 중 
발표와 최종 보고서 제출을 모두 완료해야 합니다. 기말 과제는 정해진 제출 기
한을 준수해야 하며 제출 기한을 초과한 경우 어떠한 사유로도 점수가 부여되지 
않습니다. 
 
장애 학생에 대한 지원 
이 강의는 수강생 개개인의 특성과 요구에 따라 필요한 지원이 제공될 수 있습니
다. 지원이 필요한 경우 미리 알려주시기 바랍니다.   
 
 
수업 녹음 및 촬영 
수업 중 영상∙사진 촬영 및 녹음은 허용되지 않습니다.  
 
부정행위 및 학업적 정직성 정책 
이 강의에서는 다음과 같은 행위를 부정행위 및 학업적 정직성 위반으로 간주합
니다.  
1. 시험/과제 지침 위반: 강의자의 지침을 어기거나 허가되지 않은 자료, 도구, 도
움 등을  이용하여 시험 또는 과제를 수행하는 경우 
2. 표절: 타인의 글, 아이디어, 작업을 출처 없이 그대로 사용하거나 약간의 수정 
후 자신의 것처럼 제출하는 경우 
3. 조작: 자료, 데이터, 인용 등을 임의로 조작하거나 거짓으로 작성하는 경우 
4. 부정행위 공모: 다른 학생의 부정행위를 돕거나, 도움을 받는 행위 
5. 중복 제출: 동일한 학업 작업을 같은 수업이나 다른 수업에서 허가 없이 두 번 
이상 제출하는 경우 
이와 같은 부정행위 또는 기타 부정직한 행동이 확인될 경우 해당 과제 또는 평
가에서 F학점 처리될 수 있습니다.

Spring 2026 | ENGL123(06)  
English Reading & Discussion I  
Mon/Wed 12:00-13:15 p.m. |   SK Future Hall 312 
 
Instructor: Gayeong Jung, Ph.D.  
E-mail: yeong1203@korea.ac.kr  
Office hours: By appointment only 
 
Course Description 
This course is a student-centered English reading and discussion course designed to help 
students critically engage with contemporary social issues through structured discussion. These 
reading materials will support the development of critical thinking, the construction of text-
based arguments, the personalization of ideas, and the expansion of perspectives. Students will 
participate in both group and class discussions by sharing ideas openly, listening actively, and 
respecting diverse perspectives. The course fosters a supportive environment and provides 
guidance for text-based discussion, encouraging active participation in class activities to 
improve general language skills.  
 
 
Course Objectives 
By the end of the semester, students are expected to: 
1. Analyze texts and infer intended meanings; 
2. Develop critical reading skills on various social issues; 
3. Express ideas logically and effectively by understanding key concepts related to the 
topics; 
4. Actively participate in discussions in a collaborative manner; 
5. Respect diverse perspectives and broaden viewpoints by sharing ideas openly and 
listening attentively.

Course materials will be uploaded to LMS.

Course Requirements 
1. Attendance: Class attendance is essential. One absence for any reason, including illness, job 
interviews, club activities, or conferences, will not affect your grades (except for teaching 
practicum and reservist training). However, after one absence, each absence will subtract two 
points from your final grade. Thus, “free” absence is recommended to be saved for unavoidable 
emergencies. Two late arrivals (within 15 minutes) will be counted as one absence. Being late 
for more than thirty minutes will be counted as one absence. In case of absence, it is your 
responsibility to identify any missed class information. Students who miss more than one-third 
of the course (including allowed absences) will receive an F according to university regulations, 
regardless of their performance. Students with more than four absences will not receive a grade 
higher than a B+, given the importance of attendance in this course. 
 
2. Participation & Class Preparation: Students are required to read the assigned readings, 
when necessary, and to prepare for class discussions. They are expected to engage actively in all 
class and group discussions and to make meaningful contributions to in-class activities. This 
course does not evaluate students’ discussion or debate skills per se. The primary expectations 
are that students come prepared for each session, articulate their ideas openly with peers without 
concern for judgment, and achieve the specific learning objectives designated for each lecture.   
 
3. Assignments: Students are required to complete assignments related to topics discussed in 
class. All assignments will be announced through the LMS, and students are expected to check it 
regularly and submit them by the designated due dates. 
 
4. Group presentation: In the group project, students will have the opportunity to deepen their 
understanding of a topic and explore various perspectives. Each group will select a presentation 
topic of interest. Group members are responsible for identifying relevant readings (e.g., books, 
articles, newspapers, and magazines), sharing their findings from those readings, and raising 
questions based on a thorough understanding of the topic in order to lead an active discussion. 
Presenters are expected to facilitate the class discussions during their session. All presentation 
materials must be uploaded to the LMS by the day before the presentation. Additional details 
regarding the group project will be provided during class. 
All group members must cooperate and collaborate throughout the preparation and delivery of 
the presentation. A brief peer evaluation will be conducted after the presentation via an online 
survey to assess individual contributions. 
 
 
5. Academic Integrity & Classroom Decorum: Please note that making any audio, video, or 
photo recordings of the class, the instructor, or other students is not permitted. Cheating and 
plagiarism will result in severe penalties, including possible F grades. In class, it is expected that 
you exhibit good manners.

Overview 
This studio marks a critical transition, advancing beyond the first-year 
curriculum of abstract geometric exercises and residential design 
toward the physical embodiment of architecture. The design project 
Korea University Syllabus

for this semester focuses on a small gallery space incorporating both 
natural daylight and artificial lighting. Through this program, students 
will explore how architectural form is generated via 'Tectonic Logic'—
the organic integration of structure, materials, and environmental 
conditions. Emphasis is placed on understanding the building not 
merely as a sculptural object, but as a 'Tangible Entity' that actively 
interacts with its context and accommodates human activity.

foundation of the curriculum for the Department of Architecture at

▷ Objectives  
Objectives  
General 
Transition from Abstract Form to Tectonic Reality 
This course aims to move beyond conceptual exercises to grasp the 
material reality of the built environment. Students will cultivate the 
ability to perceive and design architectural form not as a mere visual 
composition, but as a comprehensive synthesis of structural principles, 
material properties, and environmental response. 
Detailed 
Objective 1 
Geometric Order and Materialization 
 Defining Space: Students will study geometric order and spatial 
definition, translating these concepts into physical components 
(walls, columns, slabs) rather than abstract lines and planes. 
 Atmospheric Quality: Students will cultivate form-finding skills, 
evolving them into experiential spaces shaped by tangible 
elements such as light and openings. 
Detailed 
Objective 2 
Contextual Analysis and Programmatic Strategy 
 Environmental Context: Students will conduct quantitative and 
qualitative analysis of environmental factors to drive evidence-
based design decisions. 
 Spatial Organization: Students will analyze specific program 
requirements (e.g., Small Exhibition Space) to define effective 
circulation paths and spatial hierarchy. 
Detailed 
Objective 3 
Integrated Communication and Representation 
 Professional Clarity: To develop the ability to articulate design 
intentions visually and verbally with professional clarity. 
 Persuasive Representation: To train in methods that convincingly 
depict the project as an inhabitable environment, utilizing precise 
architectural drawings and scale models.

Course 
Outline
his studio focuses on the urban conditions of Dongja-dong, an inner-city neighborhood adjacent to Seoul 
Station that concentrates some of Seoul’s most critical housing challenges. Despite its central location, 
the area is characterized by aging building stock, vulnerable residents, and repeated redevelopment 
conflicts driven by displacement-oriented approaches. The studio begins by understanding these 
site-specific conditions as a foundation for architectural inquiry.
Conventional demolition-and-rebuild models are critically examined for their long construction periods, 
heavy on-site disruption, and reliance on large-scale relocation. In response, the studio introduces 
modular housing as an alternative architectural and urban strategy, emphasizing its capacity for fast and 
precise construction. Factory-based production and on-site assembly are explored as means to reduce 
uncertainty, minimize disruption, and enable development within dense and sensitive urban contexts.
The core objective of the studio is to align modular housing solutions with the given site conditions of 
Dongja-dong. Students are asked to develop housing systems that respond to existing social, spatial, 
and infrastructural constraints while maintaining the continuity of everyday life for current residents. 
Particular emphasis is placed on affordability, constructability, and the adaptability of modular systems.
Through the use of phasing strategies, the studio aims to propose a clear direction for incremental 
development on the given site. Students will articulate how modular housing can be deployed step by 
step, allowing gradual relocation, partial construction, and long-term transformation without total 
displacement. The studio ultimately positions modular housing not only as a building method, but as a 
process-driven framework for socially sustainable urban regeneration.
Class 
Objective
This studio aims to train students to address complex inner-city housing issues through modular 
housing design that integrates social responsibility, technical precision, and urban strategy. Focusing on 
Dongja-dong near Seoul Station, students will learn to apply the speed, accuracy, and cost efficiency of 
modular construction to site-specific conditions, while developing phased development strategies that 
allow incremental growth and minimize displacement. The course ultimately positions modular housing 
not only as a building system, but as a process-driven architectural approach for socially sustainable 
urban regeneration.

No grade may be assigned for absences of 1/3 or more of the class days,

Overview
This course explores the historical development of Korean popular music and 
Hallyu culture, from the early formation of modern Korean popular music to the 
global rise of K㎼pop. It examines how Korean popular music, television dramas, 
and films have evolved in relation to social, cultural, and media changes in 
Korea, and how these cultural forms collectively contributed to the emergence 
of the Korean Wave ㏖Hallyu㏗.
Through case studies of major artists, cultural texts, and media platforms, 
students will analyze the characteristics of K㎼pop as well as key Hallyu content 
such as K㎼dramas and Korean films, focusing on their production systems and 
global circulation. The course aims to provide international students with a 
comprehensive understanding of Korean popular culture as both a cultural 
expression and a global phenomenon.
Who Should Take 
This Course
㎼Students who want to build general cultural literacy about Korean popular 
music
㎼Students who aim to pursue a career in the K㎼pop / popular music industry

Yeonghyeon Choi, SunGyu Kim (kucose215@gmail.com)
Course description:
The theory of computation deals with questions such as what problems
can be solved by algorithms, how efficiently they can be solved, and
which limitations exist in the computational process. The topics include
formal languages, automata theory and computability. The theory of
computation has important applications in the design of algorithms,
programming languages, artificial intelligence, and computer security.
Text:
An Introduction to Formal Languages and Automata, 7th Edition,
Peter Linz, 2022.
Course schedule:
1. Introduction
2. Finite Automata
3. Regular Languages and Regular Grammars
4. Properties of Regular Languages
5. Context-Free Languages
6. Simplification of Context-Free Grammars
7. Pushdown Automata
8. Midterm
9. Properties of Context-Free Languages
10. Turing Machines
11. Other Models of Turing Machines
12. A Hierarchy of Formal Languages and Automata
13. Limits of Algorithmic Computation
14. Other Models of Computation
15. Computational Complexity
16. Final exam
Homeworks and Course Requirements:
Homeworks and one programming assignment will be given at the class.
English is the official language of this course. Reports and exams also
need to be written in English.
Grading:
Midterm 30%, Final 30%, H/W 30%, Others 10%
Others include quizzes, attendance, and class participation. Late work is
penalized 10% for one day, 20% for one week. No further submission will
be accepted. Copycats will get 0 point. Any form of cheating is prohibited.

개요
이 수업에서는 인류 역사의 다양한 지적 성찰 및 실천적 가치를 종합적으
로 탐구하고, 이를 바탕으로 현재의 사회를 이해하고 미래의 변화에 대응
할 수 있는 토의·토론의 장을 마련한다. 개별 전공들 간의 장벽을 넘어 비
판적·융합적·창의적 사고 능력을 함양하고, 나아가 새롭고 다양한 관점에서 
문제의식을 생성하며 타인과의 소통 및 협력을 통해 문제를 해결할 수 있
도록 하는 것이 이 교과의 목표이다. 이를 위해 플립트 클래스(Flipped 
Class) 기반의 학습자 중심 교수학습 방법을 도입하여, 질문 중심 학습
(QBL: Question Based Learning)과 토론 및 발표를 통해 학습자가 배
움의 주체가 될 수 있도록 한다.

l 연락처 : Tel. 02) 3290-2284 /Email: sangchoi@korea.ac.kr 
1. 수업개요
인사행정(public personnel administration)은 정부조직에 필요한 인적자원을 획득하고 관
리하는 기능이다. 그동안 인사행정은 사람이 중요하다는 인식하에 사람을 어떻게 확보하고 
활용하느냐에 많은 초점을 기울여 왔다. 그러나, 사람은 조직을 운영하는 핵심적인 동력이
며 조직의 목표와 성과를 실현하는 중요한 자원이기 때문에, 인사와 조직, 더 나아가 재무
까지 확장된 통섭적인 이해를 필요로 한다. 본 수업에서는 이러한 인사행정의 통섭적 이해
를 바탕으로 종합적인 인사행정의 모습을 논의하고자 한다. 
2. 학습목표
1) 인사행정의 본질, 역할, 가치 및 환경 등 행정학을 구성하는 중요 기본개념 습득
2) 인사행정활동을 추진하는 공공행정기관의 인사제도와 조직구조의 형성, 관리, 혁신 과정
의 의의와 내용 및 결과와 영향의 이해 
3) 인사행정의 내부환경요소인 실적제와 직업공무원제, 계급제와 직위분류제 등의 이해
4) 인사행정의 전략과 인적자원의 확보 및 개발, 그리고 유지·활용, 보상 등에 대한 종합적 
이해를 통하여 바람직한 행정 및 행정인의 모습을 제시함
3. 수업진행 방법
 - 강의, 사례분석(토론), 외부초빙강사(예정)

개요
이 수업에서는 인류 역사의 다양한 지적 성찰 및 실천적 가치를 종합적으
로 탐구하고, 이를 바탕으로 현재의 사회를 이해하고 미래의 변화에 대응
할 수 있는 토의·토론의 장을 마련한다. 개별 전공들 간의 장벽을 넘어 비
판적·융합적·창의적 사고 능력을 함양하고, 나아가 새롭고 다양한 관점에서 
문제의식을 생성하며 타인과의 소통 및 협력을 통해 문제를 해결할 수 있
도록 하는 것이 이 교과의 목표이다. 이를 위해 플립트 클래스(Flipped 
Class) 기반의 학습자 중심 교수학습 방법을 도입하여, 질문 중심 학습
(QBL: Question Based Learning)과 토론 및 발표를 통해 학습자가 배
움의 주체가 될 수 있도록 한다.

Evaluation/ 
Grading 
Proportion 
Attendance / Participation 30%, Midterm 30%, Final 40% 
Criteria 
Attendance: students are supposed to attend each class, punctually. Absences must be justified by a written 
document. According to the School regulation, being absent in more than 1/3 of the classes will be sanctioned 
with “F” 
Participation: students are expected to be actively involved in the classwork with interest, passion, and 
dedication (i.e., participation in class discussions, questions during lectures, active debate with instructors 
during critics, punctuality in assignments submission). Particular attention will be paid to the care and quality 
of the material shown in desk-critics and assignments reviews. Since architectural ideas cannot be expressed 
only in words, the presentation of complete, clear, and visually valid sketches, drawings, models, digital 
material, etc. will be indispensable for communicating with instructors.  
Midterm: the material of Midterm Review (see above: Assignments) will be evaluated according to:  
a) Concept (quality and complexity of the architectural idea, regarding originality, character, and study): b) 
Process (diligence, continuity, and consistency in the project development from concept generation to space 
studies, to preliminary design), and c) Final product / Presentation (completeness, clarity, and aesthetic quality 
of the material presented) 
Final: the material of Final Review (see above: Assignments) will be evaluated according to:  
a) Concept (quality and complexity of the architectural idea – and of its possible developments from the 
midterm phase - regarding originality, character, and study), b) Process (ability to turn the concept – with 
diligent, continuous, and consistent work – into a complete architectural design, where formal, functional and 
technical issues are investigated and developed), and c) Final product / Presentation (completeness, clarity 
and aesthetical quality of the material presented) 
The final grade will be given only after submitting assign. 3 whose completeness (including digital folders 
materials) is a part of the evaluation.

COURSE DESCRIPTION 
 
Dense metropolitan cities suffer from congestion. A tangled circulation web of cars, trains, buses, 
bicycles, people and other animals moving around the man‐made environment of infrastructure and 
architecture and also, the natural environment of trees and land masses. Never is this dialogue 
between architecture and the city more apparent and the issues of congestion more conflated than 
in Seongsu‐Dong. 
 
Seongsu‐Dong, currently, thriving on tourism. People flood the streets. Cars in the street seem out of 
place and out of scale. The scale and program of the architecture is equally disproportionate. There 
are old buildings coming down, new buildings going up and everything in between. There are no 
back alleys and with such commercialism every building and path seems available for public 
consumption. 
 
Your site is located halfway between two subway stations. One to the east and one to the west, 
namely Ttukseom Station and Seongsu Station, respectively. From above, the site is nestled between 
two branches of the subway’s green line. On the ground, the site takes on a different identity. It is an 
unique irregular shape ‐ the leftover block bounded by large traffic arteries. The site contains 
programs demonstrating the enduring legacy of local craftsmanship, but are housed in seemingly 
dispersed and temporary structures.    
 
When faced with such complex site conditions, the standard representations of architecture in plan, 
section and elevation seem to fall short. To fully understand the site and express the full potential of 
design, other forms of representations are needed. In addition to these standard techniques, this 
course examines other representations in architecture to explore form, program and circulation to 
express opinions that may otherwise be lost in communication.

1. Course Description  
In today’s interconnected global economy, the impact of international business (IB) is profound 
and far-reaching. From the food we eat to the clothes we wear and the technology we use, our 
lives are increasingly influenced by the operations of multinational companies. Whether you 
aim to run your own business or secure a position in a global firm, understanding international 
business is essential for managing work in a global context. 
 
We will ground ourselves in international business theories and concepts while also finding 
innovative ways, built on these conventional foundations, to navigate uncertainty and seize 
new opportunities. This will help equip you with the knowledge and skills needed to contribute 
to the competitiveness of your future business. 
 
In this sense, our course addresses three main parts: 1) National differences and international 
institutions: Explore how national differences affect business and the role of evolving 
international institutions in facilitating cross-border operations. 2) International business 
strategies: Learn how firms develop strategies to address national differences and gain 
competitive advantages in both domestic and foreign markets. 3) Drivers of change: Analyze 
the major drivers currently reshaping international business, including economic nationalism, 
climate change, and technological advancements. 
 
This comprehensive approach will provide you with the theoretical and practical knowledge 
necessary to thrive in the rapidly changing landscape of global business. 
 
2 
 
2. Course Objectives  
1) Understand conventional international business theories and concepts: Gain a 
comprehensive understanding of the traditional theories, concepts, and strategies that have 
shaped international business in the era of globalization. 
2) Develop future-oriented international business strategies: Learn to formulate effective 
international business strategies by analyzing external market environments and leveraging 
internal capabilities. 
3) Enhance team collaboration skills: Practice working collaboratively in teams with diverse 
members to achieve common goals, improving the quality and effectiveness of outputs 
through collective effort. 
 
3. Prerequisite 
There are no formal requirements for taking this course, but ideally, students are expected to 
have completed two years of business education, including introductory management courses 
and introductory economics. This is a course taught in English, and students should be able to 
communicate, present, and write a report in English. 
 
4. Required Textbook 
[DRSC] Daniels, John D., Lee H. Radebaugh, Daniel P. Sullivan, and Reid W. Click (2022) 
International Business: Environments and Operations, 17th edition(global), Pearson. 
 
5. Attendance 
Attendance will be checked every class using a seating chart for counting the minimum 
requirements of attendance by the rule of KUBS (at least 2/3 for the classes). Two late arrivals 
(more than 10 minutes) will count as one absence. If you miss more than minimum 
requirements for any reason, your grade will be automatically marked as an “F.” 
 
 
 
3

The grade for this course will be computed from the following components:
