1) In-class Participation (10 points) 
- 
Students’ contributions during classes will be assessed based on both the quality and 
quantity of their comments and questions. Active engagement is expected. Valuable 
contributions include insightful answers to the instructor’s questions, questions that 
illuminate important aspects of the topic, and comments that clarify or highlight key points 
from earlier discussions.  
- 
Students may occasionally complete in-class assignments at the instructor’s discretion. 
These assignments will count toward the in-class participation grade. 
• 
Evaluation: It will be based on the number of valuable contributions  
(0: 0 points, 1~2: 5 points, 3~4: 7 points, 5~: 10 points) 
 
2) Answering Questions for Case Study (15 points total) 
- 
We will analyze three international business cases during class sessions. Using a flipped-
learning approach, I will share a set of guiding questions for each case prior to class. You 
will be required to submit your written responses in advance. 
4 
 
• 
Evaluation: Your work will be assessed on (a) adherence to the instructions and (b) 
the quality of your answers, with scores ranging from Poor (1 point) to Excellent (5 
points) for each case study.  
 
3) Online Discussion (5 points) 
- 
I will post materials on the LMS that offer insights into the future of international business. 
You are required to: (1) submit a response indicating whether you agree or disagree with 
the viewpoints and explain why; and (2) comment on at least one classmate’s response. 
• 
Evaluation: Your work will be assessed on (a) adherence to the instructions and (b) 
the quality of your response and comment. Scores range from Poor (1 point) to 
Excellent (5 points). 
 
4-1) Team Project 1: Simulation (15 points) 
- 
A simulation project focusing on foreign market entry strategy using Harvard Business 
Simulation will be conducted as an in-class group activity.  
• 
Evaluation: It will be assessed based on the achievement of simulation targets and 
active participation throughout the project. 
 
4-2) Team Project 2: Final presentation & report (25 points) 
- 
This project consists of two parts: presentation (15 points) and report (10 points). 
- 
Each group decides on a case of a company to discuss—either 1) a Korean company in (or 
entering) a foreign country, 2) a non-Korean company in (or entering) Korea, or 3) a non-
Korean company in (or entering) a country other than Korea. 
- 
You identify and discuss a problem or issue that the company is facing or faced with 
recently regarding their IB activities (e.g., related to entries to a new country or existing 
operations) 
- 
The contents of your project must consist of (but not limited to): 
• 
A very brief overview of the company 
• 
A clear problem/issue identification 
• 
Analysis of the problem using theories and concepts from the course (and evaluation 
of the firm’s existing strategies) 
5 
 
• 
Provide two potential strategies the firm could adopt to resolve the problem, then 
select one strategy to recommend and explain why it is better than the other. 
- 
Each team has a 15-minute meeting with the instructor on the assigned team meeting day 
to get confirmation about the choice of a company, industry, and issue. 
- 
For this project, scores are awarded based on team performance. There will be a peer 
evaluation among the team members at the end of the course, which shows each team 
member’s contribution. Based on the peer evaluation, a bonus of up to 10% or a penalty of 
up to 10% could be applied to each member’s scores. 
- 
Presentation: Each team will prepare and deliver a 20-minute presentation to the whole 
class, followed by a 10-minute Q&A. The presentation should focus on the case’s key 
question. 
• 
Evaluation: (a) Analysis (Is the central issue clearly communicated? Are appropriate 
evidence and logic used to support the diagnosis of the central issue? Does the 
analysis effectively use theories and concepts learned in the course?) (b) 
Alternatives/Recommendations (Are recommendations logically drawn from the 
analysis? Do the recommended options effectively address the issue? Are the 
advantages and disadvantages of alternative options analyzed sufficiently?) (c) 
Presentation Skills (Audibility, flow of ideas, pace of delivery, time management, 
visual aids, readability) (d) Q&A Management (Does the team engage the audience 
effectively and provide well-considered answers to questions?) 
• 
Submission: Presentation slides must be uploaded to LMS by 5 PM on the day prior 
to the scheduled presentation. 
 
- 
Report: The report should convert your presentation into a written format, adding the 
detailed logic and evidence you could not fully present due to time limits. Thus, you should 
refine problem identification, analysis, and recommendations beyond the presentation draft. 
You are also expected to strengthen the report by incorporating feedback from the instructor 
and peers after your presentation. 
• 
Format: The written report should be 6 pages (Times New Roman, 12 pt, single-
spaced, 1-inch margins), excluding the title page, executive summary, tables, and 
figures. Immediately after the title page, include a one-page executive summary that 
briefly states the key problems and main recommendations. 
6 
 
• 
Evaluation: A strong presentation does not automatically translate into a strong report; 
the report will be evaluated on its own merits. (a) Analysis and 
Alternatives/Recommendations: You are expected to provide an in-depth analysis 
supported by appropriate evidence and clear logic, and to develop well-justified 
alternatives and recommendations, including a detailed discussion of the advantages 
and disadvantages of each option. (b) Feedback Reflection: You must incorporate 
the feedback and comments received from the instructor and peers after the 
presentation. (c) Writing Quality: The overall writing quality (clarity, organization, 
grammar, punctuation, and mechanics) will also be assessed as part of the evaluation. 
• 
Submission: The due date is June 22nd at 11:59 p.m. 
 
5) Exams (30 points):  
- 
There will be closed-book midterm and final exams, worth 15 points each. 
 
7. Team Building & Peer Evaluation 
The instructor will assign students to teams based on majors, seniority, nationality, and other 
relevant criteria. The purpose of this team-building approach is to simulate real-world business 
environments where team-based tasks are common, and it is rare to work exclusively with close 
friends. This course offers a valuable opportunity to experience working in teams with varying 
skills and backgrounds, similar to what you will encounter after graduation. This experience 
will help you develop the skills needed to collaborate effectively in a professional setting. 
 
8. Plagiarism and Use of Generative AI 
Students must adhere to the University’s policy on academic honesty in all areas related to the

When using generative AI and AI-assisted technologies for any course outputs, students should

outputs provide, the student will receive the lowest score in the course.

담당교수: 
이예영(연구실: 운초우선교육관 613호, 전화: 3290-2329, E-mail: young509@korea.ac.kr) 
김유경(연구실: 운초우선교육관 713호, 전화: 3290-2328, E-mail: yookyung_kim@korea.ac.kr) 
  유난숙(연구실: 운초우선교육관 627호, 전화: 3290-2324, E-mail: starwell@korea.ac.kr) 
 
 
과목 개요 
저출산으로 인한 인구구조변화에 대비해 지속가능한 가정생활문화가 요구되고 있다. 본 과목은 
팀티칭 수업 및 프로젝트 기반 수업으로 진행되며, 가정교육과 1학년 학생들이 필수로 이수해야 
하는 가정학의 입문 수업이다.  
가정생활문화의 개념을 학문적 정의와 이론을 바탕으로 이해하고, 가정생활문화의 하위 범주에 
해당하는 의, 식, 주, 가족, 소비 관련 생활문화를 중등 가정과 교육 내용과 연계해 살펴본다. 또한 
중등 가정과 교육에서 핵심 요소로 다루어지는 지속가능한 가정생활문화와 관련된 기초개념과 
방안을 한국의 전통문화, 친환경, 4차 산업혁명, 다문화와 연계해 소개한다. 
 
학습 목표 
1. 가정생활문화의 개념과 가정과 교육 내용의 관계를 이해한다. 
2. 지속가능한 가정생활문화와 관련된 기초 개념을 이해한다. 
3. 한국의 전통적 가정생활문화에 대해 이해하고 지속가능성과 관련된 요소를 탐색한다. 
4. 4차 산업혁명과 가정생활문화의 관계를 이해하고 지속가능한 가정생활문화를 만들어갈 
방안을 탐색한다. 
5. 한국의 다문화가정의 가정생활문화를 중등 가정 교과의 내용과 연계해 이해한다. 
  
수업 방침 
1. 모든 학생은 수업 전 학습관리시스템(LMS: lms.korea.ac.kr)의 강의자료실에서 자료를 다운
로드 받아 수업을 준비한다.  
2. 결석 시 출석 점수 10점 만점에서 1점씩 감점하고, 세 번 지각 시 한번 결석과 동일하게 처
리한다. 30분 이상 지각한 경우 해당 수업은 결석 처리한다. 
3. 시험은 영역별로 나누어 take-home의 형식으로 출제하고 답안은 정해진 날짜에 LMS를 통
해 제출한다. 
4. 시험과 과제물 수행 시 부정행위가 적발되면 해당 시험이나 과제는 0점 처리한다. 
5. 모든 학생은 팀별 프로젝트를 수행하여 그 결과를 학기말에 구두 및 포스터 발표를 한다.

시험 
시험은 수업 내용을 통합적으로 이해하고 공부하여 기술하는 take-home 형식으로 출제하며,  
의, 식, 가족 각 영역의 4주차 수업을 마친 후 문제를 공지한다. 문제 공지 후 2주 이내 답안을 
LMS의 과제물 제출실에 제출한다. 답안은 줄간격 160%, 글꼴은 바탕체 11포인트로 작성하고, 
제출시 파일명은 학번_이름으로 적는다. 제출한 답안은 교내 표절검사 프로그램을 이용해 표절 
여부를 확인할 예정이다. 
 
기말 과제 
기말 과제는 프로젝트 결과물이며, 조별로 의, 식, 가족 중 한 영역을 배정받은 후 수업내용과 
관련된 구체적인 프로젝트 주제를 선택해 진행한다. 조별 프로젝트 계획안은 13주차 이전까지 해당 
영역 교수에게 제출해 승인을 받은 후 필요에 따라 중간점검을 받으며 진행한다.  
프로젝트 결과는 16주차에 학술 포스터 형태의 pdf 파일로 만들어 LMS 게시판의 지정된 
섹션에 게시하고, 구두 발표로 수강생들과 공유한다. 포스터는 파워포인트를 사용하여 너비 90cm, 
높이 120cm 크기로 작성하고, 제목과 조원에 대한 정보를 포함한다. 프로젝트 결과가 효과적으로 
전달될 수 있도록 소제목을 적절히 활용하여 포스터를 구성한다. 참고 포스터의 예는 각 조별 세부 
영역 배정 후 LMS를 통해 공유될 예정이다.  
수강생들은 게시판에 공유된 다른 조의 포스터를 최소 3개 선택해서 댓글을 달아야 하며, 이를 
수행하지 않을 경우 본 과제의 점수를 100점으로 환산한 점수에서 1점씩 감점한다. 16주차에 발표를 
마친 후 각 조별 동료평가를 통해 조원들의 기여도를 조사하여 개인별 최종 점수에 반영할 
예정이다.

개요
이 수업에서는 인류 역사의 다양한 지적 성찰 및 실천적 가치를 종합적으
로 탐구하고, 이를 바탕으로 현재의 사회를 이해하고 미래의 변화에 대응
할 수 있는 토의·토론의 장을 마련한다. 개별 전공들 간의 장벽을 넘어 비
판적·융합적·창의적 사고 능력을 함양하고, 나아가 새롭고 다양한 관점에서 
문제의식을 생성하며 타인과의 소통 및 협력을 통해 문제를 해결할 수 있
도록 하는 것이 이 교과의 목표이다. 이를 위해 플립트 클래스(Flipped 
Class) 기반의 학습자 중심 교수학습 방법을 도입하여, 질문 중심 학습
(QBL: Question Based Learning)과 토론 및 발표를 통해 학습자가 배
움의 주체가 될 수 있도록 한다.

Objective of Course 
The course aims to equip aspiring students with prototyping skills to articulate the interactive and multi-
dimensional attributes of design concepts. Students who are applying this course are highly required for pre-
acquisition of their 2D graphic tools techniques and 3D graphic tools techniques. The primary objectives are 
outlined as follows: 
●Acquiring narrative storytelling techniques for design concepts and scenarios. 
●Understanding the static/dynamic attributes of design and achieving optimal expression.
●Expressing sequential/interactive information flow and mastering efficient UX design.
●Learning to articulate design concepts using tools such as Adobe Suites or Quick Prototyping Tools.
Process of Course 
The course will consist of three phase through 15 weeks.  
Phase 1  : Understanding elements and structure of information design 
Phase 2  : Usability, Storyboard & Flowchart Design  
Phase 3  : Interactive Information Design Prototyping  
Phase 4  : Term Project  
(will be conducted in parallel with Phase 1 and 2).

1. Seminar: Technical book reading chapters per each student for quick understanding of the drafting theory.

4. Term Project: Designing interactive micro site or prototype for a product or a service.

Class Meetings (유연학기제, Flexible Semester Format) 
This course will adopt a flexible semester format and run as an intensive 8-week class. We 
will meet twice a week from Week 9 to Week 16, for a total of 15 class meetings. Each class 
session will be 2.5 hours (75 minutes × 2).  
 
 
Course Description 
This course introduces the basics of the analysis of discourse, or language in use. Engaging in 
discourse is a mundane, yet highly complicated, daily activity. We will take various 
approaches in this course, exploring discourse in relation to, for example, society, pragmatics, 
genre, and conversation. We will examine the assumptions and principles of discourse, the 
basic units and structures of discourse, and the role of society and culture in various genres of 
discourse. Throughout the semester, students will engage in the analysis of both spoken and 
written discourse of various kinds. As language users, our knowledge of discourse is already 
extensive, but by directing our attention to discourse itself as a scholarly subject, the course 
will expand our understanding of language in use as we observe the complexities of our own 
and others’ discourse practices. 
2 
 
 
Course Objectives 
By the end of the semester, students should be able to:   
1. understand different approaches to discourse analysis: 
2. describe the basic structures of a discourse of various forms; 
3. discuss how social actions are accomplished in discourse;  
4. discuss how identities are constructed in discourse; and 
5. critically analyze spoken or written discourse. 
 
 
Text and Other Materials 
Required textbook: Paltridge, B. (2022). Discourse Analysis: An introduction (3rd edition). 
New York, NY: Bloomsbury Publishing Plc. 
 
* All other supplementary materials are available on Blackboard. 
* Class ppt will be available on Blackboard before the class.  
 
 
Course Requirements  
 
1. Attendance and participation (20%) 
Class attendance is important, and chronic tardiness or leaving early will affect your grade. 
You may have up to three absences without penalty and without providing documentation. 
Arriving more than forty minutes late equals an absence. In addition, every 15 minutes of late 
arrival counts as one “late mark,” and three late marks equal one absence. In any case, you 
are responsible for finding out what you have missed in a class by contacting your fellow 
classmates. Chronic absences or late arrivals may affect your final grade. Students missing 
more than 1/3 of the course (including allowed absences) will automatically receive an F 
according to university regulations. 
 
The class will consist of lectures, group activities, and discussions. Because discourse 
analysis requires practice and discussions, active participation is expected during in-class 
analysis workshops and activities.  
 
 
2. Data analyses (40%) 
The course includes two individual data analysis assignments (approximately 2–3 pages 
each). Throughout the semester, students are expected to stay attentive to discourses of 
various kinds—for example, media texts, online comments, everyday conversations, 
classroom interaction, workplace communication, or human–AI dialogue. Using spoken or 
written data that they obtain on their own, students will annotate the data with analytic labels 
introduced in class and write a short analysis explaining their key annotations, the patterns 
3 
these annotations reveal, and what the patterns suggest about real-life conversation or 
professional interaction. Students will also have opportunities to briefly share their findings 
with peers during in-class activities. 
 
 
3. Open-book final exam (40%) <selected chapters> 
There will be an open-book, in-class final exam covering selected chapters and materials 
from lectures, the textbook, and in-class practice activities (specific chapters will be 
announced). The exam will assess both conceptual understanding and your ability to apply 
course tools to new discourse data and contexts. No make-up exam will be given except in 
documented cases of unavoidable emergency.

Studio Theme 
Title 
Urban Architecture and Public Space;  
Social Infrastructure for Printing Community 
Theme 
 
1. Urban Architecture and Public Space;  
The studio explores the relationship between architecture and public space in the city, understanding buildings 
not as isolated objects but as part of a larger spatial, social, and temporal system. A key objective of the course is to 
examine how architecture can mediate between production, public life, and everyday urban  
activities. 
 
1. 
Productive Industrial Architecture  
The Eulji-ro district is characterised by dynamic, productive activities housed within a dense fabric of light-industrial 
buildings. The district functions as an urban generator within the city, supporting the entire printing production 
cycle—from the sourcing of raw materials to manufacturing and retail.  
 
Recent redevelopment around Sewoon Sangga has reopened a long-standing debate: how important is this light-
industrial urban district to retain within the central Seoul, and why does it matter? Students are asked to respond to 
this urban development context by designing a piece of urban architecture that reinforces and enhances the public 
character of the site. 
 
2. Time Architecture 
Now the architecture is not about designing a static sculptural building, rather a system that can accommodate 
changes over time, a dynamic open-ended structure that is shaped by life which occupies the building. The studio 
introduces time, typology, and adaptability as central design concerns. Students are required to design 
architecture as a composition of permanent elements—such as structure, cores, and primary public spaces—
and temporary or adaptable elements that can change in response to evolving programmes, users, and 
technologies.  
 
Tasks 
 
Task 1 – Urban Space Research (Group) 
The first task is about urban public space, drawing on the Noli-map style and writings of Camillo Sitte. Through figure–
ground drawings, morphological and spatial analysis, students study how public spaces are formed by the relationship 
between buildings and voids, and how streets, squares, and urban blocks acquire spatial hierarchy and experiential 
quality. We will visit the site and do a drawing workshop after the theory based research. 
 
 
Camillo Sitte, Studio di piazze medievali (1889) (left) / A1 Figure Ground Map by Geunah Kwon (right) 
Task 2.1 – Typological Study on the Light-Industrial Architecture  (Group) 
The second case study focuses on architectural typology, with particular emphasis on printing houses and small-scale 
light-industrial buildings. Drawing on Rafael Moneo’s essay On Typology, students examine typology not as a set of fixed 
formal models, but as a body of spatial principles that have evolved and been transformed over time.  
 
Light-industrial buildings typically generate generous and universal spatial frameworks that are inherently resilient. Their 
robust and economical modes of construction allow for flexible occupation, enabling a wide range of programmes and 
accommodating future change within the Euljiro district. Such construction systems also lend themselves to simple 
assembly and disassembly, offering the potential for reuse and a second life for building components.  
 
In this context, the students will be asked to study two references as a studio group task, one is Chrystal Palace by 
Joseph Paxton, and another is Photographs of Hilla and Bernd Becher. Through the detailed case study, students are 
asked to critically reflect on the architectural qualities embedded within light-industrial typologies and to identify lessons 
that can be reinterpreted and applied within contemporary architectural design. The students will be asked to redraw the 
both cases in their own digital or hand drawing and make 1:30 model. 
 
       
 
(left) The construction of the frame, Crystal Palace, London, 1850 Illustrated London News, 1850 (right) Photographs of Hilla and Bernt Becher 
 
Task 2.2 – Typological Study on the Light-Industrial Architecture – Collage Workshop (Individual) 
The students will choose example buildings from the neighbourhood of Euji-Ro to research on architectural character of 
it.  The example building should capture the character of Euji-Ro’s typical typology and should be represented in a collage 
to show the architectural character.  
 
Previous student’s collage on anlysis of typical building found from the neighbourhood (Seungmin Yoo)  
 
Task 3 – Designing Solid and Void / Free-Form (Individual) 
The students are required to design an urban solid and void within the existing urban fabric, understanding how to create 
an organic flow and relationship to the adjacent urban context and community referring to the task 1. The study will be 
done in 1:300 massing model and figure ground mapping exercise. Here the students will be asked to design the external 
public space as well as the massing.    
 
 
1:300 Paper model and sketch; studying volume and void to create a meaningful urban inbetween space within the existing context (Jusin Park) 
Task 4 – Organisation of the building (Planning) (Individual) 
The definition of program is changing in contemporary architecture, rather scenarios are becoming more relevant. The 
next step of our studio will be designing a vague program organisation which should be open for change in the future. 
This exercise will be planning an architecture by focusing more on servant programs(BOH) with an assumption that the 
served programs(FOH) will be changed in the future.  
Task 5 – Developing a resilient infrastructure (Group + Individual) 
The structure and service elements are critical to make the building adaptable in the future. The students will be asked to 
design not only the space in aesthetic perspective, but also develop a building system. The tectonic concept here inclines 
towards “Heterogeneous” construction rather than being homogeneous. The students should propose a tectonic 
concept that responds to the contemporary climate crisis agendas which has an open-ended character.  
 
Half completed housing, Quinta Monroy housing, Chille, 2004, Elemental 
 
 
Task 6 – Urban Architecture (1:200 exercise) (Individual) 
The next stage of the project will ask students to design a building in 1:200 scale including plan, section, elevation and 
1:200 model shaping the exterior of the model. At this stage, the public space design will be developed alongside with 
architecture. The students should identify the character of the public space and the texture of it as well.  
 
Task 7 – Public interface and Facade (1:50 scale exercise) (Individual) 
The façade should show the relationship between the internal spatial and structural character, and the external spaces 
and surrounding buildings in the context. This exercise will be carried out in 1:50 scale drawings in elevation and section. 
The façade construction will be considered in this process as well as the aesthetic aspect.  
 
      
 
Example of 1:50 façade drawing, Europaallee Mixed-use Building by Caruso St John 
Task 8 – Atmosphere (1:30 scale exercise) (Individual) 
The last stage of the project will ask students to develop the key internal spaces showing not only the architectural 
concept of the internal space but also how people will occupy the space.

Criteria 
Attendance: students are supposed to attend each class, punctually. Absences must be justified by 
a written document. According to the School regulation, being absent in more than 1/3 of the classes 
will be sanctioned with “F” 
Participation: students are expected to be actively involved in the classwork with interest, passion, 
and dedication (i.e., participation in class discussions, questions during lectures, active debate with 
instructors during critics, punctuality in assignments submission). Particular attention will be paid to 
the care and quality of the material shown in desk-critics and assignments reviews. Since 
architectural ideas cannot be expressed only in words, the presentation of complete, clear, and 
visually valid sketches, drawings, models, digital material, etc. will be indispensable for 
communicating with instructors.  
Midterm: the material of Midterm Review (see above: Assignments) will be evaluated according to:  
a) Concept (quality and complexity of the architectural idea, regarding originality, character, and 
study): b) Process (diligence, continuity, and consistency in the project development from concept 
generation to space studies, to preliminary design), and c) Final product / Presentation 
(completeness, clarity, and aesthetic quality of the material presented) 
Final: the material of Final Review (see above: Assignments) will be evaluated according to:  
a) Concept (quality and complexity of the architectural idea – and of its possible developments from 
the midterm phase - regarding originality, character, and study), b) Process (ability to turn the 
concept – with diligent, continuous, and consistent work – into a complete architectural design, 
where formal, functional and technical issues are investigated and developed), and c) Final product / 
Presentation (completeness, clarity and aesthetical quality of the material presented) 
The final grade will be given only after submitting assign. 3 whose completeness (including digital 
folders materials) is a part of the evaluation.

본 과목의 주요 목적은 한국과 주요 파트너 국가 간 여러 안보 이슈와 외교 정책에 대해 
이해하는 것입니다. 본 과목에서는 한국의 주요 파트너 국가 중에서도 미국, 중국, 일본, 
러시아, 대만, 그리고 북한과의 관계를 중점적으로 다룹니다. 이 과목을 통해 수강생들은 
한국이 직면한 다양한 국제 갈등과 협력 관계를 배우고, 관련 현안을 이해하기 위해 필

대면 시험을 원칙으로 합니다. 중간고사와 기말고사 각각 두 개의 에세이 문제가

I. COURSE DESCRIPTION 
This course is designed to introduce students to the main aspects of contemporary 
Korean society, including those pertaining to culture, the family, gender, education, 
population, religion, economy, and popular culture (Hallyu). The course will 
specifically focus on topics and issues that figure prominently in the lives of the 
Korean people, such as the persistence of Confucianism and shamanism, the rise in 
divorce rate, education frenzy, gender inequality, the rise of Christianity as a major 
religion, population aging, low fertility rate, increasing ethnic diversity and 
multiculturalism, rapid industrialization, Seoul-based urbanization, and the rise of 
Hallyu as a global phenomenon. Each of these issues will be examined through 
sociological, historical, and comparative perspectives. Every effort will be made to 
make each session lively and engaging, so your active participation is extremely 
important and is a vital part of the course. 
 
II. COURSE OBJECTIVES  
The principal objective of this course is to prepare students with the knowledge and 
analytical tools needed to develop balanced views on Korean society. Toward this end, 
students are expected to:  
• 
Recognize the ways in which culture shapes individual behavior, identity, 
values, and broader social dynamics. 
 
2 
 
• 
Understand the key dimensions and major trends that characterize 
contemporary Korean society. 
• 
Analyze how social categories such as class, gender, age, and race/ethnicity 
intersect with institutions including the family, education, economy, religion, 
and politics. 
• 
Evaluate how significant social changes—such as globalization, technological 
advancement, and demographic shifts—affect the lived experiences of diverse 
groups in Korea. 
• 
Identify and critically assess pressing social challenges facing Korean society, 
including issues of “over-education” (the disproportionate pursuit of tertiary 
education), population aging, and racism, while exploring potential strategies for 
addressing these problems. 
 
III. REQUIRED READINGS  
Kim, Andrew Eungi, ed. 2018. Korean Society: An Introduction. Seoul: Korea  
 
University Press 
 
Note: The assigned “Required Readings” are not typically covered in lectures, as 
class time is devoted to instructor-prepared materials. Nevertheless, you are 
expected to be familiar with the readings for both the midterm and final exams. 
 
 
IV. REQUIREMENTS AND EVALUATION 
1. Class Attendance (10% of the final grade) 
Attendance will be recorded either before the break or near the end of each class session. 
For each unexcused absence, 3 points will be deducted from the final grade. 
 
2. Midterm Exam (40% of the final grade) 
The midterm will assess your understanding of course content from Weeks 1–7, 
including both lectures and assigned readings. At least one-fourth of the questions 
will be drawn from the required readings. The exam format consists of short and long 
essay questions. 
 
3. Final Exam (50% of the final grade) 
The final exam will assess your understanding of course content from Weeks 9–14,

will be drawn from the required readings. The exam format consists of short and long

2026학년도 전반기 임상실습 
1. 과 소개
l 영상의학과는 각 전문분야를 담당하는 교수 및 전공의, 수련의가 의료진으로 근무하고 있으
며, 방사선사와 간호사 및 업무원이 서로 협조하여 환자의 질병을 진단하고 치료하는 역할을 
수행하고 있습니다. 또한 단순촬영기, 투시촬영기, 초음파촬영기, 혈관조영촬영기, 전산화단
층촬영기, 자기공명영상촬영기 등의 검사장비를 시행, 감독을 통해 운용하며 이를 통해 얻은 
영상정보를 판독, 관리합니다.
l 임상실습학생은 담당 전공의 및 교수의 지도아래 기본적인 영상정보의 습득 방법과 중요 질
환의 소견 및 인터벤션 치료방법 등에 대하여 실습하게 됩니다.
1) 안암 병원
l 전임교수：오유환, 조성범, 성득제, 강창호, 박범진, 조규란, 김민주, 한나연, 김병준, 황성
호, 송성은. 안경식, 유성혜, 심기춘, 곽정원, 오세린
l 임상교수：김보규, 한예은, 이규정, 신재호, 이동규, 김상운
l 초빙/진료교수: 류은미, 박아림, 정윤수, 김유연, 김연수, 박상은, 임현지
2) 구로병원
l 전임교수：이기열, 김경아, 이창희, 서상일, 최재웅, 서태석, 용환석, 우옥희, 이종미(고용 
휴직, 2024.9.1. ~2025.08.31.), 유인선, 송명규, 정혜나 (해외 연수, 2024.9.1. ~ 
2025.08.31), 양우진, 김정우, 김수연
l 임상교수：신혜선, 송미진, 강우영
3) 안산병원
l 전임교수：정환훈, 서보경, 이영흔, 제보경, 염석규, 김채리, 최인영, 심으뜸, 배민선, 박
성준, 최가영
l 임상교수: 이지영, 김왕현
l 초빙/진료교수: 차상훈, 김백현, 한지성
2. 학습목표
영상의학과 공통 실습 학습 목표
<흉부>
1) 흉부 X선 사진에서 정상 해부학을 설명할 수 있다.
2) 흉부 X선 사진에서 정상과 비정상의 구분할 수 있다.
3) 흉부 X선  및 CT 영상에서 감염성 질환과 종양성 질환의 구분할 수 있다.
<심혈관>
1) 심장 및 대동맥의 정상해부학을 설명할 수 있다.
2) 허혈성심질환의 영상소견을 설명할 수 있다.
3) 급성대동맥증후군의 영상소견을 설명할 수 있다.

                                              필수 임상실습 지침서                    
     
2026학년도 전반기 임상실습 
<복부>
1) 단순복부촬영, 투시검사, 초음파 검사, CT, MR 영상검사에서 정상 해부학에 대해 이해하고 
판단할 수 있다.
2) 각 검사 방법의 역할 및 장단점에 대해 이해하고 임상 상황에 따른 적절한 검사방법을 제시
할 수 있다.
3) 복부 주요 장기의 대표적 질환의 영상소견에 대해 이해하고 감별 진단 할 수 있다.
<비뇨기>
1) 단순복부촬영, 초음파 그리고 CT 영상에서 비뇨생식기의 정상 해부학을 설명할 수 있다.
2) 급성 측복통과 하복부 복통에 있어서 각 검사 방법의 역할 및 장단점을 안다.
3) 비뇨생식기의 대표적 종양과 염증성 질환의 영상소견을 설명할 수 있다.
<신경 두경부>
1) 전산화단층촬영 및 자기공명영상, 초음파 영상에서의 뇌 및 두경부의 정상 해부학을 설명할 
수 있다.
2) 뇌졸중 (hemorrhage, infarction)의 영상소견을 설명할 수 있다.
3) 신경계 종양의 영상소견을 설명할 수 있다.
4) 갑상선 경부 초음파를 참관하고 갑상선 암의 소견을 설명할 수 있다.
<근골격>
1) 단순 뼈사진에서 사지 및 척추의 골절과 골파괴 병소 이해한다.
2) 척추의 퇴행성 질환의 단순 사진 및 MRI 소견을 설명할 수 있다.
3) 관절질환의 이해와 영상소견에 의한 진단을 할 수 있다.
<인터벤션>
1) 혈관조영술 및 인터벤션 시술의 원리 및 수기의 이해한다.
2) 혈관조영술상의 정상 해부학을 설명할 수 있다.
3) 인터벤션 시술의 적응이 되는 대표적 질환의 영상진단 및 치료를 이해한다.
<유방>
1) 유방 해부학을 알고, 영상검사에서 어떻게 보이는지 이해한다.
2) BI-RADS (breast imaging reporting and data system)에 근거한 용어와 판정을 숙지한
다.
3) 유방에서 생기는 악성, 양성 질환을 숙지하고 감별점을 이해한다.
<소아>
1) 구역/구토가 있는 아이의 원인을 진단한다. 
2) 미숙아에서 발생하는 의학적 문제와 합병증을 진단할 수 있다.
3) 신생아 발열의 감염 원인을 진단할 수 있다. 
4) 복부덩이가 있는 소아의 흔한 원인을 진단할 수 있다.
5) 소아 설사의 원인을 진단할 수 있다.

6) 성장지연이 있는 아이에게서 필요한 영상 검사를 선택할 수 있다. 
7) 신생아 응급질환을 진단할 수 있다.
8) 혈변을 본 아이에게서 출혈 정도를 평가하고 원인 감별할 수 있다.
9) 황달이 있는 신생아에게서 병적 황달을 구분할 수 있다.
3. 실습계획서

Office Hours: By appointment.
Required Textbook and References: We will use A First Course in Probability, 10th edition by
Sheldon Ross as the primary textbook.
Description: This course develops the foundations of probability with an emphasis on clear mathematical
reasoning and disciplined problem solving. We begin with axioms and counting methods, proceed to condi-
tional probability and independence, and then study discrete and continuous random variables, expectation,
and joint distributions. The latter part of the course introduces core tools such as transforms and basic
limit theorems that underpin modern statistics, actuarial science, engineering, and quantitative finance.
Please note that the course will include formal derivations and proofs when appropriate. Students should
expect a rigorous and theory-oriented presentation, complemented by substantial practice through problem
sets.
Objectives: After completing this course, successful students should be able to:
• formulate probability models using sample spaces and axioms.
• compute probabilities using counting techniques and inclusion–exclusion.
• apply conditional probability, Bayes’ rule, and independence in structured problems.
• work with discrete and continuous random variables, distribution functions, and densities.
• compute expectations, variances, and key performance measures of random quantities.
• analyze joint distributions, conditional distributions, covariance, and correlation.
• use transforms (e.g., generating functions / moment generating functions) in distributional calcula-
tions.
• interpret foundational limit results and connect them to approximation and inference.
Prerequisites: An undergraduate-level understanding of calculus (especially single-variable integration)
and mathematical maturity for proof-based reasoning. Familiarity with basic set operations and algebraic
manipulation is assumed.

수업목표 일반 
추상적 형태에서 구축적 실재로의 전환 
본 수업은 개념적 유희를 넘어, 실제로 지어지는 건조 환경의 물성적 실재
를 깊이 있게 이해하고 파악하는 것을 목표로 합니다. 학생들은 건축적 형
태를 단순한 시각적 구성으로 바라보는 시각에서 벗어나, 구조 원리와 재료
의 물성, 그리고 환경적 대응이 유기적으로 결합된 종합적 산물로서 건축을 
인식하고 설계하는 능력을 배양하게 될 것입니다. 
세부목표 1 
기하학적 질서와 재료적 구체화 
공간의 정의: 기하학적 질서와 공간 정의를 학습하되, 이를 추상적인 선이
나 면이 아닌 벽, 기둥, 슬라브와 같은 실제 건축 부재를 통해 구체적으로 
구현합니다. 
공간의 분위기: 형태 구성 능력을 배양하고, 이를 빛과 개구부 등 실체적 
요소를 통해 감각적으로 경험 가능한 공간으로 발전시킵니다 
세부목표 2 
맥락적 분석과 프로그램 전략 
환경적 맥락: 주변 환경 요소에 대한 정량적·정성적 분석을 수행하여, 이를 
바탕으로 근거 기반의 설계 의사결정을 내리는 훈련을 합니다. 
공간 조직: 소규모 전시 공간 등 구체적인 프로그램의 요구사항을 분석하
여, 효율적인 동선 체계와 명확한 공간 위계를 수립합니다. 
세부목표 3 
통합적 소통과 표현 
전문적 명료성: 자신의 설계 의도를 시각적, 언어적으로 전문성을 갖추어 
명료하게 전달하는 능력을 기릅니다. 
설득력 있는 묘사: 정교한 건축 도면과 모형을 활용하여, 계획안을 단순한 
구상이 아닌 실제로 거주 가능한 환경으로서 설득력 있게 묘사하는 방법을 
훈련합니다.

-1/3 이상 결석시 성적부여 불가, 특정 사유에 한해 출석인정신청 및 시험 불응시 신청 가능, 단 출석인정 제
외하고 1/2 이상 실제 출석 필요함 
 
∙ [학습윤리] 
 -대학의 목적과 본교 교육이념에 따라 성실하고 정직한 마음과 열정적인 태도로 모든 학습에 적극적으로 참
여 
 -고등교육을 받는 교양인으로서의 품위를 유지하며, 도덕적 민감성을 바탕으로 창의적 학문탐구에 정진 
 -교육활동과 관련하여 교원 및 동료학생과의 약속을 성실히 이행 
 -교원과 동료학생의 인격을 존중하고 기본적인 예의를 준수 
 -학문 공동체의 일원으로서 학문의 진실성을 지키며, 본교 「AI 활용 가이드」를 성실히 준수 
 -강의계획서 등을 충분히 탐색하여 자신의 학문적 탐구 방향과 미래 비전에 부합하는 교과목을 신중히 선택 
 -매 수업에 적극적으로 임할 수 있도록 수업자료를 사전에 탐독하고 준비 
 -정해진 수업시간을 준수하며, 결석·지각·중도 이탈 등으로 타인의 학습을 방해하지 않도록 유의 
 -출석 관련 위계행위(대리출석 등) 금지 
 -모든 수업활동에 주도적으로 참여하고, 토론·질의응답 등을 통해 교과목 이해와 통찰력 향상에 노력 
 -과제는 스스로 성실하게 작성하며, 인용한 모든 자료(책·논문·인터넷·AI 등)는 변조나 왜곡 없이 출처를 명확
히 표기 
 -협동학습의 경우 자신의 역할을 책임감 있게 수행하여 공동의 학습성과 달성에 기여 
 -시험의 목적과 의미를 이해하고, 부정행위 없이 정직하게 응시 
 -한 학기 수강한 교과목의 교육 품질 향상을 위해 강의평가에 성실히 참여하고, 개선이 필요한 사항을 충실히 
서술

-연구실 안전환경 조성에 관한 법률 제20조(교육·훈련)에 의거, 연구실안전법이 적용되는 과학기술분야 대상학
과에 소속된 연구활동종사자는 매학기 일정시간의 안전교육을 이수하여야 하므로 실험·실습을 수강하는 모든 
대상학과 학부생 및 대학원생은 교육참여 필수

가능함.

개요
한문학의 특징과 범주를 개관하고 개별 분야의 초보적인 사항을 소
개합니다. 이 과목은 한문학과 전공 수업을 본격적으로 듣기 시작하
는 1, 2학년이나 편입생들을 비롯하여 한문학에 관심을 가지기 시작
한 분들을 위해 마련한 수업입니다. 한 학기 수업을 통해 이루어지
는 일종의 전공 오리엔테이션, 전공 맛보기라고 생각하면 됩니다. 한
문학 전공에 대한 고민과 궁금증을 함께 나누고 나아가 개인적인 삶
의 계획까지 구상해보는, 따뜻하고 열려 있는 수업입니다.

∙ [학습윤리]
 -대학의 목적과 본교 교육이념에 따라 성실하고 정직한 마음과 열정적인 태도로 학습에 적

고에 정진
 -교육활동과 관련하여 교원 및 동료학생과 약속한 사항을 성실히 이행

 -적극적으로 토론, 질의응답 등 수업활동에 참여

1
Introduction
Urbanization is an fundamental aspect of the social and economic transformations that take
place in the process of development. On the one hand, it is necessary for industrial and eco-
nomic growth. On the other hand, the shift to urban living alters the ways we interact with
each other. Using literature from sociology, urban planning, and geography, this course will
explore how cities have been employed to foster economic development and how they have
reshaped social relations. Though the role of cities in development will be explored primarily
through an examination of Korea’s development history, examples will also be drawn from
throughout Asia and in some cases from the West.
Note that this class is being conducted with live streaming between Korea University and
select universities in China under a cultural program sponsored by the Korea Foundation
(한국국제교류재단). This creates both challenges and opportunities for communicating and
learning that students may or may not find desirable.
1
2
Objectives
By the end of this course, students will be knowledgeable on:
1. A wide range of issues that face cities and their residents in the process of economic
development.
2. The evolution of Asian cities’ position in the global network of cities.
3. The ways in which economic, social, and urban forms mutually shape each other.
4. Differences between East Asian cities and Western cities
5. A representative sampling of theories explaining the urban process.
6. Application of those theories to concrete Asian cases, especially Korean cases.
3
Course Requirements
• You will take a short quiz about this syllabus before class in the fourth week. This quiz
is designed to ensure that you are familiar with the syllabus, that you understand the
class requirements, and that I can anticipate your interests. You will have unlimited
time to take the quiz and are free to look at the syllabus as you take the quiz, but you
will only be able to take it once.
• You are expected to read all assigned readings. Lectures and discussions will be pur-
sued under the assumption that you are already familiar with the readings’ content.
• You are expected to attend class. I do not like to grade attendance, but the Ministry
of Education insists that I fail you if you miss more than one-third of the classes. So
attendance will be counted.
• Each student is required to take a short quiz electronically by 12pm TUESDAY each
week for ten out of the twelve weeks for which there are readings. This allows you to
choose which weeks to take the quiz. If you take more than ten quizzes, your grade will
be determined by the top scoring submissions.
• In preparation for the paper on an individually selected Asian city, students will pre-
pare a timeline of significant events, periods, and transformations of their selected
city. The timeline will highlight major spatial interventions, but it will also include ma-
jor economic and social policies as well as political organization. The timeline should
attempt to place the selected city’s evolution within Lefebvre’s historical framework.
• During the second half of the term, each student will write a brief political economic
history of an Asian city employing concepts we have used in class to consider whether
or not their city reflects Lefebvre’s framework. In particular, these papers will address
the ways in which urban and economic development have been intertwined. Doing so
will require discerning historical phases in your city’s development, which you should
have established in your timeline. These papers should be 1000–1500 words long, ex-
cluding title pages and bibliographies. Note that no paper on the history of a city can
be complete without including maps.

As a student you may experience a range of issues that can cause barriers to learning, such
as strained relationships, increased anxiety, alcohol/drug problems, feeling down, difficulty
concentrating, and lack of motivation. These mental health concerns or stressful events may
lead to diminished academic performance or reduce a student’s ability to participate in daily

Schedule of classes
Week 1 (03/03): Introduction and overview of urbanization and industrialization in
Asia
After introducing the class, the lecture will provide an initial overview of historical patterns
of urbanization and industrialization in Asia relative to the rest of the world. We then ask
whether Western and Eastern cities are different.
Week 2 (03/10): Industrialization and urbanization
Note: Nanjing joins.
Thisclasswillexplorethetightconnectionbetweenindustrializationandurbanization. Specif-
ically, we will discuss the economic and geographic factors that create a synergy between
increasing concentrations of production and population.
1. Henri Lefebvre. 2003. The Urban Revolution. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press,
chapter 1.
Related readings:
1. David M. Gordon. 1978. “Capitalist Development and the History of American Cities.” In
Marxism and the Metropolis: New Perspectives in Urban Political Economy, edited by William
K. Tabb and Larry Sawers, 25–63. New York: Oxford University Press.
Week 3 (03/17): Uneven development
This class will introduce the theory of uneven spatial development and consider how it might
explain the relationship between global developments and growth strategies at the national
and urban level.
4
1. Neil Smith. 1984. Unevendevelopment:nature,capital,andtheproductionofspace. New York,
NY: Blackwell, chapter 4.
Week 4 (03/24): Smart cities and planetary urbanization
Note: Syllabus quiz due before class.
In this class, we revisit Lefebvre’s urban society hypothesis through the concept of planetary
urbanization, what it means to have a right to the city, and how the development of smart
cities in East Asia reflects the planetary. We will consider it as a new form of urban life and
as a commodity.
1. Neil Brenner and Christian Schmid. 2015. “Towards a new epistemology of the urban?”
City 19 (2–3): 151–182. https://doi.org/10.1080/13604813.2015.1014712.
Related readings:
1. Simon Marvin and Andrés Luque-Ayala. 2017. “Urban Operating Systems: Diagramming
the City.” International Journal of Urban and Regional Research 41, no. 1 (January): 84–103.
https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-2427.12479.
Week 5 (03/31): Colonial planning: Japanese imperial planning in Korea
This class will examine how imperial powers have designed cities in their colonies. In par-
ticular, we will examine how Japanese urban planning in Korea—and to some extent China—
contributed to modernizing urban infrastructure and controlling the domestic population.
1. Wonsik Jeong. 2001. “The Urban Development Politics of Seoul as a Colonial City.” Jour-
nal of Urban History 27 (2): 158–177.
Week 6 (04/07): The growth machine
This class will explore how urban leaders can employ urban development to further the eco-
nomicinterestsoftheircity. Thegrowthmachineconceptisthanappliedtourbandevelopment
in China.
1. John R. Logan and Harvey L. Molotch. 1987. Urban Fortunes: The Political Economy of Place.
Berkeley, CA: University of California Press, chapter 3.
Week 7 (04/14): East Asian industrialization
ThisclassoffersanoverviewofindustrializationinEastAsiaandcomparesittoindustrialization
elsewhere in the world.
1. Bruce Cumings. 1984. “The origins and development of the Northeast Asian political
economy: industrial sectors, product cycles, and political consequences.” International
Organization 38 (1): 1–40. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0020818300004264.
Week 8 (04/21): Midterm period. No class.
Note: Timeline due.
Week 9 (04/28): Urbanism as a way of life
As populations increase and become more dense and industrialization alters work patterns,
our social relations change. This class will explore how urbanization generates new freedoms
and new communities. Discussion will draw on the challenges currently facing traditional
markets in Korea.
5
1. GeorgSimmel.2002.“TheMetropolisandMentalLife.”InTheBlackwellCityReader,edited
byGaryBridgeandSophieWatson,11–19.BlackwellReadersinGeography.Malden,MA:
Blackwell Pub.
2. Louis Wirth. 1969. “Urbanism as a Way of Life.” In Classic Essays on the Culture of Cities,
edited by Richard Sennett, 143–164. Englewood Cliffs: Prentice Hall.
Week 10 (05/05): Holiday. No class.
Week 11 (05/12): Speed and the East Asian growth machine
This class builds on the idea that one key feature of Asian cities is the speed with which
they are built by exploring the unique institutional configurations that inform this rapid
development. Case draws primarily from Chinese cities. In particular, it explores the role
tax reforms and civil servant performance criteria have played in shaping the development
strategies of Chinese cities.
1. Kyung-sup Chang. 2022. The Logic of Compressed Modernity. Newark: Polity Press. ISBN:
9781509553297, selections.
Related readings:
1. Shiuh-shen Chien and Max D. Woodworth. 2018. “China’s Urban Speed Machine: The
Politics of Speed and Time in a Period of Rapid Urban Growth.” International Journal of
Urban and Regional Research 42:723–737. https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-2427.12610.
2. Lei Wang, Cuz Potter, and Zhigang Li. 2014. “Crisis-induced reform, state-market re-
lations, and entrepreneurial urban growth in China.” Habitat International 41 (1): 50–57.
Week 12 (05/19): Building cities, building economies
This class will examine the relationship between housing and national growth strategies. In
particular, we will explore compare the role of the Korean state with that of the Singaporean
state in housing provision.
1. Bae-Gyoon Park. 1998. “Where Do Tigers Sleep at Night? The State’s Role in Housing
Policy in South Korea and Singapore.” Economic Geography 74 (3): 272–288. https://doi.
org/10.1111/j.1944-8287.1998.tb00116.x.
Week 13 (05/26): Global and entrepreneurial cities
This class will explore the evolution of world city networks over the course of globalization.
Particular attention will be paid to the rise of Asian cities like Seoul and Shanghai in this net-
work. This class will explore how globalization’s decentralization has driven cities to become
entrepreneurial entities that compete to attract residents, visitors, and firms.
1. Richard Child Hill and June Woo Kim. 2000. “Global Cities and Developmental States:
New York, Tokyo and Seoul.” Urban Studies 37, no. 12 (November): 2167–2195. https:
//doi.org/10.1080/00420980020002760.
Week 14 (06/02): Periurbanization, deindustrialization, and gentrification
In the process of economic development, successful cities tend to lose manufacturing es-
tablishments to other cities with lower labor and land costs. They also tend to expand into
6
agricultural land. As a result, industrial districts are abandoned and degenerate while farm-
lands are paved over. This class will explore efforts to regenerate declining neighborhoods,
drawing on the success of Seoul’s Cheonggyechun restoration. Using examples of Hanoi and
Hong Kong, the class will also ask whether the concept of gentrification is applicable in Asia.
1. Hyun Bang Shin. 2009. “Property-based redevelopment and gentrification: The case of
Seoul, South Korea.” Geoforum 40 (5): 906–917. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geoforum.
2009.06.009.
Week 15 (06/09): Socio-spatial change during East Asian industrialization
As populations increase and become more dense and industrialization alters work patterns,
our social relations change. This class will explore how industrialization and urbanization
generate new freedoms, new constraints, and new communities.
1. Kyung-sup Chang. 2022. The Logic of Compressed Modernity. Newark: Polity Press. ISBN:
9781509553297, chapter 7.
Related readings:
1. Anne Allison. 2013. Precarious Japan. Durham: Duke University Press, chapter 2.
2. Kyung-Sup Chang. 1999. “Compressed modernity and its discontents: South Korean so-
ciety in transtion.” Economy and Society 28, no. 1 (February): 30–55. ISSN: 1469-5766.
https://doi.org/10.1080/03085149900000023.

판적·융합적·창의적 사고 능력을 함양하고, 나아가 새롭고 다양한 관점에서 
문제의식을 생성하며 타인과의 소통 및 협력을 통해 문제를 해결할 수 있
도록 하는 것이 이 교과의 목표이다. 이를 위해 플립트 클래스(Flipped 
Class) 기반의 학습자 중심 교수학습 방법을 도입하여, 질문 중심 학습
(QBL: Question Based Learning)과 토론 및 발표를 통해 학습자가 배
움의 주체가 될 수 있도록 한다.

[과목개요] 
 
본 과목은 26 학년도 문과대 독어독문학과 신입생에게 수강 우선권이 있는 독일어 집중 
강좌로서 [독일어1] - 학수번호 GERM171 - 과 세트로 묶여 운영된다. 
[교양독일어1]을 수강하는 학생은 [독일어I]과목을 반드시 동일 학기에 함께 수강하여야 
하며 그러할 때에만 교재의 내용을 온전하게 체계적으로 학습할 수 있다. [교양독일어1]에 
다섯 시간, [독일어1]에 세 시간, 이렇게 일주일에 총 여덟 시간의 수업 시수를 
배정함으로써 독어독문학과 신입생들이 전공언어에 대해 견고한 기초지식과 실질적인 
독어구사력을 갖추도록 하는데 본 세트 강좌의 취지가 있다. [독일어I]과 [교양독일어1]은 
따라서 수업 운영방식과 교재가 동일하며 두 강좌를 세트로 신청할 때에 비로소 외국어 
학습과 평가를 위한 유럽연합 공통 참조기준 (The Common European Framework of Reference for 
Language CEFR)이 정한 독일어 A1 단계의 습득이 가능하다. 
학수번호 끝 괄호 안의 분반번호 (02)는 - GERM171(02)과 GERM161(02)-
독어독문학과 26 학번 가운데 짝수학번에 해당하는 학생들이 우선 수강생 그룹임을 
의미한다. 26 학번 이전 학생 가운데 [전공독어1] 또는 [교양독일어초급]을 미처 이수하지 
못했거나 재수강을 원하는 학생도 수강을 신청할 수 있지만 기존 교육기관에서 이미 
 
2
독일어를 학습한 수강생의 경우, A1 단계의 교재는 학습동기 부여에 다소 부족함이 있을 
것이다. 하지만 다년간의 경험을 통해 확인한 바에 따르면, 기존 학습자라 하더라도 소위 
입시를 위한 독일어 학습의 결과, 어휘나 문법면에서 그다지 체계적이지 않은 지식을 보이는 
학생들이 있는 것이 사실이다. 기존 학습자라 하더라도 성실하게 수업에 참여하여 자신에게 
최대한 이익이 되도록 수업을 이용해야 하며 조별 또는 파트너 과제를 수행할 때 교수자의 
Assistant*in 으로 조력할 수 있으리라 기대한다. 
세트강좌 [독일어I] & [교양독일어1]은 세계화 시대의 교양인에게 요구되는 제2 외국어, 그 
가운데 유럽연합(EU)의 정치.경제적 핵심국가인 독일의 언어를 학습하고 독일, 
오스트리아와 스위스로 대표되는 독일어권의 문화를 소개하는 과목이다. 이 과목은 읽기, 
말하기, 듣기, 쓰기 그리고 어휘와 문법으로 대표되는 외국어 기초 구사능력 뿐만 아니라 
일상 생활 속 문화간 차이 및 독일의 문화적 특징도 다룬다. 해당 언어권에 대한 문화 
지식과 이해는 올바른 언어 구사력 습득과 매우 밀접한 관계에 있다. 본 과목의 교재는 독일 
Klett 출판사에서 발행한 [Netzwerk neu A1]이며 여기 A1 는 “외국어 학습과 평가를 
위한 유럽연합 공통 참조기준 (The Common European Framework of Reference for Language 
CEFR)”이 정한 독일어 입문 기초 단계에 해당한다. 흔히 [Beginner] 단계라고 일컬어지며 
보통 어학원 등에서 A1.1 와 A1.2 로 나뉘어 수업이 이루어지기도 하지만 이번 학기 우리는 
세트 강좌 시스템을 이용해 총 12 과에 이르는 A1 단계 전체를 학습한다. 
 
 
[학습목표] 
 
본 강좌의 목표는 독일어의 기본 문법을 체계적으로 정리하고 일상 어휘와 구문을 
효과적으로 습득, 기초 회화를 가능하게 하고 A1 수준의 듣기, 말하기, 쓰기, 읽기 등을 
다양한 방식으로 보완하여 독일어 구사력 전반을 향상시키는데 있다. 수업 효과를 고려해 
멀티미디어를 비롯한 인터넷 관련 사이트와 다양한 놀이방법을 통해 어휘와 표현을 
학습한다. 수업은 독일어로 진행되지만 초보 단계부터 단계적으로 진행되는 만큼 처음 
배우는 학습자도 적극적으로 참여하고 성실하게 과제를 수행한다면 수강 가능하다. 
 
이 과목을 성공적으로 수강한 학생은 다음과 같은 것을 수행할 수 있다: 
1. 독일어 낱말과 문장을 정확한 발음으로 소리 낼 수 있다; 
2. 발음규칙에 따라 처음 보는 낱말도 정확하게 소리 내어 발음할 수 있다; 
3. 처음 듣는 낱말도 발음규칙에 따라 받아쓸 수 있다; 
 
3
4. 다양한 인사말을 할 수 있다 (Kapitel 1); 
5. 기본 신상에 관한 질문 – 이름, 직업, 나이 등 – 을 이해하고 답할 수 있다; 
6. 독어로 숫자를 표현할 수 있고 시간 및 날짜를 표현할 수 있다; 
7. 제 3 자의 신상에 관해 묻고 답할 수 있다; 
8. sein(to be), haben(to have) 동사의 형태변화를 익혀 정확하게 구사할 수 있다; 
9. 동사의 어미를 인칭에 따라 변화시킬 수 있다 (Kapitel 2); 
10. 유럽 지도에서 독일어권 국가를 찾을 수 있고 주변 국가를 독어로 표현할 수 있다; 
11. 독일어권 나라에서 원하는 물건을 구입하고 필요한 정보를 물어 얻을 수 있다; 
12. 여가와 취미에 관해 묻고 답할 수 있다; 
13. 독일어권 출신의 유명인사 및 관심 있는 인물에 대해 독일어로 소개할 수 있다; 
14. 주거관련 어휘를 익히고 본인의 주거환경에 대해 간단히 묘사할 수 있다; 
15. 현지에서 집을 구할 수 있다 (기숙사 등) (Kapitel 3); 
16. 서술적 형용사 및 부정문을 적절하게 구사할 수 있다; 
17. 불규칙 동사를 형태변화 시킬 수 있다; 
18. 명령형을 이용하여 청유의 표현을 할 수 있다; 
19. 다양한 의문문의 종류와 문법적 특징을 이해한다 (Kapitel 4); 
20. 식당에서 간단한 음식을 주문할 수 있다; 
21. 본인의 식생활에 대해 설명할 수 있다; 
22. 간단한 편지 및 E-Mail 을 쓸 수 있고 서식을 이해한다 (Kapitel 5); 
23. 장소관련 전치사를 적절하게 구사할 수 있다; 
24. 시간관련 전치사를 적절하게 구사할 수 있다; 
25. 과거 사실을 표현하는 구문을 만들고 이해할 수 있다; 
26. 현재완료 구문을 만들 수 있다 (Kapitel 6);

[평가방법] 
 
1. 출석: 출석은 수업 시작과 동시에 교수자가 확인해서 엑셀파일에 체크한다. 출석은 전체 
평가 총점의 10%를 차지한다. 수업 시작 15분 이후의 입실은 지각이며 사실 지각 자체
는 - 습관적인 것이 아니라면 - 양해의 여지가 있다. 그보다 심각한 것은 지각생의 태도
이다. 수업에 방해가 될 정도로 소음을 내며 입실하는 경우가 있는데 반드시 지양되어야 
할 것으로 본다. 지각 자체는 타인에게 손해를 입히지 않지만 부주의한 소음으로 타인의 
집중력을 흩트리는 것은 글로벌 매너에 심각하게 어긋나기 때문이다. 결석은 불가피한 사
안이 있을 때 미리 이메일을 통해 양해를 구할 것을 권고하며 이 때 소위 
entschuldigt/excused가 가능하다. 여학생들을 배려하는 [유고결석] 제도는 한 학기 최
대 2회까지만 인정한다. 
2. 참여도: 출석이 성실하다 해도 수업에 집중하지 않거나 참여도가 낮다면 목적한 성과를 
이루기 어렵다. 본 과목의 특성상 파트너와 하는 과제와 그룹별 과제가 수시로 주어지는데 
타인과의 소통이 중요하고 공조해야 하는 형식의 수행과제에 적극적으로 참여하는 것이 
매우 중요하다. 다양하고 적극적으로 질문을 하는 것 또한 높은 참여도를 인정받는데 중요
하다. 이와 같은 이유에서 출석과 별도로 참여도를 평가 기준으로 삼아 전체 총점의 6%
를 할애한다. 
3. 수시과제: 수시과제는 평가 총점의 8%를 차지한다. 정답 유무보다 중요한 것은 제출기한
을 지키는 것이고 모든 과제는 교정을 거쳐 제출자에게 전달된다. 쓰기과제는 요구된 분량
과 내용을 준수하여 작성하는 것이 중요하다. 과제물의 제출과 평가에 관해서는 위 과제물 
코너 참조. 
4. 필기시험(3회): 기존의 중간과 기말시험이라는 두 번의 필기시험 대신 교재의 1과부터 3

COURSE DESCRIPTION  
China has become one of the most consequential arenas for global business strategy. Firms 
operating in China or working with Chinese partners must navigate intense competition, rapid 
technological change, strong state involvement, and growing geopolitical tensions. At the 
same time, Chinese firms are emerging as global strategists, reshaping industries such as 
electric vehicles, digital platforms, semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and consumer goods. 
This course examines business strategy in the Chinese context, focusing on how firms 
formulate, adapt, and execute strategy under distinctive institutional, political, and 
competitive conditions. Rather than treating China simply as a large market, the course 
presents China as a strategy laboratory, a setting in which firms experiment with scale, speed, 
ecosystem competition, and complex state–market interactions. 
The course is organized into a clear three-part structure. 
Part 1 focuses on understanding China as a strategic environment. Students will learn how 
China’s economic system, government policies, geography, infrastructure, culture, digital 
platforms, innovation system, and ESG expectations shape firm behavior and strategic 
decision-making. This part provides the foundation for understanding why business strategy 
in China often differs from that in Western economies. 
Part 2 examines Chinese firms going global. Students will study how China participates in 
globalization and why Chinese companies expand into foreign markets. The course explores 
how Chinese firms internationalize, what competitive advantages they bring, and what risks 
and challenges they face, including political resistance, cultural differences, and global 
competition. 
Part 3 focuses on foreign multinational firms operating in China. Students will analyze why 
foreign companies enter the Chinese market, how they adapt their strategies to local 
conditions, and what challenges they encounter related to regulation, competition, and 
geopolitics. This part also discusses why some foreign firms succeed in China while others 
struggle or choose to exit. 
Throughout the course, students will engage with real-world examples and cases to develop 
a practical understanding of strategic decision-making involving China. By the end of the 
course, students will be better prepared to analyze business opportunities and risks related to 
China, whether as managers, entrepreneurs, or future decision-makers in the global economy. 
This course is designed for students interested in business strategy, international management, 
and emerging markets. It is particularly relevant for those considering careers in consulting, 
entrepreneurship, multinational corporations, policy-related organizations, or firms engaging 
with China. No prior background in China studies is required.

Self-report – Individual (10%+10%) 
Both the midterm and final exams will be replaced by self-report. Students are required to 
write a report reflecting on what they have learned throughout the course up to the 
submission date, particularly their identified strengths and weaknesses. They should also 
create a personal improvement plan for future learning and provide an overall self-
assessment of their performance. Detailed instructions on how to write and submit the 
report will be available on the LMS. 
Class Participation – Individual (20%)  
Class participation does not mean the attendance check merely; It also includes the active 
contribution to the class discussion. The contribution can help the conversation go forward. 
Therefore, participation scores (10 points) will be based on two components: base 
attendance (BA, 5 points) and active participation (AP, 5 points).  
 
Base Attendance (10%) 
 
Attendance will be checked every class since the second week, and students are 
allowed up to THREE legitimate absences without penalty. For any non-legitimate 
absences or additional absences beyond the three allowed, points will be deducted 
from the overall attendance score. The deduction increases progressively: 1 
absence results in a 1-point deduction, 2 absences result in a 2-point deduction, and 
so on. If you have no non-legitimate or excessive absences but do not participate at 
all, you will receive the base attendance score of 5 points. 
 
Student will FAIL the course automatically when BA reaches 0.  
 
Legitimate absences must apply officially on the Korea University portal. 
 
Active Participation (10%) 
 
Active participation can be achieved through two methods: (1) in-class 
participation, by engaging in discussions, answering questions, contributing 
personal insights or external knowledge, and/or asking questions that advance the 
conversation; and (2) online participation, by initiating or contributing to discussions 
related to class topics in a meaningful way. For online discussions, contributions 
should be made within 24hours of the specific lecture or discussion to be eligible for 
grading. While you may continue the discussion beyond this timeframe, comments 
made after it will not be graded. Additionally, simply agreeing with others’ ideas will 
not earn participation points. 
 
To earn the full participation score of 5, students must be recognized for active 
participation 10 or more times across in-class and online methods. Online and 
offline participation for the same-day lecture is considered as one participation. The 
score decreases incrementally based on the frequency of participation, with 9 
participations earning 4.5, 8 earning 4, and so forth, down to 0 points for 0 
participation.  
Case Discussion – Group (20%)  
 
Each group will take the role of a case discussion leader. The leading discussion group 
should consider around 20-25mins of presentations and no less than 20 mins of active 
discussions with other classmates with your discussion questions. The presentation 
must have a visual aid (PowerPoints or equivalent ones). The presentation slides should 
be submitted to the LMS no later than 9 pm the day before the designated case 
discussion session. Detailed requirements will be given later. 
 
All members are required to present.    
Final Project – Group (35%) 
The final project requires writing a comparative analysis report on two companies: one from 
China and one from another country/region outside China. These two companies must 
operate in the same product category to ensure comparability. For example, Tesla and BYD 
are both electric vehicle (EV) manufacturers, making them suitable for a comparison of their 
business strategies. Following the comparative analysis, each group should propose 2–3 
targeted recommendations for each company to further enhance its competitive advantage 
in the industry. Submission requirements for the final project include a project proposal 
(which will be discussed in oral consultations and is ungraded), a final presentation, and a 
written report. The project grade will be based on two components: the quality of the 
presentation (20%) and the content and analysis of the written report (15%). 
 
Requirements for final project presentation:  
• 
Each group should present for 25-30mins, followed by 5 mins of comments from peers 
and the instructor. 
• 
The presentation should be well organized.  
• 
All members are required to present. 
• 
The visual aids should be submitted to the LMS no later than 9 pm the day before the 
first presentation day.  
 
Requirements for report: 
• 
The report should be no more than 20 pages all-inclusive, preferably in PDF or MS Word 
format.  
• 
The report should be submitted to the LMS no later than 9 pm on the final exam day.  
• 
The detailed formats and content requirements will be given on the LMS later.  
 
Peer Evaluation – Individual (5%) 
Each student should evaluate their team members in the final session, using a 5-point Likert 
scale. The peer evaluation score will be calculated as the average of the scores given by 
team members. If you do not complete the peer evaluation, you will receive a score of 0, 
even if others evaluate you. Also, if your average peer evaluation score is below 2.5, all your 
group-based project scores will be adjusted accordingly. 
Bonus  
• 
If your average peer evaluation score is among the top 10% of the class, you will 
receive a 0.5-point bonus. 
• 
If you are recognized as an outstanding student (10% of the class) by the instructor, 
you will receive a 0.5-point bonus. 
• 
If you receive full BA and PA scores simultaneously, you will receive a 0.5-point 
bonus. 
• 
During the semester, bonus points may also be awarded during class based on the 
results of in-class exercises. 
Although bonus points can be accumulated, the maximum total bonus is 2 points.    
Group Formation   
A group will be formed in week 2. Students need to assign themselves to a group. Each team 
can have up to 4-6 members (*this is subject to change depending on the final number of 
enrollments). Students should not switch teams between tasks or throughout the course. 
 
NO Make-up Exams 
You will score 0 if you miss the midterm and the final exam for reasons not accepted by KU.  
TEXTBOOKS AND CASES

• 
Cases: The Harvard Business School cases can be purchased online. (A course package 
will be created on https://hbsp.harvard.edu/home/ . You can purchase later with a 
discount.)  
*By choosing this course, you acknowledge that you will purchase the required cases to 
complete the assigned tasks. 
CLASS RULES

• Treat classmates and instructors with respect. Disruptive behavior, including side 
conversations, inappropriate language, or unprofessional conduct, will not be tolerated.  
o The following behaviors are considered disrespectful: 
1. Arriving late, leaving the classroom during the session (except in emergencies), 
or leaving early. 
2. Creating noise by typing on a laptop or chatting on a phone or laptop. 
3. Talking to peers while others are speaking or making comments. 
• Plagiarism, cheating, or other forms of academic dishonesty will not be tolerated and will

MATH321: Algebra I (Semester 01-2026)
1. Instructor: Prof. Sangjib Kim (김상집, sk23@korea.ac.kr)
2. Lecture: Every Tuesday and Thursday 10:30-11:45am (Asan Science Hall 111)
3. Oﬃce: Asan Science Hall 521
4. Oﬃce Hours: To be announced in class
1
Course Overview 수업개요
This course introduces the fundamental structures of modern algebra, including groups, rings, and ﬁelds. Em-
phasis will be placed on developing abstract reasoning, proof-writing skills, and understanding the applications
of algebraic structures.
대수학에서는, 선형대수에서의벡터공간처럼, 추상적인대수적대상을정의하고이들의성질을유도합니다.
대수학I에서는군이론과환이론을집중적으로공부합니다.
2
Prerequisites 선수과목
• Linear Algebra I & II
• Proof-based courses for 2nd year math students (e.g., Analysis I & II, Number theory etc.)
We assume that students are prepared for the approach to handling abstract objects and the method of
deriving mathematical properties from deﬁnitions and axioms covered in the above mentioned courses. For
example, we assume that all students have thoroughly studied and can freely use the material in the following
resource (Speciﬁcally, Chapters 1–2 and 4–12): https://richardhammack.github.io/BookOfProof/Main.pdf
• 선형대수I & II
• 정의-정리-증명형식의수학과2학년과목들(해석학I & II, 정수론등)
위에언급한과목시간에통해연습하는추상적대상을다루는방식, 정의와공리로부터수학적성질을유도
하는방식에대한연습경험이있다고가정합니다.이를테면, 모든수강생이다음자료의1-2단원, 4-12단원내용을
충분히숙지하고자유롭게활용할수있다고가정합니다. https://richardhammack.github.io/BookOfProof/
Main.pdf
3
Textbook 교재
A First Course in Abstract Algebra (7th edition) by John B. Fraleigh
4
Assessment and Grades 평가
1. 이과목학점을위한평가항목은다음과같습니다. Your ﬁnal grade will be based on your scores of
Class activity (10) + Midterm exam (45) + Final exam (45).
100 ≥A+, A ≥90;
90 > B+, B ≥77;
77 > C+, C ≥60;
60 > D+, D, F.
2. Attendance & Class activity: Your attendance is important to your success in this class. Attendance is
mandatory and will be recorded at every class meeting. If you are unable to attend due to illness or other
circumstances, please notify me via email (sk23@korea.ac.kr). It is important to note that students are
accountable for all course materials, regardless of their absence from class.
You will be asked to submit your answers to daily questions after each lecture. Eight or more unexcused
absences including non-participation in these class activities will result in a grade of F.

수업활동class activity은수업내용과관련된질의응답, 토론, 퀴즈, 발표, 보고서제출등으로기본적인

Office Hours: by appointment 
 
Course Description 
This course aims to help the students obtain a comprehensive and broad understanding of the 
characteristics of effective and potent writing by reading and examining examples of such 
writing. There will be no assignments requiring you to turn in what we refer to as essays in a 
traditional format; instead, you'll have ample opportunities to ‘read’ other academic and 
journalistic essays and ‘analyze’ their rhetorical devices, style, and structure. 
 
Course Rules  
• Recordings of the class are not allowed.  
• I’ll do my best to respond to your email within 48 hours; if I don’t, please send me a 
reminder. However, I’d appreciate it if you can talk to me directly in-person after the class, 
particularly when you have urgent issues that need my support or guidance.

* Total points with decimals will be rounded to the nearest one. For example, 89.5 will be 
rounded to 90. 89.4 will be rounded to 89.  
*Final grades are non-negotiable. 
 
Attendance  
• 
Each student has one free absence to be used at any time. No questions will be asked 
about the first absence; this should be reserved for emergencies (such as mental health 
care, family emergency, appointment/interview, and/or transportation issues).   Beyond 
one free absence, each missed class will result in a one-point deduction. 
• 
Tardiness: I will take attendance at the beginning of the lecture. Please arrive on time for 
class. If you are more than 10 minutes late, you will get a tardy point. Two tardy points 
will equal one absence. If you arrive late, you must check in with me after the lecture in 
person, not via e-mail, so I can mark you tardy. If you don't get the attendance/tardy point 
on the day the lecture takes place in the classroom, that is considered an absence. 
• 
Excused absences can only be granted when you apply for them via the university system 
with a supporting document such as Military affairs such as Army Reserve training or 
duty document or any other university-approved documents. Anything like job interviews 
is not qualified as an excused absence.  
• 
University Policy: “No grade will be given for more than -1/3 absences, except for 
excused absences, which require at least 1/2 actual attendance.” This means that 10 
unexcused absences will result in a failing mark for this course. Even when all of your 
absences are excused, you must attend at least 15 classes to have the opportunity to 
receive a passing grade.  
Participation will be assessed based on your in-class engagement and professionalism.  
The criteria include: 
• 
Reach out to the instructor in a timely and respectful manner when consultation is 
needed. 
• 
Use digital devices thoughtfully and appropriately during class session. 
• 
Do your best to show a good grasp of the assigned texts through in-class activities and 
10-minute reviews administered throughout the semester. 
• 
While you may disagree with some of the theories we are learning, you should 
demonstrate your capacity to interact with the perspectives different from your own 
carefully and seriously.

Disclosure
 이 과목은 2026년  중국 뉴스와 언론에서 주목하는 시사적인 문제들을 다룬 기사를 접하
고 학생들과 함께 중국어로 토론하여 자신만의 관점을 키우고자 한다. 학생들은 매주 정치 
뉴스, 경제 뉴스, 국제 이슈, 교육 문제, 문화생활, 중국과 타이완 관계, 한중 뉴스 등의 
다양한 주제를 통해 중국을 바라보는 시선과 심오한 통찰력을 배양하게 한다.
This course engages with articles covering current issues highlighted in Chinese 
news and media in 2026, encouraging students to discuss them in Chinese and 
develop their own perspectives. Each week, students will explore diverse topics 
such as political news, economic developments, international affairs, educational 
issues, cultural life, relations between China and Taiwan, and Korea–China 
news, thereby cultivating a deeper understanding and insightful viewpoints on 
China.

∙ [학습윤리]
 -대학의 목적과 본교 교육이념에 따라 성실하고 정직한 마음과 열정적인 태도로 모든 학습에 적극적으로 참여
 -고등교육을 받는 교양인으로서의 품위를 유지하며, 도덕적 민감성을 바탕으로 창의적 학문탐구에 정
진
 -교육활동과 관련하여 교원 및 동료학생과의 약속을 성실히 이행
 -교원과 동료학생의 인격을 존중하고 기본적인 예의를 준수
 -학문 공동체의 일원으로서 학문의 진실성을 지키며, 본교 「AI 활용 가이드」를 성실히 준수
 -강의계획서 등을 충분히 탐색하여 자신의 학문적 탐구 방향과 미래 비전에 부합하는 교과목을 신중
히 선택
 -매 수업에 적극적으로 임할 수 있도록 수업자료를 사전에 탐독하고 준비
 -정해진 수업시간을 준수하며, 결석·지각·중도 이탈 등으로 타인의 학습을 방해하지 않도록 유의
 -출석 관련 위계행위(대리출석 등) 금지
 -모든 수업활동에 주도적으로 참여하고, 토론·질의응답 등을 통해 교과목 이해와 통찰력 향상에 노력
 -과제는 스스로 성실하게 작성하며, 인용한 모든 자료(책·논문·인터넷·AI 등)는 변조나 왜곡 없이 출처를 명확히 표기
 -협동학습의 경우 자신의 역할을 책임감 있게 수행하여 공동의 학습성과 달성에 기여
 -시험의 목적과 의미를 이해하고, 부정행위 없이 정직하게 응시
 -한 학기 수강한 교과목의 교육 품질 향상을 위해 강의평가에 성실히 참여하고, 개선이 필요한 사항을 충실히 서술
∙ [실험실습 안전]
 -연구실 안전환경 조성에 관한 법률 제20조(교육·훈련)에 의거, 연구실안전법이 적용되는 과학기술분
야 대상 학과에 소속된 연구활동종사자는 매학기 일정시간의 안전교육을 이수하여야 하므로 실험·실습
을 수강하는 모든 대상학과 학부생 및 대학원생은 교육참여 필수
 -신규교육(신입생 2시간), 정기교육(고위험학과 학기별 6시간, 저위험학과 학기별 3시간)

교과목 개요 및 학습 목표  
 
개요: 빅데이터, 블록 체인, 사물 인터넷(IoT)에서 인공지능(AI)에 이르기까지 새로운 
디지털 기술 혁신은 사람들의 생활양식뿐만 아니라 가치관마저 변화시키고 있다. 이 
디지털 전환은 우리 일상의 먹고 사는 문제에 장기적으로 어떤 영향을 미칠 것이며, 그것은 
우리에게 긍정적인 것일까? 본 과목은 경제와 사회를 분석하기 위한 정치경제학(political 
economy)의 융합적 개념들을 통해 디지털 전환(digital transformation)이 초래한 새로운 
사회경제적 양상들을 이해하고자 한다. 디지털 사유(digital thinking)란 기본적으로 모든 
것들을 숫자로 코드화하여 사유하는 변환 과정을 말한다. 이는 언어를 통한 정신적 사고 
활동의 물질적 환원을 용이하게 만든다. 우리가 사는 세계를 양적으로 코드화하여 
표현하고 구성하는 디지털화(digitization)와 그에 따른 사회 양상의 변화는, 인공지능 
기술발전에 따른 노동 형태의 변화, 새로운 교환 매개 또는 가치 저장 형식의 출현, 계산 
능력의 확대와 인간 합리성, 디지털 전환이 야기한 경제적 분배 문제 등 인류가 처한 
정치·경제·생태문제들에 대해 새로운 시각을 요구하고 있다. 여기서 디지털 사유와 
정치경제학의 접목은 이중적 의미를 갖는다. 첫째, ‘코드화’된 사회경제적 양식들을 
정치경제적으로 ‘문자화(해석)’하는 것이다. 둘째, 새로운 하이브리드 양식의 출현에 
조응하여 기존의 개념들을 확장하고 재구성할 필요성이 제기된다. 본 수업은 정치경제학적 
개념을 바탕으로 디지털 전환 사회에서 사회경제적 양식의 진화와 그 대안들에 대해 
학생들이 스스로 사고할 수 있는 개념적 틀을 학습하는데 그 목적을 둔다.  
 
학습 목표: 본 수업이 학생들에게 기대하는 학습 목표는 다음과 같다. 첫째, 경제학, 사회학, 
정치학, 심리학 등 사회과학에서 자주 접하게 되는 정치경제학의 기본 개념을 학습한다. 
둘째, 인간이 만들어낸 디지털 기술이 인간의 노동과 사고 활동에 어떤 피드백 효과를 
가져오는지 이해한다. 셋째, 데이터가 정보로 전환되어 경제적 의사결정으로 나타나는

세부 강의 내용 
 
1. 강의 소개 및 수업 계획  
전체 강의를 개관하고, 한 학기 동안 수업 계획에 대해 설명한다. 본 과목의 문제의식을 
공유하면서 이 수업을 통해 얻고자 하는 것은 무엇인지 수강생들과 함께 논의한다. 
 
2. 디지털 전환의 사회경제적 특성: 개관  
플랫폼 양면 시장(two-sided market)의 출현과 네트워크화, 복잡성의 증가, 가상 
세계(virtual world)의 확대와 같은 디지털 전환의 사회경제적 특성에 대해 개괄적으로 
살펴본다. 
 
3. 인공지능 기술 발전은 인간 노동을 사라지게 만들 것인가?  
디지털 기술 혁신에 따른 노동시장의 변화에 대해서는 두 가지 상반된 경제학적 시각이 
존재한다. 낙관적 시각은 기술 진보가 노동 생산성을 향상시켜 노동 수요를 증가시킬 
것이라고 전망한다. 반면, 비관적 전망은 인공지능 기술발전이 노동 대체를 초래하여 
일자리 감소를 야기할 것이라고 주장한다. 디지털 기술 변화는 과연 인간 노동의 형태와 
숙련도에 어떤 영향을 미칠 것인가? 인공지능 기술발전은 인간 노동의 소멸을 초래할 
것인가? 인공지능도 ‘노동’을 한다고 말할 수 있는가? 육체 노동이 줄어들고 ‘비물질 노동’이 
지배적인 사회, 나아가 인지 노동 마저도 인공지능이 대신하는 사회에서, 인간 ‘소외’는 
어떤 양상을 띠게 될 것인가? 일자리와 소득 안정성은 어떻게 확보될 수 있는가? 
 
4. 정보는 재화인가?  
데이터와 정보의 차이는 무엇인가? 지식은 정보와 어떻게 구별되는가? 정보는 재화(예, 
디지털 인공물)인가? 그렇다면, 정보재(information goods)의 가치는 어떻게 산정될 수 
있는가? 이는 문화, 지식 서비스 등 지적 재화를 생산하는 (비물질) 노동과는 어떻게 
관련되는가? 한 사회 내에서 데이터가 정보로 가공되고, 그 정보가 배분되어 정치경제적 
의사결정으로 나타나는 과정을 살펴보면서 지식의 유통과 통계적 사고에 대해 생각해 본다.  
 
5. 네트워크는 우리의 합리성을 향상시킬까?  
경제학이 채택하고 있는 방법론적 개인주의(methodological individualism)은 경제 
주체들이 충분히 ‘합리적’이고 ‘독립적’ 의사결정을 내린다고 가정한다. 하지만 제한적 
합리성(bounded rationality), 정보 폭포(informational cascades), 고차원 기대(higher-
order expectations) 개념들은, 인간의 인지적 제약(cognitive limitations, i.e., “limitations 
of both knowledge and computational capacity”), 정보 외부성(informational externality) 
등으로 인해, 현실에서 우리의 의사결정이 편향되거나 타인의 행동에 영향 받는다는 점을 
이론적으로 설명한다. 디지털 네트워크 사회에서 우리의 합리적 의사결정은 어떻게 
이루어지는가? 계산가능성과 네트워크의 복잡성(complexity)이란 무엇인가? 가용한 
정보가 많다는 것이 과연 우리의 합리성을 증진시킬 것인가? 
 
6. 디지털 화폐의 운명은?  
화폐란 무엇인가? 표준화된 경제학 교과서는 화폐가 교환의 매개(지불), 가치의 저장, 
그리고 가치의 척도, 이 세 가지 기능을 수행하는 것으로 정의한다. 암호 화폐, NFT 와 같은 
새로운 교환 매개 또는 가치 저장 형식의 등장과 가상 자산 시장의 확대 등 일련의 디지털 
기술 혁신은 화폐 금융시장을 어떻게 변화시키고 있으며, 그 의미는 무엇인가? 디지털

7. (종합) 디지털 기술 혁신은 공정한 분배와 지속 가능한 발전을 약속하는가?  
디지털 기술 변화와 플랫폼 모델은 경제에 새로운 생산 및 유통 형식을 도입하여 
거래비용을 절감시키고 효율성을 제고시키는 반면, 전통적 산업구조와 갈등을 일으키거나 
자연 독점을 발생시키기도 한다. 디지털 기술 혁신은 구체적으로 지식의 소유와 관련된 
재산권, 소득 불평등 등 경제적 분배를 둘러싼 다양한 논쟁을 불러일으키고 있다. 디지털 
정보 격차는 사회경제적 불평등에 어떤 영향을 미칠 것인가? 디지털 기반 서비스를 
중심으로 한 ‘공유 경제’는 과연 정보의 배타적 독점을 막고, 양극화를 해소함으로써 호혜적 
교환 원리에 입각한 사회적 경제를 지향하는가? 우리는 디지털 기술 혁신을 통해 지속 
가능한 발전(sustainable development)을 달성할 수 있을 것인가? 디지털 전환은 우리가 
자연 생태계를 보존하는 가운데 경제적 재생산을 유지할 수 있는 더 나은 대안을 제시할 수 
있을 것인가? 
 
8. 협업 연구 아이디어 발표 및 토론  
수강생들은 한 학기 동안 디지털 전환과 정치경제학적 주제들을 연결시켜 자신들의 
문제의식을 설정하고 그에 대한 연구보고서를 작성하는 과제를 수행한다. 본 과목의 
후반부는 수강생들이 자신들의 협업 연구 아이디어를 다양한 전공의 학생들과 공유하고 
그들의 의견을 청취하는 수업으로 진행된다. 이 과정을 통해 동료들의 의견을 반영하여 
자신들의 생각을 발전시키고 최종 연구보고서로 완성시킨다.

수업개요 및 목표 The Purpose and feature of the Class: 
 
1) Class participants understand the feature and concept of contemporary film and tel
evision criticism. 
2) Class participants practice “writing criticism about media” and understand the public feature of 
media criticism in this class.   
This course is recommended for junior and senior students because we examine serious and  
various humanities disciplines in this course.  
Fresh person and sophomore (any student below five semesters) are not suitable for this class. 
 
1) 강의참여자는 방송 및 영화비평의 특성과 개념을 이해한다. 
2) 강의참여자는 “미디어에 비평문을 쓰는 연습”을 하고 아울러 “미디어에 기고하는 비평문의 
공적인 성격”을 이해한다.  
강의시간에 다루는 내용이 전반적인 인문학적인 지식과 관련이 있기에 고학년 학생들에게만 
권장한다. 1, 2 학년 (4 학기 이하 등록) 학생은 아직 이 과목에 적합하지 않다. 
 
Class Management 
Class participants will be engaged in lecture, film screening, and discussion. 
In this semester, class participants watch five films (one short and four feature-length films) and 
send the class manager emails for comment or question on them.  
The class manager collects them and provides one’s response on a day.  
 
강의 진행 방식 
수업은 강의, 영화보기 및 토론으로 진행된다. 
강의 참여자는 총 다섯편의 작품 (단편 1, 장편 4)을 강의실에서 감상하고 강의 참여자는 작품에 
대한 질문을 강의진행자에게 보낸다.   
강의 진행자는 질문을 모아서 지정된 날짜에 응답한다.  
 
Evaluation and submission: Out of classroom examination with writing reviews 
 
1) Attendance 10. 
Attendance will be checked in class for offline class, if any. 
Absence without the class manager’s permission: -1 
Lateness or early departure without the class manager’s permission: -0.5 
Absences more than five times without the class manager’s permission will result in F grade.  
 
2) a short personal essay on a film or TV program 10, 0406. Monday. 300 - 400 words. 
A class participant chooses 1) one text (film, TV show, or OTT program) which was newly 
released and available in South Korea from Januar y 2026. Then, one write one’s own thought and 
impression about the text in a short personal essay.  
 
3) a short journalistic review 20, 0504. Monday. 300 - 400 words 
(the lengh of an article in newspaper, weekly magazine) 
A class participant may develop the short personal review to a short journalistic review w
hich is publishable through printed periodicals (including online media).  
S/he needs to choose other film or TV show or OTT program from Januar y, 2026 
for this assignment. 
 
4) a book review 30, 0601. Monday. 800 - 1200 words.

(the length of a column in a monthly or quarterly current issue magazine or a professional

A class participant may have one’s own opinion about an issue of popular culture, society, politi
cs,class, gender, race, ecology, ethics and so on. S/he integrate one’s opinion to one’s own

Office: LP-307, Tel: 3290-2812, Fax: 922-7220

· Course Information 
Class Room: LP-216

COURSE DESCRIPTION  
Design thinking is a creative and collaborative process that focuses on understanding the 
problem from the customer’s perspective. In this course, the concept of design thinking will be 
introduced within the context of digital innovation because no disruptive innovations can be 
made without understanding the customer’s needs and technology change. In today’s rapidly 
changing business environment, organizations face many challenges, which include disruptive 
technologies and economic pressures, as well as keeping up with changes in customer behavior. 
In this sense, design thinking provides an effective tool to cultivate an innovative thinker and 
uncover creative business opportunities. 
Therefore, this course is designed to provide two manners: (1) to understand and analyze 
the multiple, complex problems of information, systems, and design that you will encounter; and 
(2) to identify opportunities for designing better interactions, decision, and outcomes. More 
specifically, we will conduct two main themes, “design thinking”, and “digital innovation 
practice” to conduct a real problem-solving project in creating a digital innovation. During this 
class and project, you will learn how you can identify social design, innovation, information 
systems problems in the “design thinking” part with a variety of design discussions and exercises. 
In the “digital innovation practice” part, you will learn the ways of synthesizing people-centered 
design opportunities and creating tangible solutions. 
In order to do this, we will use three major activities in the class: (1) lecture with reading 
and discussion, (2) in-class exercises and presentation, and (3) real problem-solving project 
sessions. The reading and discussion sessions are assigned in order to increase your knowledge 
about the relevant issues. The in-class exercises and presentation will characterize how you can 
productively use specific techniques and tools presented this course. During the project sessions, 
________________________________________________________________________________

you will learn tangible techniques to organize a problem-solving project with these design 
thinking and digital innovation practice.  
 
TEACHING APPROACH  
Appropriate lectures, readings, presentation, and discussion for sharing different 
perspectives and diverse experiences are required to support respective topics. To do so, your 
interactive and participative attitude is essential during the semester. 
 
COURSE MATERIALS 
Most reading material and references will be provided during the class and made 
available on the LMS system, including course handouts. Readings and resources will be 
discussed in class in details. However, you can refer to the following supplemental books. 
o Brown, T. (2009). Change by design: How design thinking transforms organizations 
and inspires innovation. HarperBusiness. 
o Liedtka, J., Ogilvie, T. and Brozenske, R. (2014). The designing for growth field book: 
A step-by-step project guide. Columbia University Press. 
o Martin, R. (2009). The design of business: Why design thinking is the next competitive 
advantage. Harvard Business Review Press. 
o Rossman, J.R. and Duerden, M.D. (2019). Designing experiences. Columbia 
University Press. 
 
COURSE PROJECT AND ASSIGNMENTS 
Students will engage in a series of skill developing assignments that build upon each 
other throughout the duration of the course. The class will culminate in a final project that 
will allow students to apply what they have learned to a specific social and policy challenge 
they are passionate about. More specific details around course projects will be discussed in 
the first class. 
 
1. Class Participation and Attendance 
 
Class participation will be based on attendance, being on time, preparedness and 
contribution to class discussion. Students are required to attend all classes and to be on time. 
All students are expected to do the assigned readings before class and to participate in class 
discussions.  
 
2. Team Formation 
 
The team assignments will be done in a team of 5 students (depending on class size). 
Teams will engage in a semester-long and comprehensive real project. Teams will be formed 
in the second session of our class. In order to exactly evaluate the degree of contribution 
made by team members in a team, there will be a peer evaluation at the end of the semester. 
 
3. Ad-hoc based Assignment 
 
There will be a few individual and group assignments throughout the semester. Each 
assignment will be announced in class whenever necessary. Each student/team is asked to 
submit the answer of assignment during the class when it is due.

4. Final Team Project 
 
A final team presentation will be a key deliverable for this course. In each session, 
students will learn different tools and ways of thinking that advance project work on their 
design challenge and build toward the final presentation. Before the final presentation, each 
team will be asked to present their progress several times throughout the semester (refer to the 
course schedule). Highlights of the final presentation include at least: 
o Statement of the design challenge and overview of the problem solving approach 
o Insights based on the design research conducted 
o Key themes and opportunity areas drawn from research insights 
o Visualized concepts that address the opportunity areas 
o A plan to make the solution concepts actionable and measurable 
 
For each presentation, one team will be asked to make a 20 mins presentation using ppt file 
(15 mins PT + 5 mins Q&A) when it is due (see our course schedule). After the presentation, the 
class will discuss its related issues. Presentation materials should be uploaded to “Board -> 
Presentation and Report Submission Board” in LMS by the midnight before the class when it 
is due.
