Planetary Geology, EAES 423, Spring 2026 
 
 
Course Overview: In this course, we aim to explore planets, moons, asteroids, comets, and recently 
discovered exoplanets. Using the results observed through recent space telescopes, such as the James 
Webb telescope, we seek to understand the internal structure of various types of planets, ranging from 
rocky planets to giant gas planets. Additionally, we will delve into the formation of planets and moons 
through collisions. The course will introduce current topics and the latest findings from the scientific 
literature.  
The first class (class orientation) will be held via Zoom on Tuesday, March 3, at 9:00 AM (Seoul 
time). Please join the session using the link below. 
Topic: EAES 423, Class Orientation 
Time: Mar 3, 2026, 09:00 AM (Seoul) 
Join Zoom Meeting: 
https://korea-ac-kr.zoom.us/j/85874111181?pwd=h99fXBDIalc0zF6aABbw2rGBd33IQp.1 
 
 
Instructor: Donghoon Kim (707 Mediheal EES Hall) 
      Homepage: https://sites.google.com/view/dhkim1986/home 
 
Teaching assistant: Gunhee Lee (702 Mediheal EES Hall), gunee2922@korea.ac.kr  
 
Lecture: Tuesday and Thursday @ 9:00- 10:15  
 
Asan Science Hall Rm #111   
 
Office hours: Friday by appointment (02-3290-3185, donghoonkim@korea.ac.kr) 
 
Textbooks: Lecture Notes; No specific textbook for this course.  
 
Course requirements:  
Mid-term exam – 20%, Final exam – 40%, Oral presentation – 15%, Problem set(s) or quizzes – 20%, 
Attendance and Participation: 5%. 
If you miss more than 9 classes, then you will be failed, F automatically. Additionally, students who score 
below 30 out of 100 will also receive an F grade.  
There will be NO MAKE UP EXAMS.  
 
At the end of the course, groups of 2–3 students will give a class presentation based on a recent paper 
from the scientific literature. The presentations should be 10 minutes long, followed by 5 minutes for 
questions and discussion. A list of possible presentation papers will be provided. Grades will be based 
both on the quality of each group’s presentation and paper, as well as on individual participation in the 
discussion of other groups’ presentations. 
Prerequisites: General geology, Physical geology, and Earth Materials (Tectonics is highly 
recommended; beginning in 2026 Spring, it will also be a required prerequisite for Planetary Geology). 
One year of college-level chemistry or physics (preferably both) and calculus. You need to provide 
documentation proving that you have completed the prerequisite courses. For students from other 
departments or universities are welcome but they MUST provide proof of completion of prerequisite 
courses or alternative courses. If you have not completed the prerequisite courses, you are welcome to 
contact me in advance if you are interested in taking the class to discuss your eligibility.  
Special Opportunity: If any of you are interested in participating in laser-driven shock experiments using an 
X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL), up to three students will be supported to travel to SACLA XFEL 
(https://xfel.riken.jp/eng/sacla/index00.html) in Japan from July 7 to 9, 2026. 
This opportunity is available to students who volunteer and demonstrate a good attitude in class. Participation 
in this trip will not impact your grade, and no out-of-pocket expenses will be required from participating 
students. 
 
Academic Integrity: Each student must pursue his or her academic goals honestly and be personally 
accountable for all submitted work. Representing another person's work as your own is always wrong. 
Faculties are required to report any suspected instance of academic dishonesty to the Academic Judiciary.  
 
Critical incident management: Korea University expects students to respect the rights, privileges, and 
property of other people. Faculties are required to report to the Office of Judicial Affairs any disruptive 
behavior that interrupts their ability to teach, compromises the safety of the learning environment, and/or 
inhibits students' ability to learn.

서 디지털 인문학에 대한 관심을 가지기 위해 디지털 과거와 자료 문제 그리고 읽기와 텍스트성의 개념
부터 NOTEPAD ++를 활용한 데이터 세팅과 이를 위한 정규식 표현까지 이론과 실제를 살펴본다.
2. 교재 및 참고문헌
1. 수업 진행 후 blackboard 자료실에 한글 파일 탑재.
2. <디지털 인문학의 이해>, 김준연 외 18명, 고려대학교출판문화원 
3. 과제물
중간고사와 기말고사 모두 과제물로 대체한다.
4. 성적평가방법 및 기준
중간고사 30점 + 기말고사 40점 + 참여도 20점 + 출석 10점
2번 지각 시 1번 결석으로 간주. 1점씩 감점. 수업 태도와 관련하여 최대 10점까지 감점될 수 있다.

개요
이 수업에서는 인류 역사의 다양한 지적 성찰 및 실천적 가치를 종합적으
로 탐구하고, 이를 바탕으로 현재의 사회를 이해하고 미래의 변화에 대응
할 수 있는 토의·토론의 장을 마련한다. 개별 전공들 간의 장벽을 넘어 비
판적·융합적·창의적 사고 능력을 함양하고, 나아가 새롭고 다양한 관점에서 
문제의식을 생성하며 타인과의 소통 및 협력을 통해 문제를 해결할 수 있
도록 하는 것이 이 교과의 목표이다. 이를 위해 플립트 클래스(Flipped 
Class) 기반의 학습자 중심 교수학습 방법을 도입하여, 질문 중심 학습
(QBL: Question Based Learning)과 토론 및 발표를 통해 학습자가 배
움의 주체가 될 수 있도록 한다.

◆ Learning Plan ◆ 
▷ Course Outline 
This course is designed to study factors related quality loss of horticultural products after 
harvest, including physiological and biochemical considerations as well as compositional and 
physical changes occurring during maturation and deterioration. Major principles involved in 
postharvest physiology are explained. Subjects to be covered in Postharvest Physiology are: 
respiration (significance, measurement, factors, climacteric, alternative pathway), ethylene 
(history, physiological effects, removing methods, measurement, biosynthesis, regulation, 
treatment), ripening (compositional changes, color, flavor, textures, nutritional changes), 
temperature (refrigeration, heat source, injury, mechanism, precooling), metabolomics 
approaches for crop quality. Through this course activity, student will learn how to collect data 
from postharvest experiment and write scientific article.  
 
▷ Learning Objectives 
-Students will learn major postharvest physiology and explain real related problem. 
-Students will be able to explain factors mainly involved in horticultural quality change and 
control the factors.  
-Students will be able to how to conduct postharvest physiology experiment, to collect data 
and to write scientific article.

Business Negotiation 
Professor: Seungwoo Kwon (권성우) 
Office: LG-POSCO 513 
Phone: 02-3290-2604 
E-mail: winwin@korea.ac.kr 
Office Hours: By appointment 
Class Meetings: Thursday, 3:00 PM – 5:45 PM 
Location: LP 206 
 
Required Readings 
• Lewicki, R. J., Saunders, D. M., & Barry, B. (2020). Negotiation (8th ed.). Boston: 
McGraw-Hill. 
(Earlier or later editions are acceptable.) 
or 
• Thompson, L. (2014). The Mind and Heart of the Negotiator. Pearson. 
 
Course Objectives 
Negotiation is both an art and a science of reaching agreements between two or more 
interdependent parties who seek to maximize their outcomes. This course focuses on 
understanding the behavior of individuals, groups, and organizations in competitive and 
cooperative negotiation contexts. 
A core premise of the course is that while managers need analytical skills to identify optimal 
solutions, a broad set of negotiation skills is required to ensure that these solutions are accepted 
and effectively implemented. Through experiential learning, primarily negotiation role-play 
exercises, students will develop practical negotiation skills while also learning to analyze 
negotiation processes using rigorous analytical frameworks. 
The latter part of the course examines academic research on negotiation. This seminar introduces 
students to theories and empirical studies in negotiation within the field of organizational 
behavior, with particular attention to strategic decision making and negotiation processes. The 
course draws heavily on insights from psychology, economics, and communication. 
 
Course Format 
The course consists of lectures, class discussions, and a series of in-class negotiation exercises. 
Although the class officially meets once a week, students will be required to meet with group 
members outside of class to prepare for certain exercises and presentations. 
 
Grading Summary 
Exams (Midterm and Final): 50% (25% each) 
Group Project – Negotiation Case Presentation: 20% 
Team Member Evaluation: 5% 
Real-World Negotiation Paper: 15% 
Class Participation (including attendance): 10% 
 
1. Exams (50%) 
There will be two exams during the semester: a midterm exam and a final exam. Both exams will 
assess students’ understanding of key theoretical concepts and their ability to apply these 
concepts to negotiation situations discussed in the textbook and in class. 
 
2. Group Project: Negotiation Case Presentation (20%) 
The negotiation case presentation is a group-based project. Students will be assigned to small 
groups of approximately six to seven members, depending on class size. Each group will deliver 
a 25-minute presentation. 
Each presentation should include the following components: 
1. A brief lecture introducing the negotiation concept(s) or model(s) used in the analysis. 
2. An explanation of the negotiation case or a short video clip illustrating the negotiation in 
practice. 
3. A clear connection between the theoretical concepts/models and the case or video. 
4. Facilitation of class discussion related to the case and concepts. 
No written report is required for this project. However, each group must upload its presentation 
slides (PPT) to LMS. 
Evaluation Criteria 
Group presentations will be evaluated based on: 
• Clarity in explaining negotiation concepts and models 
• The relevance and interest level of the selected negotiation case 
• Effectiveness in applying concepts to the case 
• Overall quality of the presentation and discussion 
 
3. Team Member Evaluation (5%) 
Effective collaboration is essential for successful group work. Five percent of the final grade will 
be based on peer evaluations completed by group members. Each student will evaluate other 
members of their group on the following dimensions: 
• Contribution to the group’s work 
• Reliability and responsibility 
• Motivation and level of effort 
• Cooperation and openness to others’ ideas and suggestions 
 
4. Real-World Negotiation Paper (15%) 
Students are required to engage in a real-world negotiation involving an issue they would not 
normally negotiate. After completing the negotiation, students will write a reflective paper 
addressing the following questions: 
• What happened during the negotiation? 
• How did you feel throughout the negotiation process? 
• Why do you think the particular outcome was reached, as opposed to other possible 
outcomes? 
The paper should integrate personal experience with theories and concepts from the readings, 
lectures, and class debriefings. Rather than providing a purely chronological description, the 
paper should focus on analyzing both the negotiation process and the outcome, and explaining 
why they unfolded as they did. 
• Length: Maximum of 4 pages 
• Format: Typed, 1.5-spaced 
Evaluation Criteria 
Grading will focus on: 
• The ability to integrate course concepts and readings into insights drawn from the real-
world negotiation 
• Evidence of thoughtful analysis, reflection, and insight 
The paper may be submitted in either English or Korean. Submitting the paper in Korean will not 
result in any disadvantage or penalty. 
 
 
 
5. Class Participation (10%) 
Participation grades are based on three components: attendance, participation in class discussions, 
and preparation for negotiation exercises. 
Attendance 
Students are expected to attend all classes and to be fully prepared for negotiation exercises. 
Because these exercises are highly interactive, the absence or lack of preparation of one student 
can negatively affect the learning experience of other group members. 
Participation in Class Discussions 
Active and high-quality participation is essential to learning in this course. Students will be 
evaluated on the quality, not the quantity, of their contributions. High-quality comments 
typically: 
• Offer a unique and relevant perspective 
• Advance the discussion or deepen the analysis 
• Build on the comments of others 
• Go beyond personal opinion (“I feel that …”) by incorporating evidence, reasoning, or 
recognition of trade-offs, demonstrating reflective thinking 
While participation grading is necessarily subjective, it will not be arbitrary. Consistent, high-
quality contributions are valued more than infrequent comments.

■ 강의 개요
 이 강의는 외국인 재학생(수준: 중급)을 위한 교양필수 강의로서, 학문 세계의 핵심 주제들에 대
해 한국어로 사고하고 표현하는 능력을 향상시켜 ‘자유, 정의, 진리’를 달성하는 데에 목적이 있
다. 이를 위해 토론과 발표를 통해 자신의 생각을 한국어로 자유롭게 표현하며, 다양한 언어적 표
현과 기초 교양 지식을 익혀 대학생으로서의 정의로운 인성을 기르고, 인문, 사회, 과학 분야의 
다양한 융복합적 주제에 대한 진지한 탐구를 한다. 학문세계의 탐구Ⅰ에서는 윤리, 문화, 경제, 
과학에 대한 탐구를 통해 글로벌 인재로 성장하기 위한 학문적 소양을 기른다.
■ 학습목표

개요
이 수업에서는 인류 역사의 다양한 지적 성찰 및 실천적 가치를 종합적으
로 탐구하고, 이를 바탕으로 현재의 사회를 이해하고 미래의 변화에 대응
할 수 있는 토의·토론의 장을 마련한다. 개별 전공들 간의 장벽을 넘어 비
판적·융합적·창의적 사고 능력을 함양하고, 나아가 새롭고 다양한 관점에서 
문제의식을 생성하며 타인과의 소통 및 협력을 통해 문제를 해결할 수 있
도록 하는 것이 이 교과의 목표이다. 이를 위해 플립트 클래스(Flipped 
Class) 기반의 학습자 중심 교수학습 방법을 도입하여, 질문 중심 학습
(QBL: Question Based Learning)과 토론 및 발표를 통해 학습자가 배
움의 주체가 될 수 있도록 한다.

COURSE OVERVIEW 
Managing in the constantly changing environment of the 21st century for business success is 
a challenging job for marketing managers.  The key challenges for managers include: 
understanding the market as a fundamental premise of formulating market-driven strategy; 
strategies for undertaking market analysis and identification of current and future competitive 
positions.  This advanced level marketing course is designed to develop new skills and 
consolidate prior knowledge and skills learned in other marketing courses to develop a 
proactive strategic marketing management approach.  
 
AIMS  
The course deals primarily with an in-depth analysis of a variety of concepts, theories, facts, 
analytical procedures, techniques and models with the development, evaluation, and 
implementation of marketing strategy in complex environments.  
 
OBJECTIVES 
On successful completion of this course, students will achieve the following objectives: 
1. 
To become familiar with the range of decisions implicit in strategic market planning at 
the corporate and strategic business unit levels, and to develop skill in using a variety of 
analytical frameworks for making new market entry and resources allocation decisions. 
2. 
To develop an understanding of the complexity of markets and how the nature of 
competition in such markets is impacted. 
3. 
To develop skill in organizing for effective strategic marketing and implementing strategic 
marketing plan for sustainable competitive advantage of the firm as a whole. 
4. 
To develop students’ abilities to critically analyze/evaluate marketing strategies. 
 
TEACHING AND LEARNING APPROACHES 
 
The lectures will enable students to develop generic attributes of knowledge and problem-
solving in business through exposure to concepts, theories, tools, frameworks, models and 
contemporary issues/debates on marketing strategy.  Even if online replace offline lectures is 
the instruction format, participation is still encouraged and expected.  
 
A hands-on approach to learning and problem-solving will be used in this course where 
students will analyze a business environment in groups to retrieve, evaluate, and use relevant 
information from the environment; debate and negotiate outcomes; share information and 
knowledge for group-based independent and interdependent learning outcome.  The group 
work will foster leadership, creativity, coordination and conflict management skills of students.  
Written reports of the analysis and solution, and oral presentation in the class will enable 
students to develop interpersonal communication skills, make adventurous decisions, and 
develop confidence necessary for business managers.

Course Description 
BUSS 213 is the first course of a two-part sequence of intermediate financial accounting. This course 
is intended to develop your understanding of the theory, concepts, principles, and practices underlying

this course will, however, focus on in-depth analysis of the measurement and reporting requirements 
under the international financial reporting standards (IFRS) necessary for the preparation of statement 
of financial position, income statement, and statement of cash flows.

담당 조교: TBA
Office hours: 수요일 오전 10:30 ~ 11:30 혹은 by appointment
‣ 강의개요
본 수업은 현대사회가 마주한 정치적 역동성과 민주주의의 위기 속에서 “국가란 무엇인가?”라
는 근원적인 질문을 던집니다. 헌법 제1조가 선언하는 ‘민주공화국’의 실질적 의미를 되새기며, 
국가권력의 정당성과 시민주권의 소재를 탐구하고자 합니다. 최근의 국가적 경험들은 우리에
게 대통령과 의회의 역할, 그리고 권력분립의 엄중함을 다시금 일깨워주었습니다. 본 강의는 
공공철학의 관점에서 국가의 존재 이유를 고찰하고, 학생들이 정의로운 국가공동체의 설계자
로서 자신만의 관점을 정립하는 것을 목표로 합니다.
이를 위해 수업은 국가에 관한 이론적·경험적 논의에 주목하며, 사상적 맥락에 따라 주요 논문
과 저서를 중심으로 다음과 같은 세 가지 축을 살펴봅니다.
Ÿ
자유주의 국가론: 근대적 이행기 속 홉스와 로크의 이론부터, 개인의 경제적 자유와 시장의 
자율성에 주목하는 아담 스미스의 시장주의 국가론, 그리고 분배와 사회적 평등을 지향하
는 존 롤즈의 현대 복지국가론까지 폭넓게 다룹니다.
Ÿ
공화주의 국가론: 아테네의 고전적 공화주의와 로마공화정을 거쳐 마키아벨리, 그리고 필립 
페팃과 비롤리가 주창한 신공화주의 담론을 살펴봅니다. 비지배 자유(non-domination)의 
개념이 현대 공화국에서 갖는 헌정적 의미를 탐구하며, 마이클 샌델의 시민적 공화주의까
지 이어지는 공화국의 본질적 가치와 시민적 덕성을 탐색합니다.
Ÿ
새로운 국가론: 인간의 근원적 취약성과 상호의존성, 그리고 보편적 돌봄의 필요성을 정책
적·철학적 토대로 삼는 대안적인 국가 패러다임을 검토합니다.
동시에 본 수업은 이론적 탐구에 그치지 않고, 현실의 국가가 직면한 정책적 이슈와 제도적 
현상들이 각 국가론의 핵심 개념(Key Concept)을 통해 어떻게 해석되고 적용될 수 있는지 분
석합니다. 이를 위해 관련 신문 기사 및 비디오 클립 등 다양한 시각 자료를 적극적으로 활용
하여 비판적 토론을 전개하고자 합니다.

한다. 디자인의 관점에서는 인터랙션의 효율성을 넘어서 어떤 새로운 경험을 창출할 수 있는가가 중요하다. 
그중 미적 경험은 외형적 미감에 대한 경험에서 나아가 인터랙션 과정에서의 풍부한 경험이라는 이해를 
바탕으로, 인터랙션을 통해 인간의 미적 경험을 한층 더 고양할 수 있는 방식을 제시해야 한다. 
본 강의는 인터랙션 디자인이 도달할 수 있는 미적 경험이란 어떤 것인지, 어떻게 미적인 인터랙션을 
디자인해야 하는지 이해하고, 이를 실제 경험할 수 있도록 구현해 제시하는 것을 목표로 한다. 인터랙션의 
“디자인”과 경험을 새롭게 정의하여 이해하고, 이를 손에 잡히고 실제적인 방식으로 미적 경험을 실현해 
봄으로써 인터랙션 디자인을 학습한다.
인터랙션 디자인이 어떻게 인간의 경험을 극대화할 수 있는지에 대한 본질적인 이해를 위해 
로우테크에서부터 하이테크까지의 다양한 인터랙션 프로토타이핑 방법을 활용한 소규모 워크샵을 중심으로 
점진적으로 학습한다. 이러한 이해를 바탕으로 개별 프로젝트를 통해 창의적이고 실험적인 인터랙션 컨셉 
디자인을 개발하고 실제적인 구현까지의 과정을 실행한다.
Serene Home (고요한 집)
일상 속에 AI가 스며들어 우리 주위의 많은 것들이 AI가 내장되게 될 것이다. 인간은 이러한 AI들과 어떻게든 
상호작용해야 한다. 집이라는 장소를 중심으로, 이 많은 AI들과 어떻게 상호작용해야 할 것인가. 그러면서도, 
어떻게 고요함을 유지할 수 있을 것인가. 그것이 어떻게 나에게 새로운 경험을 줄 것인가.

개요
본 강의의 목적은 미래 사회 변화에 대한 이해를 바탕으로 직업세
계 변화에 적응할 수 있는 진로 개발 능력을 신장하여 학생들이 현

강의 전반부에는 인구 및 사회 · 문화, 기후 및 환경, 자원과 에너지
등에 따른 직업세계 변화에 대한 개괄적인 이해를 갖게 하고, 중반
부 이후부터는 직업관 설계와 대학생의 주요 진로 발달 과업으로

하게 하고 진로에 대해서 계획하고 준비할 수 있도록 조력한다.

Phone: 02-3290-2621 
E-Mail: kihoon@korea.ac.kr 
Office Hours: by Appointment 
 
T A: Jaeduk Kim, jaeduk3119@korea.ac.kr 
 
Textbook 
Managing Business Process Flows: Principles of Operations Management by Anupindi, 
Chopra, Deshmukh, Van Mieghem, and Zemel. Prentice Hall, 3rd edition, 2011. 
 
Reference for the Final Project 
§ Platform Business in the age of AI (AI 시대의 플랫폼 비즈니스) by the 
instructor, Tote, 2025. 
§ Youtube Podcast (based on the book) available in both Korean and English at 
https://www.youtube.com/@kihoon-AI 
 
Summary. This course provides an overview of modern operations management (OM). 
The first part of the course introduces the concept of operations strategy and process flow 
management. As part of the operations strategy, platform operations management will 
also be addressed. Students will learn how to formulate appropriate operations strategies 
aligned with business and corporate strategies. For process flow management, they will 
learn how to analyze the detailed process of companies focusing on how to find the 
bottlenecks and improve the flow time. The second part of the course deals with supply 
chain management issues (bullwhip effects and supply chain coordination) and lean 
operations tatics. Students will experience how to manage inventories through 
simulation-based games. They will also learn how to supply components under two 
different supply policies such as Material Requirements Planning and Just in Time. The 
course aims to (1) familiarize you with the major operational problems and issues that 
confront managers, and (2) provide you with language, concepts, insights and tools to 
deal with these issues in order to gain competitive advantage through operations. To 
achieve these goals, lectures on some topics will be followed by the related article and 
case discussions. The detailed list of the articles and cases are listed at the end of the 
syllabus.

1. Grading 
Your grade will be based on individual and group assignments. 
 
A. Class Attendance and Participation: 10% 
B. Midterm: 25% 
C. Final: 20% 
D. Final Project: 30%  
E. HWs: 15% 
 
Re-grading.  
Re-grading (of case write-ups, midterm, and final exam) request can be submitted in 
writing along with the original assignment to a TA. We are going to review the whole 
assignment, which means that your score after re-grading can be above or below your 
original score. Re-grading requests can be made within one week of the date of return of 
the graded item in question.  
 
A. Class Attendance/Participation (10%) 
You are required to contribute to the class discussion. Send me an email before the class 
if you can't come for some official reason. Mostly, our discussion will be open: anyone 
who has something to contribute can and should. The best contribution is one that informs 
the rest of us or carries the discussion forward. You are encouraged to challenge the 
statements of others, but always in a constructive way.  
 
If you miss more than two classes, you are going to receive zero for class attendance and 
participation. If you are late two times, it will be considered as one absence unless you 
have an emergency situation.  
 
B. C. Midterm and Final (25% + 20%)  
The exact requirements for the exams for this course will be announced later in class. No 
communication with others will be allowed. Exams are open-book and open-lecture-note. 
 
D. Final Project (30%) 
Each team will develop a platform business strategy by choosing one of the following 
two approaches: 
1. Propose a platform transformation strategy for a traditional company that 
o has the potential to enter the platform economy, or 
o has already started a platform transformation; or 
2. Design a new platform business model that addresses a clear market problem 
and has the potential to scale as a platform. 
The final deliverables are: 
• 
A 10-minute team presentation 
• 
A 3-page executive summary 
These should clearly explain: 
• 
What problem the platform solves and for whom, 
• 
Why the platform strategy makes sense (strategic rationale), 
• 
How the platform creates and captures value (economic mechanisms), 
• 
How AI may support or enhance the platform, if relevant. 
Teams should apply key concepts discussed in class, such as: 
• 
Network effects, 
• 
Subsidy-side and money-side users, 
• 
Platform growth and evolution models, 
to explain how value is created for users, how revenue is generated, and how the 
platform can sustain its competitive advantage over time. 
Strong projects will: 
• 
Use simple data, assumptions, or real-world examples to support arguments, 
• 
Benchmark similar platforms or services, even if the platform is new, 
• 
Discuss key trade-offs, such as growth vs. profitability, openness vs. control, 
and pricing vs. user adoption. 
Projects will be evaluated based on: 
• 
Clarity and logic of reasoning, 
• 
Feasibility and consistency of the proposed platform model, 
• 
Creativity and originality of the idea or transformation strategy. 
In addition, teams should demonstrate: 
• 
Clear and well-organized writing and presentation, 
• 
Visually clean and professional slides, 
• 
A strong connection between course concepts and real-world platform cases. 
Excellent projects will not only describe an idea but also present a practical and 
realistic platform strategy, reflecting how platform and AI-driven competition 
actually works in today’s market. 
E. HWs (15%) 
You need to submit your own version of HWs. Any plagiarism or copy (of other students’ 
hws) will result in zero score for all the HWs, and further penalties may be applied by 
KUBS and KU. 
3. Laptops and Cell phones 
You may use your laptop for the purposes of taking notes, but I reserve the right to ban 
laptops if their use becomes a distraction. I want to be very firm on the use of cell phones.  
People coming and going from class is very disruptive and nothing encourages such 
movement like cell phones.  If you have not turned off your phone and choose to answer 
a call, do not return to the room until after the class period is over to collect your 
belongings.

개요
생애설계와 자기이해 수업에서는 개별 성격특성, 발달과정 및 삶의 맥락을 기반으로 
과정 중심적 진로탐색과 목표설정, 실천전략을 구성하고자 한다. 이를 위해, 수업의 
전과정은 개인의 개별 특성을 이해할 수 있는 객관적, 주관적 심리검사 및 현재 수업 
참여자들이 처해 있는 사회, 문화, 경제적 맥락에 대한 이해를 제공하고자 한다. 이와 
같은 전체 과정을 통해 수업 참여자들은 고정된 자기 이해에서 벗어나 다양한 진로이
야기를 만들어 가는 주체적, 역동적, 능동적인 존재로서의 자기 인식이 구축될 것이
다. 
수강(권장)대상 학생
본 수업은 진로탐색과 자기이해를 위한 개방성과 능동성, 흥미를 가진 학생들은 누구
나 참여 가능하다. 다만, 실제적이고 구체적인 직업역량 향상을 목적으로 하는 학생보
다 삶의 전체 맥락에서 진로와 자신에 대한 탐구를 목적으로 하는 학생에게 좀 더 적
합한 교과이다. 
선이수과목(권장)
특별히 요구되는 선수과목은 없으나, 심리학 및 사회학에 대한 이해가 있다면 세계 
속의 자기 이해에 도움

Instructor: Gayeong Jung, Ph.D.  
E-mail: yeong1203@korea.ac.kr 
Office hours: By appointment only 
 
Course Description    
 The course provides an overview of teaching English as a foreign language (EFL) and 
materials development for EFL learners. The course offers theories of various approaches, 
methods, and materials for teaching English as a foreign language. The primary goal of this 
course is not only to acquire knowledge but also to develop and practice pedagogical skills in 
lesson planning, material design, and adaptation. Furthermore, the course helps students apply 
the theoretical principles to actual teaching for a professional career as an English teacher in 
ELT environments. 
Note: There are no prerequisites. This course is designed for students who are planning to 
become secondary school English teachers in Korea. The course, however, also welcomes any 
students who are interested in teaching English as a second or foreign language. 
 
Course Objectives 
By the end of the semester, students are expected to: 
1. Understand how English is taught in EFL contexts and acquire a solid understanding 
of the main issues surrounding the teaching of English; 
2. Examine approaches to designing a lesson plan and implementing the plan for 
effective teaching based on the learned knowledge; 
3. Gain theoretical knowledge on materials development, examine how to evaluate, 
select, and adapt the teaching materials, and ultimately develop one’s own materials. 
 
 
Course Materials 
Course materials will be uploaded to LMS.  
References:  
Brown, H. D., & Lee, H. (2015). Teaching by principles: An interactive approach to language 
pedagogy (4th ed.). Pearson Education.

teaching materials: Theory and practice (2nd ed.).  Cambridge University Press. 
McDonough, J., Shaw, C., & Masuhara, H. (2013). Materials and methods in ELT (3rd ed.). 
Wiley-Blackwell.  
Larsen-Freeman, D., & Anderson, M. (2011). Techniques and principles in language teaching 
(3rd ed.). Oxford. 
Richards, J. C. & Rodgers, T. S. (2014). Approaches and methods in language teaching (3rd 
ed.). Cambridge University Press.

Course Requirements 
Attendance: Class attendance is essential. Two absences are allowed, which do not affect 
your grades. After two absences, each subsequent absence will subtract two points from your 
final grade. Thus, “free” absences are recommended to be saved for unavoidable emergencies. 
Three late arrivals will be counted as one absence. Being late for more than thirty minutes 
will be considered one absence. It is your responsibility to identify any missed class 
information. Excused absence is accepted only in the case of a required teaching practicum. 
Students who miss more than one-third of the course (including allowed absences) will 
receive an F according to university regulations.  
 
Participation: Students are expected to actively participate in class discussions and activities. 
Class materials, including lecture slides, will be uploaded to the LMS by the day before each 
class, and students are responsible for checking them before class. Class materials should 
never be shared or posted to any online services.  
 
Mid-term Quiz: The midterm quiz is designed to check understanding of key concepts. The 
topics learned in class and the textbook will be tested. It will consist of multiple-choice 
questions only. No make-up exam will be given. 
 
Final Project (Microteaching & Lesson Plan): Students will create a lesson plan and 
present a mini-lesson (microteaching), either in groups or individually. Lesson planning is 
directly connected to the course content, and for students who have little or no prior 
experience with lesson planning, sufficient preparation time and instructor feedback will be 
provided. In addition, students will adapt or modify ELT textbooks, or develop materials 
appropriate for their lessons based on the knowledge acquired in class. Specific guidelines for 
microteaching and lesson planning will be provided later. When working in groups, peer 
evaluation may be conducted. 
 
 
Academic Honesty & Classroom Decorum: Please note that making any audio, video, or 
photo recordings of the class, the instructor, or other students is not permitted. Cheating and 
plagiarism will result in severe penalties, including possible F grades. In class, it is expected 
that you exhibit good manners.

▷ 주차별 Flipped Class 운영 설계  
 【 주차별 학습내용 작성방법 】 총 16주차의 학사일정 중 중간고사와 기말고사를 제외한 14주차에 대한 계획을 모두 기술, 필요시 셀 통합 및 조정 가능
 1. 주차: 수업주차 
 2. 운영형태: 주차별 수업 운영형태를 온라인 수업, 오프라인 수업으로 구분하여 표시(0)하되, 오프라인 수업의 경우 수업일자를 함께 기입
    *온라인과 오프라인 수업은 1주 시간 내에서 교대하되, 2주를 초과하지 않는 범위 내에서 교대 진행 기간 연장 가능함; <Flipped Class 운영 시행세칙> 제7조(강의의 개설과 운영) 4항 참조
 3. 학습주제: 주차에 해당하는 학습주제, 주요 학습내용을 기술
 4. 주차별 학습활동 계획:
    [Pre-class] 학습내용 및 온라인 학습 확인 활동: 사전에 온라인으로 학습할 내용을 기술하고 사전학습에 사용할 퀴즈 또는 수업준비와 관련한 내용을 작성
    [In-class]  도입: 수업 도입 시 교수자가 부여한 Pre-class 동영상을 학습자들이 사전에 학습을 하고 수업에 임하는지 확인하는 시간으로 학습결과에 대한 평가 전략을 작성
              심화학습 및 마무리: 수업 도입 부분을 마친 후 본격적인 심화학습을 위한 내용, 교수·학습방법, 심화학습 결과 평가 전략 및 피드백 등을 상세히 작성
    [Post-class] 성찰활동 및 수업후 활동: 학습과정에 대한 성찰활동과 수업후 학습자에게 부여되는 활동이나 과제 등을 작성
 7. 학습시간(분): 도입과 심화학습 및 마무리에 필요한 학습시간을 각각 배분하여 시간(분)을 표기
    *강의 형태별 학습시간: <Flipped Class 운영 시행세칙> 제5조(수업 시간과 구성요소) 참조    
- 주당 2시간 강의: 동영상 32-40분+온라인 학습활동 5-15분
- 주당 3시간 강의: 동영상 48-60분+온라인 학습활동 5-15분

BUSS312 Data Driven Marketing
Course Information
• Semester: Spring 2026
• Class Time & Location: Monday and Wednesday, 12pm to 1:15pm at LG-POSC 218
• Instructor: Professor Baek Jung Kim
• Office: LG-POSCO 615
• Office Hours: Wednesday 3pm to 4pm
• Email: baekjungkim@korea.ac.kr
• TA: Ahyoung Ko (lilra299@korea.ac.kr)
Course Description
This course introduces undergraduate students to data-driven decision making in marketing,
with a strong emphasis on empirical analysis, coding, and evidence-based reasoning. The
course examines how firms, consumers, and governments use data to make marketing and
policy decisions in real-world settings.
A central component of the course is hands-on data analysis using R and Python. Stu-
dents will work with real datasets, perform data wrangling, conduct empirical analyses, and
implement forecasting and regression-based methods using code. The course aims to enhance
students’ ability to translate business and economic questions into analytical workflows and
to interpret results generated through computational tools.
The course draws inspiration from empirical and quantitative marketing research, cover-
ing topics such as panel data, causal inference, demand analysis, forecasting, and customer
lifetime value. While advanced econometric methods are discussed conceptually, the focus is
on practical implementation, interpretation, and decision making rather than mathematical
derivations.
By the end of the course, students will be able to integrate perspectives from business,
economics, and computer science to analyze marketing problems and generate meaningful
insights from data.
1
Learning Objectives
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
1. Use R and Python to clean, analyze, and visualize marketing data
2. Translate marketing and policy questions into empirical and computational analyses
3. Distinguish between descriptive, predictive, and causal approaches to data analysis
4. Apply regression, panel data, and forecasting methods using real data
5. Evaluate identification assumptions and recognize limitations in observational data
6. Interpret empirical results and communicate insights to managerial and policy audiences
7. Integrate business intuition, economic reasoning, and computational tools to support
data-driven decisions

Individual Final Project and Presentations (KDD Cup
2014: DonorsChoose.org)
Each student will complete an individual final project that applies R and/or Python-
based empirical analysis to a decision-making problem using only one dataset: the
DonorsChoose.org KDD Cup 2014 dataset (Kaggle). The objective is to demonstrate
your ability to independently analyze real relational data, apply rigorous empirical methods
covered in the course, and derive meaningful insights relevant to platform strategy, donor
behavior, and/or education policy.
Context (what the platform is trying to do). DonorsChoose.org is an online charity
platform where teachers post classroom project requests and donors decide which projects
to fund. The KDD Cup 2014 task (and the dataset you will use) centers on identifying
projects that are exceptionally exciting at the time of posting, so that the platform
can recommend them effectively and improve funding outcomes and user experience.
Dataset requirement (KDD 2014 only). Your project must use only the KDD Cup
2014 DonorsChoose dataset as the data source. You may not bring in external datasets
for analysis (no census merges, no external geography files, etc.). You may use external
references for background/interpretation, but all empirical work must come from KDD 2014.
Data structure (relational files; important constraint).
The KDD 2014 data are
provided as multiple CSV files that can be merged via project identifiers.
Typical files
include:
• projects.csv: structured project, teacher, and school attributes (e.g., subject area,
grade level, poverty indicators, location fields).
• essays.csv: teacher-written text (title/short description/need statement/essay fields).
• resources.csv: requested materials (many rows per project; quantities, unit price, ven-
dor/resource type).
4
• donations.csv: donation transaction information (available for training projects).
• outcomes.csv: training outcomes, including the binary label is exciting.
Important: The competition split is date-based: projects posted before a cutoff are training
data (with outcomes), and projects after the cutoff form a test set (without outcomes). Your
analysis must respect this logic when you evaluate predictive models (e.g., holdout validation
or cross-validation within the labeled set).
Topic selection (must be a decision problem). Choose a topic that is both (i) mean-
ingful to a real platform decision and (ii) feasible using only KDD 2014 files. Examples (you
can propose your own):
• Project ranking / recommendation: How should the platform prioritize projects to
show donors, using predicted is exciting?
• Messaging and persuasion (text + structured): Which writing patterns correlate
with exciting projects? What guidance would you give teachers?
• Equity and public policy lens: Are certain communities or school contexts less likely
to be funded/exciting, even after controlling for project attributes?
• Donor behavior: How do donation patterns vary across project types? Which project
attributes attract more donor activity (within the training set)?
Minimum project components (required). The final project must include:
• A clearly defined research question or decision problem (phrased as: “What should
the platform do?” or “What policy/action follows?”)
• A clear description of the KDD 2014 files used and your unit of analysis (project-
level vs donation-level, etc.)
• Data wrangling and variable construction in R/Python:
– At least one non-trivial merge (e.g., projects + essays + aggregated resources)
– At least three constructed variables that are meaningful for the decision problem
– If you use essay text, include at least one text-derived feature (e.g., length, read-
ability proxy, sentiment proxy, topic proportions)
• Descriptive analysis and visualization:
– At least three figures (distributions, segment comparisons, trends, or relationships)
5
– At least one segmentation (e.g., by poverty level, grade level, subject area, metro
status, region/state)
• In-depth empirical analysis using methods covered in the course:
– Examples: regression/classification with interpretation, regularization, tree-based ML,
model evaluation and calibration
– Your model/evidence must be evaluated with a clear validation plan (holdout or
cross-validation)
• Discussion of assumptions, limitations, and potential sources of bias:
– Examples: selection effects (which projects get donated to), missingness, measurement
error, fairness concerns across communities
• Interpretation of results with managerial or policy implications (what decision you
recommend, and why)
Presentation (June). Each student will deliver a final presentation during June summa-
rizing the decision problem, KDD 2014 data used, methods, key results, limitations, and a
recommended action (platform strategy or policy implication).

ELED 414 
Advanced English Writing 
Instructor: Julie Yang 
Office hours: Please make an appointment by emailing me. (운초우선 603) 
Email: yykjulie@korea.ac.kr / yang.eunkyu@gmail.com 
*Please note: email is the best way to reach me. During normal business hours (M-F, 9am-6pm) I will
respond to emails within 24-48 hours (probably sooner). If you email me outside of those times or if I give
you some notice about limited email, it may take me longer to respond. On weekends, I may not respond
until Monday. If it has been more than 24 hours and you think I may have missed your email, please send
another.
Goals and Objectives of the Course 
The goal of this course is to introduce you to the challenges and pleasures of college writing. Major 
learning goals in this class include developing critical reading and writing connections for the college 
level, shaping meaning and communication, and exploring academic writing practices. 
By the end of the semester, your final portfolio should demonstrate the following course objectives: 
•
identify key arguments in published texts and the writing of your peers;
•
create and defend arguments of your own through effective rhetorical strategies and synthesis of
others’ ideas;
•
use the conventions of academic discourse, including
o
coherent and logical organization
o
Standard English grammar and syntax
o
correct citation and evaluation of research sources;
•
revise your writing through multiple drafts.
This is a class in which there are no right or wrong answers or opinions in most cases. All academic 
discourse depends on weighing evidence and presenting a strong, well-argued position. 
Course Requirements 
•
Participate by completing all weekly activities and coursework;
•
Read articles with a great deal of attention to detail;
•
Write and revise three substantial papers that involve evaluation of sources, argumentation,
synthesis, and development of original ideas;
•
Meet with me at least twice during the semester in a conference to discuss your writing;
•
Submit your final portfolio of three papers, fully revised.
Required Course Materials and Technology Specifications 
No books are required for this course. All readings will be posted on Canvas. Using Canvas and your 
university email are crucial requirements for the course. You will be submitting work online through 
Blackboard for this course, and as such, you will also need to have regular access to Microsoft Word.  
Feedback and Due Dates for Paper Drafts 
You will receive formative feedback throughout the semester on drafts of your papers. This feedback is 
intended to help you revise your papers into their best possible shape for the final portfolio. Please note 
that revision is not only about “fixing” the things I’ve commented on. You are expected to learn 
throughout the semester and incorporate everything you have learned in addition to addressing my 
comments on your papers. If you only “fix” things I’ve commented on, you will not necessarily earn an 
“A” in the course. 
You will not receive binding grades on paper drafts because we want to grade your work after you’ve 
revised, not before. In my feedback, I will give you an indication of what grade the paper might receive if 
it were submitted in the final portfolio without any revision. For example, my feedback might include a 
sentence such as, “If you do not revise this paper, it is likely to pass in the C range.” Or “This paper is not 
passing in its current form, and you must revise it up to at least the C range to pass this course.” You are 
always welcome to discuss your progress with me if you are concerned about how your overall grade is 
shaping up. If you read my comments and pay attention during our conferences, you should have a good 
sense of your grade throughout the semester and the final grade will not be a surprise. I will do my best to 
provide feedback on papers through Blackboard within two weeks, at most. 
You may want me to look at a paper you’ve revised after I’ve given feedback and before the final 
portfolio, especially if you’re not sure how well your revisions are going. If so, you may bring your 
revised paper to me during a conference or to office hours and we can discuss it in real-time. Also, I will 
always want to know what, specifically, you want me to focus on and I will have questions for you about 
the revisions you’ve made. If your initial draft was failing or very incomplete, I may require you to re-
submit it because I am concerned about your progress, and in those cases, you should always re-submit 
however I have directed you to do so (via email or during a conference/office hours). 
Drafts of your papers must be submitted on time throughout the semester. If you have an extreme 
situation or sudden crisis that prevents you from submitting a draft for feedback on time, you may ask for 
a one-week extension, no questions asked. But you must ask before the due date, and if you need more 
time than one week you may need to consider withdrawing from the course. After a deadline or a granted 
extension has passed, I will not provide you with written feedback because you have not followed the 
proper submission procedure (a procedure that is fair and allows for a compassionate extension). 
However, this is very important: A portfolio that includes one or more papers that I have never seen in 
draft form will lead to a failing grade in the course. 
In other words, if you miss a deadline and/or an extension, you must show me your drafts in order to be 
eligible to submit a final portfolio. If you show me a draft of Paper #1 or #2 after deadlines and 
extensions have passed and only because you wish to be eligible to submit a final portfolio, you will not 
receive written feedback on these drafts. I will be glad to give you verbal feedback as long as you show 
me your draft(s) at a conference or in my office hours. That is, I always want to give you feedback on 
your writing when you need it, but the feedback is verbal, not written, because you did not follow the 
proper submission procedure. My best advice: turn paper drafts in on time! Paper #3 is submitted for 
feedback fairly late in the semester, but I will still need to see it before you submit your final portfolio. 
Also, a related point about being eligible to submit a final portfolio: If you revise one of your own drafts 
so substantially that it looks completely different than the one I saw, or if you decide to start a paper over 
on a new topic with new sources, you must send the new version to me and explain what you have done 
before the final portfolio is due. Iwill not necessarily need to meet to discuss the new draft, but you 
should not expect full written feedback, either. This is only so that I know ahead of the final portfolio that 
you’ve made appropriate changes to a draft and are eligible to submit. 
One-on-One Conferences and Office Hours 
We will meet for one-on-one conferences at least twice this semester to discuss your progress. Dates and 
times for meeting will be mutually arranged. These conferences are very important. You need to be 
prepared for each conference by having questions ready for me and by having your work in front of you 
while we are talking, and if I have assigned something specific for you to bring to conference and you 
don’t have it, I will ask you to reschedule. 
Please note that you may also attend my office hours throughout the semester if you want even more time 
with me to discuss your work, and if you cannot make my office hours you may email me for help. In 
general, I will be happy to use my office hours to read revisions and provide you with extra feedback on 
your papers. 
Format for Final Portfolios 
The basic components of the final portfolio include: 
•
Final and fully revised versions of your papers #1, #2 and #3
Grading policy 
Final Portfolio: 70% 
Three Peer Review Assignments: 15% 
Attendance and Participation (including in-class writing activities): 15% 
Coursework and Class Etiquette 
A significant aspect of our coursework includes engaging with other students in the class in either 
Blackboard Discussions, peer reviews, Google Doc group work, or other interactive activities. The 
purpose is to hear different perspectives to get a better sense of audience when writing your papers. It also 
assists with understanding the readings better since everyone takes away something a little different from 
a reading depending on their experience. The point is not to advance a particular point of view but rather 
to unpack what it is the authors are saying and how they are presenting the information. Some of the 
readings include controversial ideas and you may read about topics you are not completely comfortable 
with. Using critical thinking is not always comfortable but we can enter this as a “brave space” where we 
try to examine things we don’t always like to think about. To assist with making our interactive space a 
place where we can be brave, every student has a responsibility to make others feel comfortable learning, 
participating, and asking questions (see ground rules for interaction below). 
We are all here to learn and work with others, and any activity that runs contrary to the spirit of learning 
and collaboration will not be tolerated. I will talk to students individually if posts or comments seem to 
include hostile language, discrimination, or abuse. 
Attendance Protocol  
One goal of this course is for you to feel more confident speaking up, asking questions, and participating 
more generally. Even lectures will have discussion components. We will learn more if we engage with 
each other and contribute to class discussions. Because of this, I expect students to attend all classes.  
 
. 
Policy of Academic Honesty 
Plagiarism is the unacknowledged use of another person's labor and presenting it as your own: another 
person’s ideas, words, or assistance. In general, all sources must be identified as clearly, accurately, and 
thoroughly as possible. Academic cheating is, in general terms, the thwarting or breaking of the general 
rules of academic work and/or the specific rules of individual courses. It includes submitting, without the 
instructor’s approval, work in one course that was done for another; helping others to plagiarize or cheat 
from one’s own or someone else's work; or actually doing another person’s work. Of course I do not want 
to discourage you from using other people’s ideas or data. Our aim is exactly the opposite. But you must 
always make clear your sources and you must always be sure that the work you submit is your own. 
If you plagiarize on a draft of a paper submitted before the final portfolio, I will give you one very serious 
warning and you will have a chance to revise the paper. But if you plagiarize a second time or if 
plagiarism is found in your final portfolio, you will fail the course and will be reported to the University 
as being academically dishonest. This policy is not negotiable. If you are uncertain about what constitutes 
plagiarism, ask BEFORE you hand in the work. It will be too late afterwards.

Purpose of Academic English 
 
1 - To prepare students for taking English mediated courses (EMC) in their major. 
2 - To prepare students to be part of the global community of academia. 
3 - To prepare students for studying abroad in an international-language  
       environment. 
4 - To prepare students to thrive (survive) in a foreign language environment 
5 - To prepare students to be independent learners and thinkers. 
 
 
 
 
 
Academic English focuses on developing students’ academic skills in 
critical thinking, argumentation, academic writing, academic 
discussion and presentation (all in English).  
 
These crucial skills are transferable to any course, any major,  
any language or taught in any country.

Typically, a maximum of about 40-50% of you will receive a grade of “A” or “A+”. Evaluation in 
this class is based strictly on performance, and not on English language proficiency. All parts of 
the evaluation system must be completed in an exceptional manner if you want to get an “A+”.   
 
 
Need Help? 
Getting adjusted to university life can sometimes be tough, dramatic even traumatic, especially 
during a pandemic.  Help is available, however.  The KU Student Counseling Center offers 
help to students having trouble at university or with their feelings. They are very good at 
listening. They have one to one counseling, group counseling, and even some tests people can 
take about their lives, feelings, personality, relationships, and more. During the semester, they 
are open from Monday-Friday from 9 a.m. – 5:30 p.m. (closed for lunch). They are located in 
the 과학도서관 307 호. Tel: 3290-4581~4582. Website: http://kuscc.korea.ac.kr (in Korean). 
 
 
 
 
3 
 
Class Expectations (Please READ CAREFULLY!) 
 
This class is not like your other classes.  It is NOT a lecture class, so you must be 
active instead of passive in this class.  The following are some guidelines for 
conduct that I expect in this class.  Following these expectations will assist in 
enhancing your academic skills as well as improving chances of a good grade.  
 
 
1. 
 
Ask me questions:  This course is about communication, and it is extremely 
important for us to understand each other.  Feel free to ask me at any time to 
repeat or explain something if you do not understand. I am also available in my 
office, Rm 711, by appointment or during my office hours. Please remember that  
it is your responsibility to tell me if there is something you do not 
understand or need help with. 
 
 
2. 
 
You must use English in class: You must try as best as you can to 
communicate all of your thoughts in English.  If you cannot find the correct words 
in English, try to find some other way to express yourself (body language, face 
expressions, drawing pictures, etc.).  Be creative! It is a requirement of this 
course that you use English in this class. 
 
 
3. 
 
Participate actively in the class!  Do not be afraid to speak in class, and do not 
worry about making mistakes.  Incorrect speaking is better than no speaking.  
Perfect English is not necessary, but class participation is necessary.  It is a 
part of your grade! 
 
 
4. 
 
Assignments and projects!  Any assignment or project not ready by the 
assigned deadline will receive a grade of “0”.  If you are absent, make sure to ask 
your classmates or contact me about what you missed.  Copying homework 
(plagiarism) will automatically get you an "0". Any assignments fully created 
with generative A.I. (like ChatGPT) will receive a grade of “0”. 
 
 
5. 
 
Grades!  Although important to you and your GPA, improving your skills in a 
foreign language is not only about grades.  It is a skill that can be life changing for 
your future.  Developing good English language skills can open opportunities for 
employment and future study abroad, it can help you connect to the world beyond 
the borders of your country, and it can enhance your understanding of other 
cultures.  Please view this course as an opportunity to build your future, and 
not simply as an influence on your GPA.  Furthermore, in Korea, English is 
often used as a measure of a person’s value in society, but NOT in this class!   
The grades I assign to you are not an evaluation of you personally nor 
reflective of my likes or dislikes.  It is simply an evaluation of your performance in 
class tasks and activities. 
 
 
6. 
 
Absences!  If you are going to be absent from class for any reason, I will mark 
you as absent for that class, but I allow you 3 absences in the semester 
without any academic penalty.  You can notify me about an absence through the 
Korea University portal, but it will still count as an absence, so use your free 
absences wisely.   
 
- Students missing more than 6 classes will receive a grade of “F”. 
 
 
 
4 
 
 
7. 
 
Be in class on time!  Students who are late are disturbing for the class and for 
me. If you are more than 10 minutes late, I will mark you absent for that class.  If 
you are late 3 times, I will mark you absent for one class.   
- This will NOT count as one of the allowed absences in #6. 
 
 
8. 
 
No distracted sessions!  The use of mobile telephones for communication 
purposes is not allowed in this class.  It is disruptive and rude to other participants.  
Use of cell phones for communicative purposes (including Kakao Talk) will 
result in being marked absent for that class! Use of other devices (laptops, 
tablets, etc.) for communication purposes during class will also result in being 
marked absent. If you are using your phone as a dictionary or for fact checking, 
make it clear to me that you are doing so.  No exceptions. 
 
9. 
 
Textbook materials!  On most days we will be using our textbook materials. All of 
these materials are made available through KU-LMS.  Please make sure you have 
them available for every class.  Repeated failure to do so will affect your class 
participation grade.  Textbook materials can be used in either paper (strongly 
recommended) or digital form. 
 
10. 
 
Bathroom Breaks!  Please use the break time BETWEEN CLASSES for things 
like getting drinks, making phone calls and going to the toilet.  If it is an 
emergency, you do not have to ask me for permission to go to the toilet.  If it is 
not an emergency, you do not have to go! 
 
11. Pay attention to the details!  Students who get A+ in this course tend to be those 
who read instructions carefully, ask me questions, and focus on accomplishing the 
tasks in detail. If you miss something important, refer to #1! 
 
12. 
 
Show respect and courtesy to your classmates!  Please be respectful of your 
classmates and help me to provide a positive and encouraging learning 
environment.  Your enjoyment of this class and the development of your 
academic English skills depend on the attitude you bring to this class every day.   
Please be positive, be polite and be kind.

This course is designed for those who have NO or VERY LIMITED knowledge of Korean. 
The objective of this course is to give students basic knowledge of Korean language and 
to help students acquire a basic level of communicative competence in Korean. 
But, you will learn Hangul during the first and second weeks of class. If you fail to 
memorize Hangul within that period, it will be extremely difficult to understand the 
subsequent course content, so please make sure to memorize it.

Course
This IFLS108-03 class is recommended for Exchange / Visiting / undergraduate students.
Due to the large number of students enrolled relative to our class time, it is impossible 
to cover all vocabulary, reading, and listening sections within the classroom sessions. 
Specifically, you must memorize vocabulary on your own in advance, and a thorough 
review of the grammar taught in class is mandatory.
Therefore, the recommended self-study time is 1 to 2 hours every day.

Title 
Public Thresholds : Architecture for All  공공의 경계 : 모두를 위한 건축 
Theme 
 
서울의 공공 건축과 공공 공간은 어떻게 정의될 수 있을까? 서울의 공공 공간은 과연 충분하며, 공공 건축물은 모두에게 
공평하게 열려 있는가? 이 공간들은 다양한 사용자들이 함께 공유할 수 있는 장소로 기능하고 있는가? 더 나아가, 어떤 
건축적 전략이 공공 공간을 보다 효과적이고 의미 있게 만드는가?  
본 스튜디오는 이러한 질문을 출발점으로 삼아, ‘Type & Typology’  그리고 ‘Vernacular Intelligence’ 라는 두 가지 주제를 
통해 서울이라는 도시의 특수한 조건 속에서 서울 타이폴로지로서 공공건축과 공공공간의 새로운 유형을 탐구한다.  
Type & Typology : 유형과 유형학 
유형과 유형학은 건축과 도시를 이해하기 위한 중요한 도구이다. 본 스튜디오는 건축 유형의 근본적인 개념을 탐구하고, 
이를 분석·변형·발전시키는 과정을 통해 새로운 건축적 전략을 모색한다. 도시는 다양한 건축 유형들이 축적되고 중첩된 
집합체로 이해되며, 학생들은 이러한 관점에서 새로운 공공건축의 형태, 그리고 건축과 도시의 관계를 탐구하게 된다.  
Vernacular Intelligence : 지역의 환경과 삶에 축적된 건축적 지혜 
한때 ‘경계 없는 지구(Borderless Planet)’라는 개념은 건축과 기술의 발전을 바탕으로 전 세계 도시들이 유사한 모습과 
기능을 갖추게 만들었다. 그러나 코로나19 팬데믹, 기후 위기의 심화, 지역 분쟁의 지속, 그리고 민족주의와 보호주의의 
재등장은 이러한 흐름에 균열을 가져왔다. 오늘날 사람과 자원의 이동은 예고없이 제한되기도 하고, 글로벌 조건은 빠르게 
변화하고 있다. 이러한 시대적 맥락 속에서 본 스튜디오는 ‘Vernacular’를 다시 생각하고자 한다. ‘가정의, 토착의’를 의미하는 
라틴어 vernaculus 에서 유래한 ‘Vernacular’는 과거의 지역적 전통이나 고정된 양식이 아니라, 변화하는 사회·문화적, 환경적, 
정치적 조건에 대응하는 적응적 건축 전략으로 이해될 수 있다. 학생들은 지역의 기후, 삶, 문화, 행위, 제도와 같은 요소들이 
건축에 어떻게 작용하는지를 탐구하고, 동시에 건축이 다시 사회와 문화를 변화시키는 방식을 실험하게 된다.

Elections and Voting Behavior 
2026, Spring   
 
Course Number: POLI 230 
Class Time: Tuesday / Thursday 16:30-17:45 
Class Place: #113, Department of Politics and Economics 
Office Hour: by email appointment 
Email: ananan21@korea.ac.kr 
 
1. General Introduction 
 
Elections are one of important mechanisms in a democratic society, serving as a means of connecting citizens 
to political leadership. Voting is the principal activity that legitimizes the democratic process by individuals. 
This course focuses on academic study of elections and voting behavior and practical applications to the real 
political world. 
 
By considering diverse theoretical perspectives on why people vote/don’t vote and why they vote the way 
they do, and by applying those theoretical views to the real politics, students will learn both academic 
approaches and realistic approaches toward elections and voting behavior. 
 
There are several key elements to the class. However, most importantly, your active class participation is 
strongly required and encouraged. Our time in class will be spent presenting and discussing related to the 
topics while I will also give basic lectures. Establishing your own view and expressing it in an effective and 
persuasive way will be crucial for your success in this course. 
 
2. Objectives 
 
The basic objective of this course is to introduce major theories and key issues about electoral politics. This 
course also aims to provide students, based on understanding of theoretical perspectives, with a practical and 
strategic thinking for the real political sphere. 
 
There will be 2 major areas that this course will mainly cover - First, review of important theories about 
elections and voting behavior including people’s actual vote choice in recent national-wide elections. Second, 
practice of election campaign strategy for the upcoming national-wide election for local governments (e.g., 
Mayor of Seoul) on June 3 based on theoretical and historical understanding of Korean voters’ political 
attitude and choice behaviors.  
- 2 - 
By the end of this course, students will be able to: 
- 
Demonstrate knowledge of competing theoretical and empirical explanations of elections and voting 
behavior 
- 
Have your own logical view explaining people’s electoral choice 
- 
Apply academic concepts to analyzing the real politics and making campaign strategy plan for a real 
electoral competition 
- 
Practice appropriate research skills and expand your capacity for independent academic research 
 
3. Basic Readings 
 
The books introduced here are for students’ basic understating. Some parts of them will be required readings 
for this course, but mainly consider these books for expanding your knowledge boundary of electoral politics.  
 
Books: 
-

Makes Up His Mind in a Presidential Campaign. Columbia University Press. 
-

Voter. New York: Wiley. 
-

4. Class Activity 
 
Each week is divided into two sessions. Thursday classes are a seminar format with professor lectures and in-
class discussion, in attempt to provide the theoretical framework for understanding elections and voting 
behavior including sociological, psychological, rational, institutional, and so on. The seminar session will 
cover these issues by reviewing important books, journal papers, and other different research sources. 
 
Tuesday classes are mainly given for students’ INDIVIDUAL or TEAM presentations and discussions. For 
assigned topics, ONE STUDENT or ONE TEAM will make a presentation and lead a critical discussion 
(One team will be made of 3-5 students), and there will be several discussants for the topic presenation. 
 
Additionally, it is expected that the course can be slightly helpful for students’ future careers analyzing public 
opinion polling, survey research, campaign management, political practitioners, policy analysis, and so on.

Spring 2026

Ofﬁce Hours: By Appointment
Overview
This course examines the way political factors inﬂuence economic interactions between countries,
with a particular emphasis on trade politics. This course will provide an overview of current global
economic relations and systematically analyze how politics shape them: Why do countries cooperate
economically in some situations but not in others? Why do some governments embrace and promote
globalization while others oppose it? What are the social, political and economic consequences of
globalization? We will address these questions and others with a focus on the politics of trade. The
course will approach these topics by examining alternative theoretical approaches and evaluating these
theories using contemporary and historical evidence.
Requirements and Evaluation
• Participation (10%): Students are expected to attend the lecture each week and contribute to the
class discussion. We will have two discussion sessions during the semester. Your overall contribu-
tion to the class and to the presentation/discussion sessions will count to the participation grade.
* Attendance Policy: Attendance will be called at the beginning of each lecture at 9:00 AM. Excused
absences can be accepted up to twice throughout the semester (unless there is explicit permission
from the professor). To request an excused absence, you must submit the request to the portal
system at least two hours before class starts. In the case of illness or other medical circumstances,
you may submit your request to the portal without documentation ﬁrst and provide supporting
documentation afterward within 2 days. Each unexcused absence will result in a 1-point deduction,
and each tardiness will result in a a 0.5-point deduction from your participation grade. Up to two
instances of tardiness will be excused throughout the semester.
• In-Class Tests (30%): We will have three in-class written tests at the beginning of Class 6 (April
13), Class 10 (May 11), and Class 14 (June 8). Each test will last approximately 25 minutes, consist
of short-answer questions, and be worth 10 points. Students are expected to demonstrate their
understanding of lecture and reading materials.
• Policy Memos (30%): Students are required to two 500-word essays on discussion questions. Each
essay accounts for 15% of the ﬁnal grade. The ﬁrst policy memo is due by April 10th, 9am. The
second policy memo is due by May 8th, 9am.
• Open Book Final Exam (30%): Final exam will take place on June 15th (Monday). Students are
expected to demonstrate their understanding of lecture and reading materials. The ﬁnal exam will
be open book: Students can bring their own notes although electronic devices such as laptops and
phones are not allowed.

Academic English 
 
My attendance policy is strict.  All students are required to 
attend all classes on time.  Being late twice will result in 
one absence (whether offline or online).  Attendance will 
be taken at the beginning of every class.  
I do not regularly excuse any absences, so sending me 
documents (such as prescriptions from hospitals or 
pharmacies, or notes from your major’s administration 
about a special activity) will not give you an automatically 
excused absence.  My attendance policy is not aligned with 
any exemptions other departments may use, so simply 
submitting documents into KU Portal does not excuse an 
absence. However, if there is an emergency or unique 
situation, we can discuss it in person for exemptions (I am 
reasonable about this as long as it is done in a timely 
manner - please do not wait several weeks to explain an 
absence to me). This policy is in place to prevent an 
excessive amount of exemptions that would severely affect 
participation.  
The total value for the attendance grade is 20 points, but 
for each class you miss, you will be subtracted 3 points 
from your final grade for the first 2 absences, and then 
4 points for any additional absence. I do give each 
student one free absence, with no point penalty at all 
(see, I’m not a total monster!).  I would save it for an 
emergency situation.  That may seem like a strict policy, but 
because we have only two short classes per week, I believe 
this policy to be fair for all.  Attendance is a huge part of 
learning a foreign language, so I take this grading seriously.  
Lastly, please remember that per Korea University policy, 
students may not miss 7 classes before failing the course.   
This is a general syllabus for all of my Academic English 
courses and is subject to change.  While the classes I teach 
are structurally similar, I often design different midterms or 
quizzes to fit the needs of the students I am working with.  
The midterm in one class, for example, may differ greatly 
from that of another class, but the point system is still the 
same and rarely changes. Often times, class content will be 
tailored to be relevant to the needs of the students’ majors 
or special fields of study. 
It would be a good idea to frequently check the LMS Bulletin 
Board System as well.  During the semester I put all grading 
information and announcements there.

Course Description and Objectives 
 
Overview 
Operations management can be defined as the design, operation, and improvement of the 
systems that create and deliver the firm's primary products and services. This class provides 
an understanding of the operations management function and its relationship to other 
functional areas within the firm (both services and manufacturing). 
 
In this class, we will develop frameworks to analyze the strengths and weaknesses of a firm's 
operations and to develop viable alternatives in pursuing its goals and objectives. We will 
examine the tradeoffs that managers face in emphasizing one goal (such as high capacity 
utilization) as compared to another goal (such as customer service). We will compare the 
strengths and weaknesses of different strategies and techniques, as determined by industry 
and global operating environments. 
 
Ultimately, we hope to stimulate your interest in operations management. Whether you end 
up in finance, marketing, operations, accounting, or any other field, you will have 
opportunities to consider and systematically improve the way you do things. Operations 
management provides tools, techniques, and strategies for making organizations work more 
effectively and efficiently; hence, can make you a better manager. 
 
Learning Objectives 
At the end of the course, students should be able to: 
1. Understand the trade-offs among different types of production/operations systems 
2. Understand the strategic production/operations management issues and their 
relationship to the other functional areas of the firm. 
3. Develop a basic competence with the tools and techniques used by operations 
professionals  
4. Begin to develop an understanding of the managerial implications of alternative 
operations policies and techniques  
 
Approach 
Lectures will most likely be the predominant form of presentation, but a full interchange 
between the professor and the student is expected. 
 
2 
Statistical Applications 
Effective operations management incorporates the management of variation and uncertainty 
with respect to both demand and process capacity. Students will discover that the course 
applies statistical tools, which have been introduced in prerequisite courses (e.g., Business 
Statistics), to real business problems. Students should familiarize themselves with the 
following statistical tools for the course topics listed.

the course material. Proficiency will be estimated by measuring your performance on the

Re-grading (of homework assignments and exams) request can be submitted in writing along 
with the original assignment. TA and I are going to review the whole assignment, which means 
that your score after re-grading can be above or below your original score. Re-grading requests 
can be made within one week of the date of return of the graded item in question. No such

There will be no extra credit available for outside work. 
 
Homework 
Homework sets are assigned at periodic intervals throughout the course. These assignments 
are intended for the student to become more familiar with the concepts that are covered in 
lectures and in the text. Some of the homework exercise will require the use of the computer 
3 
and computer software such as EXCEL. Although I highly encourage you to submit the work 
individually, I also allow a group submission with a member of up to three students (will be 
determined later based on the final enrolled students). You can have a different group 
member for each homework set.  
 
Homework is to be presented in a neat, orderly fashion in a manner that would be presentable 
to a supervisor on a job. You should submit a single PDF document using “File Upload” 
method on LMS. “Comment” will not be considered when grading.  
 
Six homework sets will be assigned throughout the term. You are expected to turn in all 
homework sets. However, we will drop your score from the homework set on which you lost 
the greatest number of points. 
 
Attendance 
Students are expected to attend all classes. Students are expected to arrive promptly and be 
ready at the start of class and not to leave class early. Missing a class will forfeit the 
opportunity to earn class participation points that day. If a serious conflict arises (religious 
observance, serious illness, death in the family, etc.), please notify the professor as soon as 
possible so that accommodations can be made. Note that conflicts related to such things as 
recruiting, clubs, sports, etc. are not considered “serious conflicts” and will not be 
accommodated. 
 
Students are responsible for obtaining any notes or handouts for missed classes regardless of 
the reason for missing the class. 
 
Class Participation 
Being an active participant in class discussion and activities is crucial for learning both for 
oneself and for the good of the other students in the class. This, of course, requires being 
present, being prepared for class, answering questions well when called upon, and proactively 
engaging in class discussions. The professor will keep a record of strong participants after 
each class session. One need not be a leading participant in every session to receive full class 
participation credit. Poor or distracting participation will also be noted. 
 
Examinations 
During the term, there will be two tests.

Supplementary readings will be used to illustrate how actual firms are dealing with 
operations issues. They will be distributed in class or posted on the course website. 
 
Course Policies 
 
Copyright Law 
Materials and lectures in this course are protected by Copyright Law. Materials are presented 
in an educational context for personal use and study and should not be shared, distributed, or 
sold in print - or digitally - outside the course without permission. Electronic video and/or 
audio recording is not permitted during class unless the student obtains permission from the 
instructor. If permission is granted, any distribution of the recording is prohibited. 
  
Anti-graft Law 
Do not ask the instructor to change the grade unless there is a flaw in grading. Improper 
solicitation and graft for any matters are strictly prohibited by Anti-graft Law.

1. Course Description 
The rapid advances in technology afford unprecedented ability to collect massive data, shifting 
the paradigm in which entrepreneurs make business decisions. This course is designed to 
provide students with analytical skills on exploring data and basic concepts of programming 
language (Python). More specifically, this course introduces the fundamental principles of 
programming language, allowing students to collect and process data with libraries provided 
in Python. Through this course, students will be able to effectively process and analyze data 
with the ability to explore and understand data structures by using programming language. The 
class will be accompanied by both lectures and hands-on exercises, providing opportunities for 
students to handle programming software. 
Note: All lectures will be delivered in English. 
2. Course Objectives 
Students will be able to: 
i. 
Understand basic concepts of business analytics and apply it to solve problems. 
ii. 
Use python language for data analyses. 
iii. 
Collect data and setup empirical analyses strategies. 
iv. 
Understand basics of statistics and empirical analyses. 
v. 
Setup research questions and empirical models. 
vi. 
Interpret results from empirical analyses. 
 
 
3. Textbook 
No textbook required. Class materials will be distributed to students every week. 
Reference for Python programming:  
Python tutorial is available online: https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/

4. Class Components 
Components of the course include – (i) lectures, (ii) students’ small group discussion including 
in-class exercise, (iii) two exams, and (iv) final project. Students are strongly recommended to 
participate class actively. 
• Lectures: The class material will be provided during the lectures.  
• Small group discussion & In-class exercises: Small group discussion will be conducted 
each week. Students are required to review previous lectures before participating in a small 
group discussion. During the small group discussion, students will be given in-class 
exercises and some of them will be given as assignments. Students will get chances to earn 
extra credits during the in-class exercises.  
• Exams: Two exams will be given (midterm and final). All of them will be based on the 
content from lectures, in-class exercises, and assignment.  
• Participation: Participating in class discussions and exercises is highly recommended. Also, 
feel free to ask questions during the class. If you are disruptive or disrespectful to anyone 
in the classroom, I will ask you to leave the session.

6. Policy for late homework 
Late assignment will be accepted only if the students turn in their homework within 3 days. 
The score for the late assignment will be deducted 10% per day. Assignments must be 
submitted as both physical and electronic copies on the due date. 
7. Policy for lateness and participation 
Three lateness will be considered as one absence. Excused absences include documented 
illness, deaths in the family and other documented crises, call to active military duty or jury 
duty, religious holy days, and official University activities. These absences will be 
accommodated in a way that does not arbitrarily penalize students who have a valid excuse. 
Consideration will also be given to students whose dependent children experience serious 
illness. 
8. Learning Approach  
• Students will be assigned to do hands-on exercises after lectures. Students are 
strongly recommended to actively participate for class exercises. The purpose of 
hands-on exercises is to give opportunities for students to get familiar with python. 
Copying others’ work will not help! 
• Active and enthusiastic learning is important. Students should be able to explore 
data structures with various software tools. Students are highly recommended to 
think critically so that they can solve problems more efficiently. This cannot be 
achieved in passive learning. 
• There will be two exams (Midterm and Final) during the semester. Each exam will 
be based on all lectures and class exercises covered during the course. The exams 
will test your understanding of lectures and python codes. Students should be able 
to apply knowledge attained from the course to solve advanced problems.

POLI247 Theories of Political Institutions 
 
Spring 2026 
Tuesday/Thursday 1:30—2:45pam 
 
Prof. Dong Seong (Don) Lee 
610 Poli Sci & Econ Building 
don_lee@korea.ac.kr  
 
 
1. Course overview 
This course is designed to provide a survey of the political institutions—the “rules of the 
game”—in various democracies around the world.  An institution is a set of 
incentives/constraints that affect actors’ preferences and choices.  In order to investigate political 
behaviors and outcomes, therefore, it is essential for us to understand the effects of institutions.  
The course will first introduce students to scientific approaches to analyzing the consequences of 
institutions.  Then, we will discuss constitutional designs to solve the principal-agent 
(delegation) problem in representative democracies.  Next, we will compare the varying effects 
of different political institutions, including parliamentarism versus presidentialism, federalism 
versus unitary government, majoritarian electoral system versus proportional representation, 
two-party versus multiparty systems, unicameralism versus bicameralism, direct versus 
representative democracy, and majoritarian versus consociational government.  After that, we

COURSE INTRODUCTION 
 
This course introduces students to the principles and practices of marketing in an 
international context, with a strong emphasis on micro-level processes such as consumer 
behavior, segmentation, branding, and cultural adaptation. Students will gain practical tools 
and cross-cultural awareness to develop marketing strategies tailored to diverse global 
markets. 
 
By the end of the course, students will be able to: 
 
• 
Understand how cultural, economic, and legal factors affect marketing decisions 
• 
Analyze global consumers and segment international markets 
• 
Develop positioning and branding strategies for different regions 
• 
Create and adapt product, pricing, communication, and distribution strategies 
internationally 
• 
Work in teams to present an international market entry plan

any point during the course.

Global Marketing and Advertising, Marieke de Mooij, 6th Edition, SAGE Publications 
 
Economist, Financial Times, New York Times, The Wall Street Journal*
