e-mail: jchon@korea.ac.kr
Students in this class needing accommodations relating to a disability should feel free to contact or come by Professor Chon’s office.  The location and phone number are listed above.
Course Description
This course explores the connection between environment and landscape architecture, focusing on how environmental issues around us can be understood through a landscape lens and addressed through design-based approaches.
Students examine everyday environments and urban spaces to understand how natural systems, human activities, and spatial design interact. Rather than focusing on technical design skills, the course emphasizes observation, interpretation, and strategic thinking to bridge scientific knowledge and real-world environmental problems.
Through lectures, case studies, and hands-on exercises, students learn how landscape architecture translates environmental science into spatial strategies and practical interventions. The textbook presents real-world cases that illustrate how environmental challenges are identified, interpreted, and addressed through landscape-based design thinking.
Course Objectives
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
Identify environmental issues embedded in everyday spaces and urban environments.
Interpret environmental problems through the lens of landscape architecture by connecting natural systems, human behavior, and spatial form.
Apply basic design thinking to explore landscape-based strategies for environmental challenges.
Translate scientific and ecological knowledge into spatial observations and design-oriented insights.
Analyze real-world landscape cases to understand how environmental issues are addressed through planning and design processes.
Textbook and References

Chon, Jinhyung. Landscape, Nature Close at Hand. Seoul: [Publisher], [Year].
Lecture slides and readings provided by the instructor
Case study materials and supplementary articles
DESCRIPTION OF WORK
This course consists of lectures, weekly assignments, in-class activities, and two mini projects.
Students are expected to actively participate in all components of the course, as learning outcomes are achieved through continuous observation, analysis, discussion, and application rather than through written examinations.
Lectures introduce key concepts related to environment, landscape architecture, and design-based approaches. Weekly assignments and in-class activities are designed to help students apply these concepts to everyday environments and real-world spatial conditions. Mini projects require students to synthesize accumulated knowledge and demonstrate their ability to interpret and address environmental issues through landscape-based thinking.
Instructional Format
Each class meeting comprises lectures and practical sessions, exploring fundamentals of environment and design from an ecological landscape architecture perspective. The course includes lectures, exercises, discussions, individual assignments, and group work.
Field trips and Group Discovery
Coursework may involve field trips reflecting the ecological and social systems of the environment. Fieldtrip exercises facilitate observation and study of the environmental aspects of places related to design form and expression.
Specific field trip guidelines and activities will be announced according to the schedule.
Weekly Assignments
Weekly assignments are designed to reinforce lecture content and in-class activities by encouraging students to observe, analyze, and interpret everyday environments and urban spaces.
Each weekly assignment focuses on a specific theme or concept introduced in class, such as environmental issues in daily life, human–environment relationships, landscape elements, or resilience-based thinking. Assignments typically involve short written responses, diagrams, sketches, photographs, or analytical notes rather than technical drawings.
Weekly assignments may be cumulative or non-cumulative, depending on the nature of the task. Some assignments contribute directly to the development of mini projects, while others are evaluated independently.
All weekly assignments must be submitted according to the schedule announced in class. Submission format and deadlines will be specified for each assignment.
In-Class Activities 
In-class activities are an essential component of this course and are directly linked to the course objectives and mini projects.
These activities include observation exercises, spatial analysis, group discussions, short presentations, and hands-on practice. Students are expected to actively engage in analyzing everyday environments, identifying environmental issues, and discussing landscape-based interpretations and strategies.
Participation in in-class activities is required and is reflected in the final grade. Active involvement, preparedness, and contribution to discussions are considered in the evaluation of participation.
Mini Projects 
Mini Project 1: City Vlog

Mini Project 1 focuses on observing and interpreting an everyday urban space through a landscape perspective.
Students select a familiar place and analyze how landscape elements, environmental conditions, and human activities interact. The project emphasizes visual documentation, narrative structure, and conceptual interpretation rather than technical design skills.
Detailed guidelines, submission format, and evaluation criteria will be provided separately.

Mini Project 2: Landscape-based Environmental Problem Solving
(Final Exam Replacement)

Mini Project 2 is a cumulative project that replaces the final examination.
The project is developed progressively from Week 9 through Week 16, building on concepts and analyses introduced through lectures, weekly assignments, and in-class activities related to resilience, ecological landscape design, and green infrastructure.
Students identify an environmental issue embedded in a real site, analyze vulnerabilities and system interactions, and propose a landscape-based strategic framework to address the issue. The project emphasizes problem definition, analytical reasoning, and strategic thinking rather than detailed technical design.
Mini Project 2 consists of multiple stages, including issue identification, vulnerability assessment, strategy development, and final presentation. Detailed guidelines and submission requirements will be provided separately.
POLICY
Attendance Policy
Regular attendance is required due to the practice-oriented nature of the course. Students are responsible for all materials covered in class.

Late Submission Policy
Late submissions may be penalized unless prior arrangements have been made. Specific policies regarding late work will be announced in class.

Academic Integrity
All students must adhere to university policies regarding academic integrity. Plagiarism or submission of work that is not original is not permitted.

Use of External Tools and AI
The use of external references and AI-based tools is permitted when properly cited. All submitted work must reflect the student’s own understanding and interpretation.
Grading Policy
Attendance and Participation: 15%
Weekly Assignments and In-Class Activities: 25%
Mini Project 1: 20%
Mini Project 2 (Final Exam Replacement): 40%
Grades are based on the overall learning process, quality of observation and analysis, clarity of interpretation, and consistency of engagement throughout the semester.
Instructor Expectations Regarding Classroom Behavior
Open dialogue is encouraged, but it must be controlled and respectful. Guidelines for classroom behavior are provided, aiming to create an effective learning environment.
SCHOLASTIC HONESTY
Scholastic honesty is emphasized, with violations including cheating, plagiarism, and accepting prohibited assistance. Students are expected to read and understand the departmental handout regarding plagiarism. Instances of scholastic dishonesty will result in appropriate penalties.

COURSE DESCRIPTION	
This course examines quality of life through the study of leisure, life, and happiness in contemporary society. Students will explore classical and contemporary theories, research findings, and everyday experiences to understand how leisure contributes to individual well-being and life satisfaction. While the primary focus is on personal meaning-making, the course also introduces a life-course perspective, encouraging students to consider how leisure, work, and happiness may change across different stages of life. Through lectures, discussions, presentations, and reflective assignments, students will develop a deeper understanding of leisure as a key component of a meaningful and balanced life. Active participation and several outside assignments are required.
COURSE OBJECTIVES
A student who successfully completes this course will be able to:
Understand and describe major theoretical and research-based definitions of leisure, life, happiness, and quality of life.
Reflect on and redefine their own meanings of leisure, life, and happiness based on personal experiences and academic perspectives.
Recognize how social contexts and life stages influence leisure experiences and perceptions of well-being, including age-related issues.
Explore the relationship between leisure, work, and life satisfaction across the life course.
Present and write clearly about their perspectives on leisure, life, and happiness using reflective and academic approaches.
REQUIRED TEXTBOOK & PUBLICATIONS
No required textbook.

Course Description and Objectives

      This course will focus on enhancing academic competency in English in all four areas of speaking, listening, reading and writing. While covering academic content, particularly in terms of essay writing and general competency in communication, this course is designed to be as student-centered as possible with task orientated and group presentation activity wherever possible. The goal is to increase your overall proficiency in all areas of English communication as it relates to your academic studies. 

One segment of this course will focus on English for business majors, including the topics of international marketing and negotiation. Another segment will focus on essay writing analysis and techniques. A third segment will cover logic more intensively to improve overall communication coherency. Towards the end of the semester, there will be a parliamentary style debate activity that will give further opportunity to practically apply some of the previously taught skills. 


    This course will focus on group and class interaction as much as possible. While some activities in an Academic English program have to remain teacher-student focused, ideally other activities would begin with partner interaction, expand into group interaction, and then further develop into full class interaction. For this purpose, we need to assign groups and some of your evaluation involves your group performance. A group should have a minimum of four students and this will be organized further in the first class.

 A quiz will be given on the Basic Logical Concepts topic covered in the weeks after the mid term exam.

Course Description
Sensor Theory and Signal Processing II is a senior-level course that integrates the principles of sensor operation with signal processing algorithms. The course is balanced between theoretical foundations and practical application, with programming exercises (primarily in Python) to reinforce concepts. Students will explore a wide range of sensors – from 2D sensors like imaging devices, through 3D sensors like LiDAR sensors.
Course Learning Outcomes
In this course, students will develop the ability to characterize various sensor systems and apply signal processing algorithms to analyze and interpret the data they produce, bridging theoretical understanding with practical computational skills. Specifically, students will learn the followings
Understandings of different types of sensors
Signal processing techniques
Practical implementations
Prerequisites
Sensor Theory and Signal Processing I
Texts & Materials
There is no official book for this class, but it would be helpful to read the following material:
Oppenheim, A. et al., Signals and Systems (2nd ed). Prentice-Hall
Franklin, G. et al., Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems (7th ed).  Pearson
Gonzalez, R. C. et al., Digital Image Processing, (4th ed). Pearson

Absence
If you must miss a class due to unforeseen circumstances, please follow the guidelines below:
Emergencies: Only absences due to illness and military-related, supported by an official proof, will be considered excused. In case of illness-related absences or extended medical issues, please contact me promptly to discuss possible accommodations or alternatives.
Makeup Work: It is your responsibility to make up any missed assignments, readings, or coursework. Check the course materials and collaborate with fellow students to ensure you are up to date.
Attendance Policy: If you accumulate three unexcused absences, it will result in an automatic grade of "F" for the course.
Late Assignments
Assignments must be received by the due date, no later than 11:59PM. Up to one late assignment will be taken without deducting any points. From the second late assignment, a late assignment will take 10% of the total grade of the assignment for 24-hour period, up to 3 days. After three days, the assignment will receive a zero. 
Academic Integrity
University policy will be followed.  At a minimum, the student (and any student caught assisting in the misconduct) will be given an automatic “F” for the test/assignment in question and possibly an “F” for the course. COURSE DESCRIPTION AND OBJECTIVES:
This course aims to develop students’ academic English proficiency and communicative competence required for university-level study. The course is conducted using academic content to strengthen students’ overall English ability applicable across a range of academic disciplines. Emphasis is placed on practical communication skills through a variety of task-based and interactive activities designed to help students use English effectively in academic and real-life contexts.
Students will also engage with a variety of academic texts to improve reading comprehension skills and to develop an understanding of English expressions related to their fields of study.
We will achieve these goals through a combination of practical activities, in-class assignments, and mini-lectures. The following are the core activities and skills we will focus on:
Discussion skills for academic purposes.
Research skills necessary for academic writing and discussion. 
Developing ideas for writing through discussion, brainstorming and freewriting.
Learning how to write a basic academic essay with citations, and how to avoid plagiarism.
Expanding your level of academic vocabulary. 
Developing your public speaking skills/presentation skills.
ASSESSMENT: 
Your final grade will be based upon a combination of the following: 
The standard scale for grading is as follows:
ACTIVE PARTICIPATION is:
Willingly taking part in all class activities
Showing interest and motivation to share your ideas, thoughts, feelings, and questions
Completing classwork on time
Examples of active participation include:
Volunteering to answer questions
Asking questions by raising your hand
Speaking actively in group work
Staying awake and attentive during class
Following classroom rules
REGULAR ATTENDANCE is required.
Please note that while you may miss up to 3 classes without penalty, missing 10 or more classes will result in an automatic failing grade for the course.
The semester consists of 16 weeks, and we must meet for a minimum of 15 weeks (30 class sessions in total).
Midterm and final exams (or exam-related assignments/quizzes) each count as one class session.
We are required to make up any missed classes to ensure we reach the 30 required meetings. This includes cancellations due to public holidays, teacher illness, or other disruptions.
My absence/lateness policy (5% of your overall grade): 
You are allowed 3 absences for any reason without penalty. Starting with the 4th absence, you will begin to lose attendance points. If you have a valid reason (see examples below), you must contact me and make arrangements to recover lost points. 
Regardless of the reason, you are responsible for finding out what homework, quizzes, tests, announcements, or in-class work you missed—and you must complete the missed work. I understand that special situations may arise. Even in special situations, you are still responsible for making up missed work. Please talk to me or a classmate to find out what you missed. Important information—like deadline changes, handouts, or quiz details—is often given in class.
Being absent is not an excuse for turning in homework late or being unprepared for future classes. If you experience an emergency, I will be understanding—but you must speak with me personally to discuss the situation.
Officially excused absences (e.g., military check-ups, a family member’s funeral, etc.) must be supported by official documentation or must be registered online if required. Please make every effort to notify me in advance whenever possible.
You are considered late to class if you are more than 5 minutes late. You can be late to class 3 times without penalty. The fourth time you are late will count for a loss of attendance points equivalent to one absence. 
ELECTRONIC EMAIL 
Always include the following information in the subject line of your email: 
Your full name, Your student ID number, Our class name (number)
When sending assignments or documents, always use Microsoft Word (.doc or .docx) — do not use HWP (Hangul Word Processor). Most foreign professors (including me) prefer and appreciate Microsoft Word files because they are more accessible and compatible.
My email address is: laramanuel@hotmail.com (do not write lala by accident)
CLASSROOM MATERIALS
You will need access to Microsoft Word for the writing portion of our class. I do not accept HWP documents. There is no single book that can meet the needs of students whose English language levels and learning styles vary considerably. For this reason, we will use a combination of materials and handouts which I will upload to the LMS as needed.
CLASSROOM RULES AND FINAL COMMENTS
Important: a major goal of this class is to help you become a competent, independent learner. After completing this course, you should be able to continue developing your English through self-study and independent learning.
Participation: Often you will be expected to work in pairs or in small groups. Participation includes arriving on time, being prepared (bringing your book, notebook, handouts, and other required materials), listening attentively, interacting with your classmates and teacher, actively engaging in class activities, completing assignments thoroughly and on time, and asking questions when you don’t understand.
Speaking Korean: In most cases, speaking Korean in class is unnecessary. You will lose participation points if you speak Korean without permission. That said, I do allow Korean when helping classmates understand rules, grammar points, or my instructions—but you must ask for permission first.
Plagiarism: Plagiarism means presenting someone else’s ideas or work as your own. It is dishonest, unethical, and—even when unintentional—can negatively affect your grade. Accidental plagiarism is more understandable than intentional plagiarism, but both are serious. Most importantly, plagiarism prevents you from learning and growing as a student. We will discuss how to recognize and avoid plagiarism in this class.
AI (Artificial Intelligence): AI is a powerful tool and has many benefits, and we will occasionally use it as a learning tool in class. I allow the use of AI for some classroom activities, for research and preparation at home, and in any way that you feel it can be helpful in your English learning. However, you are not allowed to use AI programs during exams or quizzes.  
Important Note: 
Sometimes the pressures of university life and/or personal matters can cause students to become distressed, which can have a negative impact upon their health. Your health, both mental and physical, is extremely important. There are counseling services offered at Korea University free of charge, but few students take advantage of these services due to unnecessary fears. There is a common misconception that people who seek counseling are “crazy.” In reality, most people who seek help are regular individuals dealing with common challenges, such as:
Stress
Self-esteem issues
Relationship problems (with partners, friends, or family)
Anger management
Bullying
Anxiety
Grief
Addictions (to TV, smartphones, gaming, eating, exercise, etc.)
Alcohol-related issues
Loneliness
Depression
Fears
ADHD
Emotional instability
The Counseling Center is a safe and confidential space where you can work through your problems. Unlike talking to a friend, a counselor is professionally trained to support your personal growth and help you deal with life's challenges. They can help you understand your situation more clearly and guide you toward solutions—so you can eventually manage things more confidently on your own. You are free to say whatever you want in counseling, without fear of judgment. You will never be pressured to talk about anything you're not ready to discuss. Research shows that 70–90% of people who attend counseling report feeling better afterward. Don’t hesitate to seek support—you’re not alone, and help is available.

강의 소개
이 수업은 국제대학 글로벌한국융합학부 전공필수 수업으로, ‘한국 속의 세계, 세계 속의 한국’에 대한 입문 수준의 이해를 목적으로 한다. 학생들은 사회, 정치, 경제를 아우르는 다양한 측면에서 한국과 세계의 연결을 탐색한다.
국제사회의 원조를 받는 가난한 나라였던 한국은 이제 세계를 품은 글로벌 한국으로 탈바꿈하였고, 이 성공 사례는 국제사회의 많은 주목을 받아왔다. 그러나 이 수업은 단 순히 한국의 성공 스토리에 주목하는데 그치지 않고, 경제 불평등, 사회 양극화 등 현대 한국이 안고 있는 성공의 그늘 또한 살펴본다.  뿐만 아니라, 한국과 세계의 연계성을 바탕으로 인권 증진, 기술 혁신, 기후 위기 극복 등 인류가 함께 맞닥뜨린 도전과제에 대하여 논의한다.  이를 통하여 학생들은 한국의 특수한 경험을 이해하고, 동시에 그 경험이 가진 보편성에 대하여 탐구할 수 있다.  학생들은 이 수업을 통하여 국제사회의 요구에 부응하는 한국학 전문가로 성장하는 첫 걸음을 내딛게 될 것이다.
글로벌한국학입문 수업은 특별한 방식으로 운영된다. 국제대학의 교수진은 이 수업을 위한 교과서 『글로벌한국학』을 직접 집필하였다.  각자의 연구 주제에 맞추어 교재 집필에 참여한 교수들이 직접 해당 주제를 강의한다.  학생들은 여러 교수의 강의를 접 하며 앞으로 글로벌한국융합학부에서의 전공 학업 계획을 설계할 수 있다.

COURSE OBJECTIVES
The objective of this course is to improve students’ academic and professional skills in Business English. By the end of this course students will be more prepared to participate successfully in English-related academic and professional settings.  The course uses current topics and situations related to successfully navigating in society using English. 
REQUIRED MATERIALS
Each student is responsible for bringing the following materials to class: notebook, writing utensil, and a file folder.  Students will be expected to save all handouts, organize them in the folder, and bring it to class every day. If you are absent for class, please ask your classmates for any handouts. PPT's from class will be downloaded to blackboard. 
GRADED COMPONENTS
Final grades will be based on several different evaluations. The chart below may change slightly. 
              *Note: Attendance 
As this is a language skills course, simply attending class in not enough for a perfect attendance grade
Attendance includes active participation in group activities
Active participation in class discussions
Completion of tasks in class
Completion of homework
Use of only English in the classroom, as much as possible
Paying attention during presentations, which means respecting the presenter and NOT looking at smartphones, sleeping, etc. 
Grading Distribution
This course will follow the absolute grading policy of Korea University.  Your grade will be assigned based on a raw score you achieved throughout the semester. 
Late assignments will suffer a 50% deduction. After 1 week the assignment will not be accepted. 
Plagiarism is considered cheating and will not be tolerated. 
Attendance
A student will be marked late (1/2 absence) if he/she misses the attendance call. 
A student will be marked absent if he/she is 10 minutes or more late.

개요 | 21세기에 들어 세계적으로 환경오염에 대한 관심과 고도 산업화 사회의 지속적인 발전을 위한 에너지와 광물 자원의 부족으로 인하여 우리는 인류 역사상 지구과학에 대한 관심이 최고조에 이른 시기에 살고 있다. 그러나 지금까지 우리나라 초-중-고등학교 교육 과정에서 다루는 지질학과 지구과학은 주입식 교육으로 인하여 이해가 어렵고 무조건 암기해야 하는 것으로 여겨지며, 학생들이 근본적인 흥미를 가지게 되기 어려운 것이 현실이다. 본 강좌는 어떠한 과정을 통하여 현대 지구과학의 개념이 정립되었는지 살펴보고, 이를 바탕으로 최신 이론들을 소개하며, 향후 지구과학의 다양한 분야를 전공할 학생들에게 논리적으로 지구과학을 소개하는 것이 목적이다.

Academic English Writing for Sciences Syllabus
Professor: Mr. (Benjamin) Fallon
Objectives:
The objective of this course is to improve your academic skills in English, focusing on effective academic research, writing, and communication. Over the course of the semester, students will conduct an academic survey and submit a research report on a topic of their choosing. Similar to an academic conference, students will also present their results to their classmates. 
Below is a basic overview of the assessment requirements:
Grading Policies
(a) Grade Distribution
This course is an absolute graded course. Grades will be based on your score out of 100:
(b) Attendance and Lateness
1. You are allowed THREE class absences (for any reason) without penalty. Use these wisely.
2. There will be a penalty of 1% off your final score for every class missed after this.
3. This penalty will not apply in cases where the reason for the absence is covered by Korea University official policy: hospitalization, death in the family, military duty, or period pain. Please apply via the KU Portal. 
4. Being less than 20 minutes late to class three times will count as one absence. 
5. Being more than 20 minutes late will count as a full absence.
6. Sleeping or not participating in class will be marked as absent
7. According to Korea University policy, you must attend 70% of the class to pass. 
(c) Project Submission/Completion 
In all cases, excused absences consistent with official Korea University policy will not be subject to a reduction in score or other penalties.
1. All written assessments
There will be a 5% deduction of your final score for every day these are handed in late with no acceptable reason provided, up to a maximum of 3 days. After three days, they will not be accepted at all.
2. Meetings and individual presentations
If you are unable to come to your scheduled time for these activities, your first option is to swap with a willing student. This can be done at any time via our Google Sheet. If there is an emergency which means you don’t have a chance to swap, contact me ASAP, and we can schedule another time—as long as the reason for absence is consistent with Korea University policy. 
Classroom Handouts
There is no prescribed textbook for this semester. All necessary documents will be uploaded to the Blackboard portal. You may use your computer or tablet in class. 
Student Counseling Services 
The KU Student Counseling Centre offers help to students having trouble at University. They have one to one counseling, group counseling, and even some tests people can take about their lives, feelings, personality, relationships, and more. During the semester, they are open from Monday-Friday from 9am- 5:30pm (closed for lunch). They are located in the Central Plaza Room 114 (중앙광장). Tel: 3290-1540. Website: http://kuscc.korea.ac.kr (in Korean).

Mid-semester quiz | 10 | Students will take a quiz on survey design.

Individual
Presentations | 20 | Students will prepare their findings for an in-class individual presentation conducted during the final exam period.

Participation | 10 | You will be expected to use English and be active during class time.

개요 | 본 과목는 기업재무의 기초 과정으로, 재무관리의 기본적인 개념과 여러 분석도구를 학습합니다. 먼저, 기업의 재무상태와 현금흐름을 파악하기 위해 재무제표의 기본적인 구조를 학습하고, 자본예산, 운전자본관리 등 기업 내부의 주요 재무의사결정 유형을 살펴봅니다. 이후 적절한 분석도구와 평가방법을 활용하여 기업 내 현금흐름 및 프로젝트, 주식∙채권 등 다양한 금융상품의 위험과 수익을 평가하고, 마지막으로 자본자산가격결정모형(CAPM)과 증권시장선(SML)을 통해 위험과 수익의 관계를 이해함으로써, 기업가치를 극대화하는 의사결정을 내리는데 필요한 역량을 배양하는 것을 목표로 합니다.

주요 학습내용: (i) 재무관리 서론, (ii) 재무제표, 세금, 현금흐름, (iii) 화폐의 시간가치, (iv) 현금흐름 할인법, (v) 채권의 가치평가, (vi) 주식의 가치평가, (vii) 순현가법 및 기타 투자평가방법, (viii) 자본투자의 의사결정, (ix) 증권시장선, (x) 자본비용

Credits: 3 hours
Course Overview: Understanding of the elemental cycles (especially C, H, O, N, P, S, and metals) between earth’s major zones including atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, and lithosphere and the human influences on the natural material circulation.
Textbooks: Biogeochemistry: an analysis of global change, 4th ed. by William H. Schlesinger and Emily S. Bernhardt (Downloadable from https://library.korea.ac.kr/). Course notes will be uploaded in Black Board (BB). You will need to print them out by yourself.
Objectives of this Class:
To learn the basic chemical cycles that occur in the various Earth systems and the environments in which these reactions occur
To understand the basic geochemical concepts including redox chemistry, thermodynamics, and kinetics
To identify the typical procedures and methods used to measure these processes on the Earth
The learner will identify the chemical cycles that take place on the Earth; the learner will be able to explain the various geochemical reactions that are important in biogeochemical cycles; the learner will be able to identify the environments in which these cycles occur, how they differ, and what instrumental, laboratory, and field methods are used to measure these processes.
Prerequisite: Earth Materials Science / Atmospheric Chemistry / Geochemistry / Aqueous geochemistry / Hydrogeology / Sedimentary System etc

A mid-term, a final exam, and three homework problem sets are employed as summative assessments. Class discussions are used as formative assessments.

창의적 미디어 기획과 표현
고려대학교 미디어학부
과목개요: 본 과목의 목표는 “다양한 미디어를 기반으로 한 일련의 그룹 프로젝트들을 통해 팀워크 상황에서의 창의적인 기획과 표현 역량을 습득한다.” 이를 위해서 본 과목에서는 학생들이 주도해서 진행하는 프로젝트와 미디어 환경에 대한 학습, 관련된 특강, 이렇게 세가지 요소로 진행하고자 합니다. 그리고 특강을 제외한 기타 요소는 학생들과 함께 고민해서 만들어 나가고자 합니다. 특강은 미디어와 관련된 경험을 하면서 새로운 영역을 확장해 가고 있는 강사들을 모셔서 그들의 성공과 실패에 대해서 듣는 시간이며, 약 10회가량 진행할 예정입니다.

프로젝트 참가: 모든 학생은 수업의 모든 활동에 적극 참가하여야 한다. 이는 제작 전 과정을 포함하며, 각 학생의 참여도는 모니터링 후 반영될 것이다. 
제작과 관련하여 필요한 장비는 학생이 조달할 의무가 있으며, 교수의 조언을 구할 수 있다. 
수업이 일주일에 한번 있는 관계로 출석은 필수이다. 한번 결석은 최종 학점에서 한 단계 하락을 의미한다 (ex: A에서 A-로). 지각이나 미리 수업에서 나가는 것 두 번이 한번의 결석의 간주된다. 하지만, 아주 중요한 결석 사유가 있는 경우 (ex: 관혼상제), 수업 전에 미리 연락을 하여 예외 처리를 받을 수가 있다.

Course Description:
Wisdom of the East is an exploration of the enduring philosophical and spiritual traditions of Asia, focusing on key ancient and modern texts that illuminate timeless human concerns. From the ethical teachings of Confucius to the contemplative insights of Buddhism and the flowing harmony of Taoist thought, this course invites students to engage deeply with foundational ideas that have shaped Eastern civilizations. We will also consider how these traditions respond to and converse with global philosophical currents, offering a rich comparative perspective. Through close reading and discussion, students will gain not only historical and cultural understanding but also personal insight into ways of living wisely in a complex world.

General Approach to Instruction
Semiconductor device fabrication is analogous to cooking. This means the cleanroom is analogous to a kitchen. In other words, there will be ideas, ingredients, formulations, processes, techniques, recipes, equipment, hazards, and of course some tricks up the sleeves. There are many ways of going about achieving similar device features. The main purpose of this class is to first acquaint the students with the general idea of a MOSFET in a silicon substrate. This will provide the general direction of where the class is heading as we introduce individual processes such as lithography, thermal oxidation, deposition, and etching with their principles and key parameters. Each of these process steps will introduced in sequence in accordance to one of the many ways of fabricating a MOSFET. At the end of the course, the students should be able to retain working theoretical knowledge of basic semiconductor fabrication and processing. The caveat is that the student should understand that this class is far from exhaustive or up-to-date. After all, each of the seemingly minor processes mentioned in class has its own universe. Most importantly, they are constantly evolving or render obsolete except for certain specialized applications. In other words, any of the subtopics that we are covering in class can easily be expanded into a series of separate courses by itself.

Understand how organic chemistry underpins key biological processes and apply this knowledge to solve problems in molecular biology, biochemistry, and biotechnology.

지원사항 | 비고 | 본 강의를 수강하는 개개인의 특성과 요구에 따라, 지도교수 및 장애학생지원센터와의 상담을 통하여 적절한 수준의 지원 서비스를 제공합니다. 장애학생에 대한 지원서비스와 관련하여 문의사항이 있는 학생들은 장애학생지원센터(02-3290-1534)로 문의바랍니다.
∙ [출석] 
-1/3 이상 결석시 성적부여 불가, 특정 사유에 한해 출석인정신청 및 시험 불응시 신청 가능, 단 출석인정 제외하고 1/2 이상 실제 출석 필요함

∙ [학습윤리]
-대학의 목적과 본교 교육이념에 따라 성실하고 정직한 마음과 열정적인 태도로 학습에 적극적으로 참여
-고등교육을 받는 교양인으로서 위치를 자각하며 도덕적 민감성을 바탕으로 창의적 학문탐구에 정진
-교육활동과 관련하여 교원 및 동료학생과 약속한 사항을 성실히 이행
-교원과 동료학생들의 인격을 존중하고 기본적인 예의를 준수
-강의계획서 등을 충분히 탐색하여 학문적 지식탐구 및 미래 비전과 연결된 교과목 선택
-매 수업에 적극적으로 임할 수 있도록 미리 교육자료 탐독하고 확인
-정해진 수업시간에 결석, 지각, 중도 이탈 유의
-출석 관련 위계행위(대리출석 등) 금지
-적극적으로 토론, 질의응답 등 수업활동에 참여
-스스로 성실하게 작성한 과제를 제출하고 인용한 모든 자료는 변조, 왜곡 없이 표시
-협동학습의 경우 자신이 맡은 부분을 책임 있게 완수하고 최선의 노력을 다함
-교과목에서 요구하는 시험의 목적과 의미를 인식하고 부정행위 없이 정직하게 응시
-한학기 수강한 교과목의 강의 품질 개선을 위한 강의평가를 정직하게 수행
∙ [실험실습 안전]
-연구실 안전환경 조성에 관한 법률 제20조(교육·훈련)에 의거, 연구실안전법이 적용되는 과학기술분야 대상학과에 소속된 연구활동종사자는 매학기 일정시간의 안전교육을 이수하여야 하므로 실험·실습을 수강하는 모든 대상학과 학부생 및 대학원생은 교육참여 필수
-신규교육(신입생 2시간), 정기교육(고위험학과 학기별 6시간, 저위험학과 학기별 3시간)
-대상학과: KUPID > 지식관리 > 안전관리지식 > 연구실안전
-포털시스템 상단 메뉴에서 “정보생활” 클릭, [안전교육(서울)] 클릭하여 안전교육 페이지 접속(“크롬”으로 접속, 접속 오류 시 인터넷 설정에서 “팝업 차단 해제” 설정 필요)
-포털 아이디가 없는 경우, 국가연구안전관리본부 연구실안전교육시스템(https://edu.labs.go.kr/) 접속하여 수강 가능함. 
-외부기관에서 안전교육을 이수한 경우 별도의 등록절차를 통한 이수 가능
-미이수 시 불이익: 학부생(성적열람 제한), 대학원생(출입제한)
-문의사항: 교육문의(안전관리팀 02-3290-2763), 시스템문의(아키시스템즈 02-2664-5354)

∙ [인권성평등 교육 필수이수] 
-본교는 인권,성평등 교육 의무수강 제도를 운영(「양성평등기본법」 제31조 근거 법정의무)
하고 있으며 매학년도 1회 이상(학부생의 경우 총 4회 이상 이수필수)
 -수강방법 : LMS(https://lms.korea.ac.kr)에 로그인하여 수강(LMS 로그인 → 상단 '[비정규 과정] > [강좌 검색]' → 좌측 [구분] 메뉴에서 “법정의무 및 교내권장 교육”을 체크하거나, 강좌 이름 검색 → 신청 버튼 클릭 → ‘학습하러 가기’ 클릭 → [공지] 메뉴 클릭 → [주차학습] 메뉴 클릭 → 안내사항 확인 후 영상 클릭하여 시청

Course Description and Objectives

      This course will focus on enhancing academic competency in English in all four areas of speaking, listening, reading and writing. While covering academic content, particularly in terms of essay writing and general competency in communication, this course is designed to be as student-centered as possible with task orientated and group presentation activity wherever possible. The goal is to increase your overall proficiency in all areas of English communication as it relates to your academic studies. 

One segment of this course will focus on English for business majors, including the topics of international marketing and negotiation. Another segment will focus on essay writing analysis and techniques. A third segment will cover logic more intensively to improve overall communication coherency. Towards the end of the semester, there will be a parliamentary style debate activity that will give further opportunity to practically apply some of the previously taught skills. 


    This course will focus on group and class interaction as much as possible. While some activities in an Academic English program have to remain teacher-student focused, ideally other activities would begin with partner interaction, expand into group interaction, and then further develop into full class interaction. For this purpose, we need to assign groups and some of your evaluation involves your group performance. A group should have a minimum of four students and this will be organized further in the first class.   

Exams and other grading criteria








Mid-Term Exam 20%

    The Mid-Term Exam will be written and cover some skills in listening, vocabulary, grammar and conversation structure. After the mid-term exam you will be given your score and the class average and can check your progress in this class. The planned date is April 27th 

Final Exam  15%

    The Final Exam will be an interview. There will be a rubric for this. More information will be given closer to the actual date. The planned dates are June 16th – 22nd . 

 Participation (group activity) 15%

   There will be some group assignments: one on the topic of International Marketing which involves coming up with an advertising idea for the re launch of a brand, and another in which there will be an intergroup negotiating activity. 

Debate 15%

      Towards the end of the semester there will be a parliamentary style debate activity. 

Quizzes 20%  

 A quiz will be given on the Basic Logical Concepts topic covered in the weeks after the mid term exam. 

Attendance  15%  

  From the total of 15%, students will be deducted points for absences greater than four, and three lates is equal to one absence. See the table below. A student who has 4 or fewer absences and 3 or fewer lates will receive the full 15%. If a student has a problem coming to class on time, and it has been communicated beforehand, this will not count as a late. 9 absences will result in an F. No makeup classes or assignments are permitted. Proof of absence will only be accepted in extreme cases such as a death in the family.

CREATIVE MEDIA AND GLOBAL ASIA
Haerin Shin (helenshin@stanford.kr, Kakao Talk ID @haerinshin, 01047204853)

Transnational Storytelling, Representation, and Production
with industry collaboration through the VIKO Creative Hub
“Once you overcome the one-inch-tall barrier of subtitles, you will be introduced to so many more amazing films.”
— Bong Joon-ho, 92nd Academy Awards
“The single story creates stereotypes, and the problem with stereotypes is not that they are untrue, but that they are incomplete.”
— Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, “The Danger of a Single Story”
Course Description
In an era of unprecedented global connectivity, the production and circulation of media content has become unequivocally transnational. From the worldwide phenomenon of Korean Wave (Hallyu) to the rise of streaming platforms that commission content across borders, the contemporary mediascape demands creators who can navigate the complexities of cross-cultural storytelling, international co-production, and the politics of representation. With particular attention to Asian media industries and the global circulation of Asian content, this course invites students to engage with the creative, industrial, and ethical dimensions of transnational media development, examining how stories travel across linguistic, cultural, and national boundaries—and how the dynamics of representation shape what gets told, by whom, and for which audiences.
In conversation with industry entities and affiliates, including Korean and global content producers/creators and VIKO Creative Hub (see below) among others , students will gain firsthand exposure to the realities of international content development. At the same time, the course grounds its practical components in critical inquiry, drawing on scholarship in postcolonial media studies, cultural representation, and the politics of Asian visibility in global entertainment.
Rather than treating transnational media as a primarily economic or industrial phenomenon, this course approaches it through the lens of critical design thinking, asking students to empathize with diverse audiences, define meaningful creative problems, ideate innovative solutions, prototype their ideas, and test them against real-world constraints. The goal is not merely to produce content that "sells" across markets, but to cultivate a thoughtful, ethically grounded approach to storytelling that respects cultural specificity while aspiring toward universal human resonance.
Course Objectives (Critical Design Thinking)
EMPATHIZE: Research and understand diverse audiences across cultural contexts; analyze how stories resonate differently across borders
DEFINE: Identify meaningful creative opportunities and challenges in transnational media development
IDEATE: Brainstorm innovative approaches to cross-cultural storytelling and international co-production
PROTOTYPE: Develop concrete creative projects (treatments, pitches, pilot materials) that embody transnational sensibilities
TEST: Present and receive feedback on projects through peer review, industry guest critiques, and international collaboration frameworks
Industry Partnership
This course features collaboration with Korean and global content creators/producers and also VIKO Creative Hub (Vietnam-Korea Institute of Film Technology & Cultural Arts), an education-based content development program connecting Korean industry expertise with emerging Southeast Asian creators. During Spring 2026, VIKO will be running its inaugural development cycle, offering our class a real-time window into transnational content development.
Our class will engage with this initiative in several ways:
Guest Sessions: Industry professionals from partner companies (Desert Bloom Pictures, and PA+ Production, among others) will share insights on international co-development across Asian markets
Case Studies: We will analyze real-world project materials as examples of transnational development in action
Joint Feedback: Select tutorial sessions may involve parallel feedback between KU student projects and international creative teams
Potential Pathway: Student projects (upon application) may be considered for future industry development cycles, subject to institutional approval
Course Structure & Assignments
Each week's class will generally consist of a team presentation (Weekly Digest) covering the week's text and research topic, plenary discussion, and occasionally (during Tutorial sessions) small group discussions that expand on the above through critical design thinking. In addition, class members will brainstorm and build team projects as the semester progresses, mirroring the development process employed by professional content incubators in the global media industry.
Assignments Overview
Weekly Digest (teamwork): Research portfolio and presentation on weekly theme
Midterm Proposal (teamwork): Project proposal following design thinking stages 1-4
Poster Session (teamwork): Public presentation and feedback event
Final Review (individual): Written reflection assessment
Final Product (teamwork): Completed project with reflection essay
Final Project Options
Projects should engage with the course themes of transnational media, cross-cultural storytelling, and/or international co-production. Examples include but are not limited to:
Original screenplay or treatment for transnational co-production (film or series)
Format bible for an entertainment program adaptable across multiple cultural markets
Pitch deck for an original IP (webtoon, web novel, game) with transnational appeal
Academic research paper analyzing a case study in transnational media production
Short documentary exploring cross-cultural creative collaboration
Policy proposal for supporting international co-production
Course syllabus design for a creative media program at any institution across diverse cultural demographics

Attendance
Full attendance is mandatory. Given the class's participation and teamwork-focused design, each unexcused absence will result in a half-grade reduction. Three late arrivals (10+ minutes) count as one absence. Submit excusable absence requests through the portal with proper documentation.
Active Participation
This course does not ask you to memorize prescribed knowledge. Your role in creating new knowledge—cultivating and sharing unique ideas and making critical interventions—is what makes the class experience productive. You are the "main characters" of the world that the class is, so let's make sure to own it.
Language and AI Use
Don't worry about English proficiency—what matters is commitment and the originality of your ideas. You are welcome to use AI tools (ChatGPT, etc.) for spell-checking, grammar refinement, translation assistance, and research support. However, outsourcing the creative and analytical thinking itself to AI is counterproductive. AI-generated texts without human revision have distinctive tells. Collaborate with AI thoughtfully; uncritical AI use entails more loss.. than gain.

Peter Sylvestre, M.Sc., M.Phil., MIEM

All students regardless of year or national status are welcome! 
General Description & Course Content
This course, which should be titled Emerging/Future World of Work, is intended to prepare students to enter the ever-evolving ‘world of work’ by having them explore the dynamics that impact present and, more significantly, future employment trends and respond to that evolution through self-adaptation. Students will examine the socio-economic and business environment and career opportunities projected by futurists for the next decade and develop career strategies to meet anticipated challenges. As the BBC (2024) noted: “There are lots of jobs around today that didn’t exist ten or twenty years ago. With technology advancing rapidly, the world of work is going to look very different in the future.” 
The course is designed, on the basis of the instructor’s experience (taught Job Hunting Skills and Business English to over 1,000 Korea University students as well as business leaders and MBA students since 2000), as a response to widespread complaints by employers decrying the inadequate level of functional communication skills among potential recruits irrespective of communication channels and modes. In so doing, student will develop the communicative skills deemed essential by leaders of leading companies such as Goldman Sachs and BBC survey of CEOs. However, this course transcends merely being merely a language course as it also designed to ensure socio-pragmatic competence in professional settings through development of discourse analysis and strategies, identification of both general and specific needs and requirements in given and ever-evolving situations and development of constructive approaches to satisfying those needs based in part on multicultural perspective and sensitivity. Participants will investigate and practice the requisite skills (interpersonal, group discussion, presentations, etc. and exploit the opportunities to effectively respond to the demands of a more fluid, dynamic, global work environment.
Spoken (Verbal): (as many students perform at the C1 level of the Common European Framework of Reference for Language, students should be reasonably proficient in English, i.e., high intermediate/advanced).
Written: As written business documents (a) reflect the individual’s and organization’s professionalism, (b) are permanent and therefore form a lasting impression and (c) are legal business documents, business practitioners must be able to communicate coherently and effectively in writing that retains intellectual autonomy and originality (independent from predictable and formulaic AI, form letters, etc.).

Course Overview:
This course focuses on the theory and application of organizational behavior. Organizational behavior is a study of human behavior in organizations and deals with three levels of phenomena in the context of workplace – individual, group and organizational levels. 
The overall course objective is to teach you the skills essential to effective management of individuals, groups and organizations in today’s business environment. This objective will be achieved by exposing you to a variety of theories and applications of individual behavior, within-group and between-group interaction, and firm behavior. At the end the course, you are expected to learn tools, skills and strategies for: 
Enhancing your managerial judgment
Improving individual and group effectiveness
Managing organizational units and their activities 
Course Material:
The course’s textbook is Organizational Behavior: A Practical, Problem-Solving Approach 3rd Edition by A. Kinicki & M Fugate, which is available at the bookstore. There will also be additional readings which will be provided in class.
Assignments and grading: 
Your final grade will be based on:
Senior Manager Case Analysis                                    30%
Exams (2 @ 25% each)                                               50%
Homework						  10%	
10% Factor						  10%
Senior Manager Case Analysis (30%)
This assignment is designed to apply the knowledge you gain in class to tackle real issues in real organizations.  Each Project Group is required to interview at least one senior manager regarding their experiences.  Your group can choose to interview more managers.  This manager can be from a firm you previously worked for, from firms you would like to work for, or simply from industries that interest you. The “firm” doesn’t necessarily have to be a large firm. It could be any organization ranging from a non-profit organization to a local restaurant. 
This is an opportunity for you to explore a person or an industry in which you are interested.  You will want to pay attention to the issues from class.  Some topics you might want to cover include issues of motivation, job attitudes, decision making, conflict resolution, and organizational change. Please do not attempt to cover too many topics. It won’t be very feasible. You may want to pick one or maybe two issues that most interest you.
Presentation & Team Evaluation (15%). Each group will make a maximum 25-minute presentation of the results of the interview. Also, some background information about the organization of the manager will be a valuable component of the presentation. Each member of a group will turn in a team evaluation form that assesses the contribution of the group members. Self-assessment should be included as well. The form is included in Appendix A.
Report in Writing (15%). Each group will turn in a maximum 10-page written analysis on the day of the last group’s presentation. This could be of free format reporting whatever you have found from the interviews regarding the theories and practices based on the class concepts and their applications. 
Exams (50%)
	There will be 2 exams during the term. No time allowance is available for students who arrive late. No make-up exam will be available without emergency situation with supporting evidence.

Introduction
Political Science, Economics, Public Administration and Statistics (College of Political Science and Economics) as well as Media and International Studies are fields that require rigorous logical and process-oriented thinking. Students who cannot think autonomously and express themselves in a logical, coherent manner will have little to offer their academic field or future employer (ESPECIALLY IN COMPETITION WITH AI). Hence, this course will emphasize English language expressive capacity in academic settings through focusing on discourse (coherency of argument) in both written and spoken forms. By the end of the course, students should be able to express concepts, ideas and processes with particular relevance to their academic field.
In this class, students are strongly encouraged to express their own opinions and even challenge Mr. Sylvestre. Disagreement and challenge require greater language skills than merely nodding in agreement or passively receiving information. Accordingly, students should not fear being ‘wrong’ and incurring a penalty (no student since March 2000 has had any grade reduced for doing so). Students should keep in mind that it is Mr. Sylvestre’s job to help them express their ideas more effectively. When students challenge Mr. Sylvestre, it will be the student and Mr. Sylvestre against the professor.
Content
Primary objective: Enhance analytical and argumentative skills in major specific discourse through developing analytical and critical thinking skills and developing constructive discussion and negotiation techniques
Secondary objectives: Acquire major-related terminology and concepts by analyzing and discussing news articles and commentaries
Tertiary objectives: Identify logical fallacies; evaluate source validity
Materials
Materials will either be uploaded to the prevailing LMS, emailed or distributed in class.
Grading Policy
Typically, the group discussion (Module 1) lasts 20-25 minutes during which students identify and analyze a problem or topic. The thesis defense (Module 2) involves writing a 4-5 page academic essay and undergoing a 10-minute oral defense. The group presentation (Module 3) addresses a policy-related problem based on a generalized analytical framework.
Evaluation:
Small group discussion (20%)
Academic essay (40%)
Oral defense (interview) (20%)
Presentation (20%)
Grading is absolute.
Absences: It is the policy of the Academic English Program for the College of Political Science and Economics that 8 absences will result in a grade of F. Should you arrive after attendance is taken, inform Mr. Sylvestre upon the conclusion of that session. Plagiarism is an excellent way to ensure a lower grade. Fair warning: The instructor, a former U.S. intelligence analyst, uses textual analysis (and Blackboard software) to identify cases of plagiarism.
Use of English: The medium (indeed purpose) of this course is English. Thus, students are to refrain from using Korean in the classroom. The sole exception is when permission of Mr. Sylvestre is granted before resorting to Korean. Preferably, students should attempt to describe the concept or idea in English and Mr. Sylvestre will assist in providing the appropriate terminology.
Implications of Inappropriate Solicitation & Graft Act (2016), a.k.a. Kim Young Ran Law: Solicitations (requests) regarding grade changes or special treatment (that would not ordinarily be extended to all other similarly situated students) constitute violations of the Act. However, you may ask me to review or explain your grade. Gift giving of any sort for any reason also constitute a violation. Should you visit me for any reason, do not bring any gift (not even coffee, candy, etc.). When in doubt as to whether your request is improper, feel free to ask me.
Weekly Plan
Finally: Students globally naturally feel stressed at times. In Korea the competition to always “be the best” or “try one’s best” intensifies this stress. Added to this is the stress resulting from non-curriculum developments (including relationships). If either you or anyone you know is having difficulty managing stress, I strongly advise consulting the KU Student Counseling Center (https://kuscc.korea.edu/kuscc_en/index.do). 과목 개요
본 교과목을 통해 학생들은 한국 전통복식에 대한 역사적, 문화적, 구성학적, 디자인적 측면의 내용을 습득하고 이해한다. 수업은 이론과 실기를 병행하여 진행하며 한복의 문화 콘텐츠와 패션 상품으로의 활용 가치를 알고 활용한다. 본 교과목을 통해 공감소통, 융합적 사고, 창의적 문제해결, 글로벌, 도전적 리더 등의 역량 향상이 가능하다. 
학습 목표
한국 전통 복식의 유래와 변천 과정을 이해하고, 최근 한복에 대한 국제적 관심과 문화 콘텐츠로서 가치를 학습한다.

한국 전통복식과 공예의 구성학적 특징과 제작 과정을 이해하고, 이를 활용한 패션상품의 기획 및 디자인 과정을 실습한다.

Evaluation Method
Typically, a maximum of about 40-45% of you will receive a grade of “A” or “A+”. Evaluation in this class is based strictly on performance, and not on English language proficiency. All parts of the evaluation system must be completed in an exceptional manner if you want to get an “A+”.  
I employ rubrics where students are evaluated on organization(see below), content(see below) and language (see below). More criteria will be given when the projects are assigned. Many students ask for a word count. My philosophy is that students should be focusing on answering the question  and providing enough support for your answer. So concentrate on fully exploring your answer.  This is done through research (what have others said on the topic),planning (outline and deciding on your answer), and editing (checking your work for mistakes in organization, content and language).
Class Expectations (Please READ CAREFULLY!)
This class is not like your other classes.  It is not a lecture class, so you must be active instead of passive in this class.  The following are some guidelines for conduct that I expect in this class.  Adherence to these expectations will assist in enhancing your English proficiency as well as improving chances of a good grade.

Basic Criteria
Organization | Organization includes but is not limited to formatting including font (times new roman 12 points), double spacing, indents, APA title page, bibliography, intext citations and general paragraph formatting. Students are expected to create new file documents for each assignment.
Content | Content includes but is not limited to answering the question of the assignment, supporting your ideas with details including: quotations, statistics, concrete details and paraphrasing, explanations of why your details answer the question and context(why is your support important to the topic you are writing about). Explanations need to be longer than your evidence.
Language | Language includes but is not limited to grammar (common mistakes students make are: verb tenses, articles, prepositions, word choice, word order, and plurals),spelling and the use of first person.

Prof Betty Chung: Bio
Professor Betty J. Chung, Director of Global MBA, Korea University
Professor Betty J. Chung has over 30 years of teaching and educational program development experience in Asia and North America.  She was appointed as an Associate Professor and the Academic Director of the Global MBA program at Korea University.  She also serves as a Visiting Professor at Aalto School of Economics Helsinki. She also serves as the Executive Director to the Association of Asia Pacific Business Schools where she leads a Council of 22 Deans from the leading business schools in the region. Prior to these posts, Dr. Chung was a Professor of Cross-Cultural Management and Leadership Development for the past 25 years at KAIST College of Business. Dr. Chung’s passion focuses on developing leadership capabilities to optimize personal & organizational effectiveness. Her global outreach and footprint are highlighted as a Visiting Professor in the United States, Thailand, China; Myanmar, Vietnam, Malaysia and Japan. She has helped both domestic and multinational companies in Korea, Thailand, China, and the USA as a training specialist, coach and lecturer in the areas of Global Leadership, Cross Cultural Management, Diversity and Inclusion, Organizational Behavior, Management Communication and Doing Business Globally. 
A list of selected clients and companies include McKinsey & Co, Citigroup, Dell, Novartis, Mirae Asset, Samsung Group, SK Group, Hyundai Group, Doosan Group, CJ Group, LG Group, GMKorea, GMOnstar,Hana Bank, Standard Chartered Bank, ING Life Korea, Lundbeck Korea, Flextronics China, and Bank of Ayudhya Thailand.
Prior to working at KAIST College of Business for the past 25 years, Dr. Chung was an Assistant Prof. at the University of Illinois at Chicago teaching classes on Organizational Behavior and Diversity Management for master and doctoral level students. Prior to her teaching role in Chicago, Dr. Chung served as a consultant in PriceWaterhouseCoopers’Diversity Practice working with top leadership on diversity initiatives, strategy and education. 
Dr. Chung received her doctorate degree from the University of San Francisco in Organizations and Leadership. She conducted her field research in Vietnam, Thailand, Hong Kong and the United States researching trans-cultural leadership styles. Her Master’s is in Higher Education Student Affair’s Administration and Bachelor’s degree in education from the University of Vermont.

Course Overview | Organizational Behavior (OB) provides a basic understanding of your own and others’ behavior, particularly in teams. It enhances your ability to communicate and work effectively with others and develops core skills of leadership. Our goal is to help you strengthen your people management skills so you can be a successful leader in any field you choose. This course is a MUST for all students who are interested in developing and enhancing their own leadership capabilities. This course bridges organizational behavior and leadership theory to developing hands on practical leadership skills for effective global managers. It examines common issues and best practices for assessing and developing effective leadership and influence skills.    Topics include: Understanding YOURSELF as a leader, developing emotional intelligence, assessing your leadership style, leveraging your strengths and identifying areas for development, managing conflict, developing presence and effective communication skills, enhancing persuasion and influence skills, negotiation skills, understanding effective team dynamics, and enhancing global mindset to build global leadership skills. 
     The study of Organizational behavior enables leaders to have a good understanding both of themselves and of those whom they will lead. Leaders need to know why people behave as they do in relation to their job, work group, and organization.  The importance of effective leadership skills and the ability to lead, motivate and influence others are key success factors for effective global managers.

COURSE DESCRIPTION AND OBJECTIVES:
This course aims to develop students’ academic English proficiency and communicative competence required for university-level study. The course is conducted using academic content to strengthen students’ overall English ability applicable across a range of academic disciplines. Emphasis is placed on practical communication skills through a variety of task-based and interactive activities designed to help students use English effectively in academic and real-life contexts.
Students will also engage with a variety of academic texts to improve reading comprehension skills and to develop an understanding of English expressions related to their fields of study.
We will achieve these goals through a combination of practical activities, in-class assignments, and mini-lectures. The following are the core activities and skills we will focus on:
Discussion skills for academic purposes.
Research skills necessary for academic writing and discussion. 
Developing ideas for writing through discussion, brainstorming and freewriting.
Learning how to write a basic academic essay with citations, and how to avoid plagiarism.
Expanding your level of academic vocabulary. 
Developing your public speaking skills/presentation skills.

Important: a major goal of this class is to help you become a competent, independent learner. After completing this course, you should be able to continue developing your English through self-study and independent learning.
Participation: Often you will be expected to work in pairs or in small groups. Participation includes arriving on time, being prepared (bringing your book, notebook, handouts, and other required materials), listening attentively, interacting with your classmates and teacher, actively engaging in class activities, completing assignments thoroughly and on time, and asking questions when you don’t understand.
Speaking Korean: In most cases, speaking Korean in class is unnecessary. You will lose participation points if you speak Korean without permission. That said, I do allow Korean when helping classmates understand rules, grammar points, or my instructions—but you must ask for permission first.
Plagiarism: Plagiarism means presenting someone else’s ideas or work as your own. It is dishonest, unethical, and—even when unintentional—can negatively affect your grade. Accidental plagiarism is more understandable than intentional plagiarism, but both are serious. Most importantly, plagiarism prevents you from learning and growing as a student. We will discuss how to recognize and avoid plagiarism in this class.
AI (Artificial Intelligence): AI is a powerful tool and has many benefits, and we will occasionally use it as a learning tool in class. I allow the use of AI for some classroom activities, for research and preparation at home, and in any way that you feel it can be helpful in your English learning. However, you are not allowed to use AI programs during exams or quizzes.  
Important Note: 
Sometimes the pressures of university life and/or personal matters can cause students to become distressed, which can have a negative impact upon their health. Your health, both mental and physical, is extremely important. There are counseling services offered at Korea University free of charge, but few students take advantage of these services due to unnecessary fears. There is a common misconception that people who seek counseling are “crazy.” In reality, most people who seek help are regular individuals dealing with common challenges, such as:
Stress
Self-esteem issues
Relationship problems (with partners, friends, or family)
Anger management
Bullying
Anxiety
Grief
Addictions (to TV, smartphones, gaming, eating, exercise, etc.)
Alcohol-related issues
Loneliness
Depression
Fears
ADHD
Emotional instability
The Counseling Center is a safe and confidential space where you can work through your problems. Unlike talking to a friend, a counselor is professionally trained to support your personal growth and help you deal with life's challenges. They can help you understand your situation more clearly and guide you toward solutions—so you can eventually manage things more confidently on your own. You are free to say whatever you want in counseling, without fear of judgment. You will never be pressured to talk about anything you're not ready to discuss. Research shows that 70–90% of people who attend counseling report feeling better afterward. Don’t hesitate to seek support—you’re not alone, and help is available.

Course Information
Course Title: Global Business Ethics
Course Code: DISS232
Course Instructor: Minhye Zoh (Ph. D.)
Credits/Hours: 3 credits, 3 hours per week
Course Objectives
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
Demonstrate a working knowledge of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) practices in international contexts.
Understand the institutionalization process of corporate governance systems around the world.
Engage in collaborative learning through team-based projects, discussions, and presentations that simulate real-world ethical decision-making.
Strengthen practical academic skills in research, critical writing, and oral presentation through workshops and applied assignments.
Course Outline
Week 1: Introduction to <Global Business Ethics>
Week 2: CSR and ESG: What is it, and why is it important?
Week 3: Foundations of Corporate Responsibility: Competing Theories and Ethical Justifications
Week 4: Boards, Power, and Governance: Theories of Corporate Control and Responsibility
Week 5: ESG Disclosure and Accountability: Institutional Pressure, Transparency, and Trust
Week 6: Corporate Governance around the World
Week 7: Special Workshop: Academic Writing and Presentation
Week 8: MID-TERM Assignment
Week 9: Corporate Scandals and the Role of Law
Week 10: Asian Financial Crisis and its Impact on Corporate Responsibility
Week 11: Global Financial Crisis and its Impact on Corporate Responsibility
Week 12: CSR and ESG of Multinational Enterprises (MNEs)
Week 13: Case Study Workshop: Lessons from Failed ESG Institutions
Week 14: Individual or Group Presentations
Week 15: Round-up and Revision
Week 16: FINAL EXAM
Assessment Methods
Student performance will be evaluated based on the following components:
Mid-term Assignment: 30%
Final Exam: 30%
Individual or Group Presentation: 15% (10% course-instructor, 5% student-graded)
In-class Activity: 15%
Class Participation and Attendance: 10%
This assessment structure is designed to balance individual academic performance with collaborative learning and critical engagement throughout the semester.
Teaching Methods
This course will be conducted primarily through lectures, followed by class discussions and presentations. Students are encouraged to actively participate, share perspectives, and collaboratively develop ideas throughout the semester.

Course Description: 
In this course, we will study the major themes and stylistic innovations in modern American fiction through reading the novels written by F. Scott Fitzgerald, William Faulkner, Thomas Pynchon, and Philip K. Dick. Our readings focus on these authors’ literary representations of the U.S. society during the interwar and postwar period (1925-68), while examining the cultural origins and historical contexts of American literary modernism and postmodernism. The topics we will explore include these writers’ critiques of art and language, American history, modernity and materialism, individual alienation and collectivity, and the issues of class/race/gender. The course is designed to develop the skills of close reading and independent interpretation of literary texts. Class discussions and writing assignments will provide students with opportunities to respond to important topics expressed in the novels. 
Required Texts:

JMCO248
미디어데이터사이언스입문
Introduction to Media Data Science
	2026년 1학기	

Course Overview
본 강의는 미디어와 커뮤니케이션 영역에서 데이터 사이언스를 탐구하며, 철학적·방법론적 접근을 체계적으로 이해하고, 기초적인 데이터 분석 방법을 실제로 적용해 보는 것을 목표로 함. 수강생들은 데이터 사이언스의 개념적 기초를 다지고, 미디어 분야에서의 데이터 활용 사례와 분석 기술을 익혀, 융합적 패러다임을 폭넓게 학습할 수 있도록 설계되었음.
Course Materials 
주교재 없음
각 수업에서 필요한 수업자료는 수업일 전에 리딩 리스트와 해당 리딩자료의 pdf 파일이 제공될 예정, 자세한 내용은 추후 업데이트.  
Course Structure
본 강의는 강의자의 강의를 기본으로 하며, 이와 관련한 개인 과제, 팀별 과제를 수행하고 해당 지식에 대한 이해를 점검하기 위해 1회의 시험을 포함.  
Assessments

성적 등급에 대한 자세한 학교 규정은 아래를 참고: https://registrar.korea.ac.kr/eduinfo/info/grade_overview.do 
출석 (15%, 150점)  
강사 또는 조교가 지정 좌석을 기준으로 출석 확인. 좌석 변경은 중간고사 이후 한 번 더 이루어 질 예정. 
본 수업은 학기 중 사유 없이 사용할 수 있는 출석 패스 2회를 제공함. 적절한 때를 위해 이 패스를 효과적으로 사용 권장. 
무단 결석이 2회를 초과할 경우, 결석 1회당 총 출석 점수에서 10점이 감점됨. 
고려대학교 규정에 따라 10회(전체 수업의 1/3)를 초과하여 결석하면 성적을 받을 자격이 박탈됨.
결석이 예상되는 경우, 수업 전에 반드시 강사 혹은 조교에게 미리 알리고 유효한 사유와 증빙 서류를 제출해야 공결로 인정 가능. 수업 전에 알리지 않은 결석은 공결로 인정되지 않음.
생리 공결의 경우은 포털로 신청. 최대 4회까지 인정. 
출석 관련 고려대학교의 정책의 자세한 내용은 다음의 링크에서 확인. 
개인 리서치 과제 (15%, 3회 x 50점 = 150점)
개인 리서치 과제는 각 학생이 해당 주차 수업과 관련된 자료나 사례를 탐색, 분석을 수행. 각 주제는 추후 공지 예정.
작성 형식: A4 용지, 여백 1인치(상하 좌우), 글꼴 크기 10 point, 1-2페이지, 단일 간격(single-spaced). Page는 받지 않음 (word, pdf, hwp만 사용).
과제는 반드시 LMS 플랫폼을 통해 제출. 이메일이나 메시지를 통한 제출은 인정되지 않음. 
각 과제에 대한 제출 기한은 사전에 공지 예정. 
중간고사 (30%, 300점) 
시험은 강의실에서 진행되며, 참고자료 없이(closed-book) 다지선다형, 진위형(true/false), 또는 단답형 문제로 구성. 
시험 시간은 1시간 15분(강의 시간)입니다. 시험 전 수업일에 리뷰 및 Q&A 세션이 제공.  
시험시간 동안 스마트워치를 포함한 모든 디지털 기기의 사용은 금지. 시험 중 기기를 사용하는 것이 적발되면 부정행위로 간주되어 바로 퇴장조치. 시간 확인이 필요하지 않으며, 시험 시간은 교실 내 비치된 시계로 확인 가능.
시험을 일찍 끝낸 경우 퇴실할 수 있지만, 다른 학생들에게 방해가 되지 않도록 주의하여야 함. 
부정행위는 절대 용납되지 않음. 부정행위가 적발되면 해당 시험의 점수는 즉각 0점으로 처리됩니다.  
팀 과제 (40%, 400점)
팀은 랜덤으로 강의자 혹은 조교가 분배할 배정.
팀 과제에 대한 평가로 기말평가를 대체함. 팀 프로젝트이므로 팀 점수가 곧 개인의 점수로 반영됨. 
주제: 현대 사회가 당면한 다양한 문제 중 하나를 자유롭게 선정하여 미디어데이터사이언스를 활용한 창의적인 솔루션 기획 및 제안을 하도록 함 
팀 프로젝트 주제 프로포절 (5%, 50점): 팀 프로젝트의 주제는 강의자가 검토하고, 팀 대표자 1명이 LMS에 업로드함. 
작성 형식: A4 용지, 여백 1인치(상하좌우), 글꼴 크기 10 point, 1-2페이지, 단일 간격(single-spaced). Page는 받지 않음 (word, pdf, hwp만 사용)
포함 내용: 프로젝트 주제 제안 배경, 목적, 함의 및 중요성, 실행 계획
팀 프로젝트 결과내용 (20%, 200점): 팀 프로젝트 결과물은 프레젠테이션 파일 형식으로 작성하여  대표자 1명이 LMS에 업로드함.
팀 프로젝트 발표 역량 (10%, 100점): 팀 프로젝트 결과물은 학기 마지막 2주동안 발표하도록 하며, 준비성, 협동, 자료 완성도, 발표시간관리, 오디언스와의 인터렉션 등 발표 역량에 대해 강의자가 당일 평가. 
동료 평가 (5%, 50점): 강의자는 동료 평가 양식을 제공하고, 동료 평가는 참여도 면에서 A, B, C, D로 이루어진다. 팀 내 2/3이상이 C 혹은 D의 점수를 받은 경우, 최종 성적에서 100점을 감점한다. 그렇지 않은 경우, 5점 만점을 받음. 
Extra Credit 기회 (최대 2회 기회 x 25점 = 최대 50점) 
본 수업에서는 4회의 데이터 분석 도구 Demonstration이 진행될 예정.
학생들은 강의자가 제공한 데이터를 기반으로 SPSS, STATA, R, Python 또는 기타 소프트웨어를 사용하여 데이터를 분석하고, 분석 결과를 제출하여 점수를 받을 수 있습니다. 단, 4회의 기회 중 최대 2회만 참여할 수 있음.
평가 점수는 제출 내용에 따라 부여되며, 매우 우수한 경우 25점, 우수한 경우 20점, 보통의 경우 15점이 부여됨. 이보다 낮은 수준의 제출물의 경우에는 점수를 받을 수 없음. 
AI의 사용은 엄격히 금지됨. 
학생들은 데이터를 분석하는 과정에서 어떤 기능을 사용했는지, 분석 방법, 그리고 데이터 분석 결과를 어떻게 해석했는지를 자세히 작성해야 함. 
Course Policies
수업 시간 내 에티켓: 
수업의 성격상 노트북 및 전자기기의 사용을 허용함. 그러나, 반드시 오직 수업과 관련된 활동에만 사용하도록 한다. 교실 내 간단한 간식 섭취와 음료는 허용되나, 수업 진행에 방해가 되지 않도록 유의 바람. 
제출 기한이 지난 과제 성적 처리에 대한 규정: 
과제 마감 전 강의자가 인정한 유효한 사유를 미리 전달한 경우, 제출 기한이 지난 과제에 대한 감점은 없음. 
그러나 강의자에게 보고하지 않은 마감 후 제출된 과제는 최대 2일까지 50% 감점을 적용하여 채점함. 이 기한이 지나면 제출된 과제는 0점으로 처리.
성적 변경 요청에 대한 규정 (매우 중요): 
최종 성적이 확정된 이후에는 성적 변경이 불가능함. "부정청탁 및 금품 등 수수의 금지에 관한 법률"(제5조 및 제7조)에 따라, 학생(또는 제3자)이 강사에게 평가 오류가 없는 경우 성적 변경(상향 또는 하향)을 요청하는 것은 부정청탁으로 간주됨.
부적절한 청탁을 받은 강사는 요청자에게 해당 청탁이 부적절함을 알리고, 이를 명확히 거부해야 할 의무가 있음. 동일한 청탁이 두 번 이상 반복될 경우, 강사는 이를 대학에 보고해야 함.
부정행위 및 교칙 위반에 대한 규정: 
이외의 부정행위와 교칙 위반에 대한 구체적인 규정은 다음의 링크 참조. 이를 위반한 경우, 해당 과목의 성적은 즉시 F로 처리 됨. 
AI 이용 가이드라인(매우 중요)
허용 사용 범위
본 수업에서는 AI(예: ChatGPT)는 오로지 학생의 학습을 보조하는 도구로만 사용해야 함. 학생들은 항상 본인의 주체적인 사고를 통해 주어진 수업의 과제를 해결하도록 노력해야 함. 그것이 교육과 트레이닝의 본질임. 따라서 본 수업에서 허용되는 사용 범위는 다음과 같음: 
브레인스토밍을 위한 목적 
사례를 검색하거나 케이스를 탐색하는 목적 
아이디어를 정리하는 목적
허용되지 않는 사용 범위
AI를 통해 콘텐츠를 생성하여 그대로 사용하거나 퀴즈 혹은 시험의 답을 AI를 통해 얻는 행위는 허용되지 않음. 이는 표절 및 부정행위로 간주함. 
고려대학교에서는 CopyKiller와 같은 GPT-이용 감지 서비스를 사용 중. CopyKiller를 참조.
윤리적 사용 가이드라인 
학부대학의 가이드라인 참고
AI 오용 시 처벌 사항
AI를 오용한 학생은 본 수업의 정책을 위반한 것으로 간주되며, 표절과 같은 부정행위로 동일한 처벌을 받게 됨.  
때에 따라서 0점/F학점 처리가 될 수 있으니 유의바람.

Course Description
This intermediate course provides students with the platform to build upon their finance knowledge after taking Financial Management.  This class will be taught from a practitioner’s viewpoint where students will learn how finance concepts and theory are applied in the real world.   Finance theory will be rigorously taught however the students will not be expected to provide mathematical proofs of financial concepts.
Through real-world examples, case studies, and problem-solving exercises, students will gain practical insights to understand how finance is applied to the capital markets.
Course Material:   Lecture Slides, recommended articles, and strategic use of AI will be utilized.   
Recommended Textbook: Investments, 12 Edition by Bodie, Kane, and Marcus, McGraw Hill
Grading Policy: 
Class participation - 20%, Midterm- 30%, Final - 50%
Course Schedule:
Week 1: Financial Instruments, Capital Markets, Investment Management Landscape
Week 2: Risk and Return, Diversification
Week 3-4: Equilibrium in Capital Markets, CAPM, APT, Efficient Market Hypothesis
Week 5-6: Fixed Income Securities- Risk and return measures, Government Bonds, Corporate Bonds, Securitization, Yield Curve theory
Week 7:  Equity Valuation – Discount Cash Flow Model, Comparative Analysis, Financial Statement Analysis
Week 8:  Review and Midterm
Week 9-10 Equity Valuation – Discount Cash Flow Model, Comparative Analysis, Financial Statement Analysis
Week 11-12: Options, Futures and other Derivatives including Interest rate swaps and Credit Default Swaps
Week 13-14:  Applied Portfolio Management – Relative Value analysis, Alternative strategies including Hedge Fund and Private Equity
Week 15: Course Review
Week 16: Final
