Course Description and Objectives

      This course will focus on enhancing academic competency in English in all four areas of speaking, listening, reading and writing. While covering academic content, particularly in terms of essay writing and general competency in communication, this course is designed to be as student-centered as possible with task orientated and group presentation activity wherever possible. The goal is to increase your overall proficiency in all areas of English communication as it relates to your academic studies. 

One segment of this course will focus on English for business majors, including the topics of international marketing and negotiation. Another segment will focus on essay writing analysis and techniques. A third segment will cover logic more intensively to improve overall communication coherency. Towards the end of the semester, there will be a parliamentary style debate activity that will give further opportunity to practically apply some of the previously taught skills. 


    This course will focus on group and class interaction as much as possible. While some activities in an Academic English program have to remain teacher-student focused, ideally other activities would begin with partner interaction, expand into group interaction, and then further develop into full class interaction. For this purpose, we need to assign groups and some of your evaluation involves your group performance. A group should have a minimum of four students and this will be organized further in the first class.   

Exams and other grading criteria








Mid-Term Exam 20%

    The Mid-Term Exam will be written and cover some skills in listening, vocabulary, grammar and conversation structure. After the mid-term exam you will be given your score and the class average and can check your progress in this class. The planned date is April 27th 

Final Exam  15%

    The Final Exam will be an interview. There will be a rubric for this. More information will be given closer to the actual date. The planned dates are June 16th – 22nd . 

 Participation (group activity) 15%

   There will be some group assignments: one on the topic of International Marketing which involves coming up with an advertising idea for the re launch of a brand, and another in which there will be an intergroup negotiating activity. 

Debate 15%

      Towards the end of the semester there will be a parliamentary style debate activity. 

Quizzes 20%  

 A quiz will be given on the Basic Logical Concepts topic covered in the weeks after the mid term exam. 

Attendance  15%  

  From the total of 15%, students will be deducted points for absences greater than four, and three lates is equal to one absence. See the table below. A student who has 4 or fewer absences and 3 or fewer lates will receive the full 15%. If a student has a problem coming to class on time, and it has been communicated beforehand, this will not count as a late. 9 absences will result in an F. No makeup classes or assignments are permitted. Proof of absence will only be accepted in extreme cases such as a death in the family.

     This course will focus on enhancing academic competency in English in all four areas of speaking, listening, reading and writing. While covering academic content, particularly in terms of essay writing and general competency in communication, this course is designed to be as student-centered as possible with task orientated and group presentation activity wherever possible. The goal is to increase your overall proficiency in all areas of English communication as it relates to your academic studies. 

    This course will also focus on group and class interaction as much as possible. While some activities in an Academic English program have to remain teacher-student focused, ideally other activities would begin with partner interaction, expand into group interaction, and then further develop into full class interaction. For this purpose, we need to assign groups and some of your evaluation involves your group performance. A group should have a minimum of four students and this will be organized further in the first class.

    The required tasks for assessment include at least two pieces of writing, of which one must be a simple multi-paragraphed piece of writing, presentations (which can be done in your assigned groups), an assessed oral activity which may take the form of a debate or interview, one written exam (which will be given as a mid-term exam) and other smaller quizzes.   

    As you will see in the course schedule below, each week will be focused on one particular theme and relevant language functions and activities will be tied to that theme. 
 










Mid-Term Exam 20%

    The Mid-Term Exam will be written. After the mid-term exam you will be given your score and the class average and can check your progress in this class. (Please note, you are only competing with the other students in this class for the highest possible grades. Your grade is only determined by your score in relation to the other students’ scores in this class.) The scheduled date is April 23rd . 

Final Exam  15%

    The Final Exam will be an oral assessment using material that has been covered during the semester. More information on this will be given closer to the actual date. The scheduled dates are June 16th – 22nd 
 
 Written Assignments  15%

    There will be a couple of short written assignments that you will need to upload to the LMS. These assignments will be used also in the final 1-1 interview. 


Quiz  20% 

      One quiz will be given on material that has been covered. It is important not to miss this quiz because it will have an impact on your grade.  





   (v)  Debate / Participation 20%

      There will be a parliamentary style debate activity towards the end of the semester. (More information will be given about this closer to the time). 

(vi)  Attendance  10%  

    Please note that while attendance is only ten percent of the total grade, I will use it to separate grades if necessary. Also, if you are absent from group presentations, it can affect your score. (It is the responsibility of the group to ensure all members are in attendance for a presentation, or to be prepared in advance if a member needs to be absent.)

    Also please note that you cannot be absent from over 33.3% of classes and still receive a credit. This is due to the Korean government’s education policy.

개요 | 오늘날 중국은 세계에서 가장 많은 인구를 가진 국가로 세계 양대 열강의 하나로 자리매김하고 있다. 이런 거대한 중국이라는 나라가 형성된 것은 수천년간 단속적으로 이어져온 전란의 결과라는 것은 주지의 사실이다. 강력한 전제왕권과 이에 억눌렸다가 폭발하는 민중봉기는 중국을 수백 년에 한 번씩 뒤흔들었고 북방초원에서 중국의 부를 노리던 북방민족도 중국의 번영을 지속하지 못하게 만드는 중요한 원인이었다. 이에 비추어보면 중국은 세계의 그 어떤 나라보다도 전란이 그 역사의 진행과정에 영향을 많이 끼친 국가 중 하나라고 할 수 있겠다. 본 수업은 이런 중국사의 전란을 이해하는 것을 통해 중국을 이해하고 더 나아가 중국을 중심으로 돌아갔던 동아시아 세계에 대한 이해를 넓히는 것을 목표로 할 것이다.
수강(권장)대상 학생 | 고등학교 세계사 혹은 동아시아사 수업을 듣고서 동아시아사에 대해 보다 심화된 지식을 필요로 하는 학생, 대학교양 한국사 수업을 듣고 한국사와 관련된 주변국의 역사에 관심이 가는 학생. 
기본적으로 한국어 교양 강의를 듣고 이해하는데 무리가 없는 한국인 학생 및 외국인 유학생.

Exploring Korean Thought Across Contexts 
(한국사상 산책: Introduction to Korean Philosophy)
Instructor: Soyoung You 
Email: ketssaa@korea.ac.kr
Office Hours: After the class and by appointment
Semester: Spring 2026
Class Time : Wed & Fri, Period 3 (12:00 PM – 1:15 PM) 
Location: Room 403, Seogwan
Course Description:
Exploring Korean Thought Across Contexts invites students on a journey through the evolution of Korean intellectual traditions—from ancient myths and indigenous beliefs to Buddhist metaphysics, Confucian ethics, and modern reformist thought. Engaging a wide range of sources and perspectives, students will examine how Koreans have asked and answered enduring questions about life, society, and the cosmos.
    The course introduces key figures such as Wŏnhyo, Chinul, Yi Hwang (T’oegye), Yi I (Yulgok), and Chŏng Yagyong (tasan), reading their works within their historical and cultural contexts. Students will explore the shifting boundaries and intersections between myth, superstition, religion, culture, and philosophy, developing a nuanced understanding of how Korean thinkers have interpreted the world and shaped it through action.
Emphasizing accessibility, critical thinking, and contextual analysis, the course fosters lively discussion and close reading. By the end, students will gain deeper insight into how Korean philosophical thought has informed—and continues to influence—the broader currents of Korean intellectual and cultural life.
Learning Goals: 
This course is designed to help students:
Understand foundational concepts and major themes in Korean philosophical traditions.
Recognize and explain the contributions of key Korean philosophers.
Analyze how Korean philosophical ideas have responded to historical and cultural challenges.
Explore the role of Korean philosophy within the broader East Asian intellectual context.
Engage critically with Korean philosophical reasoning and apply it to modern issues.
Critically examine and distinguish myth, superstition, religion, culture, and philosophy as overlapping yet distinct categories of human thought.
Student Learning Outcomes: 
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
Explain the foundational concepts and themes in Korean philosophy.
Identify the contributions of major Korean philosophers. 
Analyze how Korean philosophical ideas developed in response to historical and cultural challenges.
Compare Korean philosophical perspectives with other East Asian traditions, such as Chinese Confucianism and Buddhism.
Apply philosophical reasoning from Korean traditions to contemporary ethical or cultural issues.
Distinguish and debate the differences and intersections among myth, superstition, religion, culture, and philosophy.
Course Policies  
Diversity and Inclusion
This course upholds the University’s commitment to diversity, equity, inclusion, and respect for all individuals. I value each and every one of my students, and our classroom will be a safe and supportive space for all identities. Mutual respect for differing perspectives and experiences is expected from all participants.
  Class rosters are provided with your legal names, but I will gladly use your preferred name and pronouns. Please inform me early in the semester of any such preferences so I can address you appropriately.
Accommodations
If you require any specific accommodations—whether related to learning, health, or other circumstances—please notify me at the beginning of the semester. You may do so via email or a scheduled Zoom appointment. I am committed to creating an inclusive learning environment that supports your success.
Academic Integrity
This course strictly adheres to the University’s policies on academic integrity. All submitted work must be your own. Acts such as plagiarism, cheating, or fabrication will result in a failing grade for the assignment and may lead to further disciplinary action as outlined in the University’s Academic Code.
    Students are responsible for reading and understanding the University’s guidelines on academic honesty.
Late Work and Extensions
All assignments are due on the dates indicated in the syllabus. Unexcused late submissions will be penalized by a deduction of 1 points per day. For example, if a reflection paper is worth a maximum of 15 points, it will receive a maximum of 14 points if submitted one day late, 13 points if two days late, and so on. 
Extensions may be granted only in cases of medical emergencies or other compelling circumstances, and must be approved in advance. Appropriate documentation, such as a signed note from a medical practitioner or a dean, may be required. Failure to complete a required component of the course may result in a failing grade.
AI Usage & Research Ethics Guidelines
This course allows the use of AI tools (such as ChatGPT, Gemini, etc.) as auxiliary aids for learning (e.g., understanding concepts, brainstorming, translation). However, any actions that forfeit the autonomy of thought are strictly prohibited. In particular, ghostwriting or the outsourcing of thought—submitting essays that lack the student’s own critical thinking and unique voice—will not be recognized as an academic achievement.
If evidence of excessive reliance is found, such as submitting AI-generated sentences directly or with only minor edits, it will be treated as academic misconduct equivalent to plagiarism, and severe penalties will be imposed during grading. As AI-driven ghostwriting contradicts the course’s core learning objective of strengthening independent thinking, any discovery of such acts will result in measures equivalent to non-submission (e.g., an “F” grade). Furthermore, please be advised that spot interviews may be conducted to verify whether the submitted work aligns with the author’s actual reasoning.
(* Distinction between Translation Aids and Ghostwriting: For non-native English speakers, the use of AI as a translation aid (to improve clarity of your own original thoughts) is permitted. However, using AI to generate content or construct arguments that do not originate from the student is considered ghostwriting. The final submission must reflect the student’s actual level of understanding, and any “logical gap” identified during spot interviews will be subject to academic scrutiny.)
Course Changes
If it becomes necessary to alter any course content, readings, or assignments, students will be notified in advance. Every effort will be made to ensure transparency and fairness in such cases.
Course Requirements and Evaluation
Detailed instructions and grading rubrics for each assignment will be provided on the course website. Written assignments may be submitted electronically or as hard copies; all submissions are due by 11:59 p.m. on the assigned due date unless otherwise noted.
Participation, Preparation, and Attendance – 10%
Regular attendance, attentive reading of assigned materials, and active participation in class discussions are expected. This portion of your grade reflects your engagement with the course and your contributions to a collaborative learning environment.
Class Engagement & Discussion – 10%
This grade reflects your active and thoughtful contribution to our collective learning. Rather than simply counting the frequency of comments, I prioritize the depth of your reflection and the quality of your insights.
Quality over Quantity: I value questions and comments that demonstrate a serious engagement with the texts and challenge our perspectives.
Alternative Participation: To ensure an inclusive environment for all, students who are less comfortable with verbalizing their thoughts in class can participate through the online discussion board (LMS). Submitting thoughtful posts or responding to peers online will be weighed equally in this category.
Reflection Papers – 30% (2 papers, 15% each)
Instead of a midterm exam or essay, students will submit two reflection papers (2–3 pages each) in response to the assigned readings. The due dates are as follows: 
April 3 (Week 5): Covering Weeks 1–4
May 15 (Week 11): Covering Weeks 5–10
Submissions should demonstrate thoughtful engagement with course themes and readings.
Reading Presentation – 10% (Peer Evaluation)
In groups of two to three students, you will lead a class discussion by serving as discussion facilitators for assigned readings. Your task is to present the key ideas, terms, and questions raised by the text and guide a thoughtful conversation with your peers. Presentations should be clear, concise, and designed to foster engagement and critical dialogue. After each presentation, students will submit a brief written comment along with a suggested grade to the instructor. Please be respectful to your presenters and offer constructive, thoughtful feedback. Peer evaluations will play a significant role in determining the final facilitation grade, though the instructor will make the final decision.
Final Project – 40% (broken down as follows):
a. Final Project Proposal – 5%
Due: May 22 (Week 12)
A brief proposal outlining your topic, key research questions, and a preliminary bibliography. 
b. Final Project Presentation – 5% (Peer Evaluation)
Scheduled: Weeks 13–15
A 7–10 minute in-class presentation summarizing your final project. Peer feedback will follow each presentation.
c. Final Project Paper or Equivalent – 30%
Due: June 19 (Week 16)
A final paper (6–8 pages, plus bibliography) or an approved creative/research equivalent that engages critically with course materials and themes.
Extra Credit: “Living Philosophy” (Max 5%)
Opportunities for extra credit are designed to encourage students to experience Korean thought and culture firsthand. These points can be earned through various activities, including but not limited to:
Experiential Learning: Submit a 1–2-page reflection paper after participating in activities such as visiting the National Museum of Korea (Buddhist/Confucian galleries), attending a Temple Stay, or watching a designated documentary on Korean philosophy.
Class Events & Assignments: Additional opportunities may be offered based on specific class activities, event participation, or optional assignments. These will be announced in class or posted on the course website as they become available.
Note: Extra credit is awarded based on the quality of engagement and reflection, and is added to the final grade after all regular evaluations are completed.
Readings:
All required readings will be available through the LMS, the course website, or are reserved at the library.
Students are expected to be familiar with the assigned readings every week and come to class prepared to discuss them. Descriptions of each session in the Course Outline will provide some guidance and context for approaching the readings. Rather than attempting to absorb every page passively, prioritize the parts that you find intellectually engaging or personally meaningful. If you’re short on time, focus your attention on the sections that spark curiosity, raise questions, or prompt reflection—especially those you’d like to bring up in our online discussion forum or during in-class conversations. Active, selective reading is not only acceptable, but encouraged.
Discussion Facilitation (Starting Week 2):
Each week, two or three assigned facilitators will lead the class discussion. This role is central to our collaborative learning environment. The primary focus is on in-class engagement, though online tools may be used to enhance the conversation.
Responsibilities include:
Lead the In-Class Dialogue: Prepare critical questions and highlight key themes or passages to guide our synchronous discussion.
Optional Online Engagement: Facilitators are encouraged (but not required) to post initial thoughts or questions on the LMS discussion board before class. This serves as an "ice-breaker" to help peers prepare.
Respond and Synthesize: If classmates post online, facilitators may use those insights to refine their in-class discussion points, creating a bridge between online reflection and in-class dialogue.
Fair Participation: Each student will serve as a facilitator at least once. The final frequency will be adjusted based on class size to ensure a balanced workload.
Discussion facilitation is a vital part of the course’s collaborative learning approach. Thoughtful preparation and active engagement in this role will greatly enhance the quality of our shared intellectual experience.
Below are some examples of discussion facilitation questions to help guide your preparation:
1. Textual Understanding & Interpretation
What do you think the author means by [key term or concept]? How is this different from or similar to other terms we’ve encountered?
Can someone summarize the main argument or idea in this reading? What evidence or examples does the author use?
Are there any passages or ideas that you found confusing or surprising? Why?
2. Historical and Cultural Context
How does the historical context influence the philosopher’s or thinker’s ideas?
In what ways do these ideas respond to the social or political challenges of their time?
How might this text reflect broader East Asian philosophical traditions, or how does it differ?
3. Thematic and Conceptual Connections
How does this reading relate to the concepts of myth, superstition, religion, culture, or philosophy as discussed in previous weeks?
What tensions or overlaps can you identify between these categories in the text?
How does the text address questions of self, society, or the cosmos?
4. Critical Reflection and Application
What questions does this reading raise for you about modern Korean culture or society?
How might the ideas in this text be applied to contemporary ethical or cultural issues?
Do you agree or disagree with the author’s perspective? Why?
5. Personal Engagement
Which part of the reading did you find most engaging or challenging, and why?
Did the reading change how you think about a particular idea or tradition? How so?
What would you like to ask the author if you could?
Papers:
Papers make up the largest portion of the course grade. They are expected to clearly express and argue a specific point of view on the chosen topic. All arguments must be supported with appropriate citations of sources (preferably using Chicago style citations or MLA style, links to guides will be provided with suggested paper topics). Although it is not required to find or use sources beyond the assigned readings, students are allowed and encouraged to do so to deepen their analysis.

Week-by-Week Schedule
Week 1: Introduction to Korean Philosophy
Topics: What counts as philosophy? What counts as Korean? Exploring the distinctions and overlaps between myth, superstition, religion, culture, and philosophy
Readings:
Don Baker, Korean Spirituality, ch. 1: “Korean Spirituality”, 1-17.
______, “Introduction,” in Religions of Korea in Practice, ed. Robert E. Buswell, 1-31; hereafter Religions of Korea in Practice will be abbreviated as RKP. 
Activity: This session introduces students to key questions about the nature of philosophy and its relevance to Korea. Through group discussion, students will reflect on their preconceptions about Korean philosophy and explore distinctions and overlaps among philosophy, religion, culture, and spirituality. The activity lays the groundwork for critical reflection throughout the course.
Week 2: Introducing the Three Teachings – Core Concepts and Worldviews
Topics: Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism in early East Asian thought 
Baker, “Three Teachings in Korea” (ch. 3), in Korean Spirituality, 30-57.
Daniel Gardner, Confucianism: A Very Short Introduction (chs. 1-2), 1-32.
Karyn Lai, An Introduction to Chinese Philosophy: (*suggested reading)
Ch. 5: “Daoism, and the Daodejing”, 92-128.
Ch. 10: “Chinese Buddhism”, 265-273; 281-303.
Activity: Students will explore the core ideas, values, and worldviews of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism by discussing their views on human purpose, reality, and the individual’s role in society. The activity will also consider how these teachings may complement or conflict with each other and how this foundational understanding will support later analysis of their development in Korean history.
Week 3: Foundations of Indigenous Korean Thought
Topics: Early Korean cosmology, the Tan’gun myth, animism, shamanism, and the blurred boundaries between myth, superstition, religion, and philosophy.
Readings:
Baker, “Folk Religion and Animism” (ch. 2), in Korean Spirituality, 18-29.
Peter H. Lee and Wm. Theodore de Bary eds., “The Foundation Myth: Tangun” in Sources of Korean Civilization Vol. 1: From Early Times to the Sixteenth Century, 3-6; hereafter Sources of Korean Tradition will be abbreviated as SKT.
Buswell ed., “A Shamanic Ritual for Sending on the Dead” in RKP, 325-352.
Video clips
- https://youtu.be/0Dxvc2XP7I0?feature=shared 진도 씻김굿
- https://youtu.be/s5n7LYxs_E0?feature=shared 불교 49재
Activity: Students will explore Korea’s indigenous worldview by comparing animism and shamanism, interpreting the Tan’gun myth, and reflecting on the cultural roles of myth and superstition. They will collaboratively map how myth, superstition, religion, and philosophy overlap and differ, building a foundation for later discussions on tensions between elite and popular beliefs.
Week 4: Popular Beliefs under Scrutiny: Confucian and Buddhist Engagements
Topics: Tension between elite philosophy, i.e., Confucianism and Buddhism, and folk religion.
Readings:
Lee and de Bary eds., “Popular Beliefs and Confucianists” (Native Beliefs; Geomancy; Taoism and Shamanism; Chǒng Tojǒn: Philosophical Rebuttal of Buddhism and Taoism) in SKT Vol. 1, 240-251 and 254-256.
Buswell ed., “Buddhist Rite in Exorcism”; “Confucianism and the Practice of Geomancy”; “Yi Kyubo’s “Lady of Old Shaman” in RKP, 112-129; 205-222; 233-243.
Boudewijin C. A. Walraven, "A Meeting of Extremes: The Symbiosis of Confucians and Shamans" (Ch. 14), in Dao Companion to Korean Confucian Philosophy, ed. Young-chan Ro (Berlin: Springer, 2019), 311-335; hereafter Dao Companion to Korean Confucian Philosophy will be abbreviated as DCKC. (*suggested reading) 
Activity: Building on week 3, this session examines elite critiques of popular beliefs in late Koryŏ and early Chosŏn. Students will compare Confucian and Buddhist responses to practices like Daoism, geomancy, and shamanism, considering how figures like Chŏng Tojŏn distinguished “high” religion from folk traditions and whether their critiques were philosophical, political, or both. The class will analyze how intellectuals absorbed, suppressed, or reinterpreted popular practices.
Week 5: Buddhism in Korea I — Philosophy, Practice, and State 
Topics: Buddhism as philosophy, religion, and state ideology. Introduction to Wŏnhyo and Chinul: synthesizing doctrinal and practical approaches
Readings:
Lee and de Bary eds., “The Introduction to Buddhism”; “The Rise of Buddhism” (Wǒnhyo’s Buddhist Philosophy); “Buddhism: Ch’ŏnt’ae and Chogye Schools” (Buddhism in Early Koryǒ; Buddhism and Koryǒ Society; Chinul and the Chogye School), in SKT Vol. 1, 34-35; 78-90; 216-224 and 228-237.
Buswell ed., “A Miraculous Tale of Buddhist Practice during the Unified Silla”; “The P’algwanhoe: From Buddhist Penance to Religious Festival,”; “Hell and Other Karmic Consequences: A Buddhist Vernacular Song,” in RKP, 76-85; 86-99; 100-111.
Activity: Students will critically examine Buddhism through two lenses: (1) As philosophy: What metaphysical or ethical systems are present in Wŏnhyo and Chinul’s writings? How do they compare with Confucian thought? (2) As religion: How did Buddhism function as a devotional or institutional practice, particularly as a state religion in early Korea? We will also explore questions of secularization and state power.
Assignment: Reflection Paper (2–3 pages) due April 3. Respond to core ideas from Weeks 1-4.
Week 6: Buddhism in Korea II — Syncretism and Confucianization
Topics: Buddhist strategies of adaptation and syncretism. Confucian critiques of Buddhism and the ideological shift from Koryŏ to Chosŏn.
Readings:
Lee and de Bary eds., “Opposition to Buddhism”; “Buddhism” (ch. 19), in SKT Vol. 1, 311-313; 382-391.
Buswell ed., “The Great Confucian-Buddhist Debate,” in RKP, 177-204.
A. Charles Muller, "Philosophical Bases of the Goryeo-Joseon Confucian-Buddhist Confrontation: The Works of Jeong Dojeon and Hamheo Deuktong" (Ch. 13), in DCKC, 285-309 (*suggested reading)
Activity: Students will look into the Confucian critiques of Buddhism and Buddhist attempt to reconcile Buddhism with Confucianism under the social change from the Koryǒ to the Chosǒn. What were the core arguments? Were they philosophical, moral, or political? How did the Confucianization of the Chosǒn state reshape religious discourse and public life?
Week 7: Confucianism and Neo-Confucianism – Continuity and Transformation
Topics: Core values of classical Confucianism (e.g., ren, li, xiao 仁禮孝) vs. Neo-Confucian metaphysics (li-qi cosmology); self-cultivation; Sage Learning, Zhu Xi, Yi Hwang (T’oegye), and Yi I (Yulgok)
Readings:
Lee and de Bary, eds., “Thought”; “Yi Hwang and the Sage Learning”; “Yi I,” in SKT Vol 1, 342; 349-375; 375-381.
Gardner, “The Reorientation of the Confucian Tradition after 1000 CE: The Teachings of Neo-Confucianism” (ch. 5); “Confucianism in Practice” (ch. 6), in Confucianism: A Very Short Introduction, 70-86; 87-100.
Michael C. Kalton, "Korean Neo-Confucian Thought" (Ch. 2), in DCKC, 17-46. (*suggested reading) 
Activity: Students will identify major differences and continuities between classical Confucian texts and Neo-Confucian commentaries (e.g., Analects vs. Zhu Xi’s interpretations). They will trace how Neo-Confucianism reframed Confucian moral goals using cosmological and metaphysical frameworks (e.g., li–qi theory, inner morality, sage learning, etc.). How does Neo-Confucianism retain or revise the ethical concerns of classical Confucianism? They will also discuss how Korean Confucian thinkers, such as Yi Hwang and Yi I, reinterpret Confucian self-cultivation and moral nature in uniquely Korean ways. Is Korean Neo-Confucianism more metaphysical or ethical in orientation?”
Week 8: Mid-term
No Class meeting
Week 9: Debates on Human Nature – The Four-Seven Debate and the Horak Controversy
Topics: Li-ki (principle and psycho-physical energy 理氣) dualism, ; the nature of emotions and moral agency in Neo-Confucian psychology, the Four-Seven Debate and the Horak Controversy; contributions of Yi Hwang and Yi I
Readings:
Michael C. Kalton, and Kim Oaksook, et al., “Introduction to the Four-Seven Debate,” in The Four-Seven Debate: An Annotated Translation of the Most Famous Controversy in Korean Neo-Confucian Thought (Albany: State University of New York Press, 1994), xv-xxxv.  
Lee and de Bary eds., “Introduction”, in SKT Vol. 1, 268-269; “The Horak Controversy”; “The Continuing Debate Over Principle and Material Force”, in SKT Vol. 2, 194-200; 200-202.
Activity: Students will unpack the significance of the Four-Seven and Horak debates as deeply philosophical engagements with moral psychology, emotion, and human nature. Discussion questions include: What are the Four Beginnings (sadan 四端) and Seven Emotions (ch’iljŏng 七情)? Why did they become a topic of such sustained debate? What is the core issue behind the Four-Seven Debate? How do Yi Hwang and Yi I differ in their interpretations? What does the Horak Controversy contribute to understanding moral nature and human emotion? How does the li–ki framework shape these debates? Why did Korean thinkers devote so much intellectual energy to such subtle philosophical distinctions?
Week 10: Confucianism and Statecraft – Reform after Crisis
Topics: Social dislocation and intellectual responses following the Japanese (Imjin War, 1592–98) and Manchu invasions (1627, 1636); critiques of Neo-Confucian orthodoxy; emergence of Practical Learning (Silhak 實學) as a reformist movement within Confucianism; key thinkers such as Pak Chega (Sŏgye) of the Northen Learning (Bukhak 北學) movement; Chŏng Yagyong (Tasan)
Readings:
Baker, “Introduction”, in SKT Vol. 2, 3-11.
“Reform Proposals” (Chŏng Yagyong: On Land; Pak Chega: On Revering China), in SKT Vol. 2, 70-73; 84-88; 101-104.
Chŏng Yagyong, Choi Byonghyon, tr., “Translator’s Introduction”; “Author’s Preface” in Admonitions on Governing the People: Manual for All Administrators (Berkeley: University of California Press, 2010), xv-xxxvii; 1-4.
James B Palais, Confucian statecraft and Korean Institutions: Yu Hyǒngwon and the late Chosǒn Dynasty (Seattle: University of Washington Press, 1996), 25-60. (*suggested reading)
Hongkyung Kim, "Dasan Jeong Yak-yong: A Synthesizer of Korean Confucianism" (Ch. 15), in DCKC, 363-379. (*suggested reading) 
Activity: Students will explore how the trauma of foreign invasions prompted a crisis in Confucian statecraft and catalyzed the rise of Silhak reformers. They will analyze and present one reform proposal (e.g., land reform, civil service reform, or educational restructuring), assessing the problem it addressed, its Confucian foundations, its continuity or break with tradition, and its feasibility in historical context. The discussion will focus on the following questions: How did war reshape Korean Confucian priorities? How did Silhak critique or revise Neo-Confucian orthodoxy? Can Silhak be seen as a form of early modern reform?
Week 11: Encounters with the West – Crisis, Curiosity, and Adaptation
Topics: Introduction of Western science, Christianity, and technology through Qing Chinese channels; rise of Western Learning (Xixue 西學) and Evidential Learning (Kaozhegxue 考證學); responses from Korean thinkers such as Yi Ik (Sŏngho) and Chŏng Yagyong; tensions between intellectual curiosity, Confucian orthodoxy, and political suspicion. 
Readings:
Baker, “Korean Christianity” (ch. 4), in Korean Spirituality, 58-70.
Lee and de Bary eds., “The Encounter with the West” (The Western Calendar; Criticism of Catholicism; the Persecution of Catholicism), in SKT Vol. 2, 117-118; 120-121; 124-130; 133-142.
Baker, “Western Learning and New Directions in Korean Neo-Confucianism” (ch. 15), in DCKC, 337-361. (*suggested reading)
Activity: Students will analyze the types of Western knowledge (science, religion, and philosophy) that entered Korea through Chinese sources. They will consider: What Western ideas attracted Korean scholars, and why? How did intellectuals like Yi Ik and Chŏng Yagyong evaluate Western ideas? Was Confucianism seen as an intellectual opening or a cultural, spiritual, or political threat? 
Assignment: Reflection Paper (2–3 pages) due May 15. Respond to core ideas from Weeks 5-10.
Week 12: Confucianism and Women
Topics: Confucian rites (esp. ancestral rituals), women’s role and status in Confucian society, and the culture of gyu-bang (women’s quarters)
Readings:
Gardner, “Confucianism and the Family”; “Confucianism and Women,” in Confucianism: A Very Short Introduction, 100-104; 105-111.
Lee and de Bary eds., “Funerary and Ancestral Rites”; “The Position of Women”; “Propagation of Confucian Values,” in SKT Vol 1, 315-316; 316-321; 321-326.
Buswell ed., “Voices of Female Confucians in Late Chosǒn Korea,” in RKP, 223-232.
Kyungmi Kim, “Formation of the Gyu-Bang and the Culture of Women,” in The Culture of Gyu-Bang in Korea, eds. Kyungmi Kim, et al. (Seoul: Pagijong Press), 15-42. 
Jisoo M. Kim, "Neo-Confucianism, Women, and the Law in Choson Korea" (Ch. 17), in DCKC, 383-395 (*suggested reading) 
Un-sunn Lee, "Korean Confucianism and Women's Leadership in the Twenty-First Century--A Religious Reflection on Gang Jeongildang, a Woman Confucian Scholar in the Late Joseon Dynasty" (Ch. 18), in DCKC, 397-422 (*suggested reading) 
Keith N. Knapp, “Learning Confucianism through Filial Sons, Loyal Retainers, and Chaste Wives,” in Teaching Confucianism, ed. Jeffrey L. Richey (Oxford; New York: Oxford University Press, 2008), 39-54. (*suggested reading)
Video clips: 
- https://youtu.be/i5WcamaGDOE?feature=shared (The Tradition of the Head Family (jongga) in Hahoe Village: Honoring Ancestors and Welcoming Guests) 
- https://youtu.be/sfhBBkDzwJQ?si=AndDZDzoFGEj3SR1 (Gyu-Bang tea ceremony )
Activity: Students will explore the intersection of Confucianism and gender by discussing the following questions: How did women find themselves in premodern Confucian society? Did Confucianism inherently suppress women? If not, why has it often been perceived as discriminatory toward women? How did they respond to the world around them? In what ways they create did they create their own space and culture (e.g., gyubang)?

평생교육실습
조대연
chodae@korea.ac.kr
평생교육실습은 학기 중 실습과 방학 중 실습, 시간제 실습과 근무지 실습으로 구분됩니다. 학기 중 실습의 경우 학기 중 특정 요일을 지정하여 이루어지는 실습으로, 반드시 과목을 신청한 학기 안에 실습이 완료되어야 합니다.
방학 중 실습의 경우, 방학기간을 이용하여 실습을 이수하는 것으로 여름방학 실습생은 실습 후 가을 학기인 2학기에 평생교육실습 교과목을 수강 신청하도록 되어 있으며, 겨울방학 실습생은 실습 후 다음 학기인 봄학기(1학기)에 평생교육실습 교과목을 수강하여 성적을 산출하도록 되어 있습니다. 시간제 실습은 직장이나 특별한 사정으로 인해 야간이나 특정 요일, 특정 시간을 이용하여 실습기회를 갖는 것이며, 기관에서 담당하는 업무내용 중 특정한 부분을 선정하여 실습 지도교수와 상의하여 실습 목표를 세우고 컨설팅을 받으면서 실시하여야 합니다. 
평생교육 현장실습기관
평생교육법 상의 현장실습기관은 평생교육법 시행령 제69조제2항에 따라 문자해득 교육프로그램 으로 지정 받은 기관, 평생교육법 제19조부터 제21조까지의 규정에 해당하는 평생교육기관(평생교육진 흥원, 시도 평생교육진흥원, 시군구 평생학습관을 비롯하여 평생교육기관(제2조제2항), 지자체 평생학 습추진기구(제5조), 평생학습도시(제15조), 평생교육 관련사업 수행학교(제29조)등을 포함합니다.
관계법령: 평생교육실습 과목은 평생교육법 시행령 제69조제2항에 따라 문자해득교육프로그램으 로 지정 받은 기관, 평생교육법 제19조부터 제21조까지의 규정에 해당하는 평생교육기관에서의 4주 간 현장실습을 포함한 수업과정으로 구성한다. 구체적인 실습기관 정보는 국가평생교육진흥원 평생교 육사 홈페이지(https://lledu.nile.or.kr/)를 참조하세요.

수업내용의 구성
평생교육실습은 실습에 앞서 a)선수과목에서 학습한 평생교육 관련 제 이론을 점검하고, b)자
신의 경력목표로서 평생교육전문가가 적합한지를 실습을 통해 확인하며, c)자신의 경력개발과 정을 성찰해 보는 기회를 갖도록 구성합니다. 따라서 본 과목은 실습 전 활동, 실습활동, 실습 후 활동으로 구분하여 이루어지며, 개인별 실습일정을 고려하여 운영합니다. 이를 구체적으로 살펴보면, 평생교육실습은 실습 전 수업 3회, 실습, 실습 중 방문수업 1 회, 실습 후 평가수업 2회로 구성되어 있습니다. 또한 교수와 학생이 1:1 개별 면담 3 회를 통해 경력개발에 관한 상담을 실시합니다.

태권도나 무도 경험이 없더라도, 기초부터 차근차근 배우고 싶은 학생
신체활동에 자신감이 부족하지만, 자기방어 능력과 신체 자신감을 함께 기르고 싶은 학생

Attention
Course Objectives and Descriptions
The objectives of this class are to develop; 
A basic level of understanding and knowledge on Marketing Channels Management,
Problem solving capabilities such as analytical ability and creativity, and
Communication capability
This course will be a combination of lecture, discussion, and case analyses. The purpose of lecture is to provide students background knowledge in marketing channels. Materials from the reading assignment may not be covered in the lecture fully. Lecture will be used to point out important concepts in marketing channels management that students should acquire in this course. 
More emphasis will be put on case analyses and discussions as well as group project. Case teaching method provides students the opportunity to apply theoretical understanding to real world situations. Extensive class participation for assigned cases is expected from students. Each group of students will be asked to present their case analysis in class. For the type of discussion and application that I envision being worthwhile, you will have to do a lot of work. 
In addition, students will work with a group of students in a project that covers any issues related to the development and evolution of marketing channels field as we are embracing more of digital technologies in our society. 
Class Materials
Textbook (Optional)
Any books related to Marketing Channels Management are OK!
Required Cases to be procured from Harvard Business Impact
Grade:
Class participation					30%
Executive summary reports of assigned cases		40%
Full case analysis report and presentation		30%
Class Participation
Just as in a business, we learn from each other through a meaningful discussion. To a substantial degree, the benefits that a student gets from the course is related to his/her willingness to expose his/her viewpoint to the critical judgment of the class, to share his/her experience with others, and to actively participate in class discussion to learn from classmates. As the participation grade is critical in getting a good final grade, you will have to be very analytical in the case discussions and provide solid answers on top of doing well in all other aspects.
For productive class discussion, I would like to ask that everyone should be alert to the flow of class discussion. Sometimes the comments or opinions that you would like to express in class discussion might be mentioned by others before you have a chance to do so. In such cases, you need to come up with newer points to contribute to class discussion to get a good grade for class discussion.
In addition, a few selected students will be asked to prepare questions for the case analysis presented by other group. If you are not prepared to ask questions, then it will be considered that you are not fully prepared for the class and penalty will be imposed on you. Without active participation from students, teaching and learning from case methods are impossible. It is your responsibility to be ready for class discussion.
The factors that will go to the consideration in the determination of this grade include:
Managerially useful analytical interpretation of case facts,
Making insightful comments rather than repeating case facts,
Relevance and depth of comments as well as frequency of comments,
Ability to synthesize and add to others’ comments
How well you respond to my questions as well as peers’ comments in class, etc.
Executive summary reports of assigned cases
We come together to discuss a business situation and apply what we have learned in various classes or from real-life experience to the problems at hand. A student group will be asked to present their analysis in class. Other students will be required to prepare relevant questions to ask to the presenting group. To do so you are responsible for thoroughly analyzing each case and be ready to discuss any aspect of a case and must take a position and defend it.	
The format of executive summary reports is as follows:
A three-page report which includes a cover page and two pages on the main content.
The main content should include; 
Problem statement
A list of alternatives
Recommendation and the logic behind your choice of an alternative.
Font size of 11 and a single space.
Any tables and figures can be put under Appendix which is not included in the three pages limit.
Students, who are not presenting their assigned case in class, should submit a three-page executive summary of each case before the start of each class. Any late submission will not be accepted. 
Full case analysis report
This exercise is to help you to enhance your business writing skills. You should be able to organize your thoughts logically when analyzing problems in your hands and present alternative solutions and recommendations in logical pattern. The written report will form the base for your oral presentation and make your presentation more effective and efficient so that you can convey your analysis in better way to your audience. The guideline for how to write case analysis proposal is 
Executive summary
One page summary of problems and recommendations.
Problem/Issue Statement
There are usually one or more core problems that a firm in the case is facing. If your diagnosis of the core problem(s) were wrong, the following analysis would be a complete waste. It is critical for you to identify the right problems to be a successful manager. This section should be in maximum of two paragraphs. Do not waste limited space giving background information or case facts.
Listing of Alternatives that may be used to resolve focal problem(s)
You have to list a set of alternatives logically. Some cases included suggested alternatives to be considered which might be a decoy to cloud your analysis. You have to develop your own alternatives and show how each alternative would help in solving the focal problem(s). 
Recommendations
This section should describe the recommendation offered and they should be keyed to the issues identified previously. When making your recommendation, make sure that you have considered the feasibility and ramifications of enacting your action plan (identify why it is a good plan and how it overcomes the problems). You need not provide the rationale for your recommendation in this section. The rationale should be provided in the following section.
Rationale and Analysis
In this section you justify your recommendations. This section would usually be the longest part of your report. The logic can be established using any quantitative analyses, evaluations, projections, and qualitative analyses that you feel relevant. Also address the impact of potentially negative outcomes of your plan and address counter-arguments like “but what if” questions.
Attachments
These attachments are exhibits, tables, graphs, or whatever, and consist of support materials. Make sure that they specifically address the questions in the proceeding sections. Also make clear references to the particular attachments in the main body of the report. A reasonable number of appendices are allowed and will not be counted toward the limit. Appendices should not be used to provide a written explanation of your argument points. The violation of this limit will result in deduction of points.
Please refer all attachments and appendices properly in the main text. All attachments and appendices should have a clear heading.
The physical formats for written case reports are;
The maximum length of the content should not exceed 10 pages, double-spaced, triple spaced between each paragraph. Exhibits and cover page are not included in the maximum length for the report.
The cover page should include the name of the case, names and students ID numbers of your group members, date of submittal, and course number.
It should be page-numbered either on the middle of each page bottom or on the upper right corner.
The font of characters should be 11.
The overall appearance should be very professional. Remind yourself that you are writing the report for either your clients as a consultant or a member of a task force for a company. If your report has more than five misspelling, you will be penalized by one letter grade.
The deadline for every report is by the beginning of the class for which a case is assigned. Any late report will not be accepted!
Presentation
You will be asked to present your case analysis to the class to facilitate the discussion of the case. You will be given maximum of 30 minutes to present your case analysis and, during the next 60 minutes, you should entertain any questions from fellow students. The final minutes will be used for my comments on the presentation and case wrap-up. How professional you are in delivering the content of your case analysis and in handling the questions will be reflected on the grade for this part of class requirement. The evaluation of your presentation will be based on the level of professionalism, presentation materials, attire (you are required to have at least a semi-business casual on), presentation manner, and the effectiveness in answering questions from other students and me.
In preparing and presenting an assigned case, every group member should share equal responsibility. Especially, allotted presentation time should be equally divided among your group members. It is not allowed for a student to present a whole case.
Attendance
Attendance is required and will be monitored every class. If you miss more than three-week class time, you will be automatically given F. In other cases, there will be no penalty regarding attendance. However, students with perfect attendance record might receive extra credit at the end of the semester.

Economic Sociology
Instructor: SeungJin Kim
Class Time: Tue. And Thurs. 1:30-2:45 PM 
Office Hours: Tue, Thurs, before and after classes (or by appointment)
Email: mafaldakim@gmail.com 
[Course Description] 
The “economic behavior/activity” means conscious “choices” that actors make for their own objectives or interests “under constraints”. 
“Constraints” could be the budgetary constraints of individual actors, but it could also be time constraints, information constraints, network constraints, or broader institutional and infrastructural conditions. “Objectives” and “interests,” i.e., the economic “values” pursued by actors, also operate within the framework of cultural, political, and social concepts of value. Therefore, the “choices” of individual economic actors are not atomic but inextricably linked to their “institutional contexts.” 
 Thus, this course focuses on the institutional context of economic behavior. 
 Throughout the semester, we will explore the social relations, especially power relations, that are implicit in economic behavior. We will examine the social implications of basic economic concepts and institutions such as markets, commodities, credit [money], scarcity, and ownership. Also we will pay particular attention to “firms” as political and social actors, not just economic actors, and to “information/knowledge” as a major source of monetary value.
[Course Structure, assignments and Grading]
This course is manly composed of lectures. Yet, during the semester we will have two one-hour discussion sessions. Before each discussion session, students are required to submit discussion questions (in a short essay form) for the designated topics.
The overall grading structure consists of 1) attendance 10%, 2) discussion participation 20%, 3) mid-term exam 35%, and 4) final exam 35%. In the exams, students are expected to fully understand main theories and concepts covered during the lectures and make proper applications to specific cases. 
Following the university policy, you will get an automatic F,
if you fail to meet the minimum attendance requirement,
or in case of plagiarism 
or if you fail to participate in the final exam.
For all written assignments (for exams that are supposed to be individually submitted to me, rather than to be shared in the classroom), you can write either in English or in Korean. All classroom activities (lectures, discussions, etc.) will be done in English.

Overview | This course provides a foundational introduction to AI. It covers essential mathematical concepts such as linear algebra, calculus, and probability that are necessary for understanding modern AI and deep learning methods. Students will also learn basic Python programming skills and apply them to simple computational experiments. In addition, the course introduces core deep learning concepts, including neural networks, training processes, and loss functions, with an emphasis on building a solid theoretical and practical foundation for advanced AI coursework.
Who Should Take This Course

General | The general objective of this course is to equip students with the fundamental knowledge and skills required to study artificial intelligence and deep learning. Through the study of basic mathematics, Python programming, and introductory deep learning theory, students will develop the ability to understand core AI concepts and prepare for more advanced coursework in artificial intelligence and related fields.
Detailed Objective 1 | Develop the ability to understand fundamental mathematical concepts required for artificial intelligence and deep learning, and to apply them to basic problem-solving tasks.
Detailed Objective 2 | Develop the ability to implement computations and experiments related to artificial intelligence and deep learning using fundamental Python programming syntax and libraries.
Detailed Objective 3 | Develop a foundational understanding of core deep learning concepts to prepare for advanced artificial intelligence courses.

1. Course Description 
Statistical technique has become of great importance in wide areas of social sciences such as business and economics as well as political science and sociology. Decision makers in firms and government organizations are more likely to make decisions anchored in quantitative and qualitative analysis of data. 
Statistics can be described as the collection, summarization, analysis, and reporting of numerical findings relevant to a decision or situation. Given the great diversity of social science, statistics can be applied to various kinds of social situations. Regardless of eventual career paths, knowledge of statistical techniques in this course will offer a great advantage to students making critical decisions and resolving problems in the relevant fields.    
There are two major goals in this course: 1) explain statistical methods used in business, 2) draw case material from real-world situations in order to demonstrate the practical applications of those methods.

Course Overview
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to Industrial and Organizational (I/O) Psychology, with an emphasis on developing the knowledge and applied skills required to work effectively as an I/O psychologist in real organizational settings. The course covers core topics in personnel and organizational practice, including individual differences, job analysis, employee selection and assessment, performance measurement and appraisal, and training and development.
Throughout the course, students will learn to connect theory and research to practice by analyzing organizational challenges, interpreting data and evidence, and designing practical interventions. By the end of the course, students will be able to apply foundational I/O psychology principles to diagnose organizational problems and propose evidence-based solutions, preparing them for professional work in a wide range of organizational contexts.
Class Sessions
This course is delivered using a flipped classroom format. Students will engage with key concepts through a pre-recorded video lecture uploaded each Tuesday, along with assigned readings to be completed prior to class. The class will meet on Thursdays for a 75-minute session dedicated to in-class application and active learning. In-class sessions will include brief lectures, structured learning activities and demonstrations, and facilitated discussions.
Instruction will incorporate multiple learning methods, including:
Watching weekly pre-recorded lecture videos and completing assigned readings prior to class
Participating in instructor-facilitated whole-class discussions of major course topics
Engaging in small-group activities and collaborative discussions during class sessions
Working in a team to complete a semester-long training development project
Textbook and Readings
Conte, J. M., & Landy, F. J. (2025). Work in the 21st century: An introduction to industrial and organizational psychology (7th ed.). Wiley. 
The textbook is available at the University library. During the course of the semester, additional required readings will be distributed or uploaded on LMS system. To obtain maximum benefit from the classes, students should read the assigned textbook chapters and other readings before each class.
Assessment and Evaluation
To promote active learning style, students will be evaluated based on the following five components. Details of each component will be provided with details in class.
Class Attendance                                10%
In-Class Assignments                         20%
Mid-Term Exam	                        25%
Final exam		                        20%
Group Project                                      25% (Training Program 15%; Presentation 10%)
Attendance 
Class attendance is the responsibility of each student. Students are expected to arrive on time and remain for the full class period (or until formally dismissed). Repeated late arrivals or early departures may be considered absences and can disrupt the learning environment. 
If you must miss class due to a legitimate reason (e.g., military service, medical appointment, or family emergency), you are required to submit appropriate documentation to the TA on your first day back. Acceptable documentation includes a medical note, hospital record, or other official document that verifies the reason for the absence. An unexcused absence will be recorded as an absence and will count toward the course attendance limit. 
Students who miss more than one-third (1/3) of class sessions will not be eligible to pass the course.
In-Class Assignments
Throughout the semester, students will complete brief in-class exercises (e.g., pop quizzes, short activities, or task-based group work). The number of in-class exercises may vary depending on the course schedule and instructional needs. These assignments are designed to help students stay on pace with the course, reinforce key concepts, and deepen understanding of the course material through active participation.
If you miss a class due to an excused absence (i.e., an absence supported by appropriate documentation), you may make up the missed in-class assignment by completing an open-ended make-up quiz on Tuesday 2pm based on the assigned reading for that week. It is the student’s responsibility to contact the TA within one week of the absence to request the make-up quiz and to submit the required documentation. Make-up opportunities will not be provided for unexcused absences.
Exams
There will be two exams in this course: a midterm and a final. The exams are non-cumulative and are designed to assess students’ understanding and application of the key concepts covered in the assigned textbook chapters, class discussions, and in-class activities within the exam units specified in the course schedule.
Upon arrival for an exam, students must place all personal belongings—including cell phones, smart watches, and other electronic devices—in their bag and move the bag to the designated area at the front of the classroom.
Group Project
In this semester-long group project, students will work in teams to design an employee training program addressing a real-world organizational need. Teams will identify a target training (e.g., dental assistants, café receptionists), articulate clear learning objectives, and develop a structured program that reflects best practices in I/O psychology.
The project includes two components:
Written Training Program (approximately 10 pages) (15%): A formal paper outlining the training needs assessment, learning objectives, program content and structure, delivery method, and evaluation plan.
Training Program Presentation (10%): A professional in-class presentation of the proposed training program, highlighting key design decisions and demonstrating how the program would be implemented in an organization.
Peer evaluation will be conducted at the end of the project, where each individual will be rated in terms of fair contribution to the group project. Those individuals who fail to contribute to the group project will receive a lower grade.
OTHER ISSUES
 Please silence all cell phones and other electronic messaging devices during class.
 If you use a laptop or tablet in class, please do so in a respectful and minimally distracting manner. Excessive browsing, messaging, or non-class-related typing may distract others and disrupt the learning environment.
 When emailing the TA or the instructor, please include your full name and the course number in the email subject line (e.g., [PSYC241]).
Policy on Scholastic Dishonesty
The University defines academic dishonesty as cheating, plagiarism, unauthorized collaboration, falsifying academic records, and any act designed to avoid participating honestly in the learning process. Scholastic dishonesty also includes, but is not limited to, providing false or misleading information to receive a postponement or an extension on a test, quiz, or other assignment, and submission of essentially the same written assignment for two courses without the prior permission of the instructor. Any instance of academic dishonesty in an assessment will result in a grade of zero (0) for the entire class. Students who violate University rules on scholastic dishonesty are subject to disciplinary penalties, including the possibility of failure in the course and/or dismissal from the University. By accepting this syllabus, you have agreed to these guidelines and must adhere to them.

Course Introduction
Economic theory consists of micro- and macroeconomics. Principles of Economics II introduces students to macroeconomics, the branch of economics that examines the economy as a whole. Central questions in macroeconomics include how short-run economic fluctuations can be mitigated and how long-run economic growth can be sustained.
Over the course of the semester, the class will cover topics such as the measurement of national income, economic growth, unemployment, inflation, money, international trade and exchange rates, short-run economic fluctuations, the effectiveness of monetary and fiscal policy, and the Phillips curve.
By the end of the course, students are expected to have a general understanding of macroeconomic phenomena and theory. They should be able to appreciate the distinctive perspective macroeconomists bring to the study of society and human behavior, as well as understand the methods used in macroeconomic analysis and how these methods are applied to decision-making.
Required Text 
N. Gregory Mankiw, Principles of Economics, 10th Edition, ISBN: 978-0357722718
Please note that older editions are still fine.
Grading Policy (applicable to all students)
The course assessment consists of one midterm examination and one final examination, both conducted in English and weighted equally. Examination questions are in multiple-choice and/or short-answer formats. Please note that attendance at more than two-thirds of all class sessions is mandatory. Students who fail to meet this minimum attendance requirement will automatically receive a failing grade for the course.
Class Policy
Attendance is mandatory once you have registered for the course. In case you are going to be absent, it is your responsibility to inform me in advance and provide me with a document confirming the reason for your absence. If you report to class after the roll has been called out, you will be marked as absent. In case of illness or other unforeseeable circumstances, you must document those circumstances as soon as possible to be marked as excused.

work well in a team by participating in group discussions (initiate discussions, generate ideas, express opinions, agree/disagree, ask for clarification, and make group decisions)
use specific techniques of academic writing (integrating sources, hedging, creating coherence, etc.)

English Reading and Writing
Spring 2026
Class Times:		Friday, 9:00 – 11:45am
Location:		148-311
Instructor:			Stewart John Cooper
Office: 		Euncho-Useon Education Hall, Room 614
Office hours: 		By appointment
E-mail:				sjcooper@korea.ac.kr
Text and Materials
Longman Academic Writing Series 4 – Essays (required text)
Supplemental handouts may also be provided on the LMS or in class.
Class Description 
This class is designed to improve students’ reading and writing abilities. Class time will be focused on discussing reading and writing skills, on reading and writing, as well as on critical thinking exercises.
This Course is for high-intermediate to advanced students, and is designed to enhance their basic reading and writing skills. The focus is on more advanced skills, such as making inferences, separating facts from opinions, as well as identifying bias, and extending these sophisticated reading skills to writing skills.
https://eled.korea.edu/eled_en/info/u_syllabus.do
Lessons will consist of a variety of activities including discussions, pair work, critical thinking exercises, writing practice, as well as peer review.  
Aims
Develop mastery and confidence when reading and writing in English
Improve ability to understand more nuanced meanings within a text
Use grammatically correct sentences when writing
Produce a well-organized and coherent 5 paragraph essay
Enjoy reading in English for study as well as for pleasure
Instructor’s expectations of students
Arrive on time and be prepared for class
Participate actively in every class and in all activities 
Be respectful of your classmates and the instructor 
Challenge one’s self whenever possible 
Ask questions when necessary 
Participation - Attendance Policy
Students arriving 5 or more minutes after the start of class will be marked ‘late.’ Students missing more than 50% of a class will be marked ‘absent.’ Because the goal of this class is to improve reading and writing through discussion, critical thinking, and sharing ideas attendance and active participation are essential. As a result, student grades depend on attendance and any unexcused absences and lateness will count against a student’s participation grade.  
Participation
I am aware that studying reading and writing in English can bring unique challenges, however I strongly believe that the more effort we put in to our classes then the better the results will be. To this end I require all students to actively participate in each class, and each activity, and to push themselves at all times. This will not only help us to work well together in class, but it also allows students to take responsibility for their own learning.
Evaluation
	Participation – 30%
Homework/reading – 20% 
Assignments – 20%
Midterm – 10%
Final – 20 %
Assignment 1: Paragraph Writing and Peer Review: You will choose from several topics and prepare a 10 to 15 sentence paragraph, using the writing model from the textbook and following the steps in the writing process. Part of your assignment will also be to peer review your classmate’s writing, as this is an extremely useful skill to develop and a great way to practice recognising good writing.
Homework and reading: Homework given in class will mainly be reading, but also occasionally the editing and uploading of a final draft of a piece of written work from class. It is very important that all homework is completed on time, as without undertaking the reading you will not be able to participate actively in class discussions.
Midterm: Writing Assignment: You will write a summary of one chapter chosen from one of the required texts read in class. Summarising is an important skill that combines reading and writing skills.
Assignment 2: Create an Outline for your final essay: A formal outline and essay plan will be created and submitted for review. This outline will form the basis for your final five paragraph essays, so it is an important chance to practice planning and preparing before you write. 
Final: Five Paragraph Essay: You will write a five-paragraph essay, incorporating what you have learned in class, and using the outline and plan created in the second assignment.
This syllabus is subject to change by the instructor to fit the needs of the students and/or achieve specific educational goals.

COURSE DESCRIPTION	
본 수업은 고려대학교 사범대학 체육교육과 체육특기학생들을 대상으로, 현대 사회에서 여가와 레크리에이션의 의미와 역할을 이해하는 것을 목표로 한다. 학생들은 여가·레크리에이션의 기본 개념을 바탕으로 현대 사회의 다양한 여가 레크리에이션 프로그램을 살펴보고, 자신의 여가 생활을 성찰함과 동시에 여가·레크리에이션 관련 직업군에 대한 이해를 넓히게 된다.
한 학기 동안 강의, 토론, 발표, 다양한 과제를 중심으로 수업이 진행된다.
본 수업은 협동학습을 기반으로 한 소그룹 활동과 전체 토론으로 운영된다.
소그룹별 현장 방문 및 시설 탐방은 필수 활동이다.
최종 과제는 KUSF 프로젝트와 연계하여 진행될 수 있다.
COURSE OBJECTIVES
이 수업을 성공적으로 이수한 학생들은 다음을 할 수 있게 된다.
현대 사회에서 여가 및 레크리에이션의 다양한 역할을 이해한다.
여가 및 레크리에이션 분야의 주요 문제점과 이슈를 파악한다.
스포츠 및 여가 관련 직업과 기업을 탐구하고 조사 결과를 발표한다.
교과서
박세혁 (2020). 행복을 탐구하는 여가 및 레크리에이션. 대한미디어 (필수 도서)
LMS
강의계획서, 강의자료, 수업 PPT 및 공지사항은 LMS를 통해 제공된다.
학생들은 LMS를 정기적으로 확인해야 하며, 공지사항 확인은 의무 사항이다.
학점
학점 : 강사의 개산 착오가 아닌 어떤 상황에서도 절대 반올림 이나 성적 변경 없음!!!!!!! 
시험 및 과제 점수:
자세한 시험 및 과제 설명
시험
수업 내용과 교재를 바탕으로 기말고사 1회가 실시된다.  
주제별 리포트
수업 진도에 따라, 3-4회의 과제가 제시되며, 지정된 기한 내에 제출해야 한다.  
여가관련 직업 알아보기(그룹)
3-4명이 한 조가 되어 여가 및 레크리에이션 시설을 방문하고, 해당 시설에서 일하는 전문가를 인터뷰 하는 과제이다. 보고서는 시설에 대한 각종 분석 및 인터뷰 내용을 포함해야 하며, 보고서 분량은 5장 이상이다.
시설 방문: 수업 내용과 교재를 바탕으로 시설, 프로그램, 서비스, 종사자 역할 등에 대한 분석을 포함해야 한다. 시설의 자료(안내 책자, 홍보물 등)도 포함되어야 한다. 
인터뷰: 인터뷰 질문은 업무적 책임과 의무, 각종 기회, 스트레스, 문제점, 좋은 점, 유행/트랜드 등과 학생들에 대한 조언 등이 포함할 수 있다. 7문항 이상의 인터뷰 질문을 포함한 질문지를 미리 만들어 준비해야 하며,  질문을 만들 때 창의력은 필수이다. 인터뷰보고서에는 학생들의 소감, 의견 필수. 인터뷰한 사람 연락처, 인터뷰 시간 장소 등 포함해야 한다. 
발표는 모든 조원이 참여하여야 하며 원고를 읽는 형식이 아닌, 전문적인 자세로 발표해야 한다.   
발표는 영상촬영으로 진행될 수 있다.
출석 및 수업 태도:
수업 출석은 필수사항이다. 모든 출석 기준은 고려대학교 학부 수업 출결 기준과 교육부와 고려대학교의 학생선수 학업 관련 가이드라인을 따른다. 
출석체크를 별도로 하지 않더라도, 수업 중 수행하는 과제와 활동을 통해 출석확인이 이루어질 수 있다.
수업 중 과제는 해당 수업 시간 내에 완료해야 점수가 부여된다. 
퀴즈나 수업 중 과제, 시험 등은 어떤 대체도 가능하지 않다. 
수업 태도가 불성실하거나 수업 중 수면을 취할 경우, 결석으로 처리될 수 있다. 
CLASS REQUIREMENTS
교재는 반드시 읽고 수업에 참여해야 한다. 예습은 필수이며, 수업 중 질문에 답하지 못할 경우 불이익이 있을 수 있다.
수업 출석은 의무 사항이다. 정해진 수업 시간 이후 입실은 지각으로 처리되며, 반복될 경우 결석으로 간주된다.
휴대전화는 반드시 전원을 끄고 가방에 보관해야 한다. 노트북 사용은 사전 허가를 받은 경우에만 가능하며, 수업과 관련된 용도로만 사용해야 한다. 수업 중 휴대전화 또는 노트북으로 채팅, 인터넷 사용, 과제 수행 등 수업과 무관한 행위가 적발될 경우 즉시 퇴실 조치될 수 있다.
모든 과제는 컴퓨터 문서로 작성하여 LMS를 통해 기한 내 제출해야 한다. 출력본 제출은 인정되지 않는다.
지각 제출된 과제는 즉시 감점 처리된다. 제출 당일 지각은 5%, 이후 하루가 지날 때마다 10%씩 감점되며, 감점에 대한 이의 제기는 허용되지 않는다.
결석이 예정되어 있거나 과제 또는 시험을 기한 내 제출할 수 없는 경우 반드시 사전에 담당 교수에게 통보해야 한다. 사전 통보 없이 발생한 결석이나 미제출에 대해서는 어떠한 사정도 고려되지 않는다.
모든 시험과 과제는 지정된 날짜와 시간에만 실시된다. 해당 시간에 응시하거나 제출하지 않을 경우 0점 처리되며, 추가 기회는 제공되지 않는다.
모든 부정행위는 엄격히 금지된다. 표절은 중대한 학문적 위반으로 간주되며, 타인의 글이나 아이디어를 한 문장이라도 인용 표시 없이 사용하는 경우 표절로 처리된다. 부정행위 적발 시 해당 과제 또는 시험은 즉시 0점 처리되며, 성적 F 부여 및 학칙에 따른 추가 조치가 이루어진다.
부상 또는 장애로 인해 학습 지원이 필요한 학생은 즉시 담당 교수에게 보고해야 한다. 사후 통보는 인정되지 않는다.
본 수업은 교육부 및 고려대학교 학생선수 출석 및 학업 지침을 근거로 운영되며, 해당 지침을 위반할 경우 수업 참여 및 성적 평가에 불이익이 발생한다.
** 이 수업 담당 교수가 수업 계획서 내용을 변경할 권리를 가지고 있으며, 진도나 상황에 따라 변경할 수 있다. 변경 내용은 학생들에게 LMS나 수업을 통해 통보 될 것임. **

BUSS164(03): 경영과 사회
2026년 1학기
과목개요
본 과목은 신입생들이 고려대학교 경영대학의 미션인 “Business for Society - Inspiring Next Leaders”를 바탕으로 인격과 실력을 갖춘 사회적 리더로 성장할 수 있도록 경영학의 기본 이론과 다양한 세부 분야에 대해 소개합니다. 근대 경영학 교육에 지대한 영향을 미친 Joseph Wharton은 “경영 교육은 우리 문명에 내재한 사회적 문제들에 대한 해결책을 찾는 것이어야 하며, 비즈니스 리더란 사회적 요구에 책임을 지는 공동체의 건설자여야 한다”고 역설하였습니다. 본 과목의 전반부에서는 이러한 교육 철학에 기반하여 경영학에 대한 철학적 고민, 리더십에 대한 고찰, 경영 윤리에 대한 이해, 그리고 기업의 존재 이유에 대한 논쟁 들을 바탕으로 기업과 사회의 관계를 조망합니다. 더불어, 기업경영에서 이윤과 사회적 가치를 함께 추구하는 것이 왜 중요한지, 그리고 어떻게 가능한지를 탐구합니다. 한편, 과정의 후반부에서는 KUBS의 8개 세부 전공(경영관리, 경영전략, 글로벌 비즈니스, 마케팅, 재무금융, 회계, IS, LSOM,)에 대한 전공별 소개와 함께 각각의 세부 전공 범위 내에서 어떻게 기업가치와 사회적 가치가 함께 추구될 수 있을지에 대해서 알아봅니다.
학습목표
기업의 존재 목적에 대한 이해
기업 활동에서 사회적 가치 추구의 중요성에 대한 이해

경영학 세부 전공과 사회적 가치 추구의 관계에 대한 이해
수업방식
수업은 학교 LMS를 통한 비대면(온라인) 방식으로 진행됩니다.

출석 및 참여
수업 중 토론참여는 효과적인 학습을 위해 매우 중요한 요소이므로 수업내용의 예복습뿐만 아니라 여러분의 경험을 적극 토론에 반영해 주기 바랍니다.

시험
시험은 대면방식의 중간과 기말시험이 있고, 시험범위는 강의내용이 해당됩니다. 
과제: 강의 내용 요약
강의 내용 요약은 세부 전공(총 여덟 개)의 강의에 대해서 제출해야 합니다.
각 전공마다 배정된 두 번의 강의가 끝나면 그 다음 첫번째 수업이 시작하기 1시간 전까지 제출합니다(학교 LMS 사용). 제출기한을 넘긴 과제는 0점 처리됩니다.
요약은 각 전공 마다 진행되는 두 번의 강의를 통합하여 작성합니다. 첫째, 전공별 두 번 강의 각각에 대한 핵심 주제를 문장으로 요약합니다. 둘째, 두 번 강의 전체를 통합한 해당 전공 전반에 대한 개괄적인 설명을 합니다.
A4 용지 2장 이내로 워드 (또는 한글)로 작성하여 PDF 파일로 변환합니다.
웹사이트, 출판물, 타인의 보고서 등의 자료를 무단으로 표절했을 경우에는 해당 요약은 0점 처리하며, 무단 표절이 2회 이상 발견되면 과목 낙제(F학점)에 해당합니다.

Office: LP509 
Phone: 010-2997-0367

Course description: 
This introductory finance course provides students with the fundamental building blocks to take on upper level advanced finance classes as well as preparation for finance internships. Throughout the semester the class will be learning necessary topics such as time value of money, stock and debt valuation, risk return, diversification, CAPM, corporate finance and an understanding of different roles and jobs in the financial world. 
Through real-world examples, case studies, and problem-solving exercises, students will gain practical insights to understand how to value financial assets. 
Course textbook: 
Corporate Finance by Ivo Welch. This is available for free online https://corpfin.ivo-welch.info/home/ 
This textbook is the one of the most often used books. Optional 
Principles of Corporate Finance by Richard Brealey, Stewart Myers 
Grading Policy: 
Class participation - 20%, Midterm- 30%, Final - 50% 
Course Schedule: 
Week 1 - Introduction to finance, time value of money, present and future value 
Week 2 - Compounding, Annuity, Amortization 
Week 3 - Financial decision making - NPV, IRR 
Week 4 - Bond valuation 
Week 5 - Bond valuation

Overview | Through this course, students will learn to recognize various types of financial and non-financial risks, and study various quantitative and qualitative tools necessary for risk-management-related decisionmaking. Additionally, students will learn about various topics for understanding risk transfer markets, and gain diverse perspectives on insurance markets along with information asymmetry issues such as moral hazard and adverse selection. In keeping with the course title 'Insurance and Risk Management,' the course also focuses on various discussions about the characteristics of domestic and international insurance markets, and seeks to continue discussions on various cases of risk management failures that have occurred recently.
Who Should Take This Course | This course is designed to be suitable for students in all subject areas within KUBS, but is considered most appropriate for students in finance and accounting fields who are contemplating careers related to insurance and/or risk management.
Prerequisites (Recommended) | Any subject covering key topics in introductory microeconomics would be helpful.
Class Rules | The instructor emphasizes the importance of two-way communication, which is only possible through students' active participation in class, and seeks to create a classroom environment where everyone's opinions can be respected by empathizing with others' opinions and providing positive feedback. While the use of generative AI to a certain extent is possible and encouraged in submitting assignments and other works, the output must be self-directed and include one's own opinions. There is a zero-tolerance principle for cheating on exams and other assessments.

Objectives 
General | Students should have an accurate understanding of insurance and risk management as a whole, and are able to provide in-depth discussions based on their understanding of various recent developments in the field.
Detailed Objective 1 | Students understand what risk management is and how risk management is conducted.
Detailed Objective 2 | Students understand the insurance market in general and how insurance pricing is determined.
Detailed Objective 3 | Students can provide diverse and comprehensive perspectives on several recent cases of risk management failures.

∙ [출석] 
-1/3 이상 결석시 성적부여 불가, 특정 사유에 한해 출석인정신청 및 시험 불응시 신청 가능, 단 출석인정 제외하고 1/2 이상 실제 출석 필요함

∙ [학습윤리]
 -대학의 목적과 본교 교육이념에 따라 성실하고 정직한 마음과 열정적인 태도로 모든 학습에 적극적으로 참여
 -고등교육을 받는 교양인으로서의 품위를 유지하며, 도덕적 민감성을 바탕으로 창의적 학문탐구에 정진
 -교육활동과 관련하여 교원 및 동료학생과의 약속을 성실히 이행
 -교원과 동료학생의 인격을 존중하고 기본적인 예의를 준수
 -학문 공동체의 일원으로서 학문의 진실성을 지키며, 본교 「AI 활용 가이드」를 성실히 준수
 -강의계획서 등을 충분히 탐색하여 자신의 학문적 탐구 방향과 미래 비전에 부합하는 교과목을 신중히 선택
 -매 수업에 적극적으로 임할 수 있도록 수업자료를 사전에 탐독하고 준비
 -정해진 수업시간을 준수하며, 결석·지각·중도 이탈 등으로 타인의 학습을 방해하지 않도록 유의
 -출석 관련 위계행위(대리출석 등) 금지
 -모든 수업활동에 주도적으로 참여하고, 토론·질의응답 등을 통해 교과목 이해와 통찰력 향상에 노력
 -과제는 스스로 성실하게 작성하며, 인용한 모든 자료(책·논문·인터넷·AI 등)는 변조나 왜곡 없이 출처를 명확히 표기
 -협동학습의 경우 자신의 역할을 책임감 있게 수행하여 공동의 학습성과 달성에 기여
 -시험의 목적과 의미를 이해하고, 부정행위 없이 정직하게 응시
 -한 학기 수강한 교과목의 교육 품질 향상을 위해 강의평가에 성실히 참여하고, 개선이 필요한 사항을 충실히 서술

-연구실 안전환경 조성에 관한 법률 제20조(교육·훈련)에 의거, 연구실안전법이 적용되는 과학기술분야 대상학과에 소속된 연구활동종사자는 매학기 일정시간의 안전교육을 이수하여야 하므로 실험·실습을 수강하는 모든 대상학과 학부생 및 대학원생은 교육참여 필수

Purpose of Academic English

Evaluation Method
Typically, a maximum of about 40-45% of you will receive a grade of “A” or “A+”. Evaluation in this class is based strictly on performance, and not on English language proficiency. All parts of the evaluation system must be completed in an exceptional manner if you want to get an “A+”.  
I employ rubrics where students are evaluated on organization(see below), content(see below) and language (see below). More criteria will be given when the projects are assigned. Many students ask for a word count. My philosophy is that students should be focusing on answering the question  and providing enough support for your answer. So concentrate on fully exploring your answer.  This is done through research (what have others said on the topic),planning (outline and deciding on your answer), and editing (checking your work for mistakes in organization, content and language).
Class Expectations (Please READ CAREFULLY!)
This class is not like your other classes.  It is not a lecture class, so you must be active instead of passive in this class.  The following are some guidelines for conduct that I expect in this class.  Adherence to these expectations will assist in enhancing your English proficiency as well as improving chances of a good grade.

Basic Criteria
Organization | Organization includes but is not limited to formatting including font (times new roman 12 points), double spacing, indents, APA title page, bibliography, intext citations and general paragraph formatting. Students are expected to create new file documents for each assignment.
Content | Content includes but is not limited to answering the question of the assignment, supporting your ideas with details including: quotations, statistics, concrete details and paraphrasing, explanations of why your details answer the question and context(why is your support important to the topic you are writing about). Explanations need to be longer than your evidence.
Language | Language includes but is not limited to grammar (common mistakes students make are: verb tenses, articles, prepositions, word choice, word order, and plurals), spelling and the use of first person.
